What Aseprite is, and what this stage is:
A 2001 program that does one thing, the version this curriculum is pinned to, and the reason to learn all of it in a fortnight rather than a third of it over a year.

**What it is.** Aseprite is a raster image editor built specifically for pixel art and sprite animation, first released in 2001 and maintained by **Igara Studio**. It is not a general image editor with a pixel mode; **every default in it assumes you want hard-edged, deliberate pixels**, and that is why it is the right tool for this work.

**The version this is written against:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Aseprite** | **1.3.18.6-x64** |
| **Where it is installed** | **the Steam copy**, at `~/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite` |
| **The configuration folder** | **`~/.config/aseprite/`** — holding `aseprite.ini`, `palettes/`, `sessions/`, `files/`, `user.aseprite-brushes` and `user.aseprite-layouts` |
| **Extensions installed** | **none.** `~/.config/aseprite/extensions/` does not exist |
| **Palettes installed** | **one — `default.ase`.** The Shepherds master palette has never been installed as a preset |

**That last row is the first thing this stage fixes.** The palette exists in the Shepherds repository as `media/reference/Palette/shepherds-master-v0-1.gpl` and has been loaded by hand when needed. **A palette you have to go and find is a palette you will sometimes not use.**

---

**Why the whole program, deliberately, and why first.**

**The argument against** is reasonable: most of Aseprite's surface is not needed for a single sprite, and learning a menu you will not use for six months is wasted. **The argument for is stronger, and it has three parts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Habits are expensive to unlearn** | a person who learns the pencil and nothing else develops a way of working that **routes around the features they do not know.** Six months later the workaround is the habit, and the feature that would have replaced it now costs more to adopt than it would have cost to learn |
| **2 — Two subsystems are prerequisites** | **Tilemap mode** is what terrain tiles want, and **Slices** is what a 9-slice interface border wants. Both are later stages here, and neither is learnable in passing |
| **3 — It is small enough** | **the official manual has about eighteen pages.** This stage has twenty-two lessons. That is a fortnight of evenings, once, forever |

**And the thing the first version of this curriculum got wrong:** it called Aseprite *"a small program"* whose whole can be learned *"in a few sittings"*, and then never mentioned Tilemap, Slices, the command line or the Lua API. **It is a small program with four large rooms in it.**

---

**What this stage covers, in order:**

| Lessons | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1–2** | this one, and the workspace |
| **3–5** | **the sprite** — canvas and image, colour modes, and the palette |
| **6–9** | **drawing** — the tools, the brush settings that matter, selection, and transforms |
| **10–11** | **layers** — the stack, and blending |
| **12–14** | **animation** — the timeline, frames and tags, onion skin and playback |
| **15–16** | **the two rooms** — Tilemap and Slices |
| **17–19** | **getting files out** — saving, export, and the command line |
| **20–22** | **making it yours** — preferences, shortcuts, extensions and scripting |

**What this stage is not.** It is not pixel art. **Nothing in it teaches a judgement** — no value, no colour choice, no silhouette. Stage 2 starts that. **This stage is the keyboard, and a keyboard is not music.**

**Practice.** Open Aseprite and check the version under Help › About — it should read 1.3.18.6. Then open `~/.config/aseprite/` in a file manager and look at what is there. Then read the Aseprite documentation's index page and count the sections, so you know the size of what you are about to learn.
The workspace:
The parts of the window, what each is for, and the layout worth saving.

**The window has six regions**, and Aseprite 1.3 lets you rearrange and save them:

| Region | Where | What it holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The menu bar** | top | File, Edit, Sprite, Layer, Frame, Select, View, Help |
| **The tool bar** | left edge | every drawing tool, one column |
| **The context bar** | under the menus | **the options for the tool you have selected** — this is the one beginners never look at, and it is where brush size, ink mode, pixel-perfect and tolerance live |
| **The canvas** | centre | the sprite, with tabs along the top when several files are open |
| **The colour bar** | right edge | the palette, the foreground and background colour, and the colour wheel or sliders |
| **The timeline** | bottom | **frames as columns, layers as rows, cels in the grid.** Toggle it with **Tab** |

**The context bar changes with the tool and nothing announces it.** Select the pencil and it shows brush and ink; select the paint bucket and it shows tolerance and contiguity; select a marquee and it shows the selection mode. **If an option you need seems missing, you have the wrong tool selected.**

---

**Navigation, which should become automatic:**

| Action | Key |
| --- | --- |
| **Pan** | **hold `Space` and drag** — the fastest, and it works inside every tool |
| **Hand tool** | `H` |
| **Zoom tool** | `Z` |
| **Zoom to a level** | **`1`, `2`, `3`** and so on — **`1` is 100%, which is the only level where you may make a decision** |
| **Zoom in and out** | **`` ` `` or `~`**, or the scroll wheel if enabled in preferences |
| **Toggle the timeline** | **`Tab`** |
| **Toggle a distraction-free canvas** | **`Ctrl+F`** — Advanced Mode, which hides everything but the canvas |
| **Cancel anything** | **`Esc`** |

**`1` is the most important key in the program.** From the contract, §10.1: *"Draw at native 1× resolution."* Everything in this curriculum is decided at 100%, and **the single most common failure in pixel art is deciding at 800%.**

---

**Two editors, not one.** Aseprite has a **Preview window** (`F7`) and a **full-screen preview** (`F8`):

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`F7` — Preview** | a small floating window showing **the sprite at 100% while you work zoomed in.** This solves the 1× problem without giving up the ability to place a pixel |
| **`F8` — Fullscreen Preview** | the sprite alone, centred, no interface |
| **Why `F7` matters here** | **it is the answer to "how do I draw at 8× and judge at 1×".** Keep it open, on the second screen if there is one, and look at it constantly |

**That is the single most useful habit in this stage**, and it is worth setting up before anything else.

---

**Saved layouts.** Aseprite 1.3 stores window arrangements in `~/.config/aseprite/user.aseprite-layouts`, which already exists on this machine — so a layout has been saved at some point. **A layout worth having for this project:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Timeline** | **visible and tall enough to show 24 frame columns at once** — the idle is 24 frames and scrolling through it hides the shape of the animation |
| **The preview window** | **open, at 100%**, positioned where it is always in view |
| **The colour bar** | wide enough to show the whole palette without scrolling, because 132 entries in 33 ramps is a lot of swatches and **the ramps are only legible when the rows line up** |

**Practice.** Open a 112 × 112 sprite. Press `Tab` to show and hide the timeline, `F7` to open the preview, `1` to go to 100% and `3` to go to 300%. Then select the pencil and read every control in the context bar; then select the paint bucket and read them again, and note what changed. Then arrange the window the way the table above describes and save the layout.
Canvas, sprite and image:
The three things Aseprite keeps separate, the geometry the contract fixes, and the operations that change size without changing content.

**Three words that are not synonyms:**

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Sprite** | **the whole document** — its canvas size, colour mode, palette, layers, frames and tags. One `.aseprite` file is one sprite |
| **Canvas** | **the rectangle the sprite occupies.** Changing it does not change what is drawn; it changes how much room there is |
| **Image** | **the pixels in a single cel** — one layer on one frame |

**The operations, and which of the three each one touches:**

| Menu | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Sprite › Sprite Size** | **resamples the pixels** — the drawing changes. **Dangerous**: see below |
| **Sprite › Canvas Size** | **changes the rectangle only**, anchoring the existing content where you choose. Safe |
| **Sprite › Crop to Selection** | canvas down to the marquee |
| **Sprite › Trim** | canvas down to the non-transparent content. **Never use this on a character master** — see below |
| **Sprite › Properties** | colour mode, and the transparent colour index in indexed mode |
| **Edit › Resize** / `Sprite Size` | the same resample |

---

**The geometry this project fixes, all from the contract §4:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal viewport** | **960 × 540** |
| **A normal adult gameplay frame** | **112 × 112** |
| **The standard pivot** | **(56, 96)** — bottom-centre, *"unless an asset-specific exception is deliberately approved"* |
| **Approximate adult height** | **about 80 px sole-to-crown**, with the approved idle reference measuring **81 to 87 px by direction** |
| **One world tile** | **16 px**, with an **8 px** collision and detail subgrid (§9.2) |
| **Scale** | **the game draws one art pixel as 3 × 3 screen pixels** at 1080p — 960 × 540 into 1920 × 1080 is 2×, and the run reference's note records the practical figure as 3 × 3 |
| **Larger frames** | permitted for *"large bodies, wide attacks, transformations, weapons and effects"*. **"Do not shrink a character merely to fit an effect"** |

**Set up a character canvas like this:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **File › New** | **112 width, 112 height** |
| **Colour mode** | **Indexed** — the next lesson but one explains why |
| **Background** | **Transparent.** Not white |
| **Then** | **a guide at the pivot** — View › Guides, or a locked one-pixel layer with a mark at (56, 96) |

**The pivot is (56, 96) on a 112 × 112 canvas**, which is the horizontal centre and **sixteen pixels up from the bottom edge**. Those sixteen pixels are deliberate: they are the room a pose needs to drop, a shadow needs to spread, and a frame needs for the feet to leave the ground without being clipped.

---

**Two destructive operations to understand before you ever use them.**

**1 — Sprite Size resamples, and in pixel art that is almost always wrong.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **scaling 112 → 224 at anything but Nearest Neighbor interpolates**, which invents colours that are not in the palette and soft edges that are not pixels |
| **§10.1's words** | *"Draw at native 1× resolution with deliberate clusters rather than resized or filtered source art."* |
| **When it is legitimate** | **exporting at an integer multiple for a contact sheet or a preview** — and even then, Nearest Neighbor |
| **The rule** | **never scale a master.** If a sprite needs to be bigger, draw it bigger |

**2 — Trim destroys the pivot.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What Trim does** | crops the canvas to the drawn content's bounding box |
| **Why that is fatal here** | **the pivot is defined relative to the canvas.** Trim a 112 × 112 frame whose figure happens to be 80 px tall and the pivot is no longer at (56, 96); the sprite will sit wrong in the game, and **every frame will sit wrong differently** |
| **The contract's version of the same warning** | §4: *"Never normalize each frame's bounding-box height independently; doing so makes prone bodies grow"* |
| **The rule** | **the canvas is 112 × 112 in every frame of every direction of every action**, and the figure moves inside it |

**Practice.** Create a 112 × 112 indexed sprite with a transparent background and put a single pixel at (56, 96). Then try Sprite › Trim and watch where that pixel ends up; undo it. Then use Canvas Size to make it 224 × 224 anchored at the centre, and note that the pixel moved relative to the canvas while the drawing did not change.
Colour modes, and why indexed:
Three modes, what each stores, and the argument for working in indexed on this project.

**The three modes** — Sprite › Color Mode:

| Mode | What a pixel stores | Colours available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **RGB** | **the colour itself** — eight bits each of red, green, blue and alpha | **any** |
| **Indexed** | **a number**, which is a position in the sprite's palette | **at most 256**, and exactly the ones in the palette |
| **Grayscale** | value and alpha only | 256 greys |

**In indexed mode the palette is part of the image.** A pixel does not hold `#7C6D63`; it holds *"entry 7"*, and entry 7 holds `#7C6D63`. **Change entry 7 and every pixel using it changes at once.**

---

**Why indexed is the right mode for this project.** Four reasons, in order of weight:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — It makes palette discipline automatic** | **you cannot use an off-palette colour, because there is nowhere to put it.** `colour-palette.md` says *"Do not invent substitute colours"*; in indexed mode that is not a rule to remember, it is a property of the file |
| **2 — It makes the colour count visible** | §10.1's bands — **12–18 for a hero, 8–26 for an ordinary enemy, 4–10 for a small prop** — are a glance at the palette rather than an audit |
| **3 — It makes a recolour one operation** | changing a character's cloth ramp means editing four palette entries, not repainting a hundred frames |
| **4 — It forbids accidental anti-aliasing** | a soft edge needs intermediate colours. **In indexed mode there are none to reach for** |

**And the costs, honestly:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Blending is constrained** | layer blend modes and opacity produce colours the palette may not hold, and Aseprite resolves them to the nearest entry. **So a 50%-opacity layer in indexed mode is not what you drew** |
| **Index 0 is special** | by default **index 0 is the transparent colour** in indexed mode, set in Sprite › Properties. **A visible colour must never sit at index 0**, or it will export as holes |
| **Some filters misbehave** | anything that wants to interpolate — blur, gradients with dithering off, resampling — has nowhere to go |
| **Importing art** | an RGB image converted to indexed is quantised, and the result depends on the dithering algorithm chosen |

**The practical position for this project:** **work indexed for sprites**, and if a specific effect needs RGB, do that effect in RGB in a separate file and convert deliberately. **UI art is a separate case entirely** — §3 says UI uses *"transparent PNG where practical"* and *"does not inherit sprite canvas, pivot or animation rules"*, so UI work can be RGB.

---

**Converting between modes**, and what each conversion costs:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **RGB → Indexed** | **quantisation.** Aseprite asks which palette to use and whether to dither. **Choose the Shepherds palette and dithering "none"** — §10.1 bans indiscriminate dithering, and a dithered conversion produces exactly that |
| **Indexed → RGB** | **lossless**, and it throws away the discipline |
| **Anything → Grayscale** | **lossy, and useful**: this is one way to run §10.1's grey test, though copying to a greyscale duplicate is safer than converting the master |

**The command line does both**, which matters for stage 19 and stage 12:

```
aseprite -b sprite.aseprite --color-mode indexed   --palette shepherds-master-v0-1.gpl --dithering-algorithm none   --save-as out.aseprite
```

**Practice.** Make a small RGB sprite with a soft gradient in it, then convert it to indexed with the Shepherds palette and dithering set to none, and see what happens to the gradient. Then convert a copy with ordered dithering and compare. Then open Sprite › Properties on an indexed sprite and find the transparent colour index.
The palette:
How Aseprite holds colour, how to install the Shepherds palette as a preset, and the colour bar's controls.

**The colour bar, on the right edge, has three parts:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The palette** | **the sprite's swatches**, in index order. In indexed mode these are the only colours the sprite can contain |
| **The foreground and background colour** | the two active colours. **`X` swaps them** |
| **The colour selector** | a wheel, sliders or spectrum, switchable — **and in indexed mode, picking here picks the nearest palette entry rather than an arbitrary colour** |

**The controls worth knowing:**

| Action | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Open the palette editor** | **`A`** or `F4` |
| **Step the foreground colour along the palette** | **`9` and `0`** — and **`[` and `]`** change the brush size |
| **Pick a colour from the canvas** | **`I`**, or **hold `Alt`** inside any tool |
| **Add the current colour to the palette** | the `+` button under the palette, or Edit › Add Color |
| **Load a palette** | **the folder icon's menu under the palette, then Load Palette** |
| **Save a palette as a preset** | **Save Palette › Save as Preset**, which writes into `~/.config/aseprite/palettes/` |
| **Sort or rearrange** | the palette menu's Sort and the palette editor's drag |

---

**Installing the Shepherds palette, which is the point of this lesson.**

> **As of 14 October 2026 this has not been done.** `~/.config/aseprite/palettes/` contains only `default.ase`.

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the file is `media/reference/Palette/shepherds-master-v0-1.gpl`** in the Shepherds repository — 132 entries, and a companion `.json` with the same contents |
| **2** | **palette menu › Load Palette**, and choose the `.gpl` |
| **3** | **palette menu › Save Palette › Save as Preset**, named something unmissable — `shepherds-v0-1` |
| **4** | it is now in **`~/.config/aseprite/palettes/`** and appears in the preset list for every new sprite |
| **5** | **and in File › New, the palette for a new sprite can be set** — so a new 112 × 112 indexed sprite starts with the right 132 entries and nothing else |

**`.gpl` is the GIMP palette format** — a plain text list of `R G B Name` lines with a header. It is readable, diffable and the right choice for a palette under version control. **The `.json` beside it is for tooling**, and `colour-palette.md` names both as *"the files to load in drawing and validation tools"*.

---

**What the palette's order means here.** This is colour theory's business and stage 5's lesson, but the mechanical consequence belongs now:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The palette is 33 ramps of four** | in the fixed value order **`Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light`** |
| **So the swatches run in fours** | and **the colour bar's width decides whether you can see that.** Set it so each row holds a multiple of four, and the ramps line up as columns |
| **Stepping with `9` and `0`** | **walks along a ramp** when the ramps are contiguous, which is what makes the keys useful rather than random |
| **Index 0** | **is the transparent index in indexed mode.** Check that the loaded palette has not put a visible colour there |

---

**Three other palette facts worth having:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A sprite's palette is saved inside the `.aseprite` file** | so a master carries its own colours and does not depend on the preset still existing |
| **Palette presets are per-machine** | they live in the config folder, not in the project. **Which is why the `.gpl` lives in the repository** and the preset is a convenience |
| **The Lospec tools can check a finished image** | the palette identifier and analyzer will tell you which palette an image uses and how many colours are in it — **a free external check on §10.1's bands** |

**Practice.** Load `shepherds-master-v0-1.gpl` and save it as a preset named `shepherds-v0-1`. Then create a new 112 × 112 indexed sprite with that palette selected in File › New, and confirm the palette has 132 entries and that index 0 is transparent. Then widen the colour bar until the four-step ramps line up as columns, and step through a ramp with `9` and `0`.
The drawing tools:
Every tool in the left column, what it is for, and which of them you will actually use.

**The tool bar, with the real default shortcuts** — read from the shipped `gui.xml` rather than from a tutorial:

| Tool | Key | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pencil** | **`B`** | **the tool.** Places the brush, hard-edged, no interpolation |
| **Spray** | `Shift+B` | scatters pixels. Noise by design — §10.1 bans *"isolated noise"*, so this is for texture studies and not for masters |
| **Eraser** | **`E`** | removes to transparent, or to the background colour on a background layer |
| **Eyedropper** | **`I`**, or **hold `Alt`** | picks a colour. **The held `Alt` is the one to learn** |
| **Rectangular marquee** | **`M`** | |
| **Elliptical marquee** | `Shift+M` | |
| **Lasso** | `Q` | |
| **Polygonal lasso** | `Shift+Q` | |
| **Magic wand** | **`W`** | selects a contiguous colour region, with tolerance in the context bar |
| **Paint bucket** | **`G`** | fills. **Tolerance and "contiguous" are in the context bar and both matter** |
| **Gradient** | `Shift+G` | **dithered or smooth.** §10.1 bans smooth gradients; this is for studies |
| **Line** | **`L`** | and **`Shift`-click with the pencil draws a line from the last point**, which is faster |
| **Curve** | `Shift+L` | a four-point curve |
| **Rectangle / filled rectangle** | **`U`** | |
| **Ellipse / filled ellipse** | `Shift+U` | |
| **Contour** | `D` | a freehand closed shape |
| **Polygon** | `Shift+D` | |
| **Blur** | `R` | **do not use it.** It invents intermediate colours |
| **Jumble** | `R` | shuffles pixels locally. A texture toy |
| **Text** | `T` | **for notes and mock-ups, never for shipped UI text** — the game draws text with a font |
| **Move** | **`V`**, or **hold `Ctrl`** | moves the selection or the cel |
| **Hand** | **`H`**, or **hold `Space`** | pans |
| **Zoom** | **`Z`** | |
| **Slice** | **`Shift+C`** | lesson 16 |

---

**The five you will actually use**, and it is worth saying which:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pencil at 1 px** | **the overwhelming majority of every sprite in this project.** An 80-pixel figure is built one pixel at a time |
| **Eyedropper, held on `Alt`** | constantly. Picking the neighbouring value is how a cluster grows |
| **Rectangular marquee plus Move** | shifting a limb two pixels, which is most of what animating a 24-frame idle consists of |
| **Paint bucket with contiguous on** | blocking in a shape before shading it |
| **Line and `Shift`-click** | the straight edges of props and architecture |

**Everything else is a study tool or a trap.** The blur and the smooth gradient are both explicitly against §10.1; the spray is noise; the text tool produces an image of text rather than text.

---

**Ink modes**, in the context bar, which almost nobody looks at:

| Ink | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Simple Ink** | replaces the pixel with the colour. **The default and the right one** |
| **Alpha Compositing** | blends by the colour's alpha. In indexed mode this resolves to the nearest entry |
| **Copy Color** | writes the colour including its alpha, so a semi-transparent colour stays semi-transparent |
| **Lock Alpha** | **paints only where there is already something.** Extremely useful: it lets you recolour a shape without touching its silhouette |
| **Shading** | **paints along the palette.** Pick a ramp as the shading range and the tool moves each pixel one step lighter or darker. **This is the ink mode that matters most for this project** |

**The Shading ink deserves its own note, because it is the one Aseprite feature that is directly about the craft this curriculum teaches.** Select a four-step ramp in the colour bar, choose Shading ink, and the pencil **shifts pixels along that ramp** rather than setting a colour. Left button moves one way, right the other. **With `Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light` ramps, that is shading as a verb.**

**Practice.** Draw a 32 × 32 blob with the pencil at 1 px, fill it with a ramp's Mid value using the bucket, then select that ramp in the colour bar, switch to Shading ink, and shade the blob by dragging. Then switch to Lock Alpha and recolour it without changing its edge. Then draw the same blob's outline with `Shift`-clicked pencil lines instead of the Line tool.
The brush, and the settings that must be:
Brush size and shape, pixel-perfect mode, dynamics, and the three settings that will quietly ruin a sprite if they are wrong.

**The brush, in the context bar when a paint tool is selected:**

| Control | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Size** | **`[` and `]`** change it. **1 px is the working size for this project** |
| **Shape** | **Circle, Square, Line**, or a custom brush made from a selection |
| **Angle** | for the Line brush |
| **Pixel-perfect** | **a toggle. See below** |

**Making a custom brush** is worth knowing: select a region, then **Edit › New Brush** (or the brush dropdown), and the selection becomes the brush. Useful for a repeated detail — a fence post, a tuft of grass — and dangerous for exactly the same reason, because §10.1's deliberate clusters are not a stamp repeated.

---

**Pixel-perfect mode**, which is the single most useful toggle in the program.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem it solves** | a freehand diagonal stroke at 1 px leaves **L-shaped doubled corners** — two pixels where the line turns, which reads as a lump |
| **What it does** | **removes the redundant pixel at each turn as you draw**, leaving a clean single-pixel line |
| **When to have it on** | **drawing lines and outlines freehand** — most of the time |
| **When to have it off** | **when you want the doubled pixel**, which happens in deliberate anti-aliasing and in some texture work; and when drawing single dots, because it can eat them |
| **Where it is** | the context bar, with the brush controls |

**This is the tool's answer to stage 2's jaggy problem, and it is only half an answer.** Pixel-perfect fixes the doubled corner; it does not fix an uneven stair pattern, and an uneven stair pattern is what makes a curve look wrong. **The tool cannot do that part.**

---

**Dynamics**, new in the 1.3 line and worth knowing exists so you can turn it off:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | brush size, angle and colour varying with **pressure, velocity or a stabiliser**, configured from the brush dropdown |
| **Why it matters here** | **a tablet with pressure dynamics on will give you a brush that changes size as you draw**, which in pixel art is never what you want |
| **The setting** | **all dynamics off**, stabiliser off. The hand does the work |

---

**The three settings that will ruin a sprite quietly.**

| Setting | Where | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Any interpolation on a transform** | **Edit › Preferences › Editor**, and the Rotate/Scale dialogs | **rotation and scaling can be set to interpolate**, which invents colours. In indexed mode it quantises them back to the nearest entry, which is worse than either outcome — it produces off-ramp colours that look almost right. **Nearest neighbour always** |
| **A non-transparent background layer** | File › New, and Layer › Background | **a sprite with an opaque background exports with that background.** Every character master is transparent, and the eraser on a background layer paints the background colour instead of erasing |
| **Grid snapping, left on** | **View › Grid › Snap to Grid** | useful for 16 px tiles, **actively harmful for a character** — it will move your two-pixel limb adjustment to the nearest grid line |

**And one setting that should be on:** **View › Show › Pixel Grid** (`Ctrl+Shift+'`). At high zoom it draws a line between every pixel, which makes counting possible. The ordinary grid (`Ctrl+'`) is the 16 px one and is a different thing.

**Practice.** Draw a freehand diagonal line with pixel-perfect off, then undo and draw it again with pixel-perfect on, and compare the corners at 100% and at 800%. Then check Preferences for any interpolation setting and set it to nearest neighbour. Then turn on the pixel grid and off snap-to-grid, and confirm you can nudge a selection by one pixel with the arrow keys.
Selection:
Making a selection, the modes, and the operations that only exist once you have one.

**The four selection tools:**

| Tool | Key | For |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Rectangular marquee** | **`M`** | **the one you will use** — a limb, a frame region, a tile |
| **Elliptical marquee** | `Shift+M` | |
| **Lasso / polygonal lasso** | `Q` / `Shift+Q` | irregular regions, freehand |
| **Magic wand** | **`W`** | **a contiguous region of one colour** — with **tolerance** and **contiguous** in the context bar |

**The modes**, in the context bar and on modifier keys:

| Mode | Key |
| --- | --- |
| **Replace** | default |
| **Add** | **hold `Shift`** |
| **Subtract** | **hold `Alt`** |
| **Intersect** | `Shift+Alt` |

**The commands:**

| Command | Key |
| --- | --- |
| **Select all** | **`Ctrl+A`** |
| **Deselect** | **`Ctrl+D`**, or `Esc` |
| **Invert** | **`Ctrl+Shift+I`** |
| **Reselect** | Select › Reselect |
| **Modify** | Select › Modify › **Border, Expand, Contract** — see below |

---

**What a selection makes possible.** This is the part worth learning, because several of these are the only sensible way to do the job:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Move content by exact pixels** | **select, then arrow keys.** One press, one pixel. **This is how a 24-frame idle gets animated** — a limb is selected and nudged, not redrawn |
| **Move without the arrow keys** | hold **`Ctrl`** to get the Move tool temporarily |
| **Fill the selection** | **`F`** fills with the foreground colour. Also Edit › Fill |
| **Constrain drawing** | **a tool only draws inside the selection.** So select a shape, then paint freely across it, and only the inside changes — the poor relation of Lock Alpha ink and sometimes the right one |
| **Copy a cel's content between frames** | select, `Ctrl+C`, go to the next frame, `Ctrl+V` |
| **Copy merged** | **`Ctrl+Shift+C`** copies the flattened result of all visible layers, not just the active one |
| **Make a new sprite from a selection** | **`Ctrl+Alt+N`** — useful for pulling one frame out to study |
| **Make a brush** | Edit › New Brush |
| **Crop the canvas to it** | Sprite › Crop to Selection |
| **Use it as the grid** | **Select › Selection as Grid** — draw a 16 × 16 marquee and the grid becomes 16 × 16, aligned to it |

---

**Select › Modify, which is how an outline gets made mechanically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Expand** | grows the selection by N pixels |
| **Contract** | shrinks it |
| **Border** | **turns the selection into a ring N pixels wide** |
| **The outline recipe** | **select the figure with the magic wand on the transparent area, invert, Border by 1, fill with the outline colour** — a one-pixel outline in four operations |
| **And why not to rely on it** | **§10.1 bans *"automatic double outlines"* and outlines *"that merge equipment into the torso"*.** An automatic border does exactly the second thing: it cannot tell a satchel strap from a chest. **The recipe is a starting point that must then be corrected by hand** |

**That tension is the lesson.** Aseprite will outline a sprite for you in a second, and the contract requires an outline that **varies in colour by what it surrounds** and **preserves negative gaps**. The automatic version gets you 80% of the pixels and all of the wrong ones.

**Practice.** Draw a filled shape with a gap in it. Select the transparent area with the magic wand, invert, Select › Modify › Border by 1, and fill — then look at what happened to the gap. Then undo and do the same outline by hand with the pencil, and compare how long each took and which one you would ship. Then select a 16 × 16 region and use Select › Selection as Grid.
Transformations:
Flip, rotate, scale and skew — what each costs, and the one this project forbids.

**Where they are:** Edit › Transform once a selection exists, and Sprite › Flip / Rotate for the whole sprite, with the Move tool's handles for interactive transforms.

| Transform | Key | What it costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Flip horizontal** | **`Shift+H`** | **nothing. It is lossless** — every pixel moves to a mirrored position and no colour changes |
| **Flip vertical** | **`Shift+V`** | nothing, same reason |
| **Rotate 90° or 180°** | Sprite › Rotate | **nothing**, for those angles only |
| **Rotate by an arbitrary angle** | the Move tool's rotation handle | **a great deal.** Pixels do not rotate; they are resampled, and a 23° rotation of pixel art produces a mess of stray pixels and, with interpolation on, invented colours |
| **Scale** | the Move tool's handles, or Sprite Size | **a great deal, unless it is an integer multiple with nearest neighbour** |
| **Skew** | the Move tool, 1.3 | the same as arbitrary rotation |

**The rule for this project:** **flips and right-angle rotations are free; everything else is a drawing decision you are asking the computer to make for you, and it will make it badly.** §10.1: *"deliberate clusters rather than resized or filtered source art."*

---

**Now the one that is not a technical question but a contract question: the horizontal flip.**

**Flipping is free, lossless and fast. It halves the work of an eight-direction character. And §5.4 forbids it here.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What the contract says** | *"Use eight authored directions whenever asymmetry or the approved motion reference requires them. Mirroring is permitted only for an explicitly approved asset whose handedness, costume and action geometry survive the flip."* |
| **Why, concretely** | **Timon's reference ties limb colours to a side** — `media/reference/Animation/README.md`: *"The limb colours are tied to a side, so a flipped west would swap them."* And a character with a crook over one shoulder and a satchel on one hip has a handedness that a flip reverses |
| **What the industry normally does** | **draws five orientations and flips to get eight.** Slynyrd's Pixelblog 55 teaches exactly that, and it is the right advice for most games |
| **What the runtime does** | **`authored_sprite_body.gd` uses a direction's own drawing when it has one, unmirrored, and mirrors only a direction with no drawing of its own.** So the engine supports both, and the contract chooses one |

**Stage 9 argues this properly.** Here the mechanical point is enough: **`Shift+H` is one keystroke and it is the most consequential keystroke in this curriculum.**

---

**Two transform facts that are easy to miss:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A transform is live until you commit it** | move the handles, and the result is a floating preview. **`Enter` commits; `Esc` cancels.** While it floats, you can change the interpolation |
| **Transforming across frames** | **select a range in the timeline first**, and a transform applies to all of it. This is how you shift an entire 24-frame animation two pixels left without doing it twenty-four times |

**Practice.** Draw an asymmetric shape — something with a clear left and right. Flip it horizontally and confirm no pixel changed except its position. Then rotate it 17° with the Move tool and look at the result at 100%; count the colours before and after with the palette, and then undo. Then select a four-frame range in the timeline and nudge all four by one pixel at once.
Layers and groups:
The stack, the kinds of layer, and the contract's rule about how finely to split.

**A cel is a layer on a frame.** The timeline's grid is layers down the side and frames across the top, and each filled square is a cel holding an image. **An empty square is an empty cel, which is not the same as a transparent one** — an empty cel has no image at all and inherits nothing.

**The kinds of layer:**

| Kind | How | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Normal layer** | **`Shift+N`** | the ordinary kind |
| **Background layer** | Layer › Background from Layer | **opaque, cannot be moved above others, and the eraser paints the background colour on it.** Character masters never have one |
| **Group** | Layer › New Group | **a folder.** Collapsible, and hiding or moving the group does so to its contents |
| **Tilemap layer** | **`Space+N`**, or Layer › New › New Tilemap Layer | lesson 15 |
| **Reference layer** | Layer › New › New Reference Layer | **an image shown behind the sprite for tracing or comparison, which does not export.** The right place for a reference frame |

**Per-layer controls:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Visibility** | the eye. **Alt-click to show only that one** |
| **Lock** | the padlock — prevents editing |
| **Continuous** | the icon that makes a new cel on this layer link rather than copy |
| **Opacity and blend mode** | the next lesson |
| **Properties** | **`Shift+P`** or `F2` |

---

**Linked cels**, which matter for animation and are easy to create by accident:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What a link is** | **two or more frames sharing one image.** Edit one and both change |
| **How to make one** | **`Ctrl`-drag a cel**, or Frame › Link Cels on a selected range |
| **Why it is useful** | **a held pose.** The idle reference holds its last pose from frame 10 through 24 — fourteen frames of the same image. **Linked cels make that one image rather than fourteen copies** |
| **Why it is dangerous** | you edit frame 14 to fix a pixel and frames 10 to 24 all change |
| **How to tell** | **a linked cel is drawn differently in the timeline**, and Cel Properties says so |
| **And note** | **Timon's run reference has frames that are byte-identical to their neighbours** — `media/reference/Animation/README.md` calls them *"Timon's two-frame holds, kept"*. Those are copies, not links, and both approaches survive export |

---

**Now the contract's rule, which is the point of this lesson.**

> **§3.1:** *"Layers should separate only things that require independent editing or runtime treatment — body, equipment, shadow and effects — not every small colour cluster."*

**So four layers, not forty:**

| Layer | Why it is separate |
| --- | --- |
| **Body** | the base figure |
| **Equipment** | **because it changes.** A character who gains a different crook needs the body unredrawn |
| **Shadow** | **because the runtime may treat it separately**, and because a contact shadow is not part of the silhouette for the black test |
| **Effects** | because they may be tinted, hidden or driven by code |

**And the reason the rule exists.** It is tempting to put every material on its own layer — cloth, skin, metal, leather — because it makes recolouring easy. **The costs are real:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The silhouette becomes invisible** | you cannot judge a shape you are seeing in six pieces |
| **The outline cannot be drawn** | a one-pixel coloured outline is a decision about **what is next to what**, which requires seeing the whole |
| **Frame count multiplies** | 24 frames × 8 directions × 6 layers is 1,152 cels to keep in register |
| **And the export does it for you anyway** | **Wizard's split-layer importer** takes layers to separate textures — stage 12 — so if the runtime needs them separate, that is where it happens |

**Practice.** Build a 112 × 112 sprite with exactly four layers named body, equipment, shadow and effects, in that stacking order, and save it as a template. Then make a two-frame animation and link the cels on one layer and copy them on another, and edit one of each to see the difference. Then add a reference layer with a reference image and confirm it does not appear in an export.
Blend modes and opacity:
What the twenty blend modes do, which three are useful here, and why most of them are a trap in indexed mode.

**Opacity and blend mode are per-layer and per-cel.** The layer's values apply to the whole layer; a cel can also carry its own opacity.

**The modes Aseprite offers**, grouped as it groups them:

| Group | Modes |
| --- | --- |
| **Normal** | Normal |
| **Darken** | Darken, Multiply, Color Burn, Linear Burn, Darker Color |
| **Lighten** | Lighten, Screen, Color Dodge, Linear Dodge (**Addition**), Lighter Color |
| **Contrast** | Overlay, Soft Light, Hard Light, Vivid Light, Linear Light, Pin Light, Hard Mix |
| **Inversion** | Difference, Exclusion, Subtract, Divide |
| **Component** | Hue, Saturation, Color, Luminosity |

---

**Why almost all of them are a trap on this project.** Two reasons, and the second is the contract:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Indexed mode** | **a blend produces a colour, and indexed mode has nowhere to put it.** Aseprite resolves the result to the nearest palette entry, so Multiply at 60% on a Shepherds ramp gives you *some* entry, chosen by distance, which is not a decision you made. **§10.1's "deliberate clusters" and a blend mode are opposites** |
| **2 — The flattened export** | **what Wizard imports is the flattened image.** Any blend is baked in at export, so the mode is a drawing convenience and never a runtime behaviour. **Runtime blending is Godot's job** — `CanvasItem`'s blend mode, `Light2D`, and the material on the sprite |

**So the working rule: layers in a master are Normal at 100%, and anything that needs to blend at runtime is done in Godot.**

---

**The three legitimate uses**, all of them temporary:

| Use | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Checking value separation** | **a black layer in Color or Saturation mode above everything desaturates the sprite** — which is §10.1's grey test, done non-destructively and toggled with one click. **This is the most useful blend mode in the program for this project** |
| **Checking the silhouette** | a solid-colour layer in **Color** mode, or simply a locked layer filled with black behind a hidden body — the black test |
| **Judging a light direction** | a soft **Multiply** layer to mock up where a shadow should fall, drawn properly afterwards and then deleted |

**All three are scaffolding.** They go in the file while you work and come out before it is a master — and §3's rule applies: *"Rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived."*

---

**Opacity has one legitimate permanent use and it is not a sprite:** **UI art**, which §3 puts outside the sprite rules entirely. A HUD panel at 85% opacity is a real design decision, lives in a PNG, and does not inherit any of this.

**And one genuine pixel-art use of partial alpha:** **a semi-transparent pixel is a colour the palette does not contain**, and §10.1's colour counts are of *"opaque base colours"*. So a glow or a veil drawn with alpha is outside the count — and in indexed mode it is barely possible, which is one more argument for doing effects in Godot.

**Practice.** Build the grey test as a toggle: a new top layer, filled with any colour, blend mode Color, visibility off. Turn it on and your sprite is greyscale; turn it off and it is not. Save that in your 112 × 112 template. Then try Multiply at 50% on a shaded shape in indexed mode and look at which palette entries the result actually used.
The timeline:
Frames across, layers down, cels in the grid — and the controls that make a 24-frame animation workable.

**Toggle it with `Tab`.** The timeline is the animation editor and it is also the layer manager, which is why it is the part of the window to make tall.

| Part | What |
| --- | --- |
| **Columns** | **frames**, numbered from 1 |
| **Rows** | **layers**, bottom-most at the bottom |
| **Cells** | **cels** — a layer's image on a frame. A filled cell has an image; an empty one has none |
| **The header strip** | **tags**, drawn as coloured bars spanning their frame ranges |
| **The left column** | layer names, with visibility, lock and continuous toggles |
| **The bottom strip** | onion skin, playback, loop range and the thumbnail toggle |

---

**Navigation and editing:**

| Action | Key |
| --- | --- |
| **Next / previous frame** | **`Right` / `Left`** |
| **Next / previous frame with the same tag** | **`.` / `,`** |
| **Play the animation** | **`Enter`** |
| **Play in the preview window** | **`Shift+Enter`** |
| **New frame (copy of the current)** | **`Alt+N`** |
| **New empty frame** | `Alt+B` |
| **Duplicate the cel** | `Alt+M` |
| **Frame properties — the duration** | **`P`** |
| **Layer properties** | **`Shift+P`** or `F2` |
| **Toggle onion skin** | **`F3`** |
| **Set the loop range** | **`F2`** on a selected frame range — *SetLoopSection* |
| **Cel thumbnails in the timeline** | **`F6`** |

**`F6` deserves a note.** With thumbnails on, the timeline shows a tiny picture of every cel, which turns 24 frames into something you can read at a glance — **you can see the shape of the motion without playing it.** For a 24-frame idle with a 14-frame hold, the hold is immediately visible as fourteen identical thumbnails.

---

**Ranges, which is how bulk work gets done:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Select a frame range** | click a frame header and shift-click another |
| **Select a cel range** | drag across the grid |
| **What then applies to the whole range** | **nudging with arrow keys, transforms, copy and paste, deleting, reversing, and linking** |
| **Reverse frames** | Frame › Reverse Frames on a selected range |
| **Move a range** | drag it |

**This is the mechanism behind most animation editing in this project.** Shifting an entire direction's 24 frames one pixel left, reversing a swing to make its recovery, or copying frames 1–10 of the idle to start another direction — all of it is a range operation.

---

**One structural fact about frame duration, because it governs stage 12.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Duration is per frame, in milliseconds** | set with **`P`**, and a frame range can be set at once |
| **There is no sprite-level frame rate** | **Aseprite has no "12 fps" field.** The playback speed is entirely a consequence of the per-frame durations |
| **So "12 fps" means a duration** | and the contract's 12 fps means **84 ms**, not 83 — because of how Aseprite Wizard converts duration to a frame rate on import. **Stage 12 does the arithmetic; for now, 84** |
| **And a longer frame is a hold** | a frame at 168 ms is two frames' worth of time in one cel, and it survives the import as a relative duration |

**Practice.** Make a 24-frame sprite. Turn on thumbnails with `F6` and set the timeline tall enough to see all 24 columns. Set every frame's duration to 84 ms by selecting the whole range and pressing `P`. Then set the loop section to frames 1–10 with `F2` and play it with `Enter`, and then play the whole thing. Then select frames 5–8 and nudge them one pixel with the arrow keys.
Frames, durations and tags:
The animation's structure: what a tag is, what it carries, and the naming grammar the import pipeline reads.

**A tag is a named frame range.** Right-click the timeline header and choose New Tag, or Frame › Tags › New Tag. It is drawn as a coloured bar above the frames it spans.

**What a tag carries:**

| Property | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | **the animation's name in Godot.** This is the important one |
| **Colour** | a label for your benefit only |
| **Animation direction** | **Forward, Reverse, Ping-pong, Ping-pong Reverse** |
| **Repeat** | a count, or infinite |
| **User data** | free text |

**Aseprite Wizard reads all of this.** The tag name becomes the `SpriteFrames` animation name; the direction becomes the frame order, with ping-pong expanded into a there-and-back sequence; the repeat count makes the animation non-looping and repeat that many times.

---

**The contract's naming grammar**, §3.1 and §5.4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One master per asset, action and direction** | named **`<asset-key>_<action>_<direction>.aseprite`** |
| **One tag per file** | and it is **`<action>_<direction>`**, **lower-case snake-case** |
| **The names state the action and direction plainly** | **`idle_s`, `move_ne`, `staff_attack_1_se`** |
| **Not sequence names** | *"Do not use sequence names such as `animation1` or `walk2`"* |
| **A one-shot tag begins with `_`** | **`_dodge_s`**, **`_death_e`** — and Wizard strips the underscore and imports it with looping disabled |

**So a file called `eli_idle_s.aseprite` contains one tag called `idle_s`** covering all 24 frames, and that is the whole structure. **The redundancy is deliberate:** `media/README.md` explains it — *"Aseprite Wizard imports animations from tags, so `death_s` in its own file imports identically to a tag inside a merged family file. Separate files keep each direction independently reviewable."*

---

**The underscore prefix, confirmed in the addon's source.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The contract** | §5.3: *"Aseprite tags for one-shot actions begin with `_`; Aseprite Wizard strips the prefix and imports them with looping disabled."* |
| **The addon** | `addons/AsepriteWizard/config/config.gd` holds **`const _DEFAULT_LOOP_EX_PREFIX = '_'`** |
| **So the rule is the addon's default**, not a Shepherds invention — and it is a **project setting**, which means it could be changed and must not be | |
| **What it actually does** | `sprite_frames_creator.gd`: if the name begins with the prefix, **strip it and invert the default loop setting.** The default is loop-enabled, so a prefixed tag becomes loop-disabled |
| **The consequence of forgetting it** | **a death animation that loops forever.** The character dies, and dies, and dies |

**Which tags take the underscore**, from §5.3: *"Locomotion and idle cycles loop. Attacks, interactions, reactions, downing and other one-shot actions do not."*

| Loops — no underscore | One-shot — underscore |
| --- | --- |
| `idle_s` | `_crook_attack_1_s` |
| `move_ne` | `_dodge_e` |
| `graze_s` | `_stoop_s` |
| `pace_w` | `_death_se` |
| | `_get_up_s` |
| | `_sling_throw_n` |

---

**Two practical notes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Tags can overlap and nest** | Aseprite permits it. **Do not** — the contract says one tag per file, and overlapping tags make the import ambiguous |
| **A tag can be shorter than the sprite** | so a file can hold 30 frames with a 24-frame tag, and only the tagged 24 import. **Useful for keeping working frames beside a finished animation; dangerous because the untagged ones are invisible in Godot and easy to forget** |

**Practice.** Make a 24-frame sprite, tag frames 1–24 as `idle_s`, and set the tag's direction to Forward and its repeat to infinite. Then make a second file with 8 frames tagged `_dodge_s` and confirm the underscore is in the tag name, not just the filename. Then open `addons/AsepriteWizard/config/config.gd` and find the line that defines the prefix.
Onion skin and playback:
Seeing the frames either side of the one you are drawing, and the three ways to watch the result.

**Onion skinning shows neighbouring frames as ghosts behind the current one**, so you can see what moved. Toggle it with **`F3`**, and configure it from the onion skin button's dropdown in the timeline's bottom strip.

| Setting | What it controls |
| --- | --- |
| **Frames before / after** | how many neighbours to show. **1 and 1 is the working default; 2 and 2 for a fast action** |
| **Opacity range** | the ghosts' minimum and maximum opacity |
| **Type** | **Merge** (ghosts drawn in their own colours) or **Red/Blue tint** (previous in red, next in blue) |
| **Loop through tag frames** | **whether the onion skin wraps at the tag's boundary** |

**That last one is the setting that matters for a looping animation.** With it on, frame 1's "previous" is frame 24 — so **you can see whether the loop closes.** With it off, frame 1 has no previous and the loop's seam is invisible while you work on it.

**And for this project the seam is a known, deliberate feature.** `media/reference/Animation/README.md` records that the approved idle has **a 3 px drop when the loop returns from frame 24 to frame 1**, and that it was *"seen in the preview and kept on purpose"*. **Timon rejected evening it out.** So the onion skin's job here is not to eliminate the seam but to show you that yours matches the reference's.

---

**The three ways to watch it:**

| Way | Key | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Play in the canvas** | **`Enter`** | quick checking while zoomed in — **at the wrong scale, so not for judgement** |
| **Play in the preview window** | **`Shift+Enter`** | **at 100%, in a small window.** This is the one to use constantly |
| **Fullscreen preview** | **`F8`** | the sprite alone, no interface |

**And the loop range, `F2`:** select a frame range, press `F2`, and playback loops just that range. **Essential for a 24-frame idle whose motion is in frames 1–10** — you can watch the motion without sitting through the fourteen-frame hold every time.

---

**What the contract requires you to check, and where.** §5.3's last line:

> *"Every animation is checked at native scale, in motion, against the real ground and under representative lighting."*

**Four conditions, and Aseprite can only give you two of them:**

| Condition | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **At native scale** | **Aseprite's preview window at 100%**, and the game at its real zoom |
| **In motion** | **Aseprite's playback** |
| **Against the real ground** | **Godot only.** A walk cycle that reads against a transparent checkerboard can disappear against grass |
| **Under representative lighting** | **Godot only** — `Light2D` changes value relationships, which is why §10.1 keeps static shading restrained |

**So the loop in this project is: animate in Aseprite, check the first two there, and then take it into Godot for the other two.** Stage 7 closes that round trip for the first time and stage 12 makes it routine. **An animation approved on Aseprite's checkerboard is not approved.**

**Practice.** Make a six-frame bouncing dot. Turn on onion skin with one frame either side and the red/blue tint, and watch what it tells you about the spacing. Then turn on "loop through tag frames" and look at frame 1's previous. Then set a loop range over frames 2–5 and play it in the preview window with `Shift+Enter`, at 100%.
Tilemap mode:
The 1.3 feature this project's terrain depends on: what a tileset is, the two drawing modes, and the three submodes that decide whether tiles get created.

**A tilemap layer is a layer where every grid cell holds a reference to a tile**, and the tiles live in a **tileset** attached to that layer. The documentation's own comparison is the useful one:

| Indexed colour | Tilemap |
| --- | --- |
| a pixel holds an **index** | a cell holds a **tile index** |
| the **palette** holds the colours | the **tileset** holds the tiles |
| indices run 0 to N | tile indices run 0 to N |
| **change a palette entry and every pixel using it changes** | **change a tile and every cell using it changes** |

**That last row is the whole point.** Edit one grass tile and every grass cell in the map updates.

---

**Creating one:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Layer › New › New Tilemap Layer**, or **`Space+N`** | |
| **The grid** | **set the grid first** — the tile size comes from it. For this project **16 × 16**, from §9.2: *"One world tile is 16 px"* |
| **Setting the grid** | View › Grid › Grid Settings, or **draw a 16 × 16 marquee and use Select › Selection as Grid** |
| **The Tileset window** | shows the layer's tiles with their indices, and is where you select a tile to stamp |

---

**Two drawing modes, swapped with `Space+Tab`:**

| Mode | What drawing does |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw Pixels** | **edits the content of the tile under the cursor** — you are painting the artwork |
| **Draw Tiles** | **stamps tile references into cells** — you are assembling the map, and the tile artwork is untouched |

**And three submodes that apply while drawing pixels**, which decide what happens to the tileset when you paint:

| Submode | Key | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Manual** | **`Space+1`** | **edits the tile in place and never reorders the tileset.** Use this when tile indices must stay put — which is always, once a Godot `TileSet` has been built against them |
| **Auto** | **`Space+2`** | **the default.** Creates a new tile or reuses an existing one as you draw, and **removes tiles that stop being used** |
| **Stack** | **`Space+3`** | creates a new tile for every modification, stacking versions |

**Manual versus Auto is the trap.** Auto is the pleasant one to draw in — it builds your tileset as you work. **And it reorders and deletes.** Once the tileset has been exported and a Godot `TileSet` resource references tile 37, an Auto-mode edit that removes an unused tile can renumber everything above it. **The rule: Auto while building, Manual once anything downstream knows the indices.**

---

**Why this matters here.** §9.1:

> *"terrain and transitions: hand-drawn 16 × 16 tiles assembled as Godot terrain sets"*

**And the import route exists:** `addons/AsepriteWizard/importers/tileset_texture_import_plugin.gd` — Wizard has a **tileset texture importer**, so a tilemap master becomes a texture a Godot `TileSet` can be built on. **Stage 8 does the drawing and stage 12 does the pipeline.**

**Two further Aseprite features that belong to tiles:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Tiled mode** | **View › Tiled Mode** — repeats the canvas in both axes as you draw, so **a tile's seams are visible while you are making them.** This is the single most useful feature for terrain work |
| **Tile flipping** | tiles can be stamped flipped or rotated in Draw Tiles mode, and Godot's `TileSet` supports flipped alternatives — **which means the no-mirroring rule does not apply to terrain.** §5.4 is about characters |

**Practice.** Create a 64 × 64 sprite, set the grid to 16 × 16, and make a tilemap layer. Draw one grass tile in Auto mode and watch the Tileset window gain a tile. Switch to Draw Tiles with `Space+Tab` and stamp it across the canvas. Then switch to Manual with `Space+1`, edit the tile, and confirm every stamped cell changed. Then turn on View › Tiled Mode and look at your tile's seams.
Slices:
Named rectangles inside a sprite, the 9-slice centre, and what the interface work needs them for.

**A slice is a named rectangle on the canvas**, with optional extra data. It is not a layer and not a selection; it is metadata that travels with the sprite and comes out in the export.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The tool** | **`Shift+C`** |
| **Making one** | press, drag, release |
| **Selecting one** | click it; overlapping slices select together |
| **Moving and resizing** | drag the body or the corner and edge handles |
| **Deleting** | select and press `Delete` |
| **Properties** | **double-click the slice** |

**The properties dialog holds three things:**

| Property | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Bounds** | the rectangle |
| **9-slices** | **"an internal rectangle to sub-divide the bounds into sub-slices"** — the stretchable centre |
| **Pivot** | a reference point inside the slice |

**Plus a name and free-text user data.** And slices are **per-frame** — a slice's bounds can change from frame to frame, and the exported data records the frame.

---

**What the 9-slice centre is for**, which is the reason this lesson exists.

**A nine-slice border is a panel that can be any size drawn from one small image.** The image is divided into nine regions by the inner rectangle:

| | | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **corner** | **top edge** | **corner** |
| **left edge** | **centre** | **right edge** |
| **corner** | **bottom edge** | **corner** |

| Region | How it scales |
| --- | --- |
| **The four corners** | **never stretch** |
| **The top and bottom edges** | stretch horizontally only |
| **The left and right edges** | stretch vertically only |
| **The centre** | stretches both ways, or tiles |

**So a 24 × 24 ornate frame can draw a dialogue panel of any size with its corners intact.** That is how every scalable interface element in the game works, and §8 requires exactly this: *"UI art must remain legible at the locked viewport and at 1080p, 1440p and 2160p presentation. Text contrast, scalable borders, safe areas…"*

**Godot's side of it:** `NinePatchRect`, and `StyleBoxTexture`'s margins — both take the same four margin values that Aseprite's 9-slice rectangle defines. **Set the centre rectangle in Aseprite, read the four margins off it, and type them into Godot.**

---

**The other uses of slices:**

| Use | How |
| --- | --- |
| **Exporting several images from one file** | **one slice per image, each named** — then `--split-slices` on the command line, or JSON data from the sprite sheet export |
| **Marking a pivot** | the slice's own pivot field, which the exported JSON records |
| **Marking a region for code** | a hit box, an attachment point, a text safe area — anything the runtime needs to know in pixels. **The name and user data make it machine-readable** |
| **Keeping a sheet of related UI pieces in one master** | map markers, slot art, orbs — each sliced and named, one file |

**That last one is directly useful.** `media/ui/map/` holds six separate marker PNGs — exclaim and question in gold, red and silver. **One master with six named slices produces all six**, and keeps them in register and on one palette.

**Practice.** Draw a 24 × 24 panel border. Make a slice over the whole thing, name it `panel`, and set its 9-slice centre to leave an 8-pixel border all round. Write down the four margins. Then draw three small icons in one file, slice and name each, and export with `--split-slices` to confirm you get three files. Then find `media/ui/hud/dialogue-text-box.png` and work out what its nine-slice margins would be.
Saving, and the file formats:
The native format, what else Aseprite writes, and the one-master rule that governs all of it.

**`.aseprite` is the native format and the only editable master.** It holds everything: layers, groups, frames, cels, tags, the palette, slices, tilesets, user data and the colour mode. **`.ase` is the same format with an older extension.**

**Everything else Aseprite writes is a derived file.** §3: *"An accepted asset has one unambiguous editable master. Generated exports and Godot imports are derived files, not alternative masters."*

| Format | What it keeps | What it loses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`.aseprite` / `.ase`** | **everything** | nothing |
| **`.png`** | one image, with alpha. Indexed PNG keeps the palette | **layers, frames, tags, slices** |
| **`.gif`** | frames and timing, 256 colours, one-bit alpha | layers, tags, true alpha |
| **`.webp`** | frames, better compression | layers, tags |
| **`.jpg`** | nothing you want. **Lossy — it invents colours at every edge** | **never use it for pixel art** |
| **`.tga`, `.bmp`, `.pcx`, `.qoi`** | single images | the rest |
| **`.css`, `.svg`** | novelty exports | |
| **`.json`** | **the sprite sheet's metadata** — frames, tags, layers, slices | it is written beside a sheet and is never a master |

---

**Saving a sequence.** Give a filename with a number in it and Aseprite writes one file per frame:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`frame01.png`** | saving a 24-frame sprite as this writes `frame01.png` through `frame24.png` |
| **Why that matters here** | **Timon's references arrived exactly this way** — `media/reference/Animation/README.md` records 192 source frames named `body-part-reference_idle_<dir>_00..23.png` |
| **And why it is not the pipeline** | **the project's export route is the sprite sheet, through Wizard.** A frame sequence is for handing art to someone, not for the game |

---

**The one-master rule, which is the real content of this lesson.**

> **`media/README.md`:** *"Exactly one authoritative editable `.aseprite` master per asset, action **and direction**, and it lives here."*
>
> *"Never keep more than one editable master for the same asset, action and direction, and never keep a duplicate elsewhere… If you find two editable masters for the same asset and family, that is a defect to resolve, not a convenience."*

**Where things live:**

| Location | What belongs there |
| --- | --- |
| **`media/sprites/<category>/<family>/<asset-key>/`** | **the editable masters.** Categories: `heroes`, `enemies`, `npcs`, `beacon`, `props`, `vfx`, `environment` |
| **`media/sprites/_exports/`** | **generated sheets.** *"Never edited by hand"* |
| **`media/ui/{hud,menu,map,fonts}/`** | **accepted UI PNGs by role** |
| **`media/reference/`** | **reference material only.** *"Presence there does not imply approval. Never place an editable production master there"* |
| **`media/work/`** | **in-progress work, gitignored** |
| **`media/placeholder/`** | explicit placeholders |

**And the rule about superseded files**, §3: *"Rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived."* **No `old/`, no `v2` beside `v1`, no `_backup`.** Version control holds the history; the working tree holds one answer.

---

**Two safety notes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Aseprite keeps session backups** | in `~/.config/aseprite/sessions/`, and offers recovery after a crash. **It is not version control** |
| **Save early as `.aseprite`** | because an unsaved sprite's recovery data is less useful than a saved file. And **the repository is the backup** |

**Practice.** Save a multi-frame sprite as `.aseprite`, then as a numbered PNG sequence, then as a GIF, and open all three to see what each kept. Then look at `media/sprites/` in the Shepherds repository and name the path a master of Eli's south-facing idle would occupy. Then check `~/.config/aseprite/sessions/` to see what is in it.
Export, and the sprite sheet:
The two export commands, the sheet layout options, and which combination this project's import route expects.

**There are two different commands and they do different things:**

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **File › Export** | **writes the current sprite as an image**, optionally scaled, one file or a frame sequence |
| **File › Export Sprite Sheet** | **writes all the frames into one image**, with an optional data file describing where each frame is |

**The second is the one that matters**, because a sprite sheet plus its data is what a game engine consumes.

---

**The Export Sprite Sheet dialog:**

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Sheet type** | **Horizontal strip, Vertical strip, By rows, By columns, Packed** |
| **Columns / rows** | for the rows and columns layouts |
| **Constraints** | fix a width or height and let the other dimension follow |
| **Padding** | **spacing between frames, and a border around the sheet** |
| **Trim** | **trims each frame to its content.** See the warning below |
| **Merge duplicates** | one cell for identical frames |
| **Split layers** | one sheet section per layer |
| **Split tags** | one section per tag |
| **Output file** | the image |
| **JSON data** | **the metadata** — frame rectangles, durations, tags, layers and slices |
| **Meta: tags / layers / slices** | which of those to include in the JSON |

---

**The two traps.**

**1 — Trim.** It is on by default in some paths and it will destroy the pivot:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | crops each frame to its own non-transparent bounding box, and records the offset in the JSON |
| **Why it is fatal here** | **the pivot is (56, 96) relative to a 112 × 112 frame.** Trimmed frames have different sizes and different offsets, so unless every consumer reads the offsets correctly, **every frame sits in a different place** |
| **The contract's own version of the warning** | §4: *"Never normalize each frame's bounding-box height independently; doing so makes prone bodies grow"* |
| **The rule** | **trim off. Every frame is 112 × 112** |

**2 — Scaling on export.** The Export dialog has a scale factor. **Export at 1×.** The game does the scaling, and §10.1 bans *"resized or filtered source art"*. A 3× export is for a contact sheet to look at, and it is not an asset.

---

**And now the point: for this project, you mostly do not use this dialog at all.**

> **§3:** *"Accepted `.aseprite` masters import through Aseprite Wizard; no competing sprite export pipeline is established."*
>
> **`media/README.md`:** *"`_exports/` holds generated sheets. **Aseprite Wizard is the Godot import route** — do not establish a competing export pipeline, and do not hand-edit anything under `_exports/`."*

**Aseprite Wizard runs the export for you.** It invokes the Aseprite executable on the command line, writes the sheet and its JSON into the project, and builds a `SpriteFrames` resource from the result — which is why Godot's editor settings need the Aseprite path (`aseprite/general/command_path`), and why `CLAUDE.md` records that **without it every import silently fails with `valid=false`**.

**So what the dialog is still for:**

| Use | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A contact sheet to look at** | all 24 frames of all 8 directions in one image, at 2× or 4×, for review. **The references in the repository are exactly this** |
| **Handing art to someone** | Timon, or a tool |
| **Understanding what Wizard is doing** | **run the export by hand once, look at the sheet and the JSON, and the import stops being magic** |
| **UI art** | **which is not sprite work.** A HUD PNG is a plain File › Export |

**Practice.** Export a 24-frame sprite as a packed sheet with JSON, trim off and scale 1×, and read the JSON — find a frame's rectangle and its duration. Then export the same sprite as a 4× contact sheet by rows, with padding, and look at it. Then find a `.json` in `media/sprites/_exports/` or in the reference tree and compare its structure with yours.
The command line:
Aseprite without a window: the options worth knowing, and why the pipeline depends on them.

**`aseprite` is a command-line program with a window attached.** Everything the interface does, `--batch` can do without one — which is how Aseprite Wizard works, how a validator would work, and how a hundred files get changed at once.

**The executable on this machine:** `~/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite`.

---

**The options, grouped:**

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`-b`, `--batch`** | **do not start the interface.** The flag that makes everything else useful |
| **`-p`, `--preview`** | **print what would be done without doing it.** Use it first, every time |
| **`--shell`** | an interactive Lua console |
| **`--save-as <file>`** | save the last-given sprite as something else |
| **`--sheet <file>`** | **write a sprite sheet** |
| **`--data <file>`** | **write the sheet's JSON** |
| **`--sheet-type <type>`** | horizontal, vertical, rows, columns, packed |
| **`--sheet-pack`** | the packed layout |
| **`--split-layers`** | one output per layer |
| **`--split-tags`** | one output per tag |
| **`--split-slices`** | **one output per slice** — the interface-art case from lesson 16 |
| **`--filename-format <fmt>`** | the naming pattern for split outputs, with `{tag}`, `{layer}`, `{frame}`, `{slice}` and more |
| **`--frame-range from,to`** | a subset of frames |
| **`--palette <file>`** | **replace the palette** |
| **`--color-mode <mode>`** | **rgb, indexed or gray** |
| **`--dithering-algorithm <alg>`** | **none, ordered or old** — for the RGB-to-indexed conversion |
| **`--dithering-matrix <id>`** | bayer2x2, bayer4x4, bayer8x8, or a PNG |
| **`--scale <n>`** | resize. **Integer only, for previews** |
| **`--list-layers`, `--list-tags`, `--list-slices`** | **print the sprite's structure.** The inspection commands |
| **`--all-layers`** | include hidden layers |
| **`--script <file>`** | **run a Lua script** |
| **`--script-param k=v`** | pass it a parameter |

---

**Four commands worth having.**

**Inspect a master without opening it:**

```
aseprite -b --list-layers --list-tags --list-slices eli_idle_s.aseprite
```

**Check that every master in a tree has exactly one tag** — the contract's rule, as a shell loop:

```
for f in media/sprites/**/*.aseprite; do
  echo -n "$f: "; aseprite -b --list-tags "$f" | wc -l
done
```

**Convert an RGB import to the project palette with no dithering:**

```
aseprite -b in.png --color-mode indexed   --palette media/reference/Palette/shepherds-master-v0-1.gpl   --dithering-algorithm none --save-as out.aseprite
```

**Write a sheet and its data the way Wizard would:**

```
aseprite -b eli_idle_s.aseprite --sheet-type packed   --sheet out.png --data out.json
```

---

**Why this lesson is in stage 1 rather than stage 12.** Three reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — It demystifies the import** | **Wizard is a wrapper around these commands.** Run them by hand once and the addon stops being a black box, which matters when an import fails |
| **2 — It is the only way to inspect at scale** | **a project will have hundreds of masters**, and the one-tag rule, the canvas size and the palette have to be checkable without opening each one |
| **3 — It is the foundation of validation** | `colour-palette.md` asks for *"a palette validator"*. **`--list-layers` plus a Lua script is that validator**, and lesson 22 and stage 12 build it |

**And a caution:** `--batch` with `--save-as` pointed at the input **overwrites a master**. **Use `--preview` first, always, and never write to a path under `media/sprites/` from a shell loop you have not tested.**

**Practice.** Run `aseprite --help` and read all of it once. Then run `--list-layers --list-tags` on one of the reference `.aseprite` files in `media/reference/Animation/body-part-reference/converted/s/` and see what it reports. Then write the one-tag check loop above and run it over the reference tree. Then run an export with `--preview` and look at what it says it would do.
Preferences worth changing:
The defaults that are wrong for this work, and where to change them.

**Edit › Preferences**, and the settings live in `~/.config/aseprite/aseprite.ini` — which on this machine already has about forty sections, so some of this has been set before.

---

**General**

| Setting | Set it to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Screen scaling / UI scaling** | whatever makes the interface readable | independent of the sprite's zoom |
| **Show full path in the tab** | **on** | **you will have eight files called `*_idle_*` open.** The tab needs to say which |
| **Expand menu bar items on mouse hover** | taste | |

**Editor**

| Setting | Set it to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Zoom with scroll wheel** | **on** | the fastest navigation |
| **Zoom from the centre / cursor** | **cursor** | |
| **Auto-select layer** | **off** | **on, clicking the canvas changes the active layer**, which with four layers in register will move the wrong thing |
| **Right-click behaviour** | **"Paint with background colour" or "Erase"** — pick one and keep it | the right button is a second ink, and it should be predictable |
| **Scale from the centre** | off | |
| **Default interpolation** | **nearest neighbour** | **the one setting that cannot be wrong.** Anything else invents colours |

**Grid**

| Setting | Set it to |
| --- | --- |
| **Grid size** | **16 × 16** for terrain; it does not matter for characters |
| **Snap to grid** | **off by default** — on only while doing tiles |
| **Pixel grid** | **visible**, with a colour that is not in the palette |

**Timeline**

| Setting | Set it to | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Thumbnails** | **on**, and reasonably large | **the shape of a 24-frame animation at a glance** |
| **Zoom** | wide enough for 24 columns | |
| **Position** | bottom, tall | |

**Theme and background**

| Setting | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| **The canvas background checkerboard** | **its colours are a judgement hazard.** A mid-grey checker makes dark pixels look lighter than they are. **Set it to a flat colour, and change that colour while working** — a sprite that reads against both a light and a dark background is one that will read in the game |
| **Theme** | **dark.** A light interface surrounding an 80-pixel sprite biases every value decision you make |

**Experimental**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Leave it alone** | except to know that **the native file dialog** toggle lives there, and the GPU acceleration options, which are worth trying if the canvas feels slow |

---

**The one that is not a preference but belongs here: Godot's Aseprite path.**

`CLAUDE.md` records it exactly:

> *"Aseprite Wizard's importer needs the Aseprite executable path in Godot's **editor** settings (`aseprite/general/command_path`). On this rig it is the Steam install, `$HOME/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite`, with the home folder written out in full because Godot does not expand `~`. Without a working path every `.aseprite` import silently fails with `valid=false`. This is a machine-local editor setting — never commit it."*

**Three things in that paragraph:** the path must be absolute, the failure is **silent**, and the setting is **per-machine and must not be committed.**

**Practice.** Go through Preferences and set every row in the tables above. Turn auto-select layer off and confirm that clicking the canvas no longer changes the active layer. Set the canvas background to a flat mid-grey, then to near-black, and look at the same sprite against both. Then open Godot's Editor Settings and confirm `aseprite/general/command_path` is the absolute Steam path.

Extensions and scripting:
The two ways to extend Aseprite, what is installed here, and the validator this project has asked for and does not have.

**Two mechanisms, and they are different:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Extensions** | **packaged add-ons** — themes, palettes, and sets of scripts — installed as `.aseprite-extension` files from **Edit › Preferences › Extensions** |
| **Scripts** | **single Lua files**, run from **File › Scripts**, living in `~/.config/aseprite/scripts/` |

**What is installed on this machine:**

> **As of 14 October 2026: nothing.** `~/.config/aseprite/extensions/` does not exist, and `CLAUDE.md` records the same check on 2026-09-16. There is no `scripts/` folder yet either.

**Which includes the Aseprite MCP Pro extension.** `CLAUDE.md`: the MCP server is in `tools/aseprite-mcp-pro/server/` and registered in `.mcp.json`, and *"With the extension not installed it has nothing to connect to; do not assume the connection exists."* **It is an inspection tool for an assistant and it is not part of this curriculum** — **Master Roachi owns all Aseprite authoring**, and nothing here routes work through it.

---

**The Lua API**, free and documented at `aseprite.org/api`, available since 1.2.10.

**The objects worth knowing:**

| Object | What it gives you |
| --- | --- |
| **`app.sprite`** | the active sprite — its `width`, `height`, `colorMode`, `layers`, `frames`, `tags`, `slices`, `palettes` |
| **`app.sprites`** | every open sprite |
| **`app.image`, `app.cel`, `app.layer`, `app.frame`** | the active ones |
| **`Sprite(filename)`** | **open a file** |
| **`Image`** | pixel access, with `getPixel` and `putPixel` and an iterator |
| **`Palette`** | entries by index |
| **`Dialog`** | **a window with fields and buttons** — scripts can have an interface |
| **`app.command.*`** | **run any menu command**, which is how a script does something there is no API for |
| **`app.alert`, `app.transaction`** | messages, and grouping edits into one undo step |

---

**The validator this project has asked for.** `colour-palette.md`:

> *"Asset briefs and validators should use the full form (for example, `TERR-001`) and preserve the exact hexadecimal value listed here."*

**And the specification is already written for you**, in the same document's two exception notes:

| It must | Because |
| --- | --- |
| **Report every colour in a master that is not one of the 132** | the palette is the authority |
