| **Accept four specific extras** | *"Master Roachi added four colours outside the numbered palette while cleaning up `ordinary-corpse-puppet-a_death_e_v002`… the extra colors are fine, i added them so they stay."* They are **`#281E18`, `#241B16`, `#1F1F11` and `#FFFFFF`**, they have no `TERR-` IDs, they are not in the `.gpl`, and **"a palette validator run over his cleaned masters should accept them, not flag them"** |
| **Count the opaque base colours** | so §10.1's bands — 12–18, 8–26, 4–10, 32–40 — can be checked |
| **Check the canvas is 112 × 112 and the pivot guide is where it should be** | §4 |
| **Check there is exactly one tag, lower-case snake-case** | §3.1 |
| **Check the frame durations are all 84 ms** | the next stages' arithmetic |

**That is six checks, all of them mechanical, all of them available from `app.sprite` and the command line.** Stage 12 writes it. **It is named here so you know, from the first stage, that the tool can check its own work.**

---

**Three other things scripts are good for:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Frame-to-frame drift** | **compare each frame's content bounding box against the previous** and report jumps — which catches a limb that moved when it should have held |
| **Batch palette conformance** | run the validator over every master in the tree, as the command-line loop from lesson 19 |
| **Contact sheets** | assemble eight directions × 24 frames into one reviewable image, which is what the conversion tooling in `media/reference/.../conversion/` already does in Python |

**Practice.** Create `~/.config/aseprite/scripts/` and write a script that prints the active sprite's width, height, colour mode and tag count with `app.alert`. Run it from File › Scripts. Then extend it to list every colour used in the active cel, and run it on one of the reference masters. Then read the `app.sprite` page of the API and note which of the six validator checks you could already write.
What the medium actually is:
The stage's thesis: pixel art is not drawing at a small size, and the difference is that every pixel is a decision you made.

**Start with the distinction, because everything in this stage follows from it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Drawing at high resolution** | **a stroke is a gesture.** The hand moves, the tool averages thousands of samples into an edge, and the result is judged as a whole. **An individual pixel is meaningless** |
| **Pixel art** | **a stroke is a sequence of explicit decisions.** At 1 px with no anti-aliasing, **you placed every pixel, and each one is visible** |

**The arithmetic of why that matters here.** A Shepherds adult is about **80 px sole-to-crown** in a **112 × 112** frame, drawn at **3 × 3 screen pixels each**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One art pixel** | **1.25% of the character's height** |
| **On screen** | **a 3 × 3 block** |
| **A one-pixel error on an arm** | **a 3-pixel-wide visible defect, moving, twelve times a second** |
| **The whole figure** | roughly **80 × 40 pixels of usable area** — call it **3,200 pixels**, of which maybe half are body |

**So you have about 1,500 decisions to make a person recognisable.** That is the budget, and the rest of this stage is about spending it.

---

**The four properties of the medium**, each of which has a lesson of its own:

| Property | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **The unit is the cluster, not the pixel** | **a single isolated pixel reads as dirt.** Pixels do their work in groups, and a clean group is the medium's smallest meaningful mark |
| **A line is a run pattern** | a diagonal is not a line but **a sequence of horizontal runs**, and whether it looks like a line depends entirely on whether those runs are consistent |
| **Value does the work and there is very little of it** | **three or four values per material** (§10.1), so a form is described by **where the boundary between two values falls**, not by a gradient across it |
| **Everything is judged at 1×** | **§10.1's first clause**, and the hardest discipline in the subject |

---

**What this stage does not contain.** No colour — stages 4 and 5. No anatomy — stage 9. No animation — stage 10. **This stage is the alphabet**: lines, curves, circles, clusters, and the four failure modes that make a sprite look amateur regardless of how good the drawing underneath is.

**The four failure modes**, named now and each given a lesson:

| | What it looks like | §10.1's words |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Jaggies** | a diagonal with an uneven stair pattern — it reads as a wobble | — |
| **Banding** | two value boundaries running parallel and touching — it reads as a stripe instead of a form | — |
| **Noise** | isolated single pixels scattered in a surface | *"isolated noise"* |
| **Indiscriminate dithering** | a checkerboard used instead of a decision | *"indiscriminate dithering"* |

**Two of the four are named in the contract as things to avoid.** The other two are not, because they are craft failures rather than specification failures — **the contract cannot describe a wobbly line, and a reviewer can see one instantly.**

**Practice.** Open one of the reference masters in `media/reference/Animation/body-part-reference/converted/s/` and zoom to 800%. Count the pixels in the figure's forearm. Then zoom to 100% and look at it again. Then draw a 16 × 16 square and put one stray pixel of a different colour in the middle of it, view it at 100%, and then at 300% — which is what the game will show.
The cluster:
The medium's actual unit: why isolated pixels read as dirt, and what makes a group of pixels deliberate.

**A cluster is a connected group of pixels of the same colour.** It is the smallest mark that reads as a mark rather than as an artefact, and **§10.1's first requirement is about clusters**:

> *"Draw at native 1× resolution with **deliberate clusters** rather than resized or filtered source art."*

---

**Why a single pixel reads as dirt.** Three reasons, and the third is the decisive one here:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Perception** | the eye reads **groups** as shapes and **isolated points** as texture or error. A single pixel of highlight on a shoulder does not say "highlight"; it says "there is a speck on my screen" |
| **2 — It is ambiguous at distance** | at native scale a lone pixel is **below the threshold at which a shape can be identified**, so it contributes nothing but noise |
| **3 — Scale multiplies it** | **at 3 × 3 the lone pixel becomes a 3-pixel block**, which is now large enough to see and still too small to mean anything. **The worst of both** |

**And the exception, which matters:** **an isolated pixel is legitimate when it is doing a job that only a point can do** — an eye at 80 px tall, a rivet, a distant star, the glint on a blade's edge. **The test is whether you could name what it is.** If you can, it is a detail. If you cannot, it is noise.

---

**What makes a cluster deliberate.** Four properties:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Size** | **big enough to read.** At this scale, **two or three pixels is the practical minimum for a shape** that is not a point |
| **Shape** | **a cluster has a silhouette of its own.** A 3 × 2 block reads as a rectangle; three pixels in an L read as a corner; three in a diagonal read as an edge. **Choose which** |
| **Edge** | **the boundary between this cluster and its neighbour is the drawing.** A form is described by where that boundary runs |
| **Intent** | **you can say what it is for.** "The shadow under the jaw", "the lit top of the shoulder" — if the answer is "it looked a bit empty", it is noise |

---

**The three cluster failures**, which between them account for most of what makes amateur pixel art look amateur:

| Failure | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Orphans** | **single pixels not attached to a cluster**, usually left behind by a freehand stroke or an eraser |
| **Fringing** | **a ragged one-pixel border** along a cluster's edge where the stroke wobbled — a cluster whose edge was not decided |
| **Confetti** | **many small clusters of many values in a small area.** Each one may be deliberate and the result is still noise, because **nothing is large enough to read** |

**Confetti is the subtle one and it is the most common failure in a first character sprite.** It comes from trying to describe a form the way a painter would — many small value changes following the surface — in a medium that has room for four values and 1,500 pixels. **The answer is fewer, larger clusters**, which is the last lesson of this stage.

---

**The cluster and the contract.** Two further clauses are cluster rules in disguise:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§10.1: *"Preserve useful negative gaps between body, limbs and equipment"*** | **a gap is a cluster of background.** A one-pixel transparent gap between an arm and a torso is what makes the arm read as separate, and it is destroyed by exactly the fringing above |
| **§10.1: *"Avoid … high-resolution texture imitation"*** | **a texture at this scale must be made of clusters big enough to see.** Wood grain as single pixels is noise; wood grain as 3-pixel dashes is wood |

**Practice.** Draw a 32 × 32 shape in two values, deliberately leaving orphan pixels and a ragged edge. Then clean it: delete every pixel you cannot name, and make every edge a decision. Compare at 100%. Then draw the same shape as confetti — eight small clusters of four values — and then redraw it as three clusters, and look at both at 100%.
Lines: slope and the jaggy:
A diagonal is a sequence of horizontal runs, and whether it reads as a line depends entirely on whether those runs are consistent.

**There are no diagonal lines in a pixel grid.** There are **steps**, and a "line" is a pattern of them. A 45° line is runs of 1; a shallower line is runs of 2, or 3, or 4.

**The canonical clean slopes**, written as the run length:

| Slope | Run pattern | What it looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1 : 1** | 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 … | **45°** |
| **2 : 1** | 2, 2, 2, 2 … | about 26.6° |
| **3 : 1** | 3, 3, 3, 3 … | about 18.4° |
| **4 : 1** | 4, 4, 4, 4 … | about 14° |
| **1 : 2** | steps of 2 vertically | about 63.4° |
| **1 : 3**, **1 : 4** | steeper still | |

**Those are the slopes a pixel grid draws cleanly**, and they are the only ones. **Anything between them has to be approximated, and the approximation is where jaggies come from.**

---

**What a jaggy is.** A line whose run lengths are **inconsistent in a way the eye reads as a wobble**:

| Run pattern | Reads as |
| --- | --- |
| **2, 2, 2, 2, 2** | **a clean line** |
| **3, 3, 3, 3, 3** | **a clean line** |
| **2, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3** | **a clean line** — an alternating pattern is a pattern |
| **2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 3** | **acceptable** — a regular period of three |
| **2, 3, 2, 2, 3, 3, 2** | **a jaggy.** No pattern, so the eye sees bumps |
| **1, 4, 2, 3, 1** | **a mess** |

**The rule, stated usefully: a pixel line is clean when its run lengths form a pattern you could predict.** That is why 2,3,2,3 works and 2,2,3,2,2,3,3 does not — **the first is predictable and the second is nearly predictable, which is worse than random.**

---

**The L-corner, which is a different defect.** Where a freehand stroke turns, it often leaves **two pixels at the corner** — one horizontal neighbour and one vertical — making a 2 × 2-ish lump:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why it happens** | the input samples both cells as the stroke passes the corner |
| **What it looks like** | **a thickening at every turn**, so a line appears to have beads on it |
| **The fix in the tool** | **pixel-perfect mode**, from stage 1 — it removes the redundant pixel as you draw |
| **What pixel-perfect does not fix** | **the run pattern.** It gives you a single-pixel line with jaggies rather than a doubled line with jaggies |

**So the tool solves half the problem and the hand solves the other half.** A clean line requires choosing the slope, not just drawing carefully.

---

**How to draw a clean line, in practice:**

| Method | When |
| --- | --- |
| **The Line tool (`L`)** | **a long straight edge.** Aseprite computes a consistent run pattern |
| **`Shift`-click with the pencil** | **the same, faster** — draws from the last point |
| **Freehand with pixel-perfect on** | **short strokes and organic edges**, then corrected |
| **Count it** | **for a critical edge**, decide the run length and place the runs deliberately. A 16-pixel-long 2:1 edge is eight runs of two, and you can count them |

**And the practical judgement: most edges in a character are short.** A forearm's edge is six pixels long. **At that length there is no slope and no pattern — there are six pixels, and you place them.** The slope theory matters for props, architecture and long limbs; for a hand, it is just pixels.

**Practice.** Draw a 1:1, 2:1, 3:1 and 4:1 line, each 24 pixels long, with the Line tool, and count the runs to confirm the pattern. Then draw the same four freehand with pixel-perfect on and compare. Then draw a deliberately jaggy line — 2,3,2,2,3,3 — and look at it at 100%; then fix it to 2,3,2,3,2,3 and look again.
Curves:
A curve is a run pattern that changes, and it reads as a curve only when it changes monotonically.

**If a straight line is a constant run length, a curve is a changing one.** The whole of curve drawing in pixel art is in that sentence.

**A quarter-circle arc, drawn as runs**, reading from the flat end to the steep end:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Runs** | **5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 1** |
| **What that is** | the arc starts nearly horizontal (long runs) and ends nearly vertical (short runs) |
| **Why it reads** | **the run lengths decrease, and they never go back up** |

---

**The rule: run lengths must change monotonically.** Increasing or decreasing, never both:

| Run pattern | Reads as |
| --- | --- |
| **5, 4, 3, 2, 1** | **a clean curve** |
| **5, 4, 4, 3, 2, 1** | **clean** — a repeat is fine |
| **5, 5, 4, 3, 3, 2, 1** | **clean**, a slower curve |
| **5, 3, 4, 2, 1** | **a dent.** The 3 then 4 is a reversal, and the eye sees the surface go in and out |
| **5, 4, 3, 4, 3, 2** | **a lump** — the same thing the other way |
| **1, 3, 2, 4** | **not a curve at all** |

**A reversal in the run pattern is a dent in the form**, and it is the most common reason a hand-drawn pixel curve looks wrong when nothing obvious is wrong with it. **The fix is always to make the sequence monotonic**, even if that means a slightly different curve from the one you intended.

---

**The S-curve**, which is two monotonic sequences meeting:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The shape** | runs **decreasing**, reaching a minimum, then **increasing** |
| **For example** | 4, 3, 2, 1, 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| **The inflection** | **where the sequence turns.** That point is the curve's inflection and the eye finds it immediately, so **put it where you mean the form to change direction** |
| **The failure** | an inflection you did not intend, which is a reversal in the middle of what should have been one arc |

**Most organic edges are S-curves.** A shoulder into an upper arm, a calf into an ankle, the back of a head into a neck. **Drawing them as two monotonic runs with a chosen inflection is the difference between a limb and a sausage.**

---

**Three practical techniques:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Draw the extremes first** | **place the curve's two endpoints and its steepest and flattest pixels**, then fill between them. The run lengths then have targets to hit |
| **Use the curve tool as a draft** | **`Shift+L`** gives a four-point curve. Aseprite's answer is usually monotonic and usually too smooth; **use it as a guide and redraw by hand** |
| **Read it as runs, not as a shape** | **count the runs along the edge.** This is the single most useful habit for fixing a curve that looks wrong: you stop seeing a wobbly arm and start seeing `4, 3, 4, 2`, and then the fix is obvious |

---

**And a note on scale, again.** At 80 px a character's limb edges are **four to eight pixels long**. A monotonic sequence of four runs is `3, 2, 2, 1`, and there is not much curve theory left in it. **Where this lesson earns its place is in props, architecture, large creatures and anything with a long smooth edge** — a barrel, a cart wheel, a round hay bale at 53–65 px, a bow, the Beacon's sphere.

**Practice.** Draw a quarter-circle arc 12 pixels across, counting the runs, and make them monotonic. Then deliberately introduce a reversal and look at the dent at 100%. Then draw an S-curve with its inflection a third of the way along, and then again with it in the middle, and compare what each reads as. Then draw the same arc with the curve tool and compare its run pattern with yours.
Circles and ellipses:
Small circles are memorised shapes, large ones are an algorithm, and the tool's answer is not always the right one.

**A circle in a pixel grid is a compromise**, and at small diameters there are only a handful of reasonable compromises — so **the small ones are worth knowing by heart.**

**The canonical small circles**, as runs per quadrant row:

| Diameter | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | a 2 × 2 square. There is no circle |
| **3** | a plus sign, or a 3 × 3 square with the corners removed — **the corners removed is the circle** |
| **4** | **2, 4, 4, 2** — rows of two, four, four, two |
| **5** | **3, 5, 5, 5, 3** |
| **6** | **4, 6, 6, 6, 6, 4** |
| **7** | **3, 5, 7, 7, 7, 5, 3** |
| **8** | **4, 6, 8, 8, 8, 8, 6, 4** |
| **9** | **5, 7, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 7, 5** |

**Read the run sequences and notice they are monotonic to the middle and then mirrored** — which is the curve rule from the last lesson, applied twice. **A circle that looks wrong almost always has a reversal in it.**

**And notice the odd diameters are better.** 5, 7 and 9 have a single middle row and a clean centre; 4, 6 and 8 have two middle rows and no centre pixel. **For anything that needs an obvious centre — a wheel hub, an eye, the Beacon — use an odd diameter.**

---

**Large circles are an algorithm.** The standard one is **midpoint circle drawing** (often called Bresenham's), and Aseprite's ellipse tool implements it. For a radius above about 10 the algorithm's answer is good, and the sensible approach is:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **draw it with the Ellipse tool** (`Shift+U`) |
| **2** | **check the runs** along one quadrant for monotonicity |
| **3** | **fix the two or three pixels that bother you**, usually at the 45° points where the algorithm's rounding shows |

---

**Ellipses, which is what you actually need.** A circle seen in this projection is an ellipse, and §9.1 fixes the projection:

> *"The projection is rectilinear three-quarter top-down, not diamond isometric. Vertical edges stay vertical; floors do not converge toward a vanishing point."*

**So a circle lying flat on the ground — a barrel's top, a well's mouth, a round hay bale seen from above — is a horizontally wider ellipse**, and how much wider is a consequence of the projection's angle. **That is stage 3's subject.** Here, the mechanics:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The tool** | **Ellipse (`Shift+U`)**, with the aspect set by the drag |
| **Holding `Shift` while dragging** | constrains to a circle |
| **What to watch** | **the four extremes.** An ellipse's top, bottom, left and right should each be a **flat run**, and the run should be the same length top and bottom. Asymmetry there is immediately visible |
| **Odd versus even** | **same rule.** An odd width and an odd height give you a centre pixel |

---

**One thing the tool cannot do: a circle with a chosen outline.** The ellipse tool draws its outline in one colour, and §10.1 requires *"a dark coloured one-pixel outline"* that varies with what it surrounds. **So the tool gives you the shape and the outline is a separate pass.** For a round object with a light from the upper-left, the outline is darkest at the lower-right and may be absent at the top.

**Practice.** Draw circles of diameter 3, 5, 7 and 9 by hand, from the run sequences above, and check them against the Ellipse tool's version. Then draw a radius-16 circle with the tool and find the pixels at the 45° points you would change. Then draw a flat ellipse twice as wide as it is tall and check that its top and bottom runs match.
Banding:
Two value boundaries running parallel and touching, which reads as a stripe instead of a form — the most common shading failure and the hardest to see in your own work.

**Banding is when two edges of equal slope run adjacent to each other for their whole length.** The result is that the eye reads **a band of colour** rather than **a surface changing value**, and the form flattens.

**The classic case, in words.** Shading a cylinder, you place a line of Shadow and then a line of Mid immediately beside it, both running at the same slope for ten pixels:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What you intended** | a surface turning away from the light |
| **What it reads as** | **two stripes painted on a flat surface** |
| **Why** | **the two boundaries are parallel and in contact**, so they reinforce each other as lines instead of describing a transition |

---

**The two kinds, because they have different fixes:**

| Kind | What it is | The fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Line banding** | **two single-pixel-wide runs of different values side by side**, same slope | **widen one of them.** A value needs more than one pixel of width to read as an area rather than a line |
| **Edge banding** | **two value boundaries that stay exactly parallel** across a form | **vary the distance between them.** The gap should open and close as the surface turns |

**And the general principle under both: a value boundary should not be predictable from its neighbour.** If knowing where one boundary runs tells you where the next one runs, they are banding.

---

**Why it is so hard to see in your own work.** Three reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It looks tidy** | **banding is the result of being careful.** Neat parallel shading looks controlled while you are drawing it, and the defect only appears when you stop looking at the pixels and look at the form |
| **It is invisible at high zoom** | at 800% you see two clean lines doing their jobs. **At 100% you see a stripe** |
| **It is a global defect** | each individual pixel is right. **The error is in the relationship between two correct decisions**, which is not where anyone looks for errors |

**The detection methods, in order of usefulness:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Look at it at 100%, small** | **the preview window from stage 1.** Banding announces itself immediately at native scale |
| **2 — Squint, or blur mentally** | banding survives squinting as a stripe; a real value transition dissolves into a form |
| **3 — Flip it horizontally** | **`Shift+H`.** A familiar image stops being familiar, and defects you have stopped seeing become visible. Flip back afterwards |
| **4 — Greyscale it** | the toggle from stage 1. Banding is a value relationship, so removing hue makes it louder |

---

**The relationship to the contract.** §10.1 does not use the word, and three of its clauses are anti-banding rules:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***"approximately three or four purposeful values per major material"*** | **four values cannot band much.** Banding gets worse with more values, because more boundaries means more chances for two to run parallel |
| ***"Avoid smooth gradients"*** | **a gradient is banding taken to its limit** — every value boundary parallel to every other |
| ***"Static shading stays restrained so Godot's local lights can read coherently"*** | **less shading, fewer boundaries, less banding.** The contract's reason is the lighting, and the side effect is the craft |

**That last point is worth holding. The contract's restraint requirement — put in for a technical reason about `Light2D` — happens to prevent the most common shading error in the medium.**

**Practice.** Draw a 24-pixel-tall cylinder in four values with deliberately parallel boundaries, look at it at 100%, and name what is wrong. Then redraw it varying the distance between the boundaries along the length. Then take any shaded sprite you have made, flip it horizontally and greyscale it, and look for stripes.
Noise against texture:
Both are many small marks in a surface. One reads as a material and the other as dirt, and the difference is pattern.

**§10.1 bans one and requires the other:**

> *"Avoid smooth gradients, indiscriminate dithering, **isolated noise** and high-resolution texture imitation."*

**And §2 requires that places feel *"materially specific"*.** So a stone wall must read as stone, and it must not read as a stone wall with dust on the lens.

---

**The distinction:**

| | Texture | Noise |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The marks** | **clusters of two or more pixels** | **isolated single pixels** |
| **Their arrangement** | **a pattern** — regular, or irregular with a visible logic | **random** |
| **Their values** | **drawn from the material's ramp**, usually two adjacent steps | often several values, or an off-ramp one |
| **Their density** | **varies with the form** — more in shadow, less in light, following the surface | uniform, because it was sprayed or scattered |
| **What it reads as** | **the material** | **an artefact** |
| **The test** | **could you say what the marks are?** "Mortar lines", "grain", "wool tufts" | "it looked flat so I added some pixels" |

---

**How to make texture at this scale.** The constraint is brutal: **a 16 × 16 stone tile has 256 pixels and four values.** So:

| Technique | What it is | Good for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Dashes** | **two- and three-pixel runs** at a consistent angle, in the adjacent ramp step | **wood grain, thatch, fabric weave, long grass** |
| **Blocks** | **small rectangles with gaps** between them | **masonry, brick, cobbles, plank ends** |
| **Clumps** | **irregular three-to-five-pixel clusters** at varying density | **moss, foliage, wool, gravel, rust** |
| **Edge accents** | **marks only at a form's boundaries**, leaving the middle flat | **the most economical texture there is** — it implies a material from the silhouette alone |
| **A repeated motif** | **one small cluster, placed deliberately several times** | **scales, shingles, chain mail, planks** |

**And the economy rule: texture the edges and the shadow, and leave the lit middle alone.** Three reasons — the lit area is where the form reads and texture confuses it; the shadow hides the cost of detail; and **it halves the work.**

---

**The scale trap, which is specific to this project.** §10.1 bans *"high-resolution texture imitation"*, and here is what that means concretely:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The temptation** | you know what weathered wood looks like, and it has hundreds of grain lines. **So you draw grain lines one pixel apart** |
| **What happens** | **at 3 × 3 scale, one-pixel-apart grain becomes a 3-pixel-period stripe pattern** that shimmers when the sprite moves, and reads as a moiré rather than as wood |
| **And in motion it is worse** | a texture finer than the motion between frames **crawls** — the pattern appears to swim across the surface |
| **The rule** | **a texture mark must be at least two pixels, and the spacing between marks at least two.** Below that it is not texture, it is interference |

---

**Where noise is legitimate.** Rarely, and it is worth naming:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Deliberate decay** | a few isolated pixels of a darker value in a ruined wall, **placed one at a time**, reads as pitting. **Placed by the spray tool, it reads as noise** |
| **Dust, embers, rain** | **as VFX, on their own layer, animated.** A static speck is noise; a moving speck is a particle |
| **Never on a character** | §10.1: a hero must be identifiable in solid black and in greyscale. **Noise on a character is value information that means nothing** |

**Practice.** Draw the same 16 × 16 stone tile three times: once with single-pixel noise scattered through it, once with two-pixel blocks and gaps, and once with texture only at the edges and in the shadow. Compare all three at 100%, and then tile each with View › Tiled Mode. Then draw wood grain at one-pixel spacing and at three-pixel spacing and look at both at 300%.
Dithering, and where the contract bans i:
Alternating two colours to imply a third: the patterns, the three legitimate uses, and the clause that rules it out for most of this project.

**Dithering is placing two colours in an alternating pattern so that at distance they read as a mixture.** It is how a four-colour palette implied dozens of tones on hardware that had no more colours, and it is a real technique with real uses.

**The standard patterns**, by the proportion of the second colour:

| Pattern | Proportion | What it looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Checkerboard** | **50%** | the strongest and most visible |
| **Every other pixel on every other row** | **25%** | a sparse grid |
| **75%** | the inverse of 25% | |
| **Bayer 2×2, 4×4, 8×8** | **ordered matrices** giving graduated steps | what Aseprite's `--dithering-matrix` offers |
| **Diagonal lines** | 50% in stripes | reads as a direction, not a tone |
| **Irregular / hand-placed** | varying | **the only kind worth using on a character** |

**Aseprite's gradient tool and its indexed conversion both offer these**, and the command line exposes `none`, `ordered` and `old` with the Bayer matrices.

---

**The contract's clause, and it is narrow but decisive:**

> **§10.1:** *"Avoid smooth gradients, **indiscriminate** dithering, isolated noise and high-resolution texture imitation."*

**Read the adverb.** It does not say "no dithering". It says **indiscriminate** — which rules out dithering as a default behaviour and permits it as a decision. **And three facts about this project make even deliberate dithering rare:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The scale** | **at 3 × 3 screen pixels, a 50% checkerboard has a 6-pixel period.** That is large enough to see as a pattern rather than as a tone — so **it does not do the thing dithering is for** |
| **2 — Motion** | **a dither pattern on a moving sprite crawls**, exactly like the fine texture of the last lesson. The pattern is fixed to the sprite and the sprite moves, so the pattern appears to swim |
| **3 — The palette already has the tone** | **dithering exists to invent a colour you do not have. This palette has 132 entries in 33 four-step ramps.** If you need a value between Shadow and Mid, the honest answer is usually that you need a different ramp, not a mixture of two steps of this one |

**That third point is the strongest. Dithering is a workaround for a palette limitation, and this project does not have that limitation.**

---

**The three legitimate uses here:**

| Use | Why it works |
| --- | --- |
| **Large flat areas that must transition** | **a sky, a large wall, a water surface** — anywhere the area is big enough that the alternative is banding across dozens of pixels. **The area has to be large**: dithering over six pixels is noise, over sixty it is a gradient |
| **A material whose actual appearance is speckled** | **gravel, rough-cast plaster, rust, sandstone.** Here the dither is texture, not tone, and the last lesson's rules apply — **two-pixel marks, varying density** |
| **A deliberate transition between two ramps** | where a stone meets earth in a terrain tile, **a few rows of interleaving** reads as a boundary rather than a cut. **This is the one that terrain work actually needs** |

**And the three places it must not appear:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **On a character** | **§10.1's black-and-greyscale identity test.** A dithered surface has no single value, so it contributes an ambiguous grey and muddies the silhouette |
| **As the output of a conversion** | **an RGB image converted to indexed with dithering on produces exactly the "indiscriminate" case.** Stage 1's rule: `--dithering-algorithm none` |
| **From the gradient tool** | its dithered gradient is ordered and uniform, which is the definition of indiscriminate |

---

**The honest counter-argument**, because it exists. **Dithering is a style**, and some of the best pixel art in the medium is heavily dithered — it is a legible, historical, deliberate look. **§2 does not choose that look**: it asks for *"warm, earthy, weathered"* with *"silhouette, value separation, pose readability and ground contact"* taking priority over *"decorative detail"*. **That is a style decision, already made, and the dithering clause follows from it.**

**Practice.** Draw a 64 × 16 band dithered from one ramp step to the next with a 50% checkerboard, and look at it at 100% and at 300%. Then do the same over 8 pixels instead of 64 and see where it stops working. Then take a terrain boundary between two materials and interleave three rows of each, and compare it with a hard cut.
Anti-aliasing, and why it is off:
What anti-aliasing is, why the tool never does it, and the narrow case where you do it by hand.

**Anti-aliasing is placing intermediate-value pixels at an edge so that the step reads as a smoother transition.** Every high-resolution drawing tool does it automatically; Aseprite's pencil never does.

**Why not, in one sentence: it needs colours you do not have.** A step between Mid and the background requires something between them, and **in indexed mode on a 33-ramp palette there is nothing between them that belongs to this material.**

---

**The three reasons it is off for this project:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The palette** | an intermediate value is **a new colour**, and §10.1's counts are of *"opaque base colours"* — 12–18 for a hero. **Anti-aliasing an outline could double that** |
| **2 — The scale** | **at 3 × 3 an anti-aliased pixel is a 3 × 3 block of an in-between colour**, which does not read as a softer edge. It reads as **a fringe** |
| **3 — The lighting** | §10.1: *"Static shading stays restrained so Godot's local lights can read coherently."* **An anti-aliased edge has baked-in intermediate values that a coloured light will tint wrongly** |

**And a fourth, practical one:** **the transparent background.** An anti-aliased edge against transparency needs partial alpha, and partial alpha is barely available in indexed mode and is outside §10.1's colour counts. **A sprite with semi-transparent edge pixels composites differently against every background**, which is the opposite of readability.

---

**Where manual anti-aliasing is legitimate.** Three cases, all narrow:

| Case | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A long, nearly-flat curve on a large object** | a cart wheel, a barrel's rim, a round hay bale at 53–65 px. **At that length a single corner pixel of an intermediate ramp step can soften a visible step**, and the object is large enough that it reads as a curve rather than a fringe |
| **UI art** | **§3 puts UI outside the sprite rules entirely** — *"HUD and other UI artwork uses transparent PNG where practical and does not inherit sprite canvas, pivot or animation rules."* **UI art is RGB, at higher effective resolution, and may be anti-aliased**, and the accepted HUD family is hand-drawn PNG |
| **Dialogue portraits and illustrated scenes** | **§2 permits higher-resolution art** for these. Different medium, different rules |

**And how to do it when you do.** **Not with a tool.** Place a single pixel of the **adjacent ramp step** — one step, never two — at the corner of a step, on the inside of the curve. **One pixel per corner, and only at corners you can see are a problem at 100%.**

---

**The thing that replaces anti-aliasing here, and this is the lesson's real content: choosing the slope.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem anti-aliasing solves** | an edge whose steps are visible |
| **The pixel-art solution** | **make the steps consistent**, so the eye reads them as a line rather than as steps. **That is the lines lesson** |
| **And if the steps are still visible** | **the edge is at a slope the grid cannot draw cleanly.** Change the drawing, not the pixels — **move the endpoint by one pixel so the edge sits on a clean slope** |

**That substitution is the whole craft difference.** A high-resolution artist softens a bad edge; **a pixel artist moves it to a slope that is not bad.**

**Practice.** Draw a 20-pixel edge at a slope between 2:1 and 3:1 — so the runs come out as 2,3,2,2,3 — and look at it at 100%. Then fix it by moving the far endpoint one pixel so it becomes a clean 2:1 or a clean 2,3,2,3. Then try the other fix: anti-alias the three worst corners with one adjacent-ramp pixel each, and compare which looks better and which costs more colours.
Selective outlining:
The contract's outline clause as a craft technique: one pixel, dark, coloured, varying — and the three things it bans.

**§10.1's outline clause, in full:**

> *"Use a dark coloured one-pixel outline. Avoid universal pure black, automatic double outlines and outlines that merge equipment into the torso."*

**Four requirements and three prohibitions in two sentences.** Taking them in order:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One pixel** | **never two.** A two-pixel outline at 80 px eats 2.5% of the figure's height on each side |
| **Dark** | **darker than what it surrounds** — so the outline separates the sprite from the background |
| **Coloured** | **not grey, not black** — a dark version of the adjacent material's hue |
| **Not universal pure black** | the specific prohibition. See below |
| **Not an automatic double outline** | what Select › Modify › Border produces when run twice, or what some tools add by default |
| **Not merging equipment into the torso** | **the outline must keep a satchel strap readable as a separate object** |

---

**Why not black.** Four reasons, and the first is the one that decides it:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — It reads as a hole** | **pure black is darker than anything else in the palette's materials**, so a black outline is the highest-contrast element in the sprite — and the eye goes to contrast. **The outline becomes the subject** |
| **2 — It flattens** | a single outline colour all the way round says *"this is a cut-out"*. **A varying outline says "this is a form"** |
| **3 — The lighting** | `Light2D` tinting a black outline does nothing, because black has no hue to tint. **The sprite's edge stops responding to light while its interior responds** |
| **4 — The palette has the right colours** | `TERR-001` **Coal Black `#17181B`** is listed for *"Outlines, deepest recesses, undersides, contact accents"* — **and it is not pure black.** And every ramp's **Deep** step is a candidate outline for that material |

**So the working method: the outline colour comes from the Deep step of the ramp of whatever it is outlining.** Cloth's outline is `TERR-005` Burnt Cloth; leather's is `TERR-025` Blackened Leather; metal's is `TERR-009` Cold Iron. **`TERR-001` to `004` are for the deepest recesses and the places where no material's own Deep is dark enough.**

---

**Selective outlining**, which is the craft name for varying it:

| Where | What the outline does |
| --- | --- |
| **The lit side — upper-left** | **lighter, or absent.** A form turning into the light does not need a dark line; the value difference does the work |
| **The shadow side — lower-right** | **darkest.** This is where the outline is doing its job |
| **Where two materials meet** | **the darker material's Deep step**, so the boundary belongs to the darker one |
| **Where a limb crosses the torso** | **a full dark outline, and a negative gap if there is room** — this is what makes the limb read as in front |
| **Against the ground** | **the contact shadow takes over** (§9.1: *"a short contact shadow inside or immediately beside their footprint"*), and the outline can lighten |

**The simplest version that works, and the one to start with:** **a full one-pixel outline in each material's Deep step, then lighten or remove it along the upper-left.** That is two passes and it satisfies the clause.

---

**The equipment clause**, which is the one that needs the most care:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The failure** | **a satchel drawn against the torso, both outlined in the same dark colour, with the outlines touching.** The two dark lines merge into one thick line and **the satchel stops being a separate object** |
| **Fix one — a negative gap** | **one pixel of background between them.** §10.1: *"Preserve useful negative gaps between body, limbs and equipment"* |
| **Fix two — asymmetric outlining** | **outline the satchel and not the torso behind it**, so there is one line and not two |
| **Fix three — value** | **make the satchel's own value clearly different from the torso's**, so the shapes separate without relying on the outline at all. **The best fix** |
| **And the test** | **§10.1's black test.** Fill the whole sprite with solid black: if the satchel disappears, the gap is not there |

**Practice.** Draw a simple torso with a strap across it. Outline both in the same Deep step with the outlines touching, and run the black test. Then add a one-pixel negative gap and run it again. Then try the asymmetric version and the value version, and decide which you would ship. Then take any outlined sprite and lighten its upper-left outline, and compare at 100%.
Pixel density, and consistency:
Why every asset in a game must have the same pixel size, and the three ways that goes wrong.

**"Pixel density" means how large one art pixel is relative to the thing it depicts.** In a game it must be the same everywhere, and when it is not the result looks broken in a way that is hard to name.

**The project's density, from §9.2:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One world tile** | **16 px** |
| **A normal adult** | **about 80 px**, representing about **1.75 m** |
| **So the calibration** | **about 45.7 px per metre** |
| **The collision and detail subgrid** | **8 px** |

**That number — 45.7 px per metre — is the density.** Every asset in the game is drawn at it, and **"footprint governs collision and placement; real proportion governs visible size. They are separate facts and every prop brief states both."**

---

**The three ways density goes wrong:**

**1 — Mixed source scales.** The commonest and the most obvious:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | one asset drawn at 1× and another drawn at 2× and scaled down, or vice versa |
| **What it looks like** | **the scaled asset has softer edges and more colours**, and sits in the scene like a photograph pasted into a drawing |
| **Why it happens** | because drawing big is easier, and scaling down looks fine on its own |
| **§10.1's answer** | *"deliberate clusters rather than **resized or filtered source art**"* |

**2 — Mixed detail scales at the same pixel scale.** The subtle one:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **two assets at the same pixel density where one has far more detail per pixel.** A barrel with every stave and hoop against a crate that is three flat values |
| **What it looks like** | **the detailed object appears closer to the camera**, or more important, or from a different game |
| **The fix** | **a detail budget per asset class**, which §10.1's colour bands already imply: a small prop gets **4–10 colours**, and a hero gets **12–18**. **A prop with 16 colours is competing with the hero** |

**3 — Scale drift in large assets.** The one that catches out architecture:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | a building drawn to look right on its own, at a scale that does not match the 16 px tile and the 80 px adult |
| **The check** | **§9.2's door opening: "at least 88 px clear."** An 80 px adult must fit through a door. **If the door is 60 px, the building is at the wrong density** |
| **The method** | **§9.2's own instruction: "Validate them beside the real character at native scale"** — keep a character silhouette in the file as a reference layer |

---

**The York size bands**, §9.2's table, which are the density made concrete. A selection:

| Object | Visible size | Footprint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Bucket / pail** | **14–17 px high** | 1 × 1 |
| **Crate** | 21–25 px | 1 × 1 |
| **Barrel** | **37–45 px** | 1 × 1 |
| **Bench** | 19–23 px seat, 46–56 px long | 3 × 1 |
| **Table** | 31–37 px high, 55–70 px long | 4 × 2 |
| **Round hay bale** | **53–65 px** | 2 × 2 |
| **Cart / hand cart** | 53–65 px high, 100–120 px long | 6 × 3 |
| **Fence run** | 41–50 px high | 1 tile deep |
| **Door opening** | **at least 88 px clear** | architecture-defined |

**And the contract's own caveat:** *"These inherited York bands are starting calibration, not approval of an asset. Validate them beside the real character at native scale and revise the table if drawn evidence shows a systematic problem."*

**So the bands are a hypothesis, not a law** — and §9.2 explicitly invites revising them if the drawing says otherwise. **Stage 7 draws a bucket against them and stage 10 argues about them.**

**Practice.** Draw a 16 px grid in a 112 × 112 file and put an 80 px tall rectangle on it, and keep that file as your density reference. Then draw a bucket at 15 px and a barrel at 41 px against it. Then draw the same barrel at 2× and scale it down, and compare its edges and colour count with the hand-drawn one.
The detail budget:
What 80 pixels actually buys, counted — and the decisions that follow from the count.

**The arithmetic, done properly, because nothing else in this stage changes behaviour as much.**

**A Shepherds adult**, from §4 and the measured reference:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Height** | **81 to 87 px by direction** |
| **Width** | roughly **30 to 45 px** at the shoulders, depending on pose and direction |
| **The bounding box** | call it **85 × 40 = 3,400 pixels** |
| **Actually occupied by the figure** | **perhaps 45 to 55% of that** — a human silhouette is mostly not a rectangle. **So about 1,600 pixels** |
| **Minus the outline** | a one-pixel outline round a figure of that size is **roughly 200 to 250 pixels** |
| **Left for the interior** | **about 1,350 pixels** |

**And how those 1,350 divide**, as a working estimate:

| Region | Pixels | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Head** | **80–140** | about **10–14 px tall** |
| **Torso** | **350–450** | the largest single area, and where equipment goes |
| **Each arm** | **120–160** | so **240–320** for both |
| **Each leg** | **200–260** | so **400–520** for both |
| **Hands** | **8–20 each** | **two or three pixels across.** A hand is a cluster |
| **Feet** | **15–30 each** | |

---

**What that means, item by item.** These are the consequences, and they are the lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An eye is one pixel, or none** | at a 12 px head, two eyes plus a nose plus a mouth is **four pixels in a 12 × 10 area**. **The face is a suggestion, and on back views it is absent entirely.** §5.1 records that the reference's face mark appears *"on s, se, e, w and sw; not visible on the back views"* |
| **A hand cannot have fingers** | three pixels. **It has a shape and a value and nothing else** |
| **A belt is one pixel tall** | so **a belt is a value change, not an object** |
| **A weapon's blade is 2 px wide** | which is why **§10.1 allows signature equipment to break the torso silhouette** — the only way a crook reads is by sticking out |
| **A fold in cloth is a 3-pixel dash** | and **you get two or three of them**, not twenty |
| **Hair is a shape** | a silhouette plus two values. **Not strands** |

---

**The three rules that follow:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Spend on silhouette first** | **§10.1 ranks it**: *"Silhouette, value separation, pose readability and ground contact take priority over decorative detail."* **The outline and the shape are 250 of your 1,600 pixels and they do most of the work** |
| **2 — Spend the rest on the largest areas** | **the torso and legs are 60% of the figure.** Getting their value structure right matters more than anything on the head |
| **3 — Spend nothing on what cannot read** | **if a detail is one pixel and you could not name it with the sprite covered up, delete it.** That is the confetti test from the cluster lesson, applied as a budget |

---

**And the identity problem this creates**, which §10.1 states as a requirement:

> *"Every playable hero must remain identifiable in solid black, grayscale, dark lighting and a busy party scene. **Identity cannot depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail.**"*

**With 1,350 interior pixels and no face, a character is told apart by four things:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Silhouette** | **height, build, hair shape, hat, cloak, stance** |
| **Equipment shape** | **the crook, the satchel, the sling** — things that break the outline |
| **Value structure** | which parts are light and which are dark, as a pattern |
| **Palette subset** | **and this one is the weakest**, because §10.1 says identity may not depend on hue |

**Which is why stage 9 begins with silhouette and not with the face.**

**Practice.** Draw an 85 × 40 rectangle and fill the pixels you think a standing figure would occupy, then count them with the Lospec analyzer or by eye. Then draw a 12 px head with a face, and then with none, and compare at 100% and at 300%. Then take a character design you have in mind and write down its four identity carriers from the table above.
The 3× scale:
One art pixel is a 3 × 3 block on screen, and every judgement in this curriculum is made at the wrong size unless you force it not to be.

**The arithmetic:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal viewport** | **960 × 540** (§4) |
| **At 1920 × 1080** | **exactly 2× — one art pixel is 2 × 2 screen pixels** |
| **At 2560 × 1440** | 2.67×, so **integer-scaled to 2× with letterboxing, or fractionally scaled** |
| **At 3840 × 2160** | **exactly 4×** |
| **And the figure the project records** | **`media/reference/Animation/README.md`: "scale 1.0 (one art pixel is 3 × 3)"** — the practical working figure for the run reference |

**So somewhere between 2 × 2 and 4 × 4, and 3 × 3 is the number to think in.** The point does not depend on which:

---

**What a 3 × 3 scale does to each of this stage's defects:**

| Defect | At 1× | At 3× |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **An orphan pixel** | a speck | **a visible 3-pixel block** |
| **A jaggy** | a slight unevenness | **a 3-pixel bump, repeated along the edge** |
| **A banded pair of lines** | two thin lines | **a 6-pixel-wide stripe** |
| **A one-pixel dither pattern** | a texture | **a 6-pixel-period chequer that shimmers** |
| **A one-pixel-apart grain texture** | fine grain | **a 3-pixel stripe pattern that crawls in motion** |
| **A two-pixel outline** | heavy | **6 screen pixels of dark border** |

**Everything gets three times worse, and nothing gets better.** That is the whole lesson: **the scale is a magnifying glass on your mistakes and does nothing for your drawing.**

---

**And the second-order effect, which matters more: motion.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A one-pixel movement between frames** | **is a 3-pixel jump on screen** |
| **At 12 fps** | there is about **a twelfth of a second** between frames — and stage 12 explains why the duration typed into Aseprite is 84 ms rather than 83, so a 3-pixel jump is visible as a jump rather than as motion |
| **Which means** | **a one-pixel difference between two animation frames is a real, visible movement** — not a subtlety |
| **And the consequence for animation** | **an idle animation whose limbs move by one pixel is already a legible animation.** §5.1's idle reference moves *"3–5 meaningful poses"* over 24 frames, and the deliberate **3 px loop drop** is visible precisely because 3 px is 9 screen pixels |

**That is why stage 10's animation lessons work in single pixels.** At this scale, one pixel is a decision with a visible consequence, and **a limb nudged two pixels is a gesture.**

---

**How to actually judge at 1×.** Four methods, in order of usefulness:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The preview window at 100%** | **`F7`**, open always. From stage 1 |
| **2 — Zoom to 300%, which is the real size** | **this is the better habit and it is counter-intuitive.** 100% is how the file is; **300% is how the player sees it.** Judge at 300%, not at 100% |
| **3 — Step back from the screen** | the oldest trick and it works |
| **4 — In Godot** | **the only place the four §5.3 conditions are all true.** Stage 7 and stage 12 |

**Point 2 is the correction worth making to the usual advice.** "Judge at 1×" is the standard rule and it is slightly wrong for this project: **1× is smaller than the player will ever see it.** The honest version is **judge at the delivery scale**, which here is 2× to 4×, and 300% in Aseprite is the closest single number.

**Practice.** Take a sprite with a known jaggy and view it at 100%, 300% and 800%. Then set Aseprite's zoom to 300% and leave it there for a session, using `F7` at 100% as the secondary check. Then make a two-frame animation where a limb moves exactly one pixel, and play it at 12 fps at 300%, and decide whether one pixel is enough movement.
Reading your own work:
Six ways to see what you have actually drawn rather than what you meant to draw, and why they are necessary.

**The problem is specific and it is not laziness.** You have been looking at this sprite for forty minutes at 800%, placing pixels you chose. **Your eye has adapted to it, and your knowledge of what each cluster is for is doing work that the drawing is not.** A reviewer seeing it for two seconds at 300% has none of that, and **their reading is the one that counts.**

**Six methods, cheapest first:**

---

**1 — Change the zoom.** From the last lesson: **300% is the delivery scale, 100% is the file, 800% is a lie.** Cycling between them takes a second and catches most of the gross errors.

**2 — Change the background.** From stage 1's preferences: **set the canvas background to a flat colour and change it.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Against mid-grey** | catches value errors — anything that disappears has the same value as the background |
| **Against near-black** | **catches the shadow side.** §10.1 requires identity *"in dark lighting"* |
| **Against near-white** | catches the light side and the outline |
| **Against the actual ground colour** | **the real test, and Godot is where it happens** |

**3 — Flip it.** **`Shift+H`**, look, flip back.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why it works** | **the brain stops recognising the image and starts seeing it.** Every asymmetry, lean and imbalance you have stopped noticing becomes visible |
| **The caution** | **flip back.** And remember §5.4 — **a flip is a judgement tool here, not a production method** |

**4 — Greyscale it.** The Color-mode layer toggle from stage 1.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it tests** | **§10.1's grey test directly**: *"identifiable in … grayscale"* |
| **What it catches** | **two materials with different hues and the same value**, which look separate in colour and merge in grey — and `Light2D` will desaturate them in play |

**5 — Black it out.** Fill the silhouette with one dark colour.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it tests** | **§10.1's black test**: *"identifiable in solid black"* |
| **What it catches** | **everything that depends on interior detail.** If the character is unrecognisable in black, the silhouette is not doing its job and no amount of interior work will fix it |
| **How** | duplicate the layer, fill with `TERR-001` using Lock Alpha ink, hide the original |

**6 — Leave it.** Close the file and look tomorrow.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why it is on the list** | **it is the most effective of the six and the only one that costs time.** Adaptation wears off |
| **And the production version** | **§10's rule that Master Roachi approves the actual asset** — which means there is a second pair of eyes by design, and **Timon's is a third with final say on design** |

---

**The two tests the contract actually requires**, from §10.1:

> *"Every playable hero must remain identifiable in solid black, grayscale, dark lighting and a busy party scene."*

**Four conditions, and methods 4 and 5 above give you two of them.** The other two — **dark lighting** and **a busy party scene** — can only be checked in Godot, which is §10's seventh condition: *"the asset works in Godot under representative lighting, crowds and effects."*

**So the full checklist, as a habit:**

| | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **300% and 100%** | Aseprite |
| **Three backgrounds** | Aseprite |
| **Flipped** | Aseprite |
| **Greyscale** | Aseprite |
| **Solid black** | Aseprite |
| **Dark lighting** | **Godot** |
| **A busy scene** | **Godot** |
| **Tomorrow** | — |

**Practice.** Build the three toggles into your 112 × 112 template: a greyscale layer, a black-fill layer, and a background colour you can change. Then take a sprite you are happy with and run all five Aseprite methods on it in order, writing down what each one caught. Then leave it overnight and look again, and write down what that caught.
Redrawing noise as clusters:
The repair exercise: taking a surface that does not read and rebuilding it with fewer, larger, deliberate marks.

**This lesson is a procedure rather than a principle**, because the principle is already in the cluster lesson and the skill is in the doing.

**The situation it addresses.** A surface — a cloak, a wall, a flank of an animal — that you have shaded and which **looks busy and reads as nothing.** Every pixel was placed on purpose and the result is mush.

**Why it happens.** Three causes, usually together:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Too many values** | five or six where §10.1 allows *"three or four purposeful values"* |
| **Too many marks** | each one small, each describing a small undulation of the surface |
| **No hierarchy** | **nothing is the biggest shape**, so the eye has nowhere to start |

---

**The procedure. Six steps, and it is destructive on purpose.**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Count the values** | **select the region and check the palette, or use the Lospec analyzer.** If there are more than four, that is the first problem |
| **2 — Reduce to two** | **flatten the whole surface to its Mid, then add only the Shadow.** Two values. Look at it at 300% |
| **3 — Find the big shape** | **where is the boundary between light and shadow?** One boundary, one continuous line, following the form. **Draw that properly and nothing else** |
| **4 — Add the third value** | **the Light, only where the form faces the key light** — upper-left, per §10.1. **Fewer pixels than the shadow** |
| **5 — Add the fourth, if needed** | **the Deep, only in the deepest recess and under an overlap.** Often not needed |
| **6 — Stop** | **the surface is finished.** Any further mark is competing with the three boundaries you have drawn |

**The step that does the work is 3.** A surface reads because of **one clear value boundary that describes the form**, and everything else is decoration. **Noise is the result of drawing the decoration before the boundary.**

---

**The before-and-after test.** Do both versions and compare:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **At 300%** | the rebuilt version has **fewer, larger, more legible areas** |
| **In greyscale** | the rebuilt version has **a readable value pattern**; the noisy one is uniformly mid-grey |
| **In solid black** | **both are identical**, which proves the point — **all that work was interior, and the silhouette carried the sprite either way** |
| **Pixel count** | **the rebuilt one took a third of the marks** |

**That third row is the most useful thing in this lesson.** The black test is unchanged by any amount of interior work. **Which means interior detail is never what makes a sprite read — it is what makes a sprite's material legible once it already reads.**

---

**And the general principle, stated as the contract states it.** §2:

> *"Dense environmental storytelling is welcome only where traversable space, interactables, hazards and combat silhouettes remain immediately readable."*
>
> *"Silhouette, value separation, pose readability and ground contact take priority over decorative detail."*

**"Only where … remain immediately readable" is a budget clause.** Detail is permitted up to the point where it costs readability, **and the point arrives much sooner than it feels like it should.**

**Practice.** Take a 32 × 32 surface and shade it badly on purpose: six values, many small marks, no clear boundary. Then run the six steps. Compare the two at 300%, in greyscale and in solid black, and count the marks in each. Then do it again on a real asset — a cloak or an animal's flank — and keep both files until you have decided which is better.
Fewer pixels:
The stage's conclusion: the discipline that separates competent pixel art from the rest, stated as a habit rather than a rule.

**The claim.** Across every lesson in this stage, the fix has been the same:

| Lesson | The fix |
| --- | --- |
| **The cluster** | **fewer, larger clusters** |
| **Lines** | **one slope instead of an approximation of a slope** |
| **Curves** | **a monotonic run sequence, which has fewer changes in it** |
| **Banding** | **fewer value boundaries, and not parallel** |
| **Noise against texture** | **fewer marks, in a pattern** |
| **Dithering** | **choose a value instead of mixing two** |
| **Anti-aliasing** | **move the edge instead of softening it** |
| **The detail budget** | **spend on silhouette, not on detail** |
| **Redrawing noise** | **one boundary, then stop** |

**Nine lessons, one answer.** That is not a coincidence and it is not minimalism as a style. **It is what a medium with 1,350 interior pixels and four values per material can carry.**

---

**Why fewer is better here, in three claims that can be checked:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Legibility is a function of the largest shape** | **the eye identifies an object by its biggest, highest-contrast features.** Adding small features does not add information; it adds competition for the same attention |
| **2 — Motion destroys small marks** | at 12 fps with 3 px screen scaling, **anything smaller than about three screen pixels that moves becomes shimmer.** A detail that reads when the sprite is still can be noise when it walks |
| **3 — Light destroys baked detail** | **§10.1 keeps static shading restrained *"so Godot's local lights can read coherently"*.** A heavily shaded sprite under a coloured light has two lighting schemes fighting. **Fewer baked values means the runtime light does the describing** |

**The third is the project-specific one and it is the strongest.** This is a lit game. **Every value you bake in is a value `Light2D` has to argue with.**

---

**The habit, stated as a question to ask of every mark:**

> **Can I remove this and lose nothing?**

**And three subsidiary questions when the answer is unclear:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Could I name it?** | if not, it is noise — the cluster lesson's test |
| **Does it survive greyscale?** | if the mark disappears when hue is removed, **it was carrying no value information**, and §10.1's grey test will fail on it |
| **Does it survive 300% in motion?** | if it shimmers, it is costing more than it gives |

---

**And the honest limit of this stage's advice**, because "fewer" is not a complete aesthetic:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fewer is not the same as empty** | **a flat surface with one boundary is not finished; it is correct.** §2 wants environments that are *"materially specific"* and places that *"feel inhabited"*, which requires marks |
| **The order is what matters** | **silhouette, then the big value boundary, then material texture, then detail — and stop when readability starts to cost.** The error this stage corrects is doing those in reverse |
| **And some styles are dense** | **heavily dithered, heavily textured pixel art is a legitimate and beautiful tradition.** §2 chose otherwise, and the reason is gameplay readability at native scale during *"movement, combat, crowds, darkness and effects"* |

**So the stage ends where it began: the constraint is the medium.** Four values per material and 1,350 pixels is not a limitation to be worked around. **It is what makes a sprite read in a crowd at 3 × 3 under a coloured light while moving, and that is the entire job.**

**Practice.** Take the best sprite you have made in this stage and remove ten pixels — any ten you can lose. Look at it at 300%. Then remove ten more. Keep going until something breaks, and write down what broke and at how many. Then look at the version two steps before the break, and decide whether it is better than what you started with.
Why projection comes first:
The stage's thesis: projection is the decision that makes every asset sit in the same world, and it is the one the first version of this curriculum left out entirely.

**What projection is.** A game's projection is **the rule by which three-dimensional space is drawn on a flat screen.** It decides what a box looks like, what a circle on the ground looks like, whether a wall shows its top, and whether two assets drawn by two people on two days belong in the same scene.

**And it is a convention, chosen once.** §9.1 states Shepherds':

> *"The projection is rectilinear three-quarter top-down, not diamond isometric. Vertical edges stay vertical; floors do not converge toward a vanishing point."*

**Three clauses, and each one rules something out.** The rest of this stage unpacks them.

---

**Why it comes before value, colour, materials and the figure.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Because it is the only decision that cannot be fixed later** | **a wrongly shaded barrel can be reshaded. A barrel drawn in the wrong projection has to be redrawn**, because its top face is the wrong shape and its proportions are wrong |
| **Because it governs every asset class** | characters, props, terrain, architecture and effects all have to agree, and §9.3 lists projection **first** among the things every environment asset is checked for |
| **Because it is invisible when right and glaring when wrong** | **an asset in the wrong projection looks "off" in a way nobody can name**, which makes it the most expensive kind of error to diagnose |
| **And because the first version of this curriculum had no lesson on it** | eight stages, sixty-four lessons, and not one mention of projection. **That is the largest single gap the rewrite fills** |

---

**What §9.3 actually requires**, which is this stage's checklist:

> *"Every asset is checked for **projection**, visible scale, collision footprint, bottom-centre ground/Y-sort anchor, upper-left lighting, palette compatibility, silhouette at gameplay zoom, controlled detail, transparent isolation where applicable, contact shadow and absence of accidental damage or narrative wear."*

**Eleven checks, and this stage owns four of them** — projection, visible scale, the ground anchor, and the contact shadow. **The others belong to stages 4, 5, 6 and 7.**

---

**The stage's shape:**

| Lessons | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1–2** | this one, and the projections named — so the words mean something |
| **3–4** | **Shepherds' projection specifically**, and why it is not isometric |
| **5** | **the implied camera**, and what it does to a circle |
| **6–7** | **the primitives in projection** — the box, and the cylinder, sphere and cone |
| **8** | **height against depth**, which is the ambiguity this projection creates |
| **9–11** | **the measurements** — the 16 px tile, 45.7 px per metre, and footprint against visible size |
| **12** | **the ground anchor and the contact shadow** |
| **13–14** | **consistency across assets**, and the seven failures |

**And a note on what this stage is not.** It is not perspective drawing. **There is no vanishing point in this game** — §9.1 says floors do not converge, and §4 says *"The camera never rotates"*. **Those two facts together remove almost all of classical perspective from the problem**, and what is left is a convention with a handful of rules.

**Practice.** Read §9.1 and §9.3 in full. Then open a screenshot of Eastward or Sea of Stars — §2 names both as references for composition and value organisation — and find one box-shaped object in it. Write down what you can see of its top, its front and its sides. Then do the same for a screenshot of a diamond-isometric game and note what differs.
The projections, named:
The vocabulary, so that "three-quarter", "isometric" and "top-down" stop being used interchangeably.

**Every projection answers one question: how do the three axes of space map onto two axes of screen?** The families:

---

**1 — Perspective projection.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The rule** | **parallel lines converge toward vanishing points.** Things further away are smaller |
| **Where you see it** | photographs, 3D games, classical painting |
| **Why not here** | **§9.1: *"floors do not converge toward a vanishing point"*.** Convergence means an asset is only correct at one position on screen, which makes a reusable tile impossible |

**2 — Orthographic projection.** The three single-axis views:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Plan / top-down** | **straight down.** You see the ground and the tops of things, and **nothing of their sides.** Hotline Miami |
| **Elevation / side** | **straight on.** You see fronts and nothing of tops. Super Mario Bros., Castlevania |
| **Section** | a cut through |

**3 — Axonometric projections**, which show all three axes at once with no convergence:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Isometric** | **all three axes equally foreshortened, at 120° to each other.** In pixel art this is approximated as **"2:1 pixel isometric"** — lines at a 2:1 run, about 26.57° — because a true 30° line does not draw cleanly on a grid. **A ground tile is a diamond.** Diablo, Baldur's Gate, Transport Tycoon |
| **Dimetric** | two axes equally foreshortened, the third differently |
| **Trimetric** | all three differently |

**4 — Oblique projections**, where one face is drawn true and the depth axis is pushed off at an angle:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cavalier** | depth drawn at full length |
| **Cabinet** | **depth drawn at half length**, which looks far more natural |
| **Military** | the plan drawn true and the verticals raised |

---

**And the one games actually use most, which does not have a clean textbook name:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"Three-quarter top-down"** | **the ground is a square grid, vertical edges stay vertical, and you see both the tops and the fronts of things.** The Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, Stardew Valley, Eastward, Sea of Stars, and **Shepherds** |
| **Its honest classification** | **a form of oblique projection** — closest to military or cabinet oblique — **and it is not geometrically consistent.** That is deliberate, and the next lesson but one says why |
| **What it is not** | **isometric.** The ground is a square, not a diamond |

---

**The distinction that matters most**, because the words get used wrongly constantly:

| | Ground tile | Vertical edges | What you see of a box |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Top-down (plan)** | **square** | **a point** — no height at all | **only the top** |
| **Three-quarter top-down** | **square** | **vertical** | **the top and the front** |
| **Isometric** | **diamond** | **vertical** | **the top and two sides** |
| **Side view** | **a line** | vertical | **only the front** |

**Read the first column.** **A square ground tile is the signature of this projection**, and it is why §9.2's *"One world tile is 16 px"* is a 16 × 16 square rather than a 32 × 16 diamond. **If you find yourself drawing a diamond, you are in the wrong projection.**

**Practice.** Draw the same simple box four times — once in plan, once in three-quarter top-down, once in 2:1 isometric, once in side view — on a 16 px grid. Label each. Then look at Slynyrd's Pixelblog 3 and 4 on Graphical Projection and check your four against its examples. Then write down, for each of the four, what it hides.
The rectilinear three-quarter top-down:
Shepherds' projection in detail: the three rules, the convention they add up to, and the one ratio you have to choose and keep.

**The contract's definition**, §9.1, read clause by clause:

> *"The projection is **rectilinear three-quarter top-down**, not diamond isometric. **Vertical edges stay vertical**; **floors do not converge toward a vanishing point**."*

| Clause | What it fixes |
| --- | --- |
| **"rectilinear"** | **the grid is square.** A ground tile is a 16 × 16 square and the world's axes run along the screen's axes |
| **"three-quarter top-down"** | **you see the tops of things and their fronts.** Not plan, not elevation — both |
| **"not diamond isometric"** | **no 2:1 diamond tiles**, and no two-sides-visible boxes |
| **"vertical edges stay vertical"** | **a wall's corner is a vertical line on screen.** Always. No lean, no convergence |
| **"floors do not converge"** | **a tile at the top of the screen is the same size as one at the bottom** |

---

**What that adds up to, and it is worth stating plainly: the projection is not geometrically possible.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A real camera tilted down** | **would make the floor converge** — distant tiles smaller — and would make vertical edges lean toward a vanishing point |
| **This projection does neither** | so **no single camera position produces this image** |
| **Which is the point** | **it is a readability convention.** A square grid means a tile is reusable anywhere on screen; vertical verticals mean a wall is reusable at any height; no convergence means an asset is correct at every position |
| **And §4 completes it** | *"The camera never rotates"* — so **there is exactly one view of the world, and every asset is drawn for it** |

**That is a trade of correctness for consistency, and it is the right trade for a 2D game with reusable tiles.** It is also why asking "what angle is the camera at?" has no exact answer — **there is no camera. There is a convention with a ratio.**

---

**The ratio, which is the one number you choose.**

**Since you see the top of things, a flat square on the ground has to be drawn shorter than it is wide** — otherwise it would read as a vertical wall. **How much shorter is the projection's ratio**, and it governs every top face in the game:

| Ratio | What it reads as |
| --- | --- |
| **1 : 1** | **a vertical surface.** No tilt at all — this is plan view's opposite |
| **2 : 1** (half as tall as wide) | **a strong downward tilt** — close to isometric's feel, more floor visible |
| **3 : 2** | a gentler tilt |
| **1 : 1 for the floor grid, with top faces at about 1 : 2** | **the usual arrangement**, and the one to understand: **the floor is drawn as a flat square grid, and the tops of raised objects are foreshortened** |

**That last row is the subtlety.** In this convention **the ground plane is drawn un-foreshortened — a 16 × 16 tile is a 16 × 16 square** — and **the top faces of objects standing on it are foreshortened.** It is inconsistent, and it is what makes the convention work: the floor stays a usable grid while objects read as having height.

**So the practical rule: a box's top face is about half as deep as the box is wide**, and whatever you choose, **every object in the game uses the same figure.** §9.3 checks for *"projection"* precisely to catch an asset that used a different one.

---

**How to check an asset's projection in four questions:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **are the vertical edges vertical?** No lean |
| **2** | **is the top face foreshortened by the project's ratio**, and the same ratio as every other asset? |
| **3** | **are there any converging lines?** There should be none |
| **4** | **is the ground footprint a square or rectangle on the 16 px grid**, not a diamond? |

**Practice.** Draw a 32 × 32 box on a 16 px grid with vertical sides and a top face foreshortened to half depth. Then draw it again with the top face at two-thirds depth and compare which reads better at 300%. Then draw a 3 × 2 tile footprint as a square grid rectangle and confirm it is not a diamond. Then open §9.2's table and pick an object whose footprint and height you can draw to that ratio.
Why it is not isometric:
The comparison in detail, because isometric is the projection most pixel art tutorials teach and choosing it here would be wrong.

**The contract rules it out by name** — §9.1: *"not diamond isometric"*. **The reasons are worth having, because they are the reasons this projection was chosen.**

---

**The mechanical differences:**

| | Isometric (2:1 pixel) | Rectilinear three-quarter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A ground tile** | **a diamond**, typically 32 × 16 | **a square**, 16 × 16 |
| **The world's axes on screen** | **two diagonals at about 26.57°** | **horizontal and vertical** |
| **A box** | **top and two side faces visible** — a hexagonal silhouette | **top and front face** — a rectangular silhouette |
| **Vertical edges** | vertical | vertical |
| **Movement in a cardinal direction** | **diagonal on screen** | **straight on screen** |
| **A character's eight directions** | **align with the diamond's axes** | **align with the screen's axes** |

---

**The five reasons rectilinear is the right choice here.**

**1 — Movement and the grid agree.** The decisive one for a game with eight-direction movement:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **In isometric** | **pressing "up" moves the character diagonally across the screen**, or the controls are rotated 45° and the world's axes do not match the screen's. **Either way one of the two is confusing** |
| **In rectilinear** | **up is up.** §5.4's eight directions — s, se, e, ne, n, nw, w, sw — **map onto the screen's own axes and diagonals** |

**2 — Tiles are simpler.** A square tile tiles trivially; a diamond tile has to interlock, needs double-height variants for walls, and makes every transition a special case. **§9.1 asks for *"hand-drawn 16 × 16 tiles assembled as Godot terrain sets"*, and Godot's terrain matching is built for square grids.**

**3 — Y-sorting is simple.** §9.1: *"bottom-centre ground anchor"*, and §4: *"Collision and gameplay origin remain at the feet."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **In rectilinear** | **depth order is screen Y.** Lower on screen is in front. That is one comparison |
| **In isometric** | **depth order is a function of both axes**, and objects spanning several tiles need careful sorting — a known, persistent source of bugs |

**4 — Buildings and interiors are readable.** §9.1 lists *"modular architecture: reusable walls, roofs, doors, windows, gates, fences, posts and interior pieces which must pass straight-run, corner and transition seam tests"*. **A square grid makes a straight run straight and a corner a corner. In isometric every wall run is a diagonal and corners come in four different shapes.**

**5 — It is what the references do.** §2 names **Eastward** and **Sea of Stars** for *"composition and value organization"*, **and both are rectilinear three-quarter**, not isometric.

---

**And the honest case for isometric**, because it has one:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **More of each object is visible** | two sides plus a top is more information than one side plus a top, so **objects read as more three-dimensional** |
| **Depth reads better over distance** | a long diagonal space has more apparent depth than a rectangular one |
| **It suits tactical and building games** | where seeing the footprint clearly matters — hence Transport Tycoon and the Front Mission comparison Slynyrd's Pixelblog 61 makes |
| **And it is a beautiful look** | which is why so much pixel art uses it |

**None of those outweigh movement, tiling, sorting and architecture for this game.** But know that **when a tutorial teaches isometric — and Slynyrd has three articles on it, 41, 54 and 61 — it is teaching a different projection, and its box and tile geometry do not transfer.**
