**Practice.** Draw the same 2 × 2 footprint crate twice: once isometric on a 32 × 16 diamond grid, once rectilinear on a 16 × 16 square grid. Note how many faces each shows and how many pixels each took. Then draw a straight run of three fence posts in each, and a right-angle corner in each, and count how many distinct pieces each projection needs.
The implied camera, and the circle:
What a flat circle looks like on the ground, why the answer is a choice rather than a calculation, and the one ratio to keep.

**A circle lying flat on the ground is the projection's clearest test**, because its shape depends entirely on how much of the ground you are seeing.

| Viewing angle | What a ground circle looks like |
| --- | --- |
| **Straight down (plan)** | **a circle** |
| **Straight on (side)** | **a horizontal line** |
| **In between** | **an ellipse**, wider than it is tall |

**In a true projection the ellipse's height is the circle's width times the sine of the angle above the ground.** At 30° above the ground, a circle 16 wide is 8 tall. At 45°, about 11 tall.

---

**And here the calculation does not apply**, for the reason the last two lessons gave: **there is no camera.** From §9.1 the floor is drawn un-foreshortened as a square grid, which corresponds to looking straight down — and objects show their front faces, which corresponds to looking from in front. **The two are inconsistent, so there is no single angle to take a sine of.**

**So the ratio is a choice.** Make it once and keep it:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The working ratio** | **a flat circle is drawn about half as tall as it is wide** — a 16-wide circular object is an ellipse about 8 tall |
| **Why half** | **it reads as flat-on-the-ground without becoming a line**, and it matches a plausible three-quarter view |
| **Where it applies** | **every horizontal circular surface**: a barrel's top, a bucket's mouth, a well, a trough's end, a round hay bale seen from above, a cauldron, a cart wheel lying flat, a pool |
| **Where it does not** | **a vertical circle is a circle** — a cart wheel standing up, a shield face-on, a round window in a wall |

---

**The sphere, which is the exception worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A sphere is a circle from every angle** | so **the Beacon is a circle, not an ellipse**, and §6.6 confirms it: *"Beacon is spherical and does not require character-style directional facings"* |
| **What makes it read as a sphere rather than a disc** | **the shading, not the silhouette** — the upper-left highlight and the lower-right form shadow, which is stage 4 |
| **And its contact shadow** | **an ellipse at the projection's ratio**, on the ground beneath it. **The shadow is what tells you the sphere is resting rather than floating** |

---

**The three circular objects in §9.2's table, worked out:**

| Object | Footprint | Visible size | So the top ellipse is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Bucket / pail** | 1 × 1 | **14–17 px high** | **a mouth about 10–13 px wide and 5–7 px tall** |
| **Barrel** | 1 × 1 | **37–45 px high** | **a top about 14–16 px wide and 7–8 px tall** |
| **Round hay bale** | **2 × 2** | **53–65 px high** | **a cylinder lying on its side** — so its visible end is a circle, nearly un-foreshortened, and its top is a long curved surface |

**That last row is the instructive one.** A round hay bale is a cylinder on its side, so **the geometry rotates**: what was a foreshortened top is now a true circle at the end, and what was a vertical side is now the curved top. **The ratio applies to horizontal surfaces, not to objects.**

**Practice.** Draw a 16-wide flat circle at 8 tall, at 11 tall and at 16 tall, and decide which reads as lying on the ground. Then draw a bucket at 15 px high with its mouth at the ratio you chose. Then draw a sphere with an upper-left highlight and an elliptical contact shadow, and then remove the shadow and see whether it still rests on the ground.
The box in projection:
The primitive everything else is built from: what faces are visible, how the top is foreshortened, and where the outline goes.

**A box is the projection's unit test.** Get it right and crates, buildings, benches, tables, carts and walls follow; get it wrong and all of them are wrong the same way.

**What is visible**, from §9.1's rules:

| Face | Visible? |
| --- | --- |
| **Front** | **yes** — drawn true, as a rectangle, with vertical sides |
| **Top** | **yes** — foreshortened, from the implied three-quarter view |
| **Left and right sides** | **no.** This is the difference from isometric |
| **Back and bottom** | no |

**So a box's silhouette is a rectangle with a shorter rectangle on top** — not a hexagon.

---

**The construction, in five steps:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The footprint** | **the box's ground rectangle, in tiles.** A crate is 1 × 1; a table 4 × 2; a cart 6 × 3 (§9.2). **At 16 px a tile, a 1 × 1 crate occupies a 16-pixel-wide footprint** |
| **2 — The front face** | **width = the footprint's width in pixels; height = the visible height** from the bands. A crate at 21–25 px high and 1 × 1 is roughly **16 wide by 22 tall** |
| **3 — The top face** | **the same width, and a depth of the footprint's depth times the projection ratio.** A 1 × 1 footprint is 16 deep, so at a half ratio **the top face is 16 wide by 8 tall** |
| **4 — Join them** | the top face sits directly above the front face, and **its side edges are vertical** |
| **5 — The ground anchor** | **bottom-centre**, §9.1 — the pivot sits at the centre of the front face's bottom edge |

**And the arithmetic to hold: a 1 × 1 object's total drawn height is its visible height plus its top-face depth.** A 22-pixel crate with an 8-pixel top is **30 pixels of drawn sprite**, and its *visible size* in §9.2's sense is the 22.

---

**The outline, which is where boxes usually go wrong.** From stage 2's selective outlining, applied:

| Edge | Outline |
| --- | --- |
| **The top face's far edge** (upper) | **lightest or absent** — it faces the key light at upper-left |
| **The top-front edge** (where top meets front) | **present, mid-dark** — this is the box's most important line, because **it is the only thing separating the two faces** |
| **The front face's lower edge** | **darkest**, and it meets the contact shadow |
| **The vertical corners** | **present**, darker on the right than the left |

**The top-front edge deserves its own note.** Without it the top and front read as one surface and the box flattens. **With it too dark, the box reads as two stacked objects.** The usual answer: **the top face is a lighter value than the front face**, so the value difference does most of the separating and the line can be subtle.

---

**And the value structure, which is stage 4's subject and worth previewing because it is the box's whole readability:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The top face** | **lightest** — it faces up, and the key light comes from above and the upper-left (§10.1) |
| **The front face** | **mid** |
| **Any visible right side, if the box is turned** | **darkest** — facing away from the upper-left key |
| **Under it** | **the contact shadow** |

**Three values and a shadow, and the box is finished.** §10.1's *"three or four purposeful values per major material"* is exactly a box's requirement.

**Practice.** Draw a 1 × 1 crate at 22 px visible height with an 8 px top face, on a 16 px grid, in three values plus an outline. Then draw a 4 × 2 table at 34 px high and 62 px long with the same ratio, and check that its top face depth is 32 × 0.5 = 16 px. Then draw the same crate with no top-front edge and compare. Then turn one box slightly to expose a side face and decide whether that breaks §9.1's rules.
The cylinder, the sphere and the cone:
The curved primitives: how each is constructed in this projection, and the value structure that makes each read.

**Three forms, and between them they cover most props in §9.2's table** — barrels, buckets, troughs, hay bales, posts, the Beacon, roofs and haystacks.

---

**The cylinder, standing up.** A barrel, a bucket, a post, a well.

| Part | How |
| --- | --- |
| **The body** | **a rectangle** — width equals the diameter, height equals the visible height. **Vertical sides, per §9.1** |
| **The top** | **an ellipse at the projection ratio** — the diameter wide, half that tall |
| **The bottom** | **a curve, not a straight line.** The bottom edge of a cylinder is the near half of an ellipse, so **it bulges downward in the middle**. Getting this wrong is the commonest cylinder error |
| **The silhouette** | a rectangle with a curved top and a curved bottom |

**The value structure, which is what makes it a cylinder rather than a rectangle:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The top** | **lightest** — facing up into the light |
| **The body's left-of-centre band** | **light** — facing the upper-left key (§10.1) |
| **The body's right side** | **mid, then shadow** as it turns away |
| **The far right edge** | **sometimes a thin lighter band** — reflected light, and **§10.1's restraint clause argues against it.** One value, not two |
| **The boundary between light and shadow** | **a vertical line, slightly left of centre, and it must not band** — stage 2 |

**And the key point about a cylinder in four values: the value boundaries are vertical and parallel, which is the textbook banding setup.** The fix from stage 2: **vary the width of each band, and let the boundary wobble slightly where the barrel's staves or hoops are.**

---

**The sphere.** The Beacon, a ball, a round fruit.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The silhouette** | **a circle.** From every angle — which is why §6.6 says *"Beacon is spherical and does not require character-style directional facings"* |
| **What makes it read** | **the shading alone** |
| **The highlight** | **a cluster in the upper-left quadrant**, not at the edge and not at the centre — about a third of the way in from the upper-left |
| **The terminator** | **the boundary between light and shadow, which is an arc concentric with the silhouette**, offset toward the lower-right |
| **The core shadow** | **the darkest band, just inside the lower-right edge** — not at the very edge |
| **The very edge, lower-right** | **slightly lighter than the core shadow** if you have the value to spare, because light bounces. **§10.1's restraint says you probably do not** |
| **The contact shadow** | **an ellipse beneath it** — and this is what makes it rest rather than float |

**The sphere is the hardest primitive to shade in four values**, because a sphere's real appearance is a continuous gradient and there are three steps to describe it with. **The answer is concentric arcs, each at a chosen distance, and no dithering between them.**

---

**The cone.** A haystack, a conical roof, a pile, a tent.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The silhouette** | **a triangle with a curved base** — the base is the near half of a ground ellipse |
| **The apex** | a point, or a small cluster |
| **Shading** | **radial** — the light and shadow bands converge toward the apex, so **the boundary is a line from the apex to the base**, left of centre |
| **The error to avoid** | **shading it with horizontal bands**, which reads as a stack of discs rather than a cone |

**And the truncated cone** — a bucket, which is wider at the top than the bottom — **is the cylinder's construction with sloping sides.** §9.2's bucket at 14–17 px high is **about 12 wide at the mouth and 9 at the base**, and at that size the slope is two or three pixels per side.

**Practice.** Draw a barrel at 41 px high and 16 wide: vertical sides, an elliptical top at 8 px deep, and a curved bottom edge. Shade it in four values with a vertical boundary left of centre, varying the band widths. Then draw a sphere 16 px across with concentric shading and a contact shadow. Then draw a cone and shade it radially, then again with horizontal bands, and compare.
Height against depth:
The ambiguity this projection creates: moving up the screen means either taller or further away, and four devices resolve it.

**The problem, stated exactly.** In a three-quarter top-down view, **the screen's vertical axis carries two of the world's three axes at once:**

| Moving up the screen | Could mean |
| --- | --- |
| **further away** | the world's depth axis — a tile further north |
| **taller** | the world's height axis — the top of a wall |

**So a 16-pixel vertical line on screen is either a 16-pixel step northward on the ground or a 16-pixel-tall vertical surface, and nothing in the geometry distinguishes them.** This is the central problem of the projection, and every device below exists to solve it.

---

**The four devices, in order of how much work each does:**

**1 — The contact shadow.** §9.1:

> *"Sprites carry only a short contact shadow inside or immediately beside their footprint; long environmental shadows belong to Godot lighting."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | **it marks where the object meets the ground**, which converts an ambiguous shape into an object at a known position |
| **Why it is first on the list** | **it is the cheapest and most effective.** A floating sprite with a shadow under it is standing; the same sprite without one is floating |
| **The rule** | **short, inside or immediately beside the footprint.** Not a long cast shadow — that is `Light2D`'s job |

**2 — The visible front face.** From the box lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | **a vertical surface shows a front face; a flat ground surface does not.** So a 16-pixel rise with a drawn front face is a wall, and 16 pixels of continuing ground texture is a floor |
| **The corollary** | **a flat object lying on the ground must not have a front face**, or it will read as raised. A rug, a path, a scorch mark are drawn purely as top surfaces |

**3 — Y-sorting.** §9.1's *"bottom-centre ground anchor"* and §4's *"Collision and gameplay origin remain at the feet"*:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | **the engine draws lower-on-screen objects in front**, so overlap tells the player what is nearer |
| **Why it needs the anchor** | **the sort key is the anchor's Y, not the sprite's.** A tall tree anchored at its base sorts by its base, which is correct; anchored at its centre it would sort as though it stood halfway up its own trunk |
| **§9.3 checks it** | *"bottom-centre ground/Y-sort anchor"* is one of the eleven checks |

**4 — Value and atmosphere.** Stage 4's material and §2's:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | **a top surface is lighter than a front surface**, because the key light comes from above. So **value alone distinguishes a floor from a wall** |
| **And over distance** | **atmospheric perspective** — Slynyrd's Pixelblog 62 on landscape backgrounds — where further surfaces lose contrast and shift toward the sky's hue. **§2 does not ask for this at gameplay scale** and it matters for backgrounds |

---

**The practical consequence for drawing: decide a thing's height first, and draw it as a height.**

| Thing | Height | How it is drawn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A path, a rug, a scorch** | **zero** | **top surface only.** No front face, no shadow, no outline against the ground beyond a value change |
| **A low step, a kerb, a root** | **a few pixels** | **a thin front face**, a contact shadow at its base |
| **A fence, a wall** | **41–60 px** (§9.2) | **a full front face**, verticals, a contact shadow, and a top face if it is thick enough to have one |
| **A tree, a building** | **tall** | front face, no visible top (it is above the implied view), and **the anchor at the base** |

**That last row is worth noticing.** **A tall object's top eventually passes out of view** — you see a tree's canopy from the side and slightly below its top, not from above. **So the projection's "you see the top" is true for low objects and becomes less true as things get taller**, which is another of the convention's inconsistencies and one that nobody minds.

**Practice.** Draw a 16-pixel vertical rise three ways: as a wall with a front face, as a continuation of ground texture, and as a flat painted path. Look at all three at 300% and confirm which reads as which. Then add a contact shadow to the wall and remove it, and compare. Then draw a 50 px fence run and a flat 50 px path side by side.
The 16-pixel tile and the 8-pixel subgri:
Two grids, what each is for, and the arithmetic that follows from them.

**§9.2 fixes both:**

> *"One world tile is 16 px and the collision/detail subgrid is 8 px."*

| Grid | What it is for |
| --- | --- |
| **16 px — the world tile** | **terrain, placement, footprints, architecture.** The unit the map is built in, and the size of a hand-drawn terrain tile |
| **8 px — the subgrid** | **collision shapes and detail alignment.** Half a tile, so a doorway can be half-tile-aligned and a collision box can be finer than a tile |

---

**What the 16 px tile buys, and why 16 rather than 32 or 8:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Against the character** | **an 80 px adult is five tiles tall.** A tile is **about a fifth of a person**, which is a believable paving stone or floorboard width |
| **Against the viewport** | **960 ÷ 16 = 60 tiles wide; 540 ÷ 16 = 33.75 tiles tall.** So the screen is **60 × 34 tiles**, which is a generous playfield |
| **Against the metre** | **45.7 px per metre, so a tile is about 0.35 m** — roughly a floor tile or a paving slab, and **three tiles is about a metre** |
| **Against drawing effort** | **256 pixels per tile.** Enough for a material with four values and some texture; small enough that a terrain set is achievable |
| **Why not 32** | fewer, larger tiles mean less repetition but **four times the drawing per tile** and a coarser placement grid |
| **Why not 8** | **64 pixels is not enough for a material to read**, and the map becomes four times as many cells to author |

---

**The arithmetic worth having memorised:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 tile** | 16 px ≈ **0.35 m** |
| **3 tiles** | 48 px ≈ **1.05 m** — call it a metre |
| **5 tiles** | 80 px ≈ **1.75 m** — **an adult's height** |
| **A 1 × 1 footprint** | 16 × 16 px of ground |
| **A 6 × 3 footprint** (a cart) | 96 × 48 px of ground |
| **A door's 88 px clear** | **5.5 tiles** — so a doorway is **six tiles wide** in practice, or **five and a half on the subgrid** |
| **The 112 × 112 character frame** | **exactly 7 × 7 tiles** |

**That last line is a pleasing fact and a useful one: the character frame is seven tiles square**, with the figure five tiles tall and the pivot one tile up from the bottom. **16 px of clearance below the feet is exactly one tile.**

---

**Where the subgrid does its work:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Collision** | **a barrel's collision circle does not have to fill its 16 px tile.** An 8 px subgrid lets a 1 × 1 object have a smaller collision footprint than its tile |
| **Alignment of detail** | **a fence post every 8 px rather than every 16**, a window centred on a half-tile, a doorframe's jamb |
| **Half-tile architecture** | a wall thickness, a step depth |
| **And §9.2's separation** | **"Footprint governs collision and placement; real proportion governs visible size"** — the subgrid is where footprint gets finer than the tile |

---

**One warning about the grid in Aseprite.** From stage 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Set the grid to 16 × 16** for terrain and architecture work | |
| **Keep snap-to-grid off for characters** — it will move a two-pixel limb adjustment to the nearest grid line | |
| **And use Select › Selection as Grid** — draw a 16 × 16 marquee and the grid takes its size and alignment from it | |
| **Tilemap mode takes its tile size from the grid**, so getting the grid right is a precondition for stage 8 | |

**Practice.** Open a 112 × 112 file, set the grid to 16 × 16, and confirm it divides into exactly 7 × 7. Mark the pivot at (56, 96) and confirm it sits on a grid intersection one tile up from the bottom. Then draw an 80 px figure silhouette and count the tiles it spans. Then draw a 6-tile-wide doorway and check an 80 px figure fits through with the 88 px clearance §9.2 requires.
45.7 pixels per metre:
The calibration number, where it comes from, and how to use it to size anything that is not in the table.

**The derivation**, §9.2:

> *"One world tile is 16 px and the collision/detail subgrid is 8 px. A normal 80 px adult represents approximately 1.75 m, giving a calibration value of about **45.7 px per metre**."*

**80 ÷ 1.75 = 45.71.** That is the whole of it, and it is the number that lets you size an object you have never drawn.

---

**The conversions worth having:**

| Real size | Pixels |
| --- | --- |
| **10 cm** | **4.6 px** — call it 5 |
| **25 cm** | **11 px** |
| **50 cm** | **23 px** |
| **75 cm** | **34 px** |
| **1 m** | **46 px** |
| **1.5 m** | **69 px** |
| **1.75 m** | **80 px** — an adult |
| **2 m** | **91 px** |
| **2.5 m** | **114 px** |
| **3 m** | **137 px** |

**And the reverse, which is the one you use more:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 px** | **about 2.2 cm** |
| **2 px** | **about 4.4 cm** — so **a one-pixel line is about the width of two fingers** |
| **8 px (the subgrid)** | **about 17 cm** |
| **16 px (a tile)** | **about 35 cm** |

**Hold the 2.2 cm figure.** It makes the detail budget concrete: **a hand is 2–3 px because a hand is 6–8 cm across; an eye is 1 px because an eye is 2–3 cm.** **The medium is not being coy — one pixel genuinely is about the size of a thumbnail.**

---

**Checking §9.2's bands against the calibration.** This is worth doing, because it tests the table:

| Object | Band | At 45.7 px/m that is | Plausible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Bucket** | 14–17 px | **31–37 cm** | **yes** — a domestic pail |
| **Crate** | 21–25 px | **46–55 cm** | yes |
| **Barrel** | 37–45 px | **81–98 cm** | **yes** — a full-size cask |
| **Bench seat** | 19–23 px | **42–50 cm** | **yes** — seat height |
| **Table** | 31–37 px | **68–81 cm** | **yes** — dining height |
| **Round hay bale** | 53–65 px | **1.16–1.42 m** | **yes** — a modern round bale |
| **Dry-stone wall** | 50–60 px | **1.09–1.31 m** | yes |
| **Door opening** | ≥ 88 px | **≥ 1.93 m** | **yes** — and tight. An 80 px figure in a hat needs it |

**All eight check out**, which is a good sign about the table — and §9.2 invites revising it anyway: *"revise the table if drawn evidence shows a systematic problem."*

---

**How to size something not in the table.** Four steps:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **find the real object's size in metres.** A shepherd's crook is about 1.5 m. A sheep is about 1.2 m long and 0.9 m at the shoulder |
| **2** | **multiply by 45.7.** The crook is **69 px**; the sheep is **55 px long and 41 px at the shoulder** |
| **3** | **sanity-check against the figure.** The crook is **86% of the adult's height**, which looks right. The sheep's shoulder is **half the adult's height**, which also looks right |
| **4** | **adjust for readability, deliberately, and write down that you did.** §9.2's own words: *"Footprint governs collision and placement; real proportion governs visible size"* — and §10's rule is that an asset brief states both |

**Step 4 matters.** **Real proportion is the starting point and readability wins.** A sheep at 55 px is correct and might be too small to read in a flock at native scale; **the answer is to decide that deliberately and record it in the brief**, not to drift.

**Practice.** Convert these to pixels at 45.7 px/m: a 1.5 m crook, a 0.9 m sheep shoulder, a 0.6 m dog at the shoulder, a 2.4 m fence, a 0.3 m lamb. Then draw an 80 px figure and put each of those measurements beside it as a plain rectangle, and judge whether each reads at 300%. Then find one object in §9.2's table and work out its real-world size.
Footprint against visible size:
Two separate facts about every object, why the contract insists they are separate, and what each one governs.

**§9.2 states it twice, which is a sign it matters:**

> *"**Footprint governs collision and placement; real proportion governs visible size.** They are separate facts and every prop brief states both."*

And §9.1 again, for standalone props:

> *"independently placeable objects with a **deliberate footprint**, **visible size** and bottom-centre ground anchor"*

---

**The two facts:**

| | Footprint | Visible size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **the ground rectangle the object occupies, in tiles** | **how big the drawn sprite is, in pixels** |
| **What it governs** | **collision, placement, Y-sorting, whether the player can walk there** | **how big the thing looks** |
| **Who uses it** | **the engine, and the level designer** | **the eye** |
| **Measured in** | **tiles** — 1 × 1, 3 × 1, 6 × 3 | **pixels** — 14–17 px high, 100–120 px long |
| **Where it lives** | the collision shape and the tile placement | the sprite |

---

**Why they come apart. Four cases, and each one is a real object in §9.2's table:**

| Case | Example |
| --- | --- |
| **The object overhangs its footprint** | **a table at 4 × 2 tiles is 64 × 32 px of ground, and its drawn length is 55–70 px.** So the top is roughly its footprint — but **its legs are inside the footprint and its top edge is at the back**, so the drawn sprite is taller than the footprint is deep |
| **The object is taller than it is wide** | **a cabinet at 2 × 1 tiles is 32 × 16 px of ground and 74–90 px high.** The footprint says "you cannot walk on two tiles"; the visible size says "it reaches above head height" |
| **The object's collision is smaller than it looks** | **a round hay bale at 2 × 2 is 32 × 32 px of ground and 53–65 px of drawn height.** A bale is a cylinder, so its collision is roughly circular inside the 2 × 2, and **the subgrid is where that is expressed** |
| **The object is flat** | **a firepit or scorch at 1 × 1 and 10–13 px high.** Nearly no height, a full tile of footprint — and the footprint may be walkable or not depending on whether it is a hazard |

---

**And the two errors this separation prevents:**

| Error | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- |
| **Sizing the sprite from the footprint** | **a 1 × 1 barrel drawn 16 px tall because its footprint is 16 px.** A real barrel is 37–45 px. **The footprint is the ground, not the height** |
| **Sizing the footprint from the sprite** | **a cart drawn 110 px long and given a 7-tile footprint because 110 ÷ 16 ≈ 7.** §9.2 says **6 × 3**, because the cart's shafts and handles overhang and **a player should be able to walk past the end of them** |

**That second error is the more common and the more annoying in play** — invisible collision where the sprite looks like empty space. **The footprint is a gameplay decision; the sprite is a drawing.**

---

**What an asset brief therefore has to state.** §10.2:

> *"Before drawing, an asset brief identifies its **subject, states, directions, actions, frame geometry, anchor, palette subset and runtime consumer**."*

**For a prop that means, minimally:**

| Field | Example — a bucket |
| --- | --- |
| **Subject** | a domestic wooden pail, York |
| **Footprint** | **1 × 1** |
| **Visible size** | **15 px high**, about 12 px wide at the mouth |
| **Frame geometry** | **a canvas large enough with margin** — not 112 × 112; a prop needs only its own size plus room for the shadow |
| **Anchor** | **bottom-centre** |
| **Palette subset** | **4–10 colours** (§10.1), from the wood and metal ramps |
| **States** | **one** — static. (A bucket that can be kicked over would have two) |
| **Runtime consumer** | a placed prop in the York scene |

**Stage 7 writes that brief for real and then draws the bucket.**

**Practice.** For five objects in §9.2's table, write down the footprint in tiles, the footprint in pixels, and the visible size — and note which of the four cases above each one is. Then take the cart at 6 × 3 and 100–120 px long and work out how much of its drawn length overhangs its footprint. Then write a one-paragraph brief for a prop of your own choosing with all eight §10.2 fields.
The ground anchor and the contact shadow:
Where an object meets the ground, how that is recorded, and the small dark shape that does more work than any other pixel in a prop.

**Two things, and they are the same decision from two directions: where is the ground?**

---

**The anchor.** §9.1 and §4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For props** | *"a deliberate footprint, visible size and **bottom-centre ground anchor**"* |
| **For characters** | *"Standard bottom-centre pivot: **(56, 96)**"*, and *"Collision and gameplay origin remain **at the feet**"* |
| **What it does** | **it is the point the engine positions, sorts and collides from** |
| **Why bottom-centre** | **because that is where the object touches the ground**, so positioning it positions the object in the world rather than on the screen |
| **§9.3 checks it** | *"bottom-centre ground/Y-sort anchor"* |

**And the practical consequence for drawing:** **the anchor is a point on the canvas, and the drawing has to be placed relative to it.** A bucket drawn in the middle of its canvas with the anchor at the bottom-centre of the canvas **will float**, because the bucket's base is not at the canvas's base.

**So: the object's lowest ground-touching pixel sits at the anchor's row, centred on the anchor's column.** For a character at (56, 96) that means the soles are at row 96, with 16 rows of canvas below them — the clearance a jump or a crouch needs.

---

**The contact shadow.** §9.1:

> *"Sprites carry only a **short contact shadow inside or immediately beside their footprint**; long environmental shadows belong to Godot lighting. **Do not bake a floor or scenery behind a standalone object.**"*

**Three clauses:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Short, and inside or immediately beside the footprint** | **not a cast shadow.** A few pixels of darkening where the object meets the ground |
| **Long shadows belong to Godot** | **because a baked cast shadow has a fixed direction**, and a scene lit by a torch that moves would have the baked shadow pointing the wrong way |
| **No baked floor** | **the object is transparent outside itself.** §9.3's *"transparent isolation where applicable"* |

**How to draw one:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shape** | **an ellipse at the projection ratio**, matching the object's footprint — so a 1 × 1 object gets an ellipse about 14 wide and 5–7 tall |
| **Position** | **centred on the anchor**, extending a pixel or two beyond the object's base on the lower-right and barely at all on the upper-left — **because the key light is at the upper-left (§10.1)** |
| **Value** | **one or two values darker than the ground it sits on** — and since the ground varies, **the shadow is usually drawn in a dark neutral from `TERR-001`–`004`**, which is listed for *"contact accents"* |
| **Edges** | **hard.** No soft falloff — there are no intermediate values |
| **Layer** | **its own**, per §3.1's four-layer rule — so the runtime can treat it separately and so the black test can exclude it |

---

**Why the contact shadow matters more than it looks.** Three jobs:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — It resolves height against depth** | the last lesson's central ambiguity. **A sprite with a contact shadow is standing on the ground; without one it is floating at an unknown height** |
| **2 — It separates the object from the ground value** | so a mid-value barrel on mid-value earth still reads, because **there is a dark line between them** |
| **3 — It anchors motion** | **in an animation, the contact shadow is what makes the feet look planted.** §4: *"Ground contact must be stable in every frame"*, and a shadow that stays put while the body moves is how that reads |

**And one case where it changes.** **A jumping or falling character's shadow stays on the ground and shrinks** — it does not travel up with the body. §6.1 lists Eli's *"stoop-down, hold and rise"* and §6.2 Pip's *"pounce"*; **in both the shadow is a separate piece of timing from the body**, which is stage 10's work.

**Practice.** Draw a 1 × 1 crate with its base at the canvas's anchor row and a contact shadow on its own layer. Then hide the shadow layer and compare — decide whether the crate is still standing on the ground. Then draw a barrel on a mid-value earth tile and check it separates. Then draw the same barrel with a long cast shadow and note what §9.1 says about it.
Consistency across assets:
The projection's real test: two assets drawn weeks apart have to belong in the same scene, and the five things that have to match.

**A projection is only worth having if it is kept.** An asset that is internally consistent and inconsistent with its neighbours is worse than one that is slightly wrong in the same way as everything else.

**The five things that must match across every asset:**

| | What | How it goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **the top-face ratio** | one crate's top is half its depth and the next one's is two-thirds. **The two read as being seen from different heights** |
| **2** | **the key light direction** | **§10.1: upper-left, always.** An asset lit from the upper-right in a scene lit from the upper-left reads as glowing |
| **3** | **the pixel density** | stage 2's lesson — **45.7 px per metre, and the same detail budget per asset class** |
| **4** | **the palette** | **§9.3: *"palette compatibility"*.** Two stone objects from two different ramps do not look like the same stone |
| **5** | **the contact shadow's treatment** | same shape, same value, same offset. **An asset with a darker or longer shadow sits at a different height** |

---

**How to keep them, practically. Four mechanisms:**

**1 — A reference file.** From stage 1's reference layers:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it holds** | **a character silhouette at 80 px, a 16 px grid, a 1 × 1 and a 2 × 2 footprint, a shaded reference box at the project's top-face ratio, and a contact shadow** |
| **How it is used** | **as a reference layer in every new asset file.** §9.2's own instruction: *"Validate them beside the real character at native scale"* |
| **Why a file and not a memory** | **the ratio is a number you will not remember in three weeks**, and a drawn reference does not drift |

**2 — Draw in families, not one at a time.** §9.1's *"modular architecture"* implies it and §13 will state it:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The principle** | **all the crates, then all the barrels** — because consistency within a sitting is free and consistency across sittings is work |
| **And the counter-principle, from `CLAUDE.md`** | *"Work one asset, action and direction at a time so each authored animation can be reviewed in Godot before the next family expands."* |
| **The reconciliation** | **one at a time for review, in families for drawing.** Draw the family, review the first one in Godot, then accept or redraw the rest |

**3 — Check new against old at native scale.** Not against the reference in isolation:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The method** | **put the new asset in a scene with three accepted ones, at 300%, and look** |
| **What it catches** | **everything the reference file cannot** — relative detail density, relative contrast, whether it looks like it belongs |

**4 — The validator.** From stage 1 and stage 12: **palette conformance, canvas size and colour count are mechanical and can be checked by a script.** The ratio and the light direction cannot.

---

**And the honest problem: the first asset sets the standard, and the first asset is the worst one you will draw.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why** | **you are learning.** Asset one is drawn with less skill than asset fifty |
| **The consequence** | **either everything matches asset one and the whole set is weak, or the set drifts as you improve** |
| **The answer, from §3** | **"Rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived."** **Redraw the early ones.** The contract expects it — nothing is approved until Master Roachi approves the actual asset, and an asset that no longer matches is superseded |
| **And the practical version** | **expect to redraw the first three or four props and the first character.** Budget for it rather than defending them |

**Practice.** Build the reference file described above and save it as a template. Then draw three 1 × 1 props in one sitting and check them against each other at 300%. Then draw a fourth tomorrow and compare it with the three — note the five things from the table and whether any drifted. Then put all four in one image and decide which one you would redraw.
The seven projection failures:
The stage's closing checklist: what a projection error actually looks like, and how to diagnose one from the symptom.

**The diagnostic problem is that a projection error does not look like a projection error.** It looks like the asset is "off", or "doesn't fit", or "looks like a different game". **These are the seven causes, with the symptom first.**

---

**1 — The asset reads as isometric.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | the object looks rotated relative to its neighbours; the scene feels like two games spliced together |
| **Cause** | **two side faces visible, or a diamond footprint** |
| **The rule broken** | §9.1: *"not diamond isometric"* |
| **Fix** | redraw with one front face and a square footprint |

**2 — Converging or leaning edges.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | the object appears to tip over, or to be seen from a specific spot on screen |
| **Cause** | **vertical edges drawn at a slope**, usually from drawing a building "in perspective" |
| **The rule broken** | *"Vertical edges stay vertical; floors do not converge"* |
| **Fix** | every vertical is a vertical pixel line |

**3 — The wrong top-face ratio.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | the object looks taller or flatter than its neighbours, or looks like a different kind of object |
| **Cause** | **the top face foreshortened differently from the rest of the project** |
| **How to catch it** | **put it beside the reference box** |
| **And the subtle version** | **a top face not foreshortened at all**, which turns a box into an upright panel |

**4 — No top face where there should be one, or one where there should not.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | a low object floats; a flat object looks raised |
| **Cause** | **drawing a low object in pure side view** (no top), or **a flat ground marking with a front face** (which gives it height) |
| **The rule** | from the height-against-depth lesson: **zero height means top surface only** |

**5 — A baked floor or cast shadow.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | a rectangle of slightly different ground appears around the object when it is placed on different terrain; or the shadow points the wrong way when a light moves |
| **Cause** | **ground drawn into the sprite**, or **a long cast shadow baked in** |
| **The rule broken** | §9.1: *"Do not bake a floor or scenery behind a standalone object"*, and *"long environmental shadows belong to Godot lighting"* |
| **And §9.3's check** | *"transparent isolation where applicable"* |

**6 — The anchor is not at the bottom-centre of the ground contact.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | **the object sorts wrongly** — a character walks behind something they should be in front of — or the object jumps when placed |
| **Cause** | the anchor at the canvas centre, or at the sprite's bounding-box bottom rather than the object's ground contact |
| **The rule** | §9.1 and §4, and §9.3's *"bottom-centre ground/Y-sort anchor"* |
| **And the trim trap from stage 1** | **trimming a frame moves the anchor**, so this failure is often an export setting rather than a drawing |

**7 — Scale drift.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | the object is the wrong size for what it is; a door an adult cannot fit through |
| **Cause** | **drawn to look right alone rather than measured against 45.7 px per metre and the figure** |
| **The check** | **§9.2's 88 px clear door opening**, and the reference silhouette |

---

**And the single diagnostic that catches six of the seven: put the asset next to an 80-pixel character silhouette, a 16 px grid and an accepted reference box, at 300%.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Isometric** | obvious immediately |
| **Leaning verticals** | obvious against the grid |
| **Wrong ratio** | obvious against the reference box |
| **Missing or wrong top face** | obvious |
| **Baked floor** | obvious against a different ground |
| **Scale drift** | obvious against the figure |
| **The anchor** | **the one it does not catch** — that needs Godot, or a measurement |

**That is why §9.2's instruction is what it is:** *"Validate them beside the real character at native scale."*

**Practice.** Draw one asset with each of the seven failures deliberately, and look at each beside the reference file. Then take the best prop you have drawn in this stage and check it against all seven. Then write the seven as a checklist you can run in two minutes, and keep it.
Why value before colour:
The stage's thesis: value does the work and colour does identity, and almost every sprite that fails fails on value.

**The two properties, separated:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Value** | **how light or dark something is**, independent of its hue. Greyscale is value with everything else removed |
| **Hue and saturation** | **what colour it is, and how intensely** |

**And the claim: value carries form, depth, separation and readability. Hue carries identity and mood, and almost nothing else.**

---

**The evidence, from the contract itself.** §10.1's requirements, sorted by which property each one is about:

| Requirement | Value or hue? |
| --- | --- |
| *"three or four purposeful values per major material"* | **value** |
| *"The authored key light comes from the upper-left; shadows and undersides favour the lower-right"* | **value** |
| *"identifiable in solid black"* | **value — in fact, silhouette, which is value's limit case** |
| *"identifiable in grayscale"* | **value, explicitly** |
| *"identifiable in dark lighting"* | **value** |
| *"identifiable … in a busy party scene"* | **value — separation from surroundings** |
| *"Preserve useful negative gaps"* | **value** |
| *"Use a dark coloured one-pixel outline"* | **value, with a hue constraint** |
| *"Identity cannot depend on hue"* | **explicitly not hue** |
| *"a normal hero usually uses 12–18 opaque base colours"* | the only clause about colour count |

**Nine of ten clauses are value clauses, and one says identity may not depend on hue at all.** §10.1 is a value specification with a colour note attached.

---

**Why that is true of this medium specifically.** Four reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Scale** | **at 80 px a character has no detail that is not a value boundary.** A fold, an edge, a strap, a jaw — each is a place where one value stops and another starts |
| **2 — The crowd** | **§2 requires readability during *"movement, combat, crowds, darkness and effects"*.** In a crowd, hue is noise — six characters in different colours read as one coloured mass. **Value is what separates them** |
| **3 — The lighting** | **`Light2D` changes hue and saturation freely and compresses value.** A sprite whose readability depends on hue stops reading under a coloured light; **a sprite whose readability is in value survives** |
| **4 — The palette** | **the palette is built as value ramps.** `Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light` is a value sequence with hue along for the ride — so **the tool the project gives you is a value tool** |

---

**The practical order this stage establishes**, and it is the order every lesson in stages 6 to 11 follows:

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **silhouette** — the shape, in one value. §10.1's black test lives here |
| **2** | **the big value boundary** — where light becomes shadow across the whole form |
| **3** | **the third and fourth values** — Light where it faces the key, Deep in recesses |
| **4** | **then hue** — which ramp each material takes |
| **5** | **then the outline** |
| **6** | **then material texture, and stop** |

**Steps 1 to 3 are this stage. Step 4 is stage 5. Step 6 is stage 6.** And **drawing in that order is the single biggest practical change this curriculum asks for**, because the instinct is to pick colours first.

**Practice.** Take any sprite — yours or a reference — and make a greyscale copy with the Color-mode layer from stage 1. Look at both at 300%. Then look at the greyscale one alone for thirty seconds and ask whether you could still tell what it is. Then draw a small object in four greys only, and only afterwards assign a ramp to it.
The four-value material:
What each of the four values is for, in the palette's own vocabulary, and how to decide where each one goes.

**The palette names them**, and `colour-palette.md` fixes the order:

> *"Build materials and effects from purposeful four-step ramps in the fixed value order: **`Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light`**."*

**So every one of the 33 ramps is four values in that order**, and the four have jobs:

| Value | Its job | Roughly how much of a surface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mid** | **the material's local colour** — what it looks like in neutral light. **The default, and the largest area** | **50–60%** |
| **Shadow** | **where the surface turns away from the key light** — the form shadow | **25–35%** |
| **Light** | **where the surface faces the key light** directly | **10–15%** |
| **Deep** | **recesses, undersides, contact points and the outline** — where light cannot reach at all | **5–10%** |

**Those proportions are the lesson.** The commonest beginner distribution is roughly equal quarters, which produces a sprite with no dominant value and therefore no read. **A material is mostly its Mid.**

---

**Where each value goes, concretely.** Taking a cloaked figure's torso:

| Value | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **Light** | **the top of the shoulder, the upper-left of the chest** — surfaces facing up and left |
| **Mid** | **the front of the chest and most of the cloak** — surfaces facing the viewer |
| **Shadow** | **the right side of the torso, the underside of the shoulder, the cloak's far side** |
| **Deep** | **under the chin, where the arm meets the torso, under a belt, the outline** |

**And the distinction that matters most and is most often missed: Shadow and Deep are different things.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shadow is a form shadow** | **the surface is turned away from the light.** It is a function of **direction** |
| **Deep is occlusion** | **light cannot reach, because something is in the way.** It is a function of **proximity** |
| **So** | **the right side of a cylinder is Shadow. The crevice where two cylinders touch is Deep** — and it is Deep on both of them, including on the lit side |
| **Which is why** | **a sprite with Deep used only on the shadow side looks flat**, and one with Deep in the crevices reads as solid |

---

**The four values as four questions**, which is the working method:

| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| **"Does this face up or toward the upper-left?"** | **Light** |
| **"Does this face the viewer?"** | **Mid** |
| **"Does this face away from the upper-left?"** | **Shadow** |
| **"Is something else in the way of the light here?"** | **Deep** |

**Ask them in that order on every surface, and the shading is determined.** The art is in deciding what "faces up" means for a pixel cluster three pixels across — which is judgement, and judgement is what the practice builds.

---

**One note on the ramps themselves.** §9.3:

> *"The Master Palette remains the colour authority. A scene curates only the material ramps it needs."*

**So you do not choose four values. You choose a ramp, and the four values come with it.** A cloth object is `TERR-005` to `008`: Burnt Cloth, Weathered Taupe, Dust Wool, Faded Linen. **The decision is which ramp, not which greys** — which is stage 5's subject, and it is why this stage can be learned in greyscale and then applied.

**Practice.** Draw a 24 × 24 cloth form in four values at roughly 55 / 30 / 10 / 5 proportions, and then again in four equal quarters, and compare at 300%. Then take the four questions and apply them to each cluster in the first version, checking each one is answerable. Then find three places where Deep belongs on the lit side of the form.
Why three or four, and not six:
The contract's number, the four reasons behind it, and the arithmetic that shows it is not arbitrary.

**§10.1:**

> *"Use approximately **three or four purposeful values per major material**."*

**"Approximately" and "purposeful" are both doing work.** The number is a discipline, not a count to hit — and the reasons are worth having, because they tell you when the number may bend.

---

**Reason 1 — The arithmetic of the colour bands.** §10.1 again:

> *"A normal hero usually uses **12–18 opaque base colours**, an ordinary enemy **8–26** and a small prop **4–10**."*

**Divide by four:**

| Asset | Colours | ÷ 4 values | So the number of materials |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **A small prop** | **4–10** | | **one to two and a half materials** |
| **A hero** | **12–18** | | **three to four and a half materials** |
| **An ordinary enemy** | **8–26** | | **two to six** |

**A hero gets three or four materials.** Skin, cloth, leather, metal — and that is the budget. **Which means the four-value rule and the colour band are the same rule stated twice**, and either one implies the other.

**And `colour-palette.md`'s own figures are tighter still:** *"Ordinary enemies should generally use about 8–14 colours. Heroes should generally use about 12–18."*

---

**Reason 2 — Readability at scale.** From stage 2's detail budget:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A material's area on a character** | **often 200 to 400 pixels** |
| **At six values** | **each value gets 30–70 pixels**, which is **a cluster or two.** A value occupying two clusters is not a value; it is a detail |
| **At four values** | the Mid alone gets 120–220 pixels, **which is an area the eye can read as a surface** |

**Reason 3 — Banding.** Stage 2's lesson: **more values means more boundaries, and every boundary is a chance for two to run parallel.** Four values give three boundaries; six give five. **The failure rate goes up faster than the fidelity.**

**Reason 4 — The lighting, and this is the project-specific one.** §10.1:

> *"Static shading stays restrained **so Godot's local lights can read coherently**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What a runtime light does** | **shifts and compresses the whole sprite's value range** |
| **A four-value sprite under a light** | **four values, shifted. Still four distinguishable steps** |
| **A six-value sprite under a light** | **six values compressed into the range a light leaves**, so **adjacent steps merge and the sprite loses the distinctions you drew** |
| **So** | **fewer baked values survive lighting better**, and the contract's reason is a technical one with a craft consequence |

---

**When the number may bend**, because "approximately" invites the question:

| Case | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| **A large area that must transition** | **a wall, a floor, a sky** — **five steps across 200 pixels is defensible**, and dithering between two is the alternative |
| **A material with a genuine specular highlight** | **metal.** A fifth value at the very top — one small cluster of a near-white — is how metal reads as metal, and **the palette provides it**: `TERR-012` Pale Steel above the Mid, or `TERR-104` Sacred White for a true specular |
| **A supernatural effect** | **`colour-palette.md`: *"Reserve the strongest saturation and brightness for supernatural effects and gameplay telegraph accents"*.** Shepherd Light, Beacon energy and fire are not ordinary materials and are not bound by the four-value rule |
| **Where it must not bend** | **an ordinary material on a character.** §10.1's identity tests are the reason, and three materials at four values each is already eighteen colours |

**Practice.** Take a material and shade it in six values, then reduce to four by merging the two pairs that are closest, and compare at 300%. Then count the colours in a sprite you have drawn and divide by four, and check the answer against the number of materials you think it has. Then shade a metal object in four values plus one specular cluster and see whether the fifth earns its place.
The upper-left key light:
The contract's light direction, why a single fixed direction matters more than which direction it is, and what it means for each surface.

**§10.1:**

> *"The authored key light comes from the **upper-left**; shadows and undersides favour the **lower-right**."*

**And §9.1, for environments:**

> *"Use an **upper-left key** and restrained **lower-right form shade**."*

**Two documents, one direction, stated twice.** It is not a suggestion.

---

**Why a fixed direction at all.** Three reasons, and the first is sufficient:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Consistency is the whole value of it** | **every asset in the game is lit the same way, so every asset belongs in the same scene.** An asset lit from the upper-right in a scene lit from the upper-left reads as glowing or as pasted in — stage 3's consistency lesson |
| **2 — It frees the runtime** | the baked light is a **constant**, so `Light2D`'s contribution is the **variable.** If every asset's baked light pointed somewhere different, the runtime light would be fighting a different battle on each sprite |
| **3 — It is the convention** | **upper-left is the overwhelming default in pixel art and in Western painting**, so it reads as "lit" without anyone noticing it was a choice |

**And why upper-left specifically rather than upper-right:** **convention, and nothing else.** Any single direction would work. **Upper-left is what the eye expects because most art does it, and that is a good enough reason — the cost of being unconventional here is zero benefit.**

---

**What it means surface by surface.** Taking the primitives from stage 3:

| Surface | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **A horizontal top face** | **Light** — it faces up, and the light is above |
| **A vertical face pointing up-left** | **Light** |
| **A vertical face pointing toward the viewer** | **Mid** |
| **A vertical face pointing down-right** | **Shadow** |
| **An underside** | **Shadow or Deep** |
| **A crevice, whatever its direction** | **Deep** |

**And on a sphere or cylinder**, where the surface turns continuously:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The highlight** | **upper-left quadrant**, about a third in from the edge |
| **The terminator** (light-to-shadow boundary) | **running from lower-left to upper-right**, perpendicular to the light direction |
| **The core shadow** | **just inside the lower-right edge** |
| **The contact shadow on the ground** | **extending to the lower-right**, barely at all to the upper-left |

**That last row is the one people forget.** **A contact shadow is a shadow, so it goes away from the light** — down and to the right.

---

**Two practical consequences.**

**1 — The outline varies with it.** From stage 2's selective outlining:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Upper-left outline** | **lighter, or absent** |
| **Lower-right outline** | **darkest** |

**2 — The eight directions all have the same light.** This is the one that surprises people:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The question** | if a character turns to face north-east, does the light turn with them? |
| **The answer** | **no. The light is in the world, not on the character** |
| **So** | **the north-facing drawing has its light on its upper-left, and so does the south-facing one** — which means **the lit side of the character's body changes as they turn.** Facing south, their right shoulder is lit; facing north, their left shoulder is |
| **Why this matters** | **it is a real asymmetry between the eight drawings**, and **it is one more reason §5.4 forbids mirroring**: a flipped sprite has its light coming from the upper-*right* |

**That consequence is worth sitting with.** **Mirroring does not only swap handedness and costume — it reverses the lighting.** A flipped west-facing sprite is lit from the wrong side, and in a scene where everything else is lit from the upper-left it will read as wrong even if the character is perfectly symmetrical.

**Practice.** Draw a sphere lit from the upper-left, then flip it horizontally and put the two side by side — note that the flipped one is now lit from the upper-right and looks wrong beside the first. Then draw a simple box in all four cardinal orientations, keeping the light fixed at upper-left in every one, and check that the lit face changes. Then draw a contact shadow for each and confirm all four extend to the lower-right.
The lower-right form shade, and restrain:
The other half of the clause: how much shadow, and the technical reason the contract asks for less than instinct wants.

**§10.1's full sentence:**

> *"The authored key light comes from the upper-left; shadows and undersides favour the lower-right. **Static shading stays restrained so Godot's local lights can read coherently**."*

**And §9.1's version:** *"Use an upper-left key and **restrained** lower-right form shade."*

**"Restrained" is the operative word in both, and it is a technical requirement rather than an aesthetic preference.**

---

**What the technical requirement actually is.** This is worth understanding properly, because the instinct to shade more strongly is strong and the reason not to is not obvious.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How a 2D light works** | **`Light2D` multiplies or adds to the sprite's existing colours**, within a region. So the final pixel is **a function of the baked value and the light's contribution** |
| **A heavily shaded sprite** | has **a wide baked value range**. Its darkest pixels are near the bottom of the palette's range and its lightest near the top |
| **Put it under a light** | **the light's contribution has nowhere to go on the light side** — the lit pixels are already near the top — **and the dark side stays dark regardless** |
| **The result** | **the runtime light has little visible effect**, and what effect it has lands on the mid-tones only. **The sprite looks unlit** |
| **A restrained sprite** | has **a narrow baked range clustered around its Mid** — so **the light has room to work in both directions**, and the sprite visibly responds |

**So: the less you bake, the more the game can light.** And §2's whole atmospheric promise depends on it — *"Godot `Light2D`, restrained overlays and optional normal maps may add atmosphere without making characters or hazards unreadable."*

---

**What restraint means in practice. Four rules:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Mid dominates** | **50 to 60% of a material's area**, from the four-value lesson. If the Shadow is winning, the sprite is over-shaded |
| **2 — Deep is for occlusion only** | **not for "more shadow".** A sprite with large Deep areas has spent its darkest value on form rather than on contact, and **it will be unreadable in dark lighting** |
| **3 — The Light step is small** | **10 to 15%.** A broad Light area reads as a white-hot surface and leaves the runtime light nothing to add |
| **4 — No second light source** | **one key, upper-left.** No rim light from the lower-right, no bounce light, no coloured fill. **Those are the runtime's job**, and baking them makes the sprite look like a specific lighting situation |

**Rule 4 is the one that costs most to accept**, because a rim light is the single easiest way to make a sprite look professional in isolation. **It also makes it look wrong in every scene that is not lit from behind.**

---

**And the honest tension**, which is worth stating because it is real:

| The case for restraint | The case for stronger shading |
| --- | --- |
| **the runtime can light it** — so a restrained sprite looks right in many lighting conditions | **a restrained sprite looks flat in isolation**, which makes it hard to judge and hard to be proud of |
| **it survives `Light2D`, darkness and crowds** — §10.1's four identity conditions | **most beautiful pixel art is strongly shaded**, because most pixel art is not lit at runtime |
| **it is cheaper** — fewer values, fewer boundaries, less banding | **form reads better with more shading**, and §2 does want *"materially specific"* |
| **§2 and §10.1 both require it in writing** | | 

**The resolution the contract already made: readability under lighting wins.** And the practical consequence: **judge a sprite in Godot under a light, not in Aseprite on a checkerboard** — which is §10's seventh condition and stage 7's round trip. **A sprite that looks slightly flat in Aseprite and right in the game is correct.**

**Practice.** Draw the same cylinder twice: once with Mid at 55% and the Light step small, once strongly shaded with a broad Light and a large Deep. Then put both in Godot under a `Light2D` from the right and compare which responds. If Godot is not to hand, approximate it: add a layer in Multiply at 40% over both and see which retains its internal distinctions.
Ambient occlusion in four values:
The darkening where surfaces meet, why it is a different thing from the form shadow, and the one value it is allowed to use.

**Ambient occlusion is the darkening that happens where a surface is close to another surface**, because ambient light cannot get into the gap. **It has nothing to do with the direction of the key light.**

**The distinction, stated as cleanly as possible:**

| | Form shadow | Occlusion |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Caused by** | **the surface turning away from the light** | **another surface being in the way** |
| **A function of** | **direction** | **proximity** |
| **Which value** | **Shadow** | **Deep** |
| **Where** | the lower-right of every form | **every crevice, junction, overlap and contact — on the lit side too** |
| **Changes if the light moves** | **yes** | **no** |

**That last row is why occlusion is the shading you are allowed to bake generously.** A form shadow baked into a sprite is a claim about where the light is, and `Light2D` may contradict it. **Occlusion is true under any light**, so baking it costs nothing and it is what makes a sprite read as solid rather than as a flat shape with a dark side.

---

**Where occlusion goes on a character.** This list is most of what separates a solid-looking sprite from a flat one:

| Place | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Under the chin, above the chest** | the head overhangs the neck |
| **Where an arm meets the torso** | **on both sides, including the lit one** |
| **Under a belt, a collar, a hem, a cuff** | cloth overlapping cloth |
| **Where a strap crosses the body** | **on the body, under the strap's lower edge** |
| **Inside a hood, under a hat's brim** | the deepest occlusion on a figure |
| **Between the legs** | and under each foot at the ground |
| **Where equipment touches the body** | a satchel against a hip, a quiver against a back |
| **Under the nose, if there is a nose** | at 80 px there is not |

**And on environments**, §9.1's asset classes:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where a wall meets the floor** | **a one-pixel Deep line along the base.** This single line does more for an interior than any amount of wall texture |
| **Inside a doorway or a window** | the recess |
| **Under a table top, a bench seat, a shelf** | |
| **Where a prop meets the ground** | **which is the contact shadow** — occlusion by another name |
| **Between stacked objects** | crates on crates |

---

**The rule for how much.** Occlusion is **narrow and dark**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Width** | **one pixel, usually. Two where the overlap is deep** — a hood, a deep recess |
| **Value** | **Deep** — the ramp's darkest step. And `TERR-001`–`004` are listed for *"deepest recesses, undersides, contact accents"* |
| **Falloff** | **none.** There is no room and no value for it. One pixel of Deep against the Mid |
| **Extent** | **it hugs the junction.** Occlusion that spreads across a surface is a form shadow drawn in the wrong value |

**The commonest error is the last one: using Deep as "more shadow".** A sprite with large Deep areas has spent its darkest value describing form, which means **in dark lighting those areas merge with the background and the sprite loses its silhouette** — exactly the failure §10.1's *"identifiable in dark lighting"* is guarding against.

---

**And the one-pixel line that is worth more than anything else in this lesson:** **a line of Deep where the figure meets the ground.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is occlusion** | the ground and the foot are in contact |
| **It is also the contact shadow** | stage 3's device, which resolves height against depth |
| **It is also the thing that makes a figure stand** | §4: *"Ground contact must be stable in every frame"* |
| **And it is about eight pixels of work** | for the single largest readability gain available |

**Practice.** Draw a figure's torso with an arm across it and add occlusion at the junction — one pixel of Deep, on both sides of the arm, including the lit side. Then draw a wall meeting a floor with and without a one-pixel Deep line at the base, and compare. Then take a sprite with large Deep areas, reduce the Deep to junctions only, and look at both against a dark background.
The black test:
§10.1's first identity test: what it checks, how to run it, and the five things that make a sprite pass.

**The clause:**

> *"Every playable hero must remain identifiable in **solid black**, grayscale, dark lighting and a busy party scene. Identity cannot depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail."*

**Solid black is the harshest of the four**, and it tests exactly one thing: **the silhouette.**

---

**How to run it.** Two minutes, in Aseprite:

| Step | How |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **duplicate the body and equipment layers**, merged |
| **2** | **select all, then fill with `TERR-001` using Lock Alpha ink** — so only the drawn pixels change |
| **3** | **hide the original layers** |
| **4** | **look at it at 300% against a mid-value background** |
| **5** | **keep it as a hidden layer in the file** — stage 1's toggle approach, so the test is one click thereafter |

**Exclude the contact shadow layer** — it is not part of the figure's silhouette, and including it makes the figure look like it has a puddle.

---

**What passing looks like.** Three questions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Can you tell it is a person?** | the proportions and stance read |
| **2 — Can you tell which person?** | **the hard one.** With four heroes in black, are they distinguishable? |
| **3 — Can you tell what they are doing?** | **pose readability**, which §10.1 ranks alongside silhouette |

---

**The five things that make a sprite pass.** In order of how much each contributes:

| | What | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Head and hair shape** | **the single largest identity carrier.** A hood, a hat, a tied-back shape, a tall silhouette — at 80 px the head is 12 px and its outline is unmistakable |
| **2** | **Equipment that breaks the outline** | **§10.1: *"allow signature equipment to break the torso silhouette"*.** A crook over a shoulder, a satchel on a hip, a sling at a belt, a quiver. **Anything that projects beyond the body is visible in black** |
| **3** | **Build and proportion** | height, shoulder width, whether the figure is broad or slight |
| **4** | **Stance** | **feet apart or together, weight on one leg, shoulders square or turned.** §5.1's idle has *"3–5 meaningful poses"*, and the pose is part of the identity |
| **5** | **Negative gaps** | the next lesson — **the holes in the silhouette.** A gap between an arm and the torso is as recognisable as the arm |

**And the five things that do not help at all**, which is the clause's point: **colour, a glow, jewellery, facial features, and interior detail of any kind.** All of them vanish in black.

---

**What a failure looks like, and the three usual causes:**

| Cause | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The outline is closed** | **the figure is one undifferentiated blob** — arms merged into the torso, legs merged together | **negative gaps**, the next lesson |
| **The silhouette is generic** | it is clearly a person and could be any person | **add a signature**: hair shape, a hat, equipment that projects |
| **Identity was in the interior** | the character is told apart by their tunic's colour or their face | **move identity outward** — this is a design change, not a shading fix, and §2.1 puts **Terrath canon** and **`characters.md`** above the drawing for identity |

**That last row has a process consequence worth naming.** **A black-test failure caused by a generic silhouette is not fixable by drawing better** — it needs a design decision about what the character looks like, which is **Timon's, who has final say on design.** §2.1's priority order and §10's approval rule both point the same way: **surface it rather than inventing a hat.**

**Practice.** Run the black test on any character sprite and answer the three questions. Then draw the same figure's silhouette three times, adding one identity carrier each time from the list of five, and run the test after each. Then take two existing characters, put their black silhouettes side by side at 300%, and decide whether you could name each.
The grey test:
The second identity test: what greyscale reveals that colour conceals, and the specific failure it exists to catch.

**The clause, again:**

> *"identifiable in solid black, **grayscale**, dark lighting and a busy party scene."*

**Greyscale removes hue and saturation and leaves value.** It is less harsh than the black test — interior detail survives — and it catches a different and more common failure.

---

**The failure it catches: two materials with different hues and the same value.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **In colour** | **a green tunic against a red belt reads clearly** — the hues are opposite and the eye separates them instantly |
| **In greyscale** | **if both are at the same value step, they merge into one shape.** The belt disappears |
| **Why this matters in play** | **three reasons.** `Light2D` desaturates toward its own hue; at native scale in a crowd, hue blends and value does not; and **a colour-blind player sees something closer to the greyscale version than to the colour one** |
| **And it is invisible while drawing** | because you are looking at the colour version, where it reads perfectly |

**This is the most common value failure in a sprite that looks good**, and it is why the test exists as a separate requirement from the black test.

---

**How to run it.** From stage 1, as a toggle:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The method** | **a top layer filled with any colour, blend mode `Color`, visibility off.** One click to greyscale, one click back |
| **Why not convert the sprite** | **Sprite › Color Mode › Grayscale is destructive** and loses the palette. The layer toggle is non-destructive and instant |
| **Why not just squint** | squinting removes detail, not hue. **It is a different test and also worth doing** |
| **Keep it in the template** | so every file has it |

---

**What to look for, in order:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Does every material still separate from its neighbours?** | the core of the test |
| **2 — Does the figure still separate from the background?** | put a mid-grey behind it |
| **3 — Is there a readable value hierarchy?** | **the lightest thing, the darkest thing, and a clear middle.** A sprite that is uniformly mid-grey has no hierarchy and will look muddy under any light |
| **4 — Did anything you thought was a highlight disappear?** | **a saturated colour can read as bright without being light.** A saturated gold next to a mid grey looks like a highlight and is the same value — so **in greyscale the highlight vanishes** |

**Point 4 is the subtle one and it is specific to this palette.** `TERR-099` **Grace Gold `#C99B3E`** is vivid and is a **Mid**, not a Light. **A gold accent is not a highlight unless you also move it up its ramp.**

---

**How to fix a grey-test failure.** Three options, in order of preference:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Move one material along its own ramp** | **the belt was at Mid; put it at Shadow.** Costs nothing, stays on-palette, keeps the hue |
| **2 — Choose a different ramp with a different value range** | **the palette's 33 ramps have different lightness ranges** — `TERR-013`–`016` Stone runs lighter than `TERR-021`–`024` Earth. **Pick the ramp whose values separate** |
| **3 — Change the design** | **put the belt somewhere else, or make it wider** — a shape change rather than a value change |

**And the option that is not available: brightening the hue.** **Saturation is not value**, and §10.1 says identity may not depend on hue. **If the fix only works in colour, it has not worked.**

**Practice.** Build the greyscale toggle into your template. Then take a sprite with at least three materials and run it, and find any two that merge. Fix one by moving it along its ramp and check again. Then find a saturated accent colour in your sprite and check whether it is still the lightest thing in greyscale — and if not, decide whether it should be.
Negative gaps:
The holes in a silhouette: why the background showing through is a drawing decision, and the four places it belongs.

**§10.1:**

> *"**Preserve useful negative gaps** between body, limbs and equipment, and allow signature equipment to break the torso silhouette."*

**A negative gap is background visible inside the figure's outline.** One pixel is usually enough, and it does more for readability than any interior value.

---

**Why it works.** The eye separates shapes by their boundaries, and **a boundary between the figure and the background is far stronger than a boundary between two values inside the figure.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An arm against a torso, same material, two values** | **a value boundary.** Reads as a fold, or an arm, depending on how well it is drawn |
| **An arm against a torso, with a one-pixel gap** | **a silhouette boundary.** Reads unambiguously as an arm in front of a torso |
| **And in solid black** | **the value boundary vanishes and the gap survives.** Which is why the black test and this lesson are the same subject |

---

**The four places a gap belongs:**

| Place | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Between an arm and the torso** | **the commonest and the most valuable.** A standing figure with arms at its sides has two gaps, and without them it is a blob |
| **Between the legs** | **a stance reads through the gap.** Feet together with no gap is one leg; feet apart with a gap is a stance — and §5.1's idle has meaningful poses that depend on it |
| **Under and around equipment** | **a crook held away from the body, a satchel's strap clearing the shoulder, a quiver standing off the back** |
| **Under a cloak's hem, inside a hood** | where the garment stands away from the body |

**And where a gap does not belong:** **anywhere it is not describing a real separation.** A gap in the middle of a chest is a hole.

---

**The technical problem: one pixel of gap is expensive at 80 px.** This is the honest difficulty:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An arm is 4 to 6 px wide** | so **a one-pixel gap plus a one-pixel outline on each side** takes 3 px of the 6 |
| **Which means** | **the gap and the outline compete for the same pixels**, and both are required by §10.1 |
| **The resolution** | **the gap replaces the outline there.** Where there is a gap, the background is doing the outline's job — **so you do not need a dark line on both sides of a one-pixel gap.** One side, or neither |
| **And the practical sequence** | **draw the gap first, then the outline around it** — not the other way round, because an outline drawn first will close the gap |

---

**The relationship to the equipment clause.** §10.1's sentence has two halves and they work together:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***"Preserve useful negative gaps"*** | **holes inside the silhouette** |
| ***"allow signature equipment to break the torso silhouette"*** | **projections outside it** |
| **Together** | **they make the outline complicated**, and a complicated outline is a recognisable one. **A smooth oval is anonymous; an outline with two gaps and a crook sticking out of it is a specific person** |
| **And §10.1's identity list** | *"Identity cannot depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail"* — **so it has to depend on exactly these two things** |

---

**How to check.** Two ways:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The black test** | **a gap is one of the few interior features that survives it** |
| **Shrink it** | **view at 100%, or smaller.** A gap that closes up at small sizes was not wide enough — and at 3 × 3 screen scaling a one-pixel gap is three screen pixels, which is visible, so **one pixel is genuinely enough** |

**Practice.** Draw a standing figure with its arms against its sides and no gaps, and run the black test. Then add a one-pixel gap at each armpit and run it again. Then draw the same figure with its feet together and then apart with a gap, and compare the stances in black. Then draw a crook held against the body and then held an inch away, and compare.
Contact shadow against environmental sha:
Two kinds of shadow, which one you draw, and the clause that divides the labour between you and the engine.

**§9.1 draws the line:**

> *"Sprites carry only a **short contact shadow inside or immediately beside their footprint**; **long environmental shadows belong to Godot lighting**. Do not bake a floor or scenery behind a standalone object."*

---

**The two kinds:**

| | Contact shadow | Environmental / cast shadow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **the darkening right where the object meets the ground** | **the object's shape projected across the ground away from a light** |
| **Caused by** | **occlusion** — the ground and the object are in contact | **a specific light in a specific position** |
| **Direction** | **mostly none.** It hugs the footprint, extending slightly to the lower-right | **entirely determined by the light's position** |
| **Size** | **short** — a few pixels | **as long as the geometry demands** |
| **Who draws it** | **you, baked into the sprite** | **Godot, at runtime** |
| **Why** | it is true under every light | **it changes with every light** |

**The division is the point.** A baked cast shadow is a claim about where a light is, and **the moment a torch moves, a door opens or night falls, the claim is false and visibly so.** A contact shadow is true always.

---

**How to draw the contact shadow.** From stage 3, with the value detail now available:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shape** | **an ellipse at the projection ratio**, matched to the footprint |
| **Extent** | **hugging the base.** A pixel or two beyond the object on the lower-right; essentially flush on the upper-left |
| **Value** | **Deep** — one or two steps below the ground it sits on, usually from `TERR-001`–`004`, which `colour-palette.md` lists for *"undersides, contact accents"* |
| **Hard edges** | no falloff. There is no value available for one |
| **Its own layer** | **§3.1's four layers: body, equipment, shadow, effects.** The shadow is one of them by name |

**And why it gets its own layer**, which the contract specifies rather than suggests:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The runtime may want it separately** | to hide it, fade it, or offset it as the character jumps |
| **The black test excludes it** | **a silhouette with a puddle under it is not a silhouette** |
| **Animation treats it differently** | **the shadow does not follow the body up.** §6.1's *"stoop-down, hold and rise"* and §6.2's *"pounce"* both need a shadow that stays on the ground |
