| **And Wizard can import it separately** | **the split-layer importer** from stage 12 |

---

**Three related cases worth distinguishing:**

| Case | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| **An object's own self-shadow** | **the Shadow and Deep steps on the object's lower-right.** This is form shading and it is yours |
| **A shadow one object casts onto another** | **usually not drawn.** A crate casting onto a wall behind it is a cast shadow, so it is Godot's — and in practice at this scale it is often simply omitted |
| **An overhang's shadow on the ground beneath it** | **drawn, if it is short and attached** — the dark under a bench or a cart is closer to occlusion than to a cast shadow, and it is part of what makes the object read as raised |

**That third case is the useful one in practice.** §9.2's bench at 19–23 px seat height and 46–56 px long **has a readable gap underneath it**, and **the dark in that gap is what tells you it is a bench and not a solid block.** Draw it, keep it short, and keep it attached to the footprint.

**Practice.** Draw a bench at 21 px seat height and 50 px long with a dark area under the seat, then remove it and compare — decide whether it still reads as a bench. Then draw a barrel with a short contact shadow and then with a long cast shadow, and imagine each under a torch on the other side. Then check that your shadows are on their own layer in every file you have made.
Value massing across a screen:
Composition at the scene level: the value hierarchy a playable screen needs, and the colour budget the contract puts on it.

**This lesson steps back from one sprite to a whole screen**, because §2 names it as a reference criterion:

> *"**Eastward** and **Sea of Stars** inform composition and **value organization**; they are references, not templates."*

**And §9.3 puts a number on it:**

> *"A normal environment screen should usually remain near **32–40 selected master colours**, but readability and the actual material set decide the final count."*

---

**32 to 40 colours for a whole screen.** Divide by four values and that is **eight to ten material ramps** on screen at once — which is tighter than it sounds and is the reason a scene has a palette rather than a collection of assets.

**So a York exterior might curate:**

| Ramp | For |
| --- | --- |
| **`TERR-021`–`024` Earth** | paths, bare ground |
| **`TERR-045`–`048` Olive** or **`TERR-053`–`056` Sage** | grass |
| **`TERR-013`–`016` Stone** | walls, foundations |
| **`TERR-033`–`036` Timber** | fences, doors, beams |
| **`TERR-017`–`020` Slate** | roofs |
| **`TERR-005`–`008` Cloth** | thatch, sacks, awnings |
| **`TERR-049`–`052` Living Green** | trees, shrubs |
| **`TERR-001`–`004` Neutral** | outlines, contact shadows, deepest recesses |
| **Plus the character's own subset** | 12–18 |

**Eight ramps plus the characters, and the budget is spent.** Which is exactly §9.3's point: *"A scene curates only the material ramps it needs."*

---

**The value hierarchy a playable screen needs.** This is the composition rule, and it is a gameplay requirement before it is an aesthetic one:

| Priority | Element | Value treatment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Hazards and telegraphs** | **the highest contrast on screen.** §5.3: telegraphs read through *"pose, silhouette, motion and sound"* — and value |
| **2** | **Characters** | **high contrast against the ground they stand on.** The next lesson |
| **3** | **Interactables** | **distinguishable from scenery** — §2: *"traversable space, interactables, hazards and combat silhouettes remain immediately readable"* |
| **4** | **Obstacles and walls** | **clearly not walkable.** Usually darker and with a visible front face — stage 3's height-against-depth |
| **5** | **The walkable floor** | **mid-value, low contrast, and quiet.** The floor's job is to be ignorable |
| **6** | **Background and distance** | **lowest contrast** — compressed toward the mid |

**Read 5 again, because it is the counter-intuitive one: the floor is the largest area on screen and it should be the least interesting.** A beautifully textured, high-contrast floor competes with everything standing on it. **§2's clause is explicit — dense environmental storytelling is welcome *"only where traversable space … remain[s] immediately readable"*.**

---

**The practical method, which is borrowed from painting and works here:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Block the screen in three values first** | **light, mid, dark — nothing else.** Where is the light mass, where is the dark mass, and what is the field between them |
| **Check that the figure's value is not the floor's** | **at this stage, with three values, it is obvious** |
| **Then assign ramps** | each mass gets a material |
| **Then detail, in the order from stage 4's first lesson** | and stop when readability starts to cost |

**And §2's reference criterion gives you the study:** **take an Eastward or Sea of Stars screenshot, reduce it to three values, and look at the massing.** §2 is explicit that they are *"references, not templates"* and that *"Individual scenes, designs and incidental details from any reference are not copied"* — **so study the value organisation, not the content.** That is precisely what §2 names them for.

**Practice.** Take a screenshot of one of the two named references, greyscale it, and posterise it mentally to three values — then describe where the light mass, dark mass and field are. Then block out a York exterior in three greys at 240 × 135 (a quarter of the viewport) and place a figure in it. Then count how many ramps your design needs and check it against 32–40 colours.
Figure against ground:
The separation that matters most in play: keeping a character readable against every surface the game can put them on.

**§10.1's hardest condition:**

> *"identifiable in solid black, grayscale, dark lighting and **a busy party scene**."*

**And §2's version:** *"Gameplay must remain readable at native scale during **movement, combat, crowds, darkness and effects**."*

**The problem is that a character's value is fixed and the ground's is not.** A figure drawn to read beautifully on dirt may vanish on stone.

---

**The scale of the problem, concretely.** The palette's ground-capable ramps and their Mid values:

| Ramp | Mid | Lightness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Earth** `TERR-023` | `#93663D` | mid |
| **Stone** `TERR-015` | `#857D70` | **mid-light** |
| **Dry Stone / Chalked** `TERR-016` | `#B8AFA0` | **light** |
| **Olive** `TERR-047` | `#77753A` | mid |
| **Sage** `TERR-055` | `#7C8768` | mid |
| **Moss** `TERR-043` | `#5A6838` | **mid-dark** |
| **Slate** `TERR-019` | `#65717A` | mid |
| **Water** `TERR-059` | `#537488` | mid |
| **Living Green** `TERR-051` | `#48764D` | mid-dark |

**Almost all of them are mid.** Which is good news and bad news: **good, because the grounds are consistent with each other; bad, because a character's Mid will be in the same region.**

---

**The four devices that keep a figure readable, in order of reliability:**

| | Device | Why it is reliable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The one-pixel coloured outline** | **§10.1 requires it anyway**, and it is a dark boundary between the figure and any ground. **This is the single most important readability device in the game** |
| **2** | **The contact shadow** | **a second dark boundary at the base**, and it also resolves height — stage 3 |
| **3** | **Value range, not value match** | **a figure should span a wider value range than the ground does.** The ground is quiet and mid; **the figure has a real Light and a real Deep.** The contrast is what separates, not the average |
| **4** | **Silhouette complexity** | from the gaps lesson — **a complicated outline reads even at low contrast** |

**And the one that does not work:** **choosing a hue the ground does not have.** It works on dirt and fails on stone, and §10.1's greyscale clause rules it out in principle.

---

**The crowd case**, which is harder than the ground case:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **four heroes and six enemies on screen, overlapping, all of them figure-shaped** |
| **What separates them** | **silhouette first** — the black test is a crowd test in disguise. Then **value structure**: if every character is mid-dominant with the same distribution, they merge |
| **The design consequence** | **the party should have different value weights.** One character predominantly light, one predominantly dark, one mid — **which is a design decision across the cast, not a drawing decision per sprite** |
| **Where that lives** | **`characters.md` and §2.1's priority order**, and it is Timon's call on design |
| **And the accent colours** | **`hero-accent-colours.md` and `hud.md`'s `PARTY_ACCENTS`** give each hero an accent — **exempt from the palette and the violet rule** — but **those are HUD colours, not sprite colours**, and §10.1 still forbids identity depending on hue |

---

**The darkness case**, §10.1's third condition, and the one that catches people:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What a dark scene does** | **compresses everything toward the bottom of the value range** |
| **What survives** | **the light end of a figure's range** — the Light step and the lighter Mids |
| **What disappears** | **everything at Deep and Shadow.** They merge with each other and with the dark ground |
| **So** | **a figure whose readability lives in its dark values is invisible in darkness**, and **a figure whose readability lives in its light values survives** |
| **The practical rule** | **put the identity in the light half.** A pale hood, a light satchel strap, a lit shoulder — **these are what you see at night.** And it is one more reason §10.1 restrains the shading: **a lightly shaded sprite has more of itself in the light half** |

**Practice.** Draw a figure and place it on five different ground Mids from the table above, at 300%, and find the one where it reads worst. Then add or strengthen the outline and contact shadow and check again. Then make a dark version of the scene — a Multiply layer at 60% over everything — and see which parts of the figure survive. Then redraw whatever did not.
Reading in darkness:
The condition that is hardest to design for and easiest to forget, and what it changes about how a sprite is shaded.

**§10.1 lists it as one of four:**

> *"identifiable in solid black, grayscale, **dark lighting** and a busy party scene."*

**And §2 makes it a gameplay requirement:** readability during *"movement, combat, crowds, **darkness** and effects"*.

**Darkness is not a style here. The Prologue has a night, and §6.8's corpse puppets *"at the power station idle and turn toward the light in sequence"* — so a dark scene with a light source in it is literally a scripted moment.**

---

**What a dark scene does to a sprite, mechanically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`Light2D` in darkness** | **the unlit areas are multiplied toward black, and the lit region is closer to the sprite's authored values** |
| **So the sprite's value range compresses** | **the whole range is squeezed into the dark end**, and the distances between adjacent values shrink with it |
| **Which means** | **two values that were one ramp step apart become almost the same**, and a sprite with four well-chosen values reads as two |
| **And the dark end goes first** | **Deep and Shadow merge with each other and with the background** before Mid and Light do |

---

**The three consequences for how you shade:**

**1 — Put the identity in the light half.** From the last lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What survives darkness** | **the Light step and the lighter part of the Mid** |
| **So the identity carriers** — hood shape, equipment, the lit shoulder — **should be in those values** | |
| **And what to avoid** | a character whose distinguishing feature is a dark cloak against a dark body. **In daylight it reads by hue; at night it is one shape** |

**2 — Keep the Deep step small.** From the occlusion lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why** | **a large Deep area is already nearly background-coloured in darkness.** The sprite loses that part of its silhouette |
| **The rule** | **Deep hugs junctions.** One pixel, at contacts |

**3 — The outline earns its keep in darkness, and needs the right value.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The tension** | **a dark outline against a dark background disappears** — so in darkness the outline stops separating |
| **What takes over** | **the figure's lit values against the dark surroundings.** The silhouette reads as a light shape rather than as an outlined one |
| **Which argues for** | **a coloured outline rather than near-black** — `TERR-001` Coal Black `#17181B` is dark and **it is not pure black**, so it retains a little separation. **And the material's own Deep step is lighter still**, which is why §10.1 prefers it |

---

**And the one thing that is genuinely in tension with the rest of the contract:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§10.1 wants restrained shading** so runtime lights read coherently | |
| **§10.1 also wants identity in darkness**, which wants a wide, well-separated value range | |
| **The tension** | **restraint narrows the range; darkness compresses it further.** A restrained sprite in darkness has very little range left |
| **The resolution** | **restraint is about the *extremes*, not the separation.** Keep the Light step modest and the Deep step small — **and keep the Mid-to-Shadow boundary strong and well placed.** The readability comes from **where the boundary is**, not from how far apart the values are |
| **Which is this stage's recurring point** | **a form reads because of where its value boundary falls.** That survives compression; a wide range does not |

---

**How to test it.** Three ways, cheapest first:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A Multiply layer at 60–70%** over the whole sprite in Aseprite | **crude and useful.** It compresses the range the way darkness does |
| **The canvas background set to near-black** | tests the silhouette's separation, not the interior |
| **Godot, under a dim `Light2D`** | **the real test**, and §10's seventh condition. **Stage 7's round trip** |

**Practice.** Take a finished sprite and add a Multiply layer at 65% over everything, and count how many of its four values are still distinguishable. Then identify which parts of the figure you can still recognise and whether they are enough. Then move one identity carrier from the dark half to the light half and test again.
Fixing a failed test:
The repair procedure when the black test or the grey test fails: diagnosing which of five causes it is, and what each one costs to fix.

**A failed test is a diagnosis problem, not a drawing problem.** The sprite looks fine in colour and fails in black or grey, and **the first job is to find out which of five things is wrong** — because the fixes differ by an order of magnitude in cost.

---

**The five causes, cheapest fix first:**

| | Cause | Symptom | Cost to fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Two materials at the same value step** | **grey test: two shapes merge** | **minutes.** Move one along its ramp |
| **2** | **A missing negative gap** | **black test: arms or legs merged into the body** | **minutes.** Add a one-pixel gap |
| **3** | **The outline is closing the form** | **black test: the figure is a solid blob** | **tens of minutes.** Thin or remove outline where it is merging shapes |
| **4** | **Identity in the interior** | **black test: it is clearly a person and could be anyone** | **hours, and a design decision** |
| **5** | **The silhouette is wrong** | **black test: it does not read as a person, or the pose does not read** | **a redraw** |

---

**The diagnostic order**, which saves the most time:

| Step | Ask |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **Run the grey test first.** It is the less harsh one, and it isolates cause 1. **If two materials merge, fix that and re-run both tests** — a surprising number of black-test failures are grey-test failures in disguise |
| **2** | **Run the black test and look at the outline.** Are limbs separate? If not, **cause 2 or 3**, and the test is whether there is room for a gap. If there is, it is 2; if the outline has eaten the room, it is 3 |
| **3** | **If the limbs are separate and it still does not read as a specific person**, it is **cause 4** |
| **4** | **If it does not read as a person at all**, it is **cause 5** |

---

**The fixes, in detail.**

**Cause 1 — two materials at the same value.** Three options, from the grey test lesson: **move one along its own ramp; choose a different ramp with a different lightness range; or change the design so the two shapes do not touch.** The first is nearly always right.

**Cause 2 — a missing gap.** From the gaps lesson: **draw the gap first and the outline around it.** And **the gap replaces the outline there** — you do not need a dark line on both sides of one pixel of background.

**Cause 3 — the outline is closing the form.** The subtle one:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What happens** | **two outlines meeting make one thick dark line**, and the two shapes either side become one |
| **Where** | **arm against torso, satchel against hip, weapon against body, leg against leg** |
| **The fix** | **outline one of the two, not both.** §10.1's words: avoid outlines *"that merge equipment into the torso"* |
| **The better fix** | **make the two shapes different values**, so they separate without the outline — which is cause 1's fix applied preventively |

**Cause 4 — identity in the interior.** This is the expensive one and it needs naming honestly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is not a shading problem** | **no amount of redrawing the interior will fix a generic silhouette** |
| **The fix is a design change** | a hat, a hood, a hair shape, a cloak, a piece of equipment that projects |
| **And the design is not yours alone** | **§2.1's priority order puts Terrath canon and the owning product document above the drawing**, and **Timon has final say on design** |
| **So the correct action** | **§2.1: *"Art must not invent costume details, insignia, equipment, anatomy or lore to fill a gap; surface the gap instead."*** **Raise it. Do not invent a hat** |

**Cause 5 — the silhouette is wrong.** **Redraw, starting from the silhouette in one value, and do not add a second value until the first one reads.** That is stage 4's first lesson's order, and a failure here usually means it was not followed.

---

**And the rule that makes all of this cheaper: run the tests early.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The tests cost one click each**, if the toggles are in the template | |
| **Run them at the silhouette stage**, before any shading. **A silhouette that fails the black test will still fail it after four hours of shading** | |
| **Then again after the value block-in** | |
| **Then again at the end** | |
| **§10's definition of done requires them anyway** | so the only question is whether you find out now or later |

**Practice.** Take a sprite that fails one of the tests and run the four diagnostic steps to name the cause. Then fix it and re-run both tests. Then take a sprite you have not started and run the black test on its silhouette alone, before shading, and see whether it passes.
The value checklist:
The stage's conclusion: eleven checks, in the order to run them, drawn from the contract's own clauses.

**Everything in this stage, as a procedure.** The order matters — each check is cheaper than the one after it, and each one can invalidate the later ones.

---

**While drawing, in this order:**

| | Check | From |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The silhouette reads in one value, before any shading** | §10.1's black test, run early |
| **2** | **Negative gaps are in place — armpits, legs, equipment** | §10.1 |
| **3** | **Each material has three or four values, no more** | §10.1 |
| **4** | **Mid dominates — 50 to 60% of each material's area** | this stage |
| **5** | **The key light is upper-left on every surface; the form shade is lower-right** | §10.1, §9.1 |
| **6** | **Occlusion is at junctions, one pixel, in the Deep step — not spread across surfaces** | §10.1's *"deepest recesses, undersides"* |
| **7** | **No baked rim light, bounce light or second light source** | §10.1's restraint clause |
| **8** | **The contact shadow is on its own layer, short, hugging the footprint** | §9.1, §3.1 |

**Then the four tests:**

| | Test | Where |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **9** | **Greyscale** — does every material still separate from its neighbours, and from the background? | **Aseprite**, the toggle |
| **10** | **Solid black** — is it a person, is it *this* person, and is the pose readable? | **Aseprite**, the toggle |
| **11** | **Dark** — does the identity survive compression? | **Aseprite's Multiply approximation, then Godot** |
| **12** | **A busy scene** | **Godot only** — §10's seventh condition |

**Eight while-drawing checks and four tests.** Checks 1 to 8 are things you can get right; tests 9 to 12 are things you find out.

---

**The three that are worth doing first every time**, if the list is too long to run in full:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The silhouette in one value** | because a failure here invalidates everything else |
| **4 — Mid dominates** | because it is the commonest cause of a muddy sprite and it is visible at a glance |
| **9 — Greyscale** | because it is one click and it catches the commonest value failure |

---

**And the stage's thesis restated, because the checklist can obscure it:**

> **A form reads because of where its value boundary falls.** Not because of how many values there are, how far apart they are, how smooth the transition is, or what colour they are. **One boundary, in the right place, describing the form — and then two more, and then stop.**

**Everything in this stage follows from that.** Four values rather than six, because four give three boundaries and three are enough. Restraint, because the range matters less than the placement. Occlusion at junctions, because a junction is a boundary the form actually has. The black test, because the silhouette is the outermost boundary and the most important one.

**And the handover to stage 5:** **every boundary in this stage was a value boundary, drawn in greys.** Stage 5 assigns the ramps — **which decides what the material is without changing anything about where the boundaries go.**

**Practice.** Write the twelve checks on one page and keep it beside the keyboard. Run all twelve on the best thing you have drawn so far and record which fail. Then draw one new small asset running the first eight as you go, and see whether tests 9 to 12 pass first time.
Hue, saturation and value:
The three properties of a colour, which of them the palette varies, and the measurements that show what it is actually doing.

**Any colour can be described three ways**, and the useful one here is hue, saturation and lightness:

| Property | What it is | Range |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Hue** | **which colour it is** — where it sits on the wheel | **0 to 360 degrees.** Red ~0, yellow ~50, green ~120, cyan ~180, blue ~220, violet ~270 |
| **Saturation** | **how intense it is** — how far from grey | **0 to 100%** |
| **Lightness** | **how light or dark** — stage 4's value | **0 to 100%** |

**And the reason to learn the numbers rather than the words: the palette's 132 entries can be measured, and the measurements say what the palette is for.**

---

**The measurements. Here are six of the 33 ramps with hue, saturation and lightness for each step:**

| Ramp | Deep | Shadow | Mid | Light |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`005`–`008` Cloth** | H22 S10 L21 | H22 S12 L32 | H24 S11 L44 | **H27 S14 L59** |
| **`021`–`024` Earth** | H24 S33 L22 | H26 S38 L31 | H29 S41 L41 | **H30 S46 L55** |
| **`049`–`052` Living Green** | H146 S29 L17 | H136 S25 L26 | H127 S24 L37 | **H118 S20 L51** |
| **`057`–`060` Water** | H203 S33 L20 | H202 S30 L30 | H203 S24 L43 | **H201 S24 L59** |
| **`073`–`076` Warm Skin** | H17 S35 L33 | H17 S34 L45 | H19 S45 L59 | **H21 S58 L73** |
| **`125`–`128` Fire** | H13 S57 L23 | H12 S66 L34 | H15 S70 L48 | **H26 S86 L58** |

---

**Four things those numbers show, and all four are teachable rules:**

**1 — Lightness is the primary axis, and the steps are about 10 to 13 points.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Cloth** | 21 → 32 → 44 → 59 — **steps of 11, 12, 15** |
| **Earth** | 22 → 31 → 41 → 55 — **steps of 9, 10, 14** |
| **Gold `097`–`100`** | 27 → 38 → 52 → 73 — **steps of 11, 14, 21** |
| **The pattern** | **the Mid-to-Light step is always the biggest.** The ramps are weighted so the Light step is a genuine highlight rather than a fourth equal increment |

**2 — Warm and organic materials gain saturation toward the light.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Skin** | S35 → S58 |
| **Gold** | S56 → S78 |
| **Fire** | S57 → S86 |
| **Earth** | S33 → S46 |
| **What that models** | **a lit warm surface looks more colourful**, which is how sunlight on skin and earth actually behaves |

**3 — Cool and emissive materials lose saturation toward the light.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Beacon `105`–`108`** | **S51 → S29** |
| **Water** | S33 → S24 |
| **Living green** | S29 → S20 |
| **What that models** | **a glow's core goes toward white**, and a cool surface's highlight is a reflection of sky rather than of its own colour |

**4 — The greens hue-shift hard; most other ramps barely shift.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Living green** | **H146 → H118** — a 28-degree swing toward yellow |
| **Moss `041`–`044`** | **H99 → H73** — a 26-degree swing |
| **Cloth, stone, earth, skin** | **4 to 6 degrees warmer** — a small, consistent drift |
| **Water, violet** | **essentially none** |
| **Fire** | **H13 → H26** at the Light step — the flame's tip goes orange |

**So the palette hue-shifts the vegetation strongly, everything warm slightly, and the cool materials not at all.** That is a deliberate set of decisions and the next lesson is about why.

**Practice.** Open the `.gpl` or the palette table and pick three ramps you have not looked at. Work out each step's lightness, saturation and hue — by eye in Aseprite's colour sliders, or with a calculator. Then say which of the four patterns above each ramp follows. Then find a ramp that breaks all four.
Hue shifting, not darkening:
The craft principle, what the palette does about it, and the one case where you have to supply it yourself.

**The principle.** A shadow is not the same colour, darker. **Darkening a colour by lowering its lightness alone produces a muddy, lifeless shadow** — and the reason is physical: a shadow is lit by ambient light, which has a different colour from the key light, so **a shadowed surface shifts hue as well as value.**

**The standard formulation, from every pixel art tutorial:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shadows** | **shift toward the cool** — blue, violet, cyan |
| **Lights** | **shift toward the warm** — yellow, orange |
| **And saturation** | **often rises in both directions** from the mid, dropping only at the extreme highlight |

---

**Now what this palette actually does**, from the last lesson's measurements:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The warm earthy ramps** | **shift 4 to 6 degrees warmer toward the Light.** Cloth H22 → H27; earth H24 → H30; skin H17 → H21. **A small, consistent, deliberate warm drift** |
| **The vegetation ramps** | **shift hard toward yellow in light** — living green H146 → H118. **A 28-degree swing** |
| **The cool ramps** | **barely shift at all.** Water H203 → H201 |
| **Which means** | **the palette supplies the warm-light half of the principle, and only weakly supplies the cool-shadow half** |

**And the structural reason:** **`colour-palette.md`'s first usage rule.**

> *"Ordinary Terrath should remain **muted, earthy, restrained, and materially readable**."*

**A strongly hue-shifted shadow is not muted.** The palette is built for a weathered, low-saturation world, so its shadows go darker and slightly less warm rather than markedly blue. **That is a style decision already made, and it is why the ramps look as they do.**

---

**So where does cool-shadow hue shifting come from here? Three legitimate routes:**

**1 — Borrow a neighbouring ramp's Deep.** The palette is a kit:

| Material | Its own Deep | A cooler alternative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cloth `005`** | `#3A332F` H22 | **`TERR-002` Soot Ink `#27292D` H220** — a cool near-black, and listed for *"deepest recesses, undersides"* |
| **Stone `013`** | `#403C37` H33 | **`TERR-017` Night Slate `#2E3438` H199** — cool, and legitimately stone |
| **Earth `021`** | `#4A3425` H24 | **`TERR-013` Deep Stone**, or `TERR-002` |

**That is the method the palette intends.** `colour-palette.md`: *"A master palette is a bank of approved choices"* — and §9.3: *"A scene curates only the material ramps it needs."* **A cool shadow is a cool ramp's entry, not a modified warm one.**

**2 — Notice that `TERR-001`–`004` is already cool.** The measurement:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`TERR-001` Coal Black** | `#17181B` — **H225 S8 L10** |
| **`TERR-002` Soot Ink** | `#27292D` — H220 S7 L16 |
| **`TERR-003` Graphite** | `#3B3E43` — H218 S6 L25 |
| **`TERR-004` Iron Charcoal** | `#55595F` — H216 S6 L35 |

**The neutral ramp is a cool blue-grey, not a neutral grey.** Which is quietly important: **the project's outline and recess colours are cool**, so every outline is already doing a small amount of cool-shadow hue shifting. **And it is the reason §10.1 can ban pure black** — the palette's darkest is a cool dark, which reads better against warm materials than `#000000` would.

**3 — Let the runtime do it.** §10.1's restraint clause:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`Light2D` has a colour** | and a warm torch next to a cool ambient **produces hue-shifted shadows at runtime, across the whole scene, consistently** |
| **Which is better than baking it** | because the shift matches the actual light in the actual scene |
| **And it is the contract's own logic** | *"Static shading stays restrained so Godot's local lights can read coherently"* |

---

**The practical rule for this project**, which differs from the generic advice:

> **Do not hue-shift by hand. Choose the ramp whose hue you want, and use the neutral ramp or a cooler material ramp for the deepest recesses. The warm drift toward light is already in the ramps, and the cool shadow is the engine's job.**

**Practice.** Shade the same cloth form three ways: with its own four steps; with `TERR-002` substituted for its Deep; and with a hand-mixed cool shadow that is not in the palette. Compare at 300%, and note that the third is off-palette and would fail a validator. Then measure `TERR-001`'s hue and confirm it is blue rather than neutral.
The Deep to Light order:
The palette's fixed four-step structure, what each name commits to, and why the order is stated as a rule rather than a convention.

**`colour-palette.md` states it twice.** In the usage rules:

> *"Build materials and effects from purposeful four-step ramps in the fixed value order: **`Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light`**."*

And as its own section:

> *"Every ramp follows this four-step value structure: `Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light`."*

**And every one of the 132 entries carries a "Value family" column with one of those four words.**

---

**Why a fixed order and fixed names matter.** Four reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — It makes the palette machine-readable** | **a validator can check that an asset used one ramp's four steps** rather than four arbitrary colours, because the family is recorded per entry |
| **2 — It maps onto stage 4's four jobs** | Deep = occlusion and outline; Shadow = form shade; Mid = local colour; Light = key-lit. **The names are the jobs** |
| **3 — It makes substitution safe** | **swapping a material means swapping four entries, step for step.** Cloth's Shadow becomes leather's Shadow, and the value structure is preserved |
| **4 — It makes the asset brief writable** | §10.2 requires a *"palette subset"*, and *"`TERR-005`–`008` for the tunic, `TERR-025`–`028` for the belt"* is a complete and checkable specification |

---

**What each name commits to, with the measured lightness ranges across all 33 ramps:**

| Step | Typical lightness | Its job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Deep** | **L10 to L33** | **occlusion, undersides, contact, the outline.** Not "the shadow side" — stage 4's distinction |
| **Shadow** | **L16 to L45** | **the form shade** — the surface turned from the key |
| **Mid** | **L25 to L59** | **the local colour, and the largest area** |
| **Light** | **L35 to L73** | **the key-lit surface** |

**Note the overlap.** A stone's Deep at L23 is lighter than a violet's Mid at L38 is— no, darker; but **a stone's Light at L67 is lighter than a water's Light at L59, and a neutral's Light at L35 is darker than an earth's Shadow at L31 is— nearly the same.** **So the step names are relative within a ramp, not absolute across the palette.**

**That is the single most important practical consequence of this lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **"Light" does not mean light** | **`TERR-004` Iron Charcoal, the neutral ramp's Light, is L35** — darker than most ramps' Mid |
| **"Deep" does not mean dark** | **`TERR-077` Pale Skin Shadow is L?** — a pale skin's Deep is lighter than a moss's Light |
| **So two materials at the same step name can have completely different values** | which is exactly the grey-test failure of stage 4 |
| **And the fix** | **compare lightness numbers, not step names.** Two materials that must separate need different *lightnesses*, not different step names |

---

**And the one real exception to the four-step structure.** The violet ramp:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`TERR-117`–`120`** | Ash Violet L19, Bruised Violet L28, Dissonant Violet L38, Veil Violet L53 |
| **Its four steps are normal** | and **it serves two opposite meanings** — which is the violet rule, three lessons on |
| **The consequence** | **the step name tells you the value and tells you nothing about the register.** Sacred or dissonant is decided by pairing and context, not by the step |

**Practice.** Pick five ramps and write down each step's lightness. Then find two ramps whose "Mid" entries differ in lightness by more than 15 points. Then find a pair where one ramp's Deep is lighter than another's Light. Then take a two-material object and choose its ramps by comparing lightness numbers rather than step names.

Living in the palette:
Loading it, keeping to it, and the three mechanisms that make conformance automatic rather than remembered.

**From stage 1, the mechanics:** the `.gpl` is at `media/reference/Palette/shepherds-master-v0-1.gpl`, it is loaded with Load Palette, and **Save Palette › Save as Preset** installs it into `~/.config/aseprite/palettes/`. **As of 14 October 2026 that had not been done.**

**This lesson is about the three mechanisms that make it stick.**

---

**1 — Indexed colour mode.** From stage 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it gives you** | **you cannot use an off-palette colour, because there is nowhere to put it** |
| **Why it is the strongest mechanism** | **`colour-palette.md`'s rule — *"Do not invent substitute colours, rename entries, alter hex values, or break ramp relationships without an explicit palette revision"* — becomes a property of the file rather than a discipline** |
| **And the colour count becomes visible** | §10.1's bands are a glance at the palette rather than an audit |
| **The one caution** | **index 0 is the transparent colour**, so check a visible colour has not landed there |

**2 — A template file.** Everything from stages 1 to 4, in one `.aseprite`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **112 × 112, indexed, transparent, the full 132-entry palette** | |
| **A pivot mark at (56, 96)** | |
| **Four layers: body, equipment, shadow, effects** — §3.1 | |
| **A greyscale toggle layer** — a fill in `Color` blend mode, hidden | |
| **A black-fill toggle layer** — hidden | |
| **A reference layer** with the 80 px silhouette, the 16 px grid and the reference box — stage 3 | |
| **A 16 × 16 grid set, snap off** | |
| **Every frame at 84 ms** | |

**That file is the single highest-value thing to build before drawing anything.** It makes every rule in four stages into a default.

**3 — A validator.** From stage 1's specification and stage 12's implementation: **a Lua script that reports off-palette colours, counts the opaque base colours, and checks the canvas, the tag and the durations.**

---

**And the discipline the mechanisms cannot supply: choosing the smallest subset.**

> **`colour-palette.md`:** *"A master palette is a bank of approved choices, not a requirement to use every colour in an asset."*
>
> *"Use the smallest coherent subset that preserves silhouette, value separation, material identity, and gameplay readability."*

**Four things that subset must preserve, in that order.** And the next lesson is about how many colours that is.

---

**Three further rules from the document, each of which is a prohibition:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ***"Do not invent substitute colours"*** | **no hand-mixed shadow.** The last lesson's conclusion |
| ***"rename entries, alter hex values"*** | **the IDs and hexes are stable identifiers.** A validator checks the hex, so an altered one fails |
| ***"or break ramp relationships"*** | **do not use `TERR-005` with `TERR-011` as if they were a ramp.** They are not, and the value steps will not behave |
| **And the exception clause** | *"without an explicit palette revision"* — **so all three are revisable, by decision, not by drift** |

**And one permission that is easy to miss:**

> *"Runtime lighting, compositing, transparency, and effects may create transitional display colours; the entries below remain the base authoring colours."*

**So the palette governs what you author, not what appears on screen.** `Light2D` will produce thousands of colours that are not in the 132, and that is correct and expected. **The palette is an authoring constraint.**

**Practice.** Install the palette as a preset. Then build the template file described above and save it where you will find it. Then open one of the reference masters and check whether its colours are in the 132 — the body-part reference has *"its own 13-colour body-part palette"*, so it should not be, and knowing that is the point.
Choosing a subset:
The four colour bands, where they come from, and how to pick a specific asset's colours against them.

**The bands appear in both documents, with slightly different numbers**, and the difference is worth noticing.

**§10.1:**

> *"A normal hero usually uses **12–18** opaque base colours, an ordinary enemy **8–26** and a small prop **4–10**. These are **discipline ranges rather than reasons to discard a necessary material distinction**."*

**`colour-palette.md`:**

> *"Ordinary enemies should generally use about **8–14** colours. Heroes should generally use about **12–18**."*

**And §9.3, for a whole screen:** *"near **32–40** selected master colours"*.

| Asset | §10.1 | `colour-palette.md` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Small prop** | **4–10** | — |
| **Hero** | **12–18** | **12–18** |
| **Ordinary enemy** | **8–26** | **8–14** |
| **Environment screen** | — | §9.3: **32–40** |

**The enemy band differs — 8–26 against 8–14 — and the narrower figure is the later document's.** When they disagree, §2.1's priority order applies: **both are current product documents, so the sensible reading is 8–14 for an ordinary enemy and up to 26 for something that genuinely needs it**, which §10.1's *"discipline ranges"* caveat permits.

---

**How to pick a subset, in five steps.** Working a hero at 12–18:

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — List the materials** | **skin, hair, tunic, trousers, boots, belt, satchel, crook.** Eight things |
| **2 — Group them into ramps** | **skin → `073`–`076`. Hair → `005`–`008` or `033`–`036`. Tunic → `045`–`048`. Trousers → `005`–`008`. Boots and belt and satchel → `025`–`028` leather. Crook → `033`–`036` timber.** Eight things, **four or five ramps** |
| **3 — Count** | **five ramps × 4 = 20.** Over budget |
| **4 — Share and trim** | **trousers share the tunic's ramp at different steps. The crook shares the leather ramp.** Now **three ramps = 12**, plus **`TERR-001`–`002` for outline and occlusion = 14** |
| **5 — Check the four things the subset must preserve** | silhouette, value separation, material identity, gameplay readability |

**Step 4 is the craft.** **Two materials can share a ramp if they sit at different steps** — a tunic at Mid and trousers at Shadow are visibly different garments from the same four colours. **That is how a 14-colour hero has eight materials.**

---

**And the small prop at 4–10, which is tighter than it sounds.** §9.2's bucket:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The materials** | **wood staves, a metal band, a rope handle** |
| **The naive answer** | three ramps × 4 = 12. **Over budget** |
| **The actual answer** | **timber `033`–`036` for the staves (4); the band at `TERR-011` Dull Steel and `TERR-009` Cold Iron (2); the handle at `TERR-027` Harness Leather (1); `TERR-001` for the outline and contact shadow (1).** **Eight colours** |
| **The method** | **a secondary material gets one or two steps, not four.** A 15-pixel-tall bucket's metal band is three pixels of band — it does not need four values |

**That is the general rule for props: the primary material gets its full ramp; everything else gets one or two entries.**

---

**One thing the bands count and one thing they do not:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **They count** | **"opaque base colours"** — §10.1's exact words |
| **They do not count** | **semi-transparent pixels**, which are outside the count — and which indexed mode makes hard anyway |
| **Nor** | **runtime colours.** `colour-palette.md`: *"Runtime lighting, compositing, transparency, and effects may create transitional display colours"* |
| **And the Lospec palette analyzer** will count them for you from a PNG export — **a free external check** | |

**Practice.** Pick a hero design and run the five steps, writing the final list of palette IDs. Then do the same for the bucket and get to eight or fewer. Then export one of your sprites as a PNG and run it through the Lospec analyzer to count its colours, and compare with what you intended.
The coloured outline in palette terms:
§10.1's outline clause translated into specific palette IDs, with the measurements that show why each choice works.

**The clause, from stage 2:** *"Use a dark coloured one-pixel outline. Avoid universal pure black, automatic double outlines and outlines that merge equipment into the torso."*

**And the palette's own answer**, in the Intended uses column for `TERR-001`–`004`:

> *"**Outlines**, deepest recesses, undersides, contact accents"*

**So the palette nominates a ramp for outlines. The question this lesson answers is when to use it and when to use the material's own Deep instead.**

---

**The measurements that make the choice:**

| Entry | Hex | H | S | L |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`TERR-001` Coal Black** | `#17181B` | **225** | 8 | **10** |
| **`TERR-002` Soot Ink** | `#27292D` | 220 | 7 | 16 |
| **`TERR-005` Burnt Cloth** (cloth's Deep) | `#3A332F` | 22 | 10 | **21** |
| **`TERR-013` Deep Stone** | `#403C37` | 33 | 8 | 23 |
| **`TERR-025` Blackened Leather** | `#3B291F` | 24 | 31 | **18** |
| **`TERR-033` Charred Wood** | `#422B20` | 20 | 35 | 19 |
| **`TERR-049` Pine Shadow** (living green's Deep) | `#1F382A` | 146 | 29 | **17** |

**Three things that table shows:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — `TERR-001` is the darkest thing in the palette at L10**, and it is **cool** at H225 — a blue-black, not a neutral one | |
| **2 — The material Deeps cluster at L17 to L23** — all of them in a narrow band, which is why they work as outlines interchangeably | |
| **3 — And `#17181B` is not `#000000`** — which is exactly what §10.1's *"avoid universal pure black"* is asking for, and the palette already provides it | |

---

**The decision rule:**

| Use | When |
| --- | --- |
| **The material's own Deep** | **the default.** Cloth outlined in `TERR-005`, leather in `TERR-025`, timber in `TERR-033`. **This is the "coloured" in "dark coloured outline"** — the outline carries the material's hue |
| **`TERR-002` Soot Ink** | **where two materials meet and you want the boundary to belong to neither** |
| **`TERR-001` Coal Black** | **the deepest recesses and the contact shadow** — and sparingly as an outline, **only where maximum separation is needed** against a light ground |
| **A neighbouring material's Deep** | **where a cool shadow is wanted** — the hue-shifting lesson's method |

---

**And the selective variation, in palette terms.** From stage 2's selective outlining:

| Where | Entry |
| --- | --- |
| **Lower-right, against a light ground** | **`TERR-001`** — maximum separation |
| **Lower-right, ordinary** | **the material's Deep** |
| **Sides** | **the material's Deep** |
| **Upper-left** | **the material's Shadow step rather than its Deep** — one step lighter, so the outline fades into the light |
| **Upper-left, strongly lit** | **no outline at all** — the value difference against the background does the work |
| **The contact line at the ground** | **`TERR-001`**, shared with the contact shadow |

**That is five decisions and they take one pass round the figure.** The commonest mistake is doing it in one colour and the second commonest is doing it in `#000000`.

---

**One palette-specific trap: the dark materials.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **`TERR-025` Blackened Leather is L18 and `TERR-001` is L10 — only eight points apart.** So **a leather boot outlined in `TERR-001` has almost no visible outline** |
| **And worse** | **a leather object against a dark ground has no separation at all** |
| **The fix** | **outline a dark material with something lighter, not darker** — `TERR-003` Graphite at L25, or the material's own Shadow step. **An outline's job is separation, and against a dark material that means going up** |
| **Which is a genuine exception to the clause** | **§10.1 says *"dark"*, and for a dark material the separating line is lighter.** The clause's intent is separation; **follow the intent** |

**Practice.** Outline a cloth form in `TERR-005`, then in `TERR-001`, then in pure black, and compare all three at 300% against a mid ground. Then outline a leather boot in `TERR-001` and see the problem, then fix it with `TERR-003`. Then do one figure with the five-decision selective outline from the table above.
The violet rule:
One ramp, two opposite meanings, and the most carefully reasoned clause in the whole palette document.

**`colour-palette.md` gives it its own section, and it is worth reading in full before anything else.** The core:

> *"Violet carries **two opposite metaphysical registers** in this game, and the `TERR-117`–`TERR-120` ramp serves both. This is deliberate — the two are theologically related, not unrelated — but it means **hue alone never tells the player which one they are looking at. Pairing, treatment and context do.**"*

---

**The two registers:**

| | Sacred violet | Dissonant violet |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it is** | *"visions, divine encounters, Shepherd callings, the white-and-violet metaphysical language"* | *"demonic influence, Dissonance, spiritual shadow"* |
| **Always paired with** | **the sacred light ramps — Sacred White / Grace Ivory `TERR-101`–`104`**, and where warmth is wanted **Grace Gold `TERR-097`–`100`** | **ash, shadow and demonic ember `TERR-121`–`124`.** **Never** the sacred ramps |
| **Its behaviour** | **luminous and *emanating*** — *"it radiates outward from a source, clean-edged, with light at its core"* | **murky and *staining*** — *"it creeps, seeps and clings, dark at its core"* |
| **What it belongs to** | **events** — *"moments that interrupt ordinary reality"* | **entities and places** — *"things in the world that are corrupted"* |

---

**So the register is carried by four things, and the hue is not one of them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — What it is paired with** | **sacred white and gold, or ash and ember.** This is the primary signal |
| **2 — Where the light is** | **sacred violet has light at its core; dissonant violet is dark at its core.** A practical drawing rule: **sacred reads `TERR-104` or `TERR-100` at the centre with `TERR-119`–`120` around it; dissonant reads `TERR-117` at the centre with `TERR-119` around it** |
| **3 — Its edges and motion** | **clean-edged and radiating outward, or creeping and clinging** |
| **4 — Its subject** | **an event, or a thing** |

**And the document's own note on how the separation works in practice:**

> *"The practical separation is that **the two rarely share a frame**: sacred violet appears in metaphysical events and cinematic punctuation, dissonant violet appears on enemies and environments during ordinary play. **Where they must appear together, the sacred register is identified by its white core and the dissonant one by its absence.**"*

---

**Why one ramp rather than two.** The document says why: *"the two are theologically related, not unrelated"*. **That is a world-fact decision, not a palette convenience** — and it comes from the canon that `cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md` implements.

**And the escalation if it fails**, which is the clause worth admiring:

> *"**If playtesting shows the two read alike at gameplay distance, the escalation is a palette revision splitting them into separate ramps — not a per-asset workaround.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What that means for you** | **do not solve a violet ambiguity by inventing a different violet for one asset** |
| **The correct response** | **report that the two read alike**, and the palette gets revised |
| **Which is the same rule as everywhere else** | §2.1: *"Art must not invent costume details, insignia, equipment, anatomy or lore to fill a gap; **surface the gap instead**"* |

---

**And the measurement, which is a caution:**

| Entry | Hex | H | S | L |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`TERR-117` Ash Violet** | `#2D2738` | 261 | 18 | **19** |
| **`TERR-118` Bruised Violet** | `#463A56` | 266 | 19 | 28 |
| **`TERR-119` Dissonant Violet** | `#625074` | 270 | 18 | 38 |
| **`TERR-120` Veil Violet** | `#8A70A0` | 272 | 20 | **53** |

**Saturation is 18 to 20 throughout — the ramp is muted.** Which fits *"Ordinary Terrath should remain muted, earthy, restrained"*, and it means **violet at gameplay distance is a desaturated purple-grey.** **That is precisely the condition under which the two registers are most likely to read alike**, and it is why the escalation clause exists.

**Practice.** Read the violet rule section in full. Then draw the same violet shape twice: once with a `TERR-104` Sacred White core radiating outward with clean edges, once with a `TERR-117` core creeping with ragged edges, and look at both at 300%. Then ask whether you can tell them apart at 100% — and if not, note that as the escalation the document describes.
The three exemptions:
Where the palette does not apply, who decided each one, and why knowing the exemptions is part of knowing the palette.

**The palette document records three exemptions, each with a date and a decider.** They are worth knowing precisely, because an exemption misapplied is an off-palette colour with an excuse.

---

**1 — The HUD party-frame accent colours.**

> *"**HUD party-frame accent colours are exempt** from the palette and the violet rule (Master Roachi, 2026-09-17; the colours approved by Timon the same day). Each hero's party frame draws its resource-bar fill in code, and recolours the bar's painted rim at runtime, in that hero's accent colour (`PARTY_ACCENTS` in `game/scripts/presentation/ui/production_hud.gd`; see `hud.md`). **Two are off-palette**: Felix `#B04A4F` (burgundy) and Veyra `#2F4FB8` (deep mana blue). **Eli's Veil Violet (`TERR-120`) is used there under the same exemption, not as either violet register.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What is exempt** | **the party-frame accent colours only** |
| **Where they live** | **in code**, as `PARTY_ACCENTS`, not in a sprite |
| **Two are genuinely off-palette** | `#B04A4F` and `#2F4FB8` |
| **And the subtle part** | **Eli's accent is `TERR-120` Veil Violet — a palette colour used outside the violet rule.** So it is violet, and it is **neither sacred nor dissonant**; it is an identifier |
| **What this does not exempt** | **a sprite.** An accent colour is a HUD colour. §10.1 still forbids a character's identity depending on hue |

**2 — UI art.**

> *"**UI art is an exception to the violet rule** (Master Roachi, 2026-09-15). Violet painted into the hand-drawn UI art stays as painted. (The example given on 2026-09-15, the minimap's purple banner, is red in Timon's minimap border v2 of 2026-09-16; the exception itself stands.)"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What is exempt** | **the violet rule, for hand-painted UI art** |
| **And separately, §3 exempts UI from the sprite rules entirely** | *"HUD and other UI artwork uses transparent PNG where practical and **does not inherit sprite canvas, pivot or animation rules**"* |
| **Note the drafting** | **the example given for the exemption no longer exists** — the purple banner became red in v2 — **and the document says the exemption stands anyway.** That is good document hygiene and worth imitating: **a rule outlives the instance that prompted it** |

**3 — The cleanup colours**, which get their own lesson next.

---

**And two further boundaries that are not called exemptions but function as them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Nix Green ramp** | **`TERR-129`–`132`, reserved: *"Nix's interface, system graphics and Bandwidth readouts only"*.** And the reasoning is unusual and worth reading: it *"does not spend the 'supernatural effects and gameplay telegraph accents' saturation budget … because it is not world light — it is a screen, emitted by Nix's own equipment, present only where his interface renders, and dark whenever he is not working"*. **Matrix Green `#2BD44A` is S68 L50 — by far the most saturated green in the palette — and it is permitted because it is a CRT, not a world** |
| **The body-part reference's own palette** | **`media/reference/Animation/README.md`: the approved idle has *"its own 13 colours"*, not Palette v0.1.** **It is a motion reference and not a production master**, so it is outside the palette by being outside production |

---

**Why the exemptions matter as knowledge.** Three reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — A validator must know them** | **a script that flags `#B04A4F` in `production_hud.gd` is wrong**, and one that flags the reference idle's 13 colours is wrong too |
| **2 — They show the shape of the authority** | **each exemption names a person and a date.** §2.1's priority order starts with *"direct decisions by Master Roachi"*, and these are what that looks like in practice |
| **3 — They are the model for the next one** | **an exemption is decided, recorded with its reason, and kept even when its example changes.** That is how to ask for one |

**Practice.** Read the three exemption notes in `colour-palette.md`. Then find `PARTY_ACCENTS` in `production_hud.gd` and list the accent colours, marking which are off-palette. Then check whether `TERR-120` appears in any sprite you have drawn, and if so decide which violet register you intended.
The cleanup colours:
Four hex values with no palette ID, the decision that kept them, and what it teaches about how this project treats rules.

**The note, in full:**

> *"**Cleanup colours kept (decided 2026-09-11):** Master Roachi added four colours outside the numbered palette while cleaning up `ordinary-corpse-puppet-a_death_e_v002` in Aseprite, and on 2026-09-11 decided they stay: *"the extra colors are fine, i added them so they stay."* They are **`#281E18`** (dark brown for trousers and hair, replacing Soot Ink there), **`#241B16`** (boots), **`#1F1F11`** (the shirt outline where it meets hair and sleeve hem) and **`#FFFFFF`**. They have no `TERR-` IDs yet, and they are not in the `.gpl`/`.json` swatch files. **A palette validator run over his cleaned masters should accept them, not flag them.**"*

---

**The four, measured:**

| Hex | H | S | L | What it was for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`#281E18`** | 23 | 25 | **12** | **dark brown for trousers and hair, replacing `TERR-002` Soot Ink** |
| **`#241B16`** | 22 | 24 | **11** | boots |
| **`#1F1F11`** | 60 | 31 | **9** | the shirt outline where it meets hair and sleeve hem |
| **`#FFFFFF`** | — | 0 | **100** | — |

**And the instructive part is the first one's reason: it replaced Soot Ink.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`TERR-002` Soot Ink** | `#27292D` — **H220, cool**, L16 |
| **`#281E18`** | **H23, warm**, L12 |
| **So the substitution** | **swapped a cool near-black for a warm one, and went two points darker** |
| **Which is exactly the hue-shifting problem of three lessons ago** | **the palette's neutral ramp is cool, and a warm material's darkest recess sometimes wants to be warm.** The palette has no warm near-black below `TERR-005` at L21 |
| **So this is not an arbitrary addition** | **it is a real gap in the palette, found by drawing** |

---

**And `#1F1F11` is the same gap again, from the other side:** H60 — **olive-black**, for a shirt outline meeting hair. **A very dark warm-green near-black that the palette also does not have.**

**`#FFFFFF`** is a different case: **the palette's lightest is `TERR-104` Sacred White `#F3E8C5`** at L87 and warm. **Pure white is not in the palette at all**, and `colour-palette.md`'s usage rule reserves the brightest values for *"supernatural effects and gameplay telegraph accents"*. **So pure white on an ordinary corpse puppet is outside the system — and it was kept.**

---

**What this teaches, and it is three things:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The palette is incomplete, and drawing is how that gets found** | **nobody noticed the missing warm near-black until a sprite needed one.** §9.2's parallel: *"revise the table if drawn evidence shows a systematic problem"* |
| **2 — A decision beats a rule** | **§2.1's priority order puts *"direct decisions by Master Roachi"* first**, above the product documents. The four colours break the palette's own *"Do not invent substitute colours"* rule, and they stay, because he said so |
| **3 — The validator must be told** | **the document goes out of its way to say so**: *"A palette validator run over his cleaned masters should accept them, not flag them."* **A tool that is right about the rule and wrong about the decision is a broken tool** |

---

**And the open question the note leaves**, stated plainly because the document does:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **They have no `TERR-` IDs** | and **are not in the `.gpl` or `.json`** |
| **So they cannot be loaded** | **you cannot pick `#281E18` from the palette in Aseprite**, because it is not there |
| **Which means** | **in indexed mode they are unavailable**, and in RGB mode they must be typed in by hand |
| **The sensible resolution** | **either give them IDs and add them to the swatch files, or accept that they live in that one master and nowhere else** |
| **And that is a palette revision** — a decision, not a drawing choice. **Surface it** | |

**Practice.** Load the `.gpl` and confirm the four colours are not in it. Then find the darkest warm entry in the palette (`TERR-025` Blackened Leather at L18, or `TERR-005` at L21) and compare it with `#281E18` at L12 — and decide whether the gap is real. Then write down what you would propose: four new IDs, or four local exceptions.
Ramp borrowing:
Using one ramp's entries for a material it was not named for, when that is right, and the one rule it must not break.

**The permission is explicit.** `colour-palette.md`:

> *"A master palette is **a bank of approved choices**, not a requirement to use every colour in an asset."*

**And §9.3:** *"A scene curates only the material ramps it needs."*

**So the Intended uses column is guidance, not a constraint.** This lesson is about doing that deliberately.

---

**The four legitimate reasons to borrow:**

**1 — A material has no ramp of its own.** The commonest case:

| Material | No ramp named for it, so |
| --- | --- |
| **Thatch** | **`029`–`032` Ochre** (*"dry grasses"*) or **`005`–`008` Cloth** (*"dust"*) |
| **Rope** | **`029`–`032` Ochre** or **`005`–`008`** |
| **Bone** | **`013`–`016` Stone** (*"chalked stone"* at the Light end) or **`081`–`084`** |
| **Glass** | **`057`–`060` Water** or **`109`–`112` Tech** |
| **Brick** | **`037`–`040` Rust** at its Mid, or **`021`–`024` Earth** |
| **Canvas or sacking** | **`005`–`008`** or **`045`–`048`** (*"utility cloth"*) |

**2 — A hue shift is wanted.** From the hue-shifting lesson: **borrow a cooler ramp's Deep for a warm material's deepest recess** — `TERR-002` or `TERR-017` under cloth.

**3 — A value range is wanted that the material's own ramp does not have.** From stage 4's grey test:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | two materials that must separate sit at the same lightness |
| **The fix** | **borrow a ramp with a different range.** Stone `013`–`016` runs L23–67; slate `017`–`020` runs L19–62; metal `009`–`012` runs L22–66. **Three "grey" ramps with slightly different ranges and hues** |

**4 — A scene's budget demands sharing.** §9.3's 32–40 colours: **if the budget is tight, one ramp serves two materials at different steps.**

---

**The one rule borrowing must not break.** `colour-palette.md`:

> *"Do not invent substitute colours, rename entries, alter hex values, or **break ramp relationships** without an explicit palette revision."*

**"Break ramp relationships" means: do not treat four entries from different ramps as if they were a ramp.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Legitimate** | **use `TERR-033`–`036` for timber, and `TERR-002` as the outline.** Four from one ramp plus one borrowed entry |
| **Legitimate** | **use `TERR-033` and `TERR-035` only** — two steps of one ramp, skipping one |
| **Not legitimate** | **use `TERR-005`, `TERR-014`, `TERR-023`, `TERR-036` as a four-step ramp.** Their lightnesses are 21, 35, 41, 59 — **so they would behave as a ramp** — and their hues are 22, 34, 29, 20, so **they would read as one muddled material rather than as a coherent one** |
| **Why it matters** | **the ramps are designed as sets.** Their steps are spaced deliberately and their hue drift is consistent. **A home-made ramp has neither property, and a validator checking ramp coherence would flag it** |

---

**And the borrowing that is explicitly forbidden:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`TERR-129`–`132` Nix Green** | **reserved: *"Nix's interface, system graphics and Bandwidth readouts only"*, and *"Not for the world, and not for any other character's technology"*.** The most explicit prohibition in the document |
| **`TERR-097`–`104` the sacred ramps** | **not forbidden, and reserved by the usage rule** — *"Reserve the strongest saturation and brightness for supernatural effects and gameplay telegraph accents"*. **Grace Gold on an ordinary brass buckle spends the sacred budget** |
| **`TERR-121`–`124` demonic ember against `TERR-125`–`128` ordinary fire** | **two fires, and using the demonic one for a cooking fire says something untrue** |
| **The violet ramp** | **the violet rule, and the pairing requirement** |

**The pattern: material ramps borrow freely; meaning ramps do not.** The nine earthy ramps, the four vegetation ones, the two water and cold ones and the four skin ones are a kit. **The sacred, Beacon, Vale, violet, ember and Nix ramps carry meaning, and borrowing them borrows the meaning.**

**Practice.** Assign a ramp to each of these with no ramp of its own: thatch, rope, bone, glass, brick, sacking, a clay pot, a tin lantern. Then take one and justify a second choice. Then find three ramps whose lightness ranges differ and note which you would use to separate two greys. Then write down which ramps you would never borrow and why.
Saturation as a budget:
The usage rule that reserves the palette's brightest colours, and how to tell whether an asset is spending them.

**The rule, and it is the second thing `colour-palette.md` says:**

> *"Ordinary Terrath should remain **muted, earthy, restrained, and materially readable**."*
>
> *"**Reserve the strongest saturation and brightness for supernatural effects and gameplay telegraph accents**, including Shepherd Light, Beacon energy, Vale signals, demonic influence, and exceptional fire/light."*

**So saturation is a budget, and the budget is spent by meaning rather than by taste.**

---

**The measurement that shows the two tiers.** Maximum saturation by ramp group:

| Group | Peak saturation |
| --- | --- |
| **Neutral `001`–`004`** | **S8** |
| **Cloth `005`–`008`** | **S14** |
| **Stone, slate, metal** | **S14 or lower** |
| **Earth `021`–`024`** | **S46** |
| **Leather, timber, ochre** | **S35 to S46** |
| **Vegetation** | **S20 to S30** |
| **Water, ice** | **S24 to S33** |
| **Skin** | **S34 to S58** |
| **Blood `089`–`092`** | **S52** |
| | |
| **Gold `097`–`100`** | **S78** |
| **Sacred White `101`–`104`** | S50 |
| **Beacon `105`–`108`** | **S51** |
| **Vale `113`–`116`** | S47 |
| **Ordinary fire `125`–`128`** | **S86** |
| **Demonic ember `121`–`124`** | **S68** |
| **Nix Green `129`–`132`** | **S83** |

**The ordinary world tops out around S46 and the meaning ramps run S47 to S86.** That is the budget, visible in the numbers — **and the cloth, stone and metal ramps at S14 or less are the quietest things in the palette, which is why they are the ones a York scene is mostly made of.**

---

**How to tell whether an asset is overspending. Three checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Is anything above S50 that is not supernatural?** | **a saturated colour on an ordinary prop is spending the budget.** A red door at `TERR-091` Fresh Blood S52 is loud; at `TERR-039` Iron Rust S56 it is— **also loud.** Rust is a material ramp and it is the most saturated of them |
| **2 — Does the asset draw the eye before the character does?** | **saturation attracts attention regardless of value**, so a saturated prop competes with the thing the player should be looking at — the value hierarchy of stage 4 |
| **3 — Would it still read if desaturated?** | **the grey test again.** If an asset's appeal is its saturation, it has no value structure |

---

**And the one real tension in this rule**, worth naming:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§2 wants places to *"feel inhabited and materially specific"*** | which usually means variety |
| **The palette wants *"muted, earthy, restrained"*** | which means low saturation |
| **The resolution** | **variety comes from hue and value, not from saturation.** Thirty-three ramps at S8–S46 is a lot of distinguishable materials; **the palette achieves specificity by having many quiet ramps rather than a few loud ones** |
| **Which is why there are four separate greens** | moss, olive, living green, sage — **all of them muted, all of them distinguishable by hue and lightness.** That is the method |

---

**One practical consequence for telegraphs.** §5.3:

> *"Telegraphs must read through **pose, silhouette, motion and sound** rather than **colour alone**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So the saturated colours are available for telegraphs** | the usage rule names *"gameplay telegraph accents"* |
| **And colour is not sufficient for one** | §5.3 is explicit |
| **Which means a telegraph is a pose plus a motion plus a sound plus, optionally, a saturated accent** | |
| **And that accent is the one place an ordinary enemy legitimately uses a meaning ramp** — Vale signal red on a hostile machine, demonic ember on a corrupted creature's wind-up | |

**Practice.** List every entry in the palette above S50 and note which ramp each belongs to. Then take a prop you have drawn and check its highest saturation. Then design a telegraph for an enemy wind-up that reads through pose and silhouette alone, and only then add a saturated accent and ask whether it added anything.

| **`117`–`120` Violet** | **H261–272** |
| **`113`–`116` Vale** | H340–350 |

---

**Four observations, and each one is usable:**

**1 — York is warm and its materials are cool.** The ground, cloth, timber, leather and stone are all warm (H20–38); **the stone roofing, the metal and the neutral outlines are cool (H199–225).** So an ordinary scene is **warm masses with cool edges and cool hard surfaces** — which is exactly the *"warm, earthy, weathered"* of §2.

**2 — The outline ramp is cool and that is doing work.** From the hue-shifting lesson: **`TERR-001`–`004` at H216–225 means every outline is slightly blue.** Against warm cloth and earth that is **a complementary contrast**, which separates more strongly than a neutral grey would at the same value. **The palette's outline ramp is the single cleverest thing in it.**

**3 — The interruptions are at the extremes.** The meaning ramps sit where the ordinary world does not:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Beacon H182–190** | **cyan — and nothing else in the palette is cyan except the Tech and Ice ramps**, both of which are its relatives |
| **Violet H261–272** | **nothing else is violet.** It owns that part of the wheel |
| **Vale H340–350** | **crimson — adjacent to blood at H0–3, and nothing else** |
| **Nix green H132–140** | **the same hue as living green, and at S83 against living green's S20–29.** It is distinguished by saturation, not hue |

**So the palette reserves whole regions of the hue wheel for meaning.** A cyan glow in York is Beacon or technology; a violet is metaphysical; a crimson signal is Vale. **That is a legible language, and it works because the ordinary world stays in H15–45 and H180–225.**

**4 — The one ambiguity is Nix green against living green.** Same hue, and **separated only by saturation — S83 against S29.** **Which is why the exception note is so careful**: it is *"a screen, emitted by Nix's own equipment, present only where his interface renders"*. **At gameplay distance a desaturated Matrix Green and a saturated Living Green could meet in the middle**, and the escalation would be the same as the violet rule's.

---

**What to do with this.** Three habits:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Pair warm with cool for separation** | **a warm material against a cool outline, a warm figure against a cool slate roof.** Temperature contrast separates where value contrast is unavailable |
| **Keep the ordinary world inside H15–45 and H180–225** | and **notice when you have left it** |
| **Treat a cyan, a violet or a crimson as a statement** | **because the palette does.** If an ordinary prop needs one, that is a design question |

**Practice.** Sort the ramps you use most by hue and confirm which half each is in. Then draw a warm object with a cool outline and the same object with a warm outline, and compare separation at 300%. Then look at a York scene you have blocked out and list every hue in it, and check whether any are outside H15–45 and H180–225.
Accents and telegraphs:
The saturated colours as a signalling system: what each one means, and §5.3's rule that colour alone is never enough.

**The palette reserves its loudest colours for meaning. This lesson is the vocabulary.**

| Ramp | What it signals |
| --- | --- |
| **`097`–`100` Shepherd Gold** | **Shepherd Light, Grace effects, holy accents** — the player's own sacred power |
| **`101`–`104` Ivory → Sacred White** | **Shepherd Light cores and sacred highlights.** The white core that identifies the sacred register |
| **`105`–`108` Beacon Cyan** | **Beacon lights and cold machine energy** — the Prologue's central object (§6.6) |
| **`109`–`112` Tech** | **ordinary technology, displays, machinery** — the quiet relative of Beacon cyan |
| **`113`–`116` Vale** | **Vale technology, Kia accents, corporate danger** |
| **`117`–`120` Violet** | **two registers** — the violet rule |
| **`121`–`124` Demonic Ember** | **demonic heat, ash-fire, corrupted glow** |
| **`125`–`128` Ordinary fire** | **ordinary fire, lamps, combustion** |
| **`129`–`132` Nix Green** | **one hero's interface, and nothing else** |

**And the distinction that structures the whole set: `121`–`124` against `125`–`128`.** **Two fires.** A cooking fire, a lamp and a burning roof are `125`–`128`; a demonic manifestation is `121`–`124`. **The player can tell a disaster from an attack by the colour of the fire**, and spending the wrong one says something untrue.

---

**The rule that limits all of it.** §5.3:

> *"Telegraphs must read through **pose, silhouette, motion and sound** rather than **colour alone**."*

**Four channels, and colour is not among them.** So a telegraph is:

| Channel | For a fox's rear before a lunge (§6.5) |
| --- | --- |
| **Pose** | **the rear itself** — the body rising, weight back, a shape the fox has in no other state |
| **Silhouette** | **readable in solid black** — stage 4's test applies to actions, not only to characters |
| **Motion** | **the timing.** §6.5: *"The lunge currently lasts 0.22 seconds and the rear 0.62 seconds; art must be authored against the gameplay timing rather than redefining it"* |
| **Sound** | `audio.md`'s |
| **Colour** | **optional, and additive** |

**The reason is accessibility and legibility together:** a colour-blind player, a player in a cluttered scene, and a player under a coloured `Light2D` all see the pose and may not see the hue. **§10.1's identity clause says the same thing about characters — *"Identity cannot depend on hue"* — and §5.3 extends it to actions.**

---

**So where does a saturated accent legitimately go?** Three places:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **On a supernatural or technological source** | **it is the thing's actual colour.** The Beacon is cyan; Shepherd Light is gold and white |
| **As a confirming accent on a telegraph** | **after the pose reads.** A wind-up that already reads in black, with ember at the contact point |
| **In the HUD** | **where §8 and `hud.md` govern, and the party accents are exempt** — stage 5's exemptions lesson |

**And the one place it does not go: as the primary carrier of any gameplay information.**

---

**One concrete case worth working, because the Prologue needs it.** §6.6:

> *"Beacon needs inert, awakening and awake states. Awakening includes trembling, seams, rings rotating into alignment, rising, flash and settlement. Awake Beacon uses light and a subtle bob."*

| State | How the colour is spent |
| --- | --- |
| **Inert** | **no Beacon cyan at all, or only the deepest step.** A dark sphere — `TERR-105` Beacon Deep, or tech greys. **The saturation is held back** |
| **Awakening** | **seams light up** — `TERR-106` → `107` → `108` progressively. **The trembling and the rings are pose and motion; the cyan is the confirmation** |
| **Flash** | **`TERR-108` Beacon Light, and `TERR-104` Sacred White at the core** if the moment is sacred — which is the violet rule's logic applied to a different ramp |
| **Awake** | **`TERR-107` steady with a subtle bob.** The bob is motion; the cyan is identity |

**Read the progression: the colour escalates with the state, and the motion carries the event.** That is the pattern for every telegraph in the game.

**Practice.** List the nine meaning ramps and write one sentence each on what using it claims. Then design the fox's rear as pose and silhouette only, test it in solid black, and only then consider an accent. Then sketch Beacon's four states as a value progression with no cyan at all, and check whether the states are still distinguishable.
When to propose a new ramp:
The palette is designed to grow, the procedure for growing it, and the three tests a proposal should pass first.

**The palette is explicitly open.** `colour-palette.md`:

> *"It is a set of four-step ramps **with no fixed size: the palette grows to include every colour it needs, and a new ramp joins it when it is approved** (Master Roachi, 2026-09-17), as the Nix Green ramp `TERR-129`–`TERR-132` did on 2026-09-10. **It began as 32 ramps and 128 colours.**"*

**And the implementation note:** *"The palette holds 132 entries at the time of writing (33 ramps); **a new ramp takes the next free IDs**."*

**So `TERR-133`–`136` is the next ramp, whatever it turns out to be.**

---

**What the precedent shows.** Nix Green is the one worked example, and its note is a model proposal:

| Element | What Nix Green's note does |
| --- | --- |
| **The gap it fills** | *"Nix's interface, system graphics and Bandwidth readouts"* — a specific, named need |
| **Why nothing existing works** | **nothing in the palette is a saturated phosphor green** |
| **Why it does not break the saturation budget** | *"it is not world light — it is a screen, emitted by Nix's own equipment, present only where his interface renders, and dark whenever he is not working"* |
| **What it pairs with** | *"black, charcoal and dark metal … and with Tech Deep Steel/Tech Cyan Grey/System Cyan/Interface Steel (`TERR-109`–`112`) where an ordinary machine housing is wanted"* |
| **Its limits** | *"**Not for the world, and not for any other character's technology.**"* |
| **And it is dated and attributed** | decided 2026-09-10 |

**Six elements. A proposal that has all six is a proposal; one that has fewer is a request.**

---

**The three tests to run before proposing.**

**1 — Is the gap real, or is it a borrowing failure?** From the borrowing lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ask** | **which existing ramp is closest, and what specifically is wrong with it?** |
| **The common wrong answers** | *"it is not quite the right green"* — **there are four greens.** *"It needs to be darker"* — **there are four steps.** *"The hue is slightly off"* — **the palette is deliberately muted** |
| **The right kind of answer** | **"the palette has no warm near-black below L18, and a warm material's deepest recess needs one"** — which is the cleanup colours' actual finding |

**2 — Is it a material or a meaning?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A material ramp** | **cheap to add and easy to justify.** It joins a kit of nine and borrows freely |
| **A meaning ramp** | **expensive.** It claims a region of the hue wheel, spends saturation budget, and has to be distinguishable from every other meaning at gameplay distance — **which is the violet rule's whole problem** |
| **So** | **a material proposal needs the gap; a meaning proposal needs the gap *and* a legibility argument** |

**3 — Does it survive the four-step structure?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The requirement** | **`Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light`**, with the measured properties from this stage: **lightness steps of about 10 to 13, with the Mid-to-Light step biggest; saturation rising toward light if warm and falling if cool or emissive** |
| **A proposal that is one colour** | **is not a ramp.** It is either a borrowing or an exception like the cleanup colours |
| **And a four-colour proposal whose steps are evenly spaced** | **will not behave like the other 33** |

---

**And the alternative to a new ramp, which is often the right answer: an exception.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The precedent** | **the four cleanup colours** — kept, used in one master, given no IDs, and the validator told to accept them |
| **When that is better** | **when the need is local.** One sprite's outline problem does not need four new palette entries |
| **When it is worse** | **when the need recurs.** Three sprites with the same off-palette warm near-black is a missing ramp pretending to be three exceptions |
| **The test** | **has this gap appeared twice?** |

**Practice.** Write a proposal for a ramp the palette does not have, with all six of Nix Green's elements. Then run the three tests on it honestly and decide whether it survives.
