| **Why generous is fine** | **transparent pixels cost nothing** in a packed sprite sheet, and **§4's own 112 × 112 has 16 rows below the feet for exactly this reason** |

---

**Placing the anchor.** From stage 3:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where** | **bottom-centre of the ground contact** — not of the canvas, and not of the sprite's bounding box |
| **On a 24 × 24 canvas** | **column 12, and the row where the bucket's base sits** |
| **If the base is at row 20** | **the anchor is (12, 20)**, with 4 rows below it |
| **How to mark it** | **a single pixel on a locked guide layer**, or Aseprite's View › Guides |
| **And the warning from stage 1** | **never Trim.** Trim moves the anchor, and a prop's anchor is what positions it in the world |

**And how Godot learns the anchor**, which is worth knowing now:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For a `Sprite2D`** | **the `offset` property, or `centered = false` plus an offset.** The texture is positioned relative to the node |
| **So the anchor is expressed in the scene**, not in the image | which means **the drawing must be consistent so one offset works** |
| **The consequence** | **every prop of the same canvas size and anchor convention shares one offset value**, which is why having a convention matters more than having the right number |
| **The convention to adopt** | **bottom-centre of the canvas, with the object's base sitting a fixed number of rows above the canvas's bottom edge.** Then the offset is the same for every prop |

**That last row simplifies things considerably: put the base at a fixed distance from the canvas bottom** — say, always 4 rows — **and every prop's Godot offset is the same formula.**

---

**Three canvas sizes worth standardising on**, so that props are consistent:

| Size | For |
| --- | --- |
| **24 × 24** | **1 × 1 footprint props up to about 20 px tall** — buckets, crates, pails, firepits, small sacks |
| **48 × 48** | **1 × 1 or 2 × 2 props up to about 44 px** — barrels, round hay bales, cabinets at a push |
| **Wider, case by case** | **benches, tables, troughs, carts** — §9.2's 46–120 px lengths. **A cart at 100–120 px long needs a canvas around 128 × 80** |

**And §9.2's door opening at 88 px clear** is the reminder that architecture is a different problem again — stage 8's.

**Practice.** Create a 24 × 24 indexed canvas with the Shepherds palette, mark the anchor at (12, 20), and save it as a small-prop template. Then work out the canvas you would need for §9.2's bench at 23 px seat and 56 px long, and for the cart at 120 px long. Then check your template's grid is 16 × 16 so you can see the footprint.
Blocking the bucket:
The first three passes: silhouette, form, and the structure — all before any colour is chosen.

**Stage 4's order: silhouette first, in one value.** This lesson does that, and the two passes after it.

---

**Pass one — the silhouette, in one value.**

**The bucket's shape**, from stage 3's truncated cone:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Height** | **15 px** |
| **Width at the mouth** | **about 12 px** |
| **Width at the base** | **about 9 px** — so **1 or 2 px of taper per side** |
| **The mouth** | **an ellipse at the projection ratio** — 12 wide, so **6 tall** |
| **The base** | **the near half of an ellipse — a curve, not a straight line** (stage 3's cylinder rule) |
| **The handle** | **an arc above the mouth**, or omitted — **and whether it is up or down is a decision.** A bucket at rest has its handle down against the side |

**So the silhouette is: a trapezoid 12 wide at the top and 9 at the bottom, 15 tall, with an elliptical top and a curved base.** About 140 pixels.

**Run the tests now**, from stage 4: **does the shape read as a bucket in one value at 300%?** If not, the taper is wrong or the mouth ellipse is wrong — **and fixing it now costs a minute.**

---

**Pass two — the form, in two values.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fill with the Mid** | `TERR-035` Weathered Wood — though the colour is not chosen until the next lesson, so **do this in two greys if that helps** |
| **The light-to-shadow boundary** | **a vertical line slightly left of centre**, because the key light is upper-left (§10.1) |
| **Which side** | **the right side is Shadow.** On a truncated cone the boundary leans slightly with the taper |
| **The mouth's interior** | **mostly Shadow** — the inside of a bucket is in shade. **And the far rim's inner edge catches light** |
| **And the mouth's rim** | **the ellipse's upper edge is Light; its near edge is where you see the rim's thickness** |

**Pass three — the structure.**

**A bucket's structure is staves and bands**, and at 12 px wide there is room for very little:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Staves** | **two or three vertical lines of the Shadow step**, not evenly spaced — **a 12 px bucket can show three staves and no more** |
| **The metal band** | **one horizontal line, 1 px, about a third of the way down** — and **a second near the base if there is room, which at 15 px there barely is.** One band |
| **The rim** | **the mouth's edge, one pixel, and it reads as the band at the top** |
| **The handle** | **a 1 px arc**, or hanging down the side as two pixels |
| **And stop** | **three staves, one band, a rim.** That is the structure, and it is about eight pixels of line work |

---

**The three errors to avoid**, each of which comes from a previous stage:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Evenly spaced staves** | **banding** — stage 2. Three staves at 4 px intervals on a 12 px bucket is a pattern. **Vary the spacing** |
| **A straight base** | **stage 3's cylinder rule.** The base of a round object curves downward in the middle |
| **A symmetrical silhouette** | **the taper and the light make a bucket asymmetrical**, and a perfectly symmetrical one reads as a logo. **One pixel of difference between the left and right profiles is enough** |

---

**And the check that matters at this point.** Before colour:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The black test** | **does it read as a bucket in solid black?** At 15 px, **the read is the taper plus the elliptical mouth.** If it reads as a plant pot, the taper is too strong; if as a tin, too weak |
| **Against the reference** | **put it beside the 80 px figure silhouette** from stage 3's reference file. **A bucket should come to about a fifth of an adult's height** — 15 against 80 is 19%, which is right |

**Practice.** Draw the silhouette in one value and run the black test. Then add the second value with the boundary left of centre. Then add three unevenly spaced staves, one band and a rim. Then put it beside the 80 px figure and check the proportion.
The eight colours:
Choosing the subset against the 4–10 band, assigning the four values, and the arithmetic of a secondary material.

**The band:** §10.1's *"a small prop 4–10"*. **The brief said eight. This lesson spends them.**

---

**The assignment:**

| Material | Entries | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Timber staves — the primary material** | **`TERR-033` Charred Wood, `034` Old Timber, `035` Weathered Wood, `036` Dry Timber** | **4** |
| **The metal band** | **`TERR-009` Cold Iron, `TERR-011` Dull Steel** | **2** |
| **The rope or leather handle** | **`TERR-027` Harness Leather** | **1** |
| **The outline and contact shadow** | **`TERR-001` Coal Black** | **1** |
| | | **8** |

**And the reasoning for each decision:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why timber gets four and the band gets two** | **stage 5's rule: the primary material gets its full ramp; everything else gets one or two entries.** A 1 px metal band has no room for four values |
| **Why `TERR-009` and `011` rather than `010` and `011`** | **contrast.** The band must separate from the timber around it, and **`TERR-009` at L22 against `TERR-035` at L?** — a bigger gap reads better at one pixel wide |
| **Why one entry for the handle** | **a rope handle is two or three pixels.** One value |
| **Why `TERR-001` rather than the timber's own Deep** | **stage 5's outline lesson: the material's Deep is the default** — so **`TERR-033` would be the orthodox choice.** `TERR-001` is used here **because the prop also needs a contact shadow, and sharing one entry between the outline's darkest parts and the shadow saves a colour** |

**That last decision is worth noticing: a colour band makes you share entries, and sharing the outline with the contact shadow is the cheapest sharing available.** §10.1's own words: *"These are discipline ranges rather than reasons to discard a necessary material distinction"* — **so if the sharing costs a distinction, spend the ninth colour.**

---

**Assigning the four timber values to surfaces**, from stage 4's four questions:

| Surface | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **The mouth's far rim, facing up** | **`TERR-036` Dry Timber** — Light |
| **The left third of the body** | **`TERR-035`** — Mid, facing the light |
| **The right third** | **`TERR-034`** — Shadow |
| **The staves' lines** | **`TERR-034`**, and `TERR-033` on the shadow side |
| **The interior of the mouth** | **`TERR-034`**, with `TERR-033` at the deepest |
| **Under the rim, where it overhangs the body** | **`TERR-033`** — occlusion |
| **The outline** | **`TERR-033` on the upper-left, `TERR-001` on the lower-right** — stage 5's selective outline |
| **The contact shadow** | **`TERR-001`** |

**Count the pixels per value**, which is stage 4's proportion check:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`TERR-035` Mid** | **the largest area** — the body's lit two-thirds. **50–60%** |
| **`TERR-034` Shadow** | the right side, the staves, the interior. **25–35%** |
| **`TERR-036` Light** | **the rim only.** 5–10% — **less than stage 4's 10–15%, because a bucket is matte timber** |
| **`TERR-033` Deep** | occlusion and the upper-left outline. **5–10%** |

---

**And the grey test, run before going further.** Three pairs to check:

| Pair | Risk |
| --- | --- |
| **The metal band against the timber** | **`TERR-011` Dull Steel is L?; `TERR-035` Weathered Wood is L?** — **if they are close, the band disappears in greyscale.** Which is why the band uses `TERR-009` as well |
| **The handle against the body** | `TERR-027` against `TERR-034`/`035` |
| **The whole bucket against the ground** | **stage 4's figure-against-ground lesson** — put it on `TERR-023` earth and on `TERR-015` stone and check both |

**Practice.** Assign the eight entries as above and shade the bucket. Then count the pixels of each value and compare with the proportions. Then greyscale it and check the three pairs. Then try it with the metal band at `TERR-010` and `011` instead and see whether it still separates.
The outline, the shadow and the checks:
Finishing the asset: the selective outline in palette terms, the contact shadow on its own layer, and stage 4's twelve checks run in order.

**Three passes left, and then it is done.**

---

**Pass one — the outline.** From stage 5's five decisions, applied to a 15 px bucket:

| Where | Entry |
| --- | --- |
| **Lower-right of the body** | **`TERR-001`** — maximum separation, and it will meet the contact shadow |
| **Right side** | **`TERR-033`** — the timber's Deep |
| **Left side** | **`TERR-033`**, or **`TERR-034`** one step lighter |
| **Upper-left of the rim** | **none** — the rim is the lightest thing on the bucket and the background does the separating |
| **The mouth's interior edge** | **`TERR-033`** — and this is occlusion as much as outline |
| **Around the metal band** | **nothing extra.** The band is already darker than the timber; **outlining it would be the double-outline §10.1 forbids** |

**And the handle**, which is the equipment case in miniature:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **If the handle stands away from the body** | **a negative gap** — one pixel of background between handle and bucket. §10.1's *"preserve useful negative gaps"* |
| **If it hangs against the side** | **a dark line between them**, so the handle reads as a separate object |
| **And the black test will tell you** | which you achieved |

---

**Pass two — the contact shadow.** From stages 3 and 4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its own layer** | **§3.1's four layers: body, equipment, shadow, effects.** The bucket uses body and shadow |
| **Shape** | **an ellipse at the projection ratio, matched to the 1 × 1 footprint** — about **13 wide and 5 tall** |
| **Position** | **centred on the anchor**, extending a pixel or two past the base on the lower-right and flush on the upper-left |
| **Value** | **`TERR-001`** |
| **Edges** | hard |

**And the check:** **hide the shadow layer and the bucket should look like it is floating.** If it does not, **the shadow was not doing anything and something else is anchoring it** — which is usually a baked dark edge that should not be there.

---

**Pass three — stage 4's twelve checks, run in order:**

| | Check | For the bucket |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | silhouette in one value | done in the blocking lesson |
| **2** | negative gaps | **the handle, if it stands away** |
| **3** | three or four values per material | **timber 4, metal 2, handle 1** |
| **4** | Mid dominates | **`TERR-035` at 50–60%** |
| **5** | key light upper-left | **the boundary left of centre, the rim lit** |
| **6** | occlusion at junctions, one pixel | **under the rim, at the band's lower edge, inside the mouth** |
| **7** | no rim light or second source | **check: no light on the lower-right edge** |
| **8** | contact shadow on its own layer | done |
| **9** | **greyscale** | **three pairs, from the last lesson** |
| **10** | **solid black** | **does it read as a bucket?** |
| **11** | **dark** | a Multiply layer at 65% — **does the rim still read?** |
| **12** | a busy scene | **Godot**, three lessons on |

**Plus stage 5's nine colour checks** — and the three that matter: **indexed with the palette loaded; one ramp per material; nothing above S50.** `TERR-039` Iron Rust at S56 is the only risk, and there is no rust here.

**And stage 3's seven projection failures** — of which the relevant ones are: **is the top ellipse at the project's ratio; is the base curved; is there a baked floor; is the anchor at the ground contact.**

---

**Three checks is the honest minimum if the list is too long:** **the black test, the greyscale test, and "put it beside the 80 px figure".** **Those three catch most of what the other twenty would.**

**Practice.** Outline the bucket with the six decisions above. Then add the contact shadow on its own layer and test by hiding it. Then run all twelve of stage 4's checks and write down which failed. Then fix them and run the three-check minimum to confirm.
Naming it, and where it goes:
The file layout and the naming grammar, applied — and the one rule that has no exceptions.

**The layout**, from `media/README.md` and §3.1:

> *"Editable masters live under `media/sprites/<category>/<family>/<asset-key>/`."*

| Part | For the bucket |
| --- | --- |
| **`<category>`** | **`props`** — the seven are `heroes`, `enemies`, `npcs`, `beacon`, `props`, `vfx`, `environment` |
| **`<family>`** | **a grouping of related assets.** `domestic`, or `containers`, or `york` — **a choice, and it should be consistent** |
| **`<asset-key>`** | **a stable kebab-case production identifier** — **`wooden-pail`** |
| **So the path** | **`media/sprites/props/domestic/wooden-pail/`** |

---

**The filename.** §3.1:

> *"Use one master per asset, action and direction, named `<asset-key>_<action>_<direction>.aseprite`."*

**And §9.2's prop exception:**

> *"**Static prop masters are `.aseprite` files with no character direction suffix.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So for a static prop** | **`wooden-pail.aseprite`** — **no action, no direction** |
| **And its tag** | **a static prop has one frame and needs no tag at all** if it imports as a Static Texture. **If it has states, each state is a tag** |
| **Where a direction suffix would come back** | **a prop with authored directions** — rare, and §5.4's rule would apply |

---

**The one rule with no exceptions.** `media/README.md`:

> *"**Exactly one authoritative editable `.aseprite` master per asset, action and direction, and it lives here.** … Never keep more than one editable master for the same asset, action and direction, and never keep a duplicate elsewhere. … **If you find two editable masters for the same asset and family, that is a defect to resolve, not a convenience.**"*

**Which forbids, specifically:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`wooden-pail-v2.aseprite`** beside `wooden-pail.aseprite` | **§3: *"Rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived"*** |
| **A copy in `media/reference/`** | *"`media/reference/` is for **visual reference material only**. Presence there does not imply approval. **Never place an editable production master there**"* |
| **A copy in `media/work/`** once it is a master | `media/work/` is for in-progress work and is gitignored |
| **An editable copy anywhere else** | |

**And the practical workflow that respects it:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **While learning or drafting** | **work in `media/work/`**, which is gitignored — **so the bucket-as-exercise lives there** |
| **When it is a real asset** | **move it to `media/sprites/<category>/<family>/<asset-key>/`** |
| **When it is superseded** | **delete the old one.** Version control has it |
| **Never two at once** | |

---

**And the export destination**, which you do not manage by hand:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`media/sprites/_exports/`** | *"Generated runtime sheets belong under `media/sprites/_exports/` and are **never edited by hand**"* |
| **Who writes it** | **Aseprite Wizard**, when it imports |
| **So you do not put anything there**, and you do not open anything there | |

---

**One Godot-specific caution.** `.aseprite` files inside the Godot project **are picked up by Godot's import system**:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Which is the point** for masters under `media/sprites/` | |
| **And a problem** for anything else — **which is why `media/reference/` has a `.gdignore`**, recorded in `media/reference/Animation/README.md`: *"Godot never imports it (`../.gdignore`)"* | |
| **And Wizard provides an alternative** | **the "No Import" importer** — set a file's importer to that and Godot ignores it without a `.gdignore` |

**Practice.** Create `media/work/wooden-pail.aseprite` and save your bucket there. Then decide the family name and write out the full production path it would take. Then check `media/sprites/props/` and confirm it holds only a `.gitkeep`. Then find the `.gdignore` in `media/reference/` and confirm it exists.
The six importers:
Aseprite Wizard's six import modes, read from the addon's source, and which one each asset class uses.

**Wizard 9.8.0 registers six importers**, and the names are exactly as they appear in Godot's Import dock:

| Importer | Produces | Internal name |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SpriteFrames** | **a `SpriteFrames` resource** — animations from tags | `aseprite_wizard.plugin.spriteframes` |
| **SpriteFrames (Split By Layer)** | **one `SpriteFrames` per layer** | |
| **Static Texture** | **a `PortableCompressedTexture2D`** — *"Imports first frame from Aseprite file as texture"* | `aseprite_wizard.plugin.static-texture` |
| **Static Texture (Split By Layer)** | **one texture per layer** | |
| **Tileset Texture** | **a `PortableCompressedTexture2D`**, laid out for a `TileSet` | `aseprite_wizard.plugin.tileset-texture` |
| **No Import** | **nothing** — Godot ignores the file | |

---

**Which one for which asset class:**

| Asset class | Importer | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A static prop** | **Static Texture** | **one frame, one texture.** The bucket |
| **A prop with states** | **SpriteFrames**, one tag per state — **or several Static Textures**, one file each | |
| **A character animation** | **SpriteFrames** | §3.1's *"one master per asset, action and direction"*, one tag each |
| **A character needing separable layers at runtime** | **SpriteFrames (Split By Layer)** | **§3.1's body / equipment / shadow / effects** |
| **Terrain tiles** | **Tileset Texture** | **§9.1's *"hand-drawn 16 × 16 tiles assembled as Godot terrain sets"*** |
| **Reference material** | **No Import** | **or a `.gdignore`, which `media/reference/` uses** |
| **UI art** | **none of these** | **§3: UI is PNG.** Godot's own texture importer |

---

**Two facts about how the importers behave that matter.**

**1 — There is a default importer, and it is a project setting.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | **decides which importer a newly added `.aseprite` file gets** |
| **The priority mechanism** | each importer returns a priority — **2.0 if it is the configured default, otherwise 0.8** — so **the default wins** |
| **Why that matters** | **drop a tileset master into the project with the default set to SpriteFrames and it imports as the wrong thing**, silently |
| **The fix** | **change it per file in Godot's Import dock, then reimport** — and **set the project default to whatever you add most of** |

**2 — Static Texture takes the first frame only.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The docstring** | *"Imports first frame from Aseprite file as texture"* |
| **Which means** | **a multi-frame master imported as a Static Texture silently loses every frame but one** |
| **And the reverse** | **a single-frame master imported as SpriteFrames gives you a one-frame animation**, which works and is odd |
| **So the brief's "runtime consumer" field decides the importer**, and §10.2 asks for it for this reason | |

---

**And the import options worth knowing**, from the static importer's source:

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **`layer/exclude_layers_pattern`** | **a pattern of layer names to skip.** Useful: **name your toggle layers something matching the pattern and they never import** |
| **`layer/only_visible_layers`** | **import only what is visible** — the simpler version of the same idea |
| **`layer/split_layers`** | one output per layer |

**That first option is the answer to stage 1's toggle layers.** **The greyscale layer, the black-fill layer and the reference layer must not import** — and either hiding them (`only_visible_layers`) or naming them to match an exclusion pattern handles it. **A sensible convention: prefix every non-exporting layer with `_`** — and set the exclusion pattern accordingly.

**Note that is a different underscore from the tag's.** **A tag beginning with `_` means "do not loop"; a layer beginning with `_` would mean "do not import", by your own convention.** **Both are useful and they are unrelated — do not confuse them.**

**Practice.** Open Godot's Import dock with an `.aseprite` file selected and read the importer list and the options. Then find the project's default importer setting. Then add a layer called `_guides` to your bucket master and set an exclusion pattern that skips it, and confirm the imported texture does not contain it.
Importing the bucket:
The round trip's first half, step by step, and the three ways it fails silently.

**The precondition, from `CLAUDE.md` and stage 1:**

> *"Aseprite Wizard's importer needs the Aseprite executable path in Godot's **editor** settings (`aseprite/general/command_path`). On this rig it is `$HOME/Games/steam/steamapps/common/Aseprite/aseprite`, with the home folder written out in full because Godot does not expand `~`. **Without a working path every `.aseprite` import silently fails with `valid=false`.**"*

**Check that first.** Everything below assumes it.

---

**The steps:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **put the master in the Godot project** — `media/sprites/props/domestic/wooden-pail/wooden-pail.aseprite` |
| **2** | **Godot notices it and imports it** with the default importer |
| **3** | **select it in the FileSystem dock and open the Import tab** |
| **4** | **set the importer to Static Texture** if it is not already |
| **5** | **set the layer options** — exclude or hide the guide and toggle layers |
| **6** | **Reimport** |
| **7** | **the result is a `PortableCompressedTexture2D`** usable as a `Sprite2D`'s texture |
| **8** | **and a sheet appears under `media/sprites/_exports/`** — **which you never touch** |

---

**The three silent failures, and how to recognise each:**

**1 — The Aseprite path is wrong.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | **the import produces nothing and the resource is invalid.** `CLAUDE.md`'s *"silently fails with `valid=false`"* |
| **Cause** | the editor setting is missing, has a `~` in it, or points at a non-existent binary |
| **Check** | **run the Aseprite path from a terminal with `--version`** — stage 1's command line. If that works and the import does not, the setting is wrong |
| **And it is machine-local** | *"never commit it"* |

**2 — The wrong importer.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | **a single-frame prop imported as SpriteFrames**, or **a multi-frame master imported as Static Texture and showing only frame 1** |
| **Cause** | the project's default importer |
| **Check** | **the Import dock says which** |

**3 — A layer that should not have imported.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | **the texture has a grey wash over it, or a grid, or a figure silhouette behind the bucket** |
| **Cause** | **the greyscale toggle, the black-fill layer, or the reference layer was visible** |
| **Check** | **look at the imported texture, not at the master.** This is the failure that is easiest to miss because the master looks right |
| **The fix** | **hide them, or the exclusion pattern** |

---

**And one failure that is not silent and is worth expecting: the canvas.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What happens** | **the texture is 24 × 24, as drawn** |
| **Why that is a surprise** | **because you think of the bucket as 15 px tall**, and the texture is 24 — **with 9 rows of transparency** |
| **Which is correct** | and it means **the `Sprite2D`'s offset has to account for it.** From stage 7's canvas lesson: **put the base at a fixed distance from the canvas bottom and the offset is the same formula for every prop** |
| **If you had trimmed** | the texture would be 12 × 15 and the offset would be different for every prop. **Which is the Trim warning from stage 1, now concrete** |

---

**One more thing worth doing once: run the export by hand.** From stage 1's command line lesson:

```
aseprite -b wooden-pail.aseprite --sheet out.png --data out.json
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why** | **Wizard is a wrapper around that command.** Running it once makes the import stop being magic |
| **What to look at** | **the PNG's dimensions and the JSON's frame rectangle** — and then compare with what Godot produced |
| **And then delete it** | it is not a master and not an export the project wants |

**Practice.** Verify the Aseprite path with `--version` from a terminal. Then put the bucket in the project, set the importer to Static Texture, exclude the guide layers, and reimport. Then check the imported texture's dimensions and confirm no guide layer came through. Then run the command-line export by hand and compare.
Seeing it in Godot:
The round trip's second half: placing the prop, getting the anchor right, and the two conditions only the engine can test.

**§10's seventh condition:**

> *"the asset works in Godot under **representative lighting, crowds and effects**"*

**And §5.3's, for animation:** *"checked at native scale, in motion, against the real ground and under representative lighting."*

**Aseprite can give you native scale and motion. The ground, the lighting, the crowd and the effects are here.**

---

**Placing it, in five steps:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **a `Sprite2D`** with the imported texture |
| **2** | **set the anchor** — `centered = false` and an `offset`, or `centered = true` with a vertical offset. **From the canvas lesson: if every prop's base sits a fixed distance from its canvas bottom, the offset is one formula** |
| **3** | **`y_sort_enabled` on the parent**, so the prop sorts by its anchor's Y against the characters — stage 3's Y-sorting |
| **4** | **put it in a real scene**, on real ground, near a character — **not in an empty test scene** |
| **5** | **set the zoom to the game's actual zoom** |

**Step 4 is the one people skip and it is the whole point.** An asset in an empty scene against a grey background has not been tested.

---

**The four things to look at, in order:**

| | What | What it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **the scale against the character** | **§9.2's band.** A 15 px bucket beside an 80 px figure should come to about the knee |
| **2** | **the anchor** | **walk the character past it.** Does the prop sort correctly — in front when the character is behind it, behind when in front? **A wrong anchor shows up as the character's feet overlapping the bucket's rim** |
| **3** | **the ground** | **does it separate from earth, from grass, from stone?** Stage 4's figure-against-ground lesson, applied to a prop |
| **4** | **the lighting** | **put a `Light2D` near it and move it.** Does the baked shading fight the runtime light? §10.1's restraint clause is being tested here |

---

**And the two things that can only be found here:**

**1 — Does the restrained shading work?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What you are checking** | **§10.1's *"Static shading stays restrained so Godot's local lights can read coherently"*** |
| **The test** | **a `Light2D` from the lower-right, which is the opposite of the baked key** |
| **A pass** | the bucket's lit side shifts — **the runtime light visibly changes it** |
| **A fail** | **nothing happens**, because the baked values are already at the extremes. **Which means going back and reducing the contrast** |
| **And this is the feedback loop the whole of stage 4 was waiting for** | |

**2 — Does it read in a crowd?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The test** | **put six props and two characters in one screen** |
| **What fails** | **a prop whose contrast or saturation competes with a character** — stage 4's value hierarchy |
| **And §9.3's check** | *"silhouette at gameplay zoom"* |

---

**The one thing to resist: adjusting the drawing to fix an engine problem.**

| Symptom | The wrong fix | The right fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The prop sorts wrongly** | move the drawing within the canvas | **fix the `offset` or the Y-sort** |
| **The prop is too small on screen** | redraw it bigger | **check the camera zoom** — and then check §9.2's band |
| **The prop is too dark** | lighten the drawing | **check the scene's ambient light** |
| **The prop has a seam against the ground** | paint ground into the sprite | **§9.1: *"Do not bake a floor"*.** The seam is the contact shadow's job |

**That table is the round trip's real lesson: half the problems you see in Godot are Godot problems**, and learning which half is why this loop has to become routine.

**Practice.** Place the bucket in a real York scene beside a character, with Y-sort on, at the game's zoom. Walk the character round it and check the sorting. Then add a `Light2D` from the lower-right and move it, and decide whether the baked shading is restrained enough. Then put six props and two characters on screen and look at the whole thing at once.
The definition of done:
§10's eight conditions, applied to the bucket one at a time, and the honest answer for each.

**The clause, in full:**

> *"Artwork is accepted only when: 1. its subject and required actions are defined by current product documents and canon; 2. Master Roachi approves the actual asset, not merely a concept or filename; 3. the editable master is uniquely identified; 4. dimensions, pivot, transparency, tags and loop behavior are correct; 5. animation timing matches gameplay; 6. silhouette, value, ground contact and direction coverage read at native scale; 7. the asset works in Godot under representative lighting, crowds and effects; 8. superseded versions and temporary conversion material are deleted."*

---

**Condition by condition, for the bucket:**

| | Condition | The bucket |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **subject and actions defined by documents and canon** | **FAILS, honestly.** §9.2's size band is *"starting calibration, not approval of an asset"*, and no document requires a bucket. **The bench, the fence and the wool do** — the derivation lesson |
| **2** | **Master Roachi approves the actual asset** | **not yet, and it is a separate event** |
| **3** | **the editable master is uniquely identified** | **passes** — one `.aseprite`, in one place, no duplicates |
| **4** | **dimensions, pivot, transparency, tags and loop behaviour correct** | **passes** — 24 × 24, anchor at (12, 20), transparent, no tag needed for a static texture, no loop |
| **5** | **animation timing matches gameplay** | **not applicable** — one frame |
| **6** | **silhouette, value, ground contact and direction coverage read at native scale** | **the checks lesson** — and *"direction coverage"* is satisfied by the brief's decision that one direction serves |
| **7** | **works in Godot under lighting, crowds and effects** | **the last lesson** |
| **8** | **superseded versions and temporary material deleted** | **passes if you deleted the hand-run export and any earlier attempt** |

---

**So the bucket satisfies six of eight, fails one on purpose, and awaits one.** Which is the right outcome for a training asset, and the two it does not satisfy are worth separating:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Condition 1 is a scope failure** | **the asset is not required.** Fixable only by drawing something that is |
| **Condition 2 is a process step** | **not a defect.** Every asset waits on it |

---

**And the three conditions worth dwelling on, because they catch most real failures:**

**Condition 4 — "dimensions, pivot, transparency, tags and loop behavior are correct."**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Five separate things**, and each has its own failure | |
| **Dimensions** — the canvas, untrimmed | |
| **Pivot** — at the ground contact, and consistent with every other prop | |
| **Transparency** — **no background layer, and no baked floor** | |
| **Tags** — **one, lower-case snake-case**, or none for a static texture | |
| **Loop behaviour** — **the `_` prefix on one-shots**, which a bucket does not have | |

**Condition 6 — "read at native scale."**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Not "look good"** | **read.** Four things specified: silhouette, value, ground contact, direction coverage |
| **At native scale** | which stage 2 argued is really **the delivery scale, 2× to 4×** |

**Condition 8 — "superseded versions and temporary conversion material are deleted."**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The hand-run export** from the import lesson | |
| **Any `-v2` or earlier attempt** | |
| **And §3's general rule**: *"Rejected and superseded art is deleted rather than archived"* | |
| **Which means the drafting history lives in git and nowhere else** | |

---

**And the thing to build from this: a checklist that fits on one screen.** Stage 4's twelve value checks, stage 5's nine colour checks, stage 3's seven projection failures and §10's eight conditions are **thirty-six items**, which is too many to run every time. **The practical version:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The three tests** | **greyscale, solid black, beside the 80 px figure** |
| **The four numbers** | **canvas untrimmed, anchor at the ground contact, colour count in band, palette conformant** |
| **The one round trip** | **in Godot, in a real scene, under a light** |
| **And §10's eight conditions, read once at the end** | |

**Practice.** Run all eight conditions against your bucket and write down the honest answer for each. Then write the eight-item practical checklist above onto one page. Then take a genuinely required prop — the bench — and check whether it would pass condition 1.
Two more props:
Repeating the loop twice more, deliberately choosing harder cases, and the three things that get faster.

**One asset proves the pipeline. Three prove it is a pipeline.** This lesson picks the next two to make specific things go wrong.

---

**Prop two — the bench.** §9.2: **19–23 px seat, 46–56 px long, 3 × 1 footprint.**

**Why this one second:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is genuinely required** | **§6.1: *"remove-from-satchel and place-on-bench"*.** The Prologue needs a bench — so **condition 1 passes**, which the bucket's did not |
| **It is wider than it is tall** | **so the canvas is not square** — about **64 × 32** — and the anchor's horizontal centring matters |
| **It has a readable void** | **the gap under the seat**, from stage 4's contact-shadow lesson: *"the dark in that gap is what tells you it is a bench and not a solid block"* |
| **It is a 3 × 1 footprint** | **so the footprint and the drawn length differ** — 48 px of footprint against 46–56 px drawn. **Stage 3's footprint-against-visible-size lesson, concretely** |
| **And it is timber** | the same ramp as the bucket, **so the palette work is already done and the drawing is the only new thing** |

**The brief's differences:** canvas **64 × 32**; anchor **(32, 28)**; palette **`TERR-033`–`036` plus `TERR-001`** — **five colours, well inside the 4–10 band**; footprint **3 × 1**; one state.

---

**Prop three — the barrel.** §9.2: **37–45 px high, 1 × 1 footprint.**

**Why this one third:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **It is a cylinder** | **stage 3's hardest primitive** — an elliptical top, a curved base, and **vertical value boundaries that are the textbook banding setup** |
| **It is tall relative to its footprint** | **41 px of height on 16 px of ground.** So the canvas is **48 × 48** and **the sprite is two and a half times its footprint's width in height** — which is where Y-sorting starts to matter |
| **It has two materials with a one-pixel part** | **timber staves and two metal hoops**, which is stage 6's metal lesson at its smallest |
| **And it is the first one where the drawing is genuinely hard** | the bucket and the bench are boxes and trapezoids; **a barrel's silhouette has four curves in it** |

**The brief's differences:** canvas **48 × 48**; anchor **(24, 44)**; palette **`TERR-033`–`036` timber, `TERR-009` and `011` metal, `TERR-001` — seven**; one state.

---

**The three things that get faster, and they are the measure of whether this stage worked:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The brief** | **the bucket's took thinking; the barrel's is a diff against the bucket's.** Canvas, anchor, palette, footprint — four numbers |
| **2 — The import** | **the first time it is six steps and three possible silent failures. The third time it is: drop it in, set the importer, reimport** |
| **3 — The checks** | **the twelve-plus-nine-plus-seven collapse into the three tests and the four numbers**, because the others have become habits |

**And the one thing that does not get faster: the drawing.** **A barrel is harder than a bucket and will take longer**, and that is correct — **the pipeline is now free and the craft is still the work.**

---

**And a note on order, from `CLAUDE.md`:**

> *"**Work one asset, action and direction at a time** so each authored animation can be reviewed in Godot before the next family expands."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So: finish the bench, import it, look at it, then start the barrel** | not all three at once |
| **Which conflicts with stage 3's advice** to draw in families for consistency | |
| **The reconciliation, from that lesson** | **one at a time for review, in families for drawing.** Three props is small enough to do either way; **thirty is not, and `CLAUDE.md`'s rule is the one that scales** |

**Practice.** Write the bench's brief as a diff against the bucket's, then draw it, import it and place it in the scene beside the bucket. Then do the barrel. Then put all three in one screen at the game's zoom and check they look like they belong together — stage 3's five consistency properties.
A prop with a state:
The second state as a deliberate authored asset: what changes in the brief, and the two ways to ship it.

**§9.3:**

> *"**Interactive and destructible objects define their required states before drawing.**"*

**And §9.3's closing paragraph puts the rest of it out of scope:** *"Terrain transition grammar, environment material ramps, final York calibration assets, **destruction states** and VFX rules remain open work."*

**So the grammar for destruction states is undecided, and the rule about defining them first is not.**

---

**The case to work: a bucket that can be knocked over.** Two states.

**What the brief gains:**

| Field | One state | Two states |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **States** | **static** | **`upright`, `fallen`** |
| **Frame geometry** | 24 × 24 | **the fallen bucket is wider than tall** — about 17 wide and 10 high — **so the canvas must hold both**, which means **24 × 24 still works if the fallen one fits** |
| **Anchor** | (12, 20) | **the same anchor for both**, which is the constraint that matters |
| **Runtime consumer** | a static prop | **either two Static Textures or a two-frame `SpriteFrames`** |
| **Palette subset** | eight | **the fallen one shows the interior**, which may need a ninth colour — **and the band is 4–10, so there is room** |

---

**The design problem the second state creates**, which the brief lesson flagged:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An upright bucket has no visible interior** | the mouth's inside is two or three pixels of Shadow |
| **A fallen bucket shows its inside** | **so the interior has to be designed** — how deep, what the base looks like from inside, whether there is anything in it |
| **Which is why §9.3 requires the states before the drawing** | **a bucket drawn without an inside has no inside to show**, and bolting one on afterwards produces an interior that does not match the exterior's staves |
| **The specific decisions** | **the stave lines continue inside; the base is visible as an ellipse at the projection ratio; and the interior is one or two steps darker than the exterior's shadow side** |

---

**The two ways to ship it:**

**Option A — two files, two Static Textures.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Files** | **`wooden-pail.aseprite`** and **`wooden-pail-fallen.aseprite`** |
| **Or, following §3.1's grammar** | **`wooden-pail_upright.aseprite`** and **`wooden-pail_fallen.aseprite`** — treating the state as the *action* slot |
| **Pros** | **each state is independently reviewable**, which is `media/README.md`'s own argument for separate files per direction |
| **Cons** | **two files to keep in register** — the anchor must match exactly |

**Option B — one file, two tags, a `SpriteFrames`.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **File** | **`wooden-pail.aseprite`**, two frames, two tags: **`upright`** and **`_fallen`** |
| **The underscore** | **`_fallen` is a one-shot** — it does not loop. §5.3 |
| **Pros** | **one file, one anchor, guaranteed register** |
| **Cons** | **it is a `SpriteFrames` for something that is not animated**, and the runtime consumer becomes an `AnimatedSprite2D` rather than a `Sprite2D` |

**Which to choose:** **Option B if the transition is animated** — a bucket that tips over wants three or four frames, and then it is genuinely an animation. **Option A if the two states are discrete** and the game just swaps the texture.

**And §3.1's grammar favours A for discrete states**, because it says *"one master per asset, **action** and direction"* — and a state is closest to an action.

---

**The general rule this case establishes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A state that is reached instantly** | **two textures** |
| **A state reached through a transition** | **one animation, with the `_` prefix** |
| **And either way, the states are listed in the brief before the first one is drawn** | |

**Practice.** Write the two-state bucket's brief, deciding the interior's design explicitly. Then draw the fallen state and check the anchor matches the upright one exactly — overlay them and confirm. Then ship it both ways: two Static Textures, and one two-tag `SpriteFrames`, and see which the scene is easier to write.
What the round trip taught:
The stage's conclusion: the loop as a habit, the five numbers that travel with every asset, and what changes now.

**The loop, in its final form:**

| | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **brief** — §10.2's eight fields, plus footprint and visible size |
| **2** | **silhouette**, one value, black test |
| **3** | **value**, two then three then four, with the upper-left key |
| **4** | **colour**, a ramp per material, within the band |
| **5** | **outline and contact shadow**, selective, on their own layers |
| **6** | **checks** — greyscale, black, beside the figure |
| **7** | **name and place** — the path, the one-master rule |
| **8** | **import** — the right importer, the excluded layers |
| **9** | **Godot** — real scene, real ground, real zoom, a light |
| **10** | **§10's eight conditions** |

**Ten steps, and after three props they take about as long as step 3 alone.**

---

**The five numbers that travel with every asset**, which is the compressed version of the brief:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The canvas** | 24 × 24, 48 × 48, or case by case |
| **The anchor** | **bottom-centre of the ground contact**, a fixed distance above the canvas bottom |
| **The footprint** | in tiles |
| **The visible size** | in pixels, against §9.2's band |
| **The colour count** | against §10.1's band |

**Write those five on the master's own layer, or in the brief, or in the filename's folder.** **An asset whose five numbers are recoverable can be checked; one whose numbers are in your head cannot.**

---

**What changes now that the loop is routine. Three things:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Drawing decisions get feedback** | **before this stage, every value decision was a guess about how it would look in the game.** Now it is a question with an answer, ten minutes away. **Which is why stage 4's restraint clause only becomes real here** |
| **2 — The checks become cheap** | **and therefore get run.** A check that takes a minute gets skipped; one that is a keystroke does not |
| **3 — The scary assets get smaller** | **a character is 192 drawings and one pipeline.** The pipeline is now free, so **a character is 192 drawings** — which is a lot, and it is not frightening in the way it was |

---

**And the two honest limitations of what this stage achieved:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The bucket is not a production asset** | **§10's condition 1.** The derivation lesson was explicit, and the bench is the first one that passes it |
| **Nothing has been approved** | **§10's condition 2 is a separate event, and Master Roachi is the only one who can satisfy it** — and `CLAUDE.md` is explicit that he owns all Aseprite authoring. **The curriculum can get an asset to the point of being submittable and no further** |

---

**And the handover.** Three stages use this loop immediately:

| Stage | What it adds |
| --- | --- |
| **8 · Terrain and architecture** | **the Tileset Texture importer, Tilemap mode, and seam tests** — the loop with a different importer and a tiling constraint |
| **9 · The figure** | **eight directions and the 80-pixel problem** — the loop times eight |
| **10 · Animation** | **24 frames, tags, the `_` prefix and the 84 ms arithmetic** — the loop times 192, and the first time the SpriteFrames importer matters |

**The loop does not change. Only the count does.**

**Practice.** Write the ten steps and the five numbers on one page. Then time yourself doing the whole loop on one more simple prop — §9.2's crate, or a firepit — and see how long it takes end to end. Then write down which of the ten steps took longest, because that is the one to practise.
What a tile has to do:
The stage's opening constraint: a tile is drawn once and seen ten thousand times, and everything about authoring one follows from that.

**§9.1's first asset class:**

> *"**terrain and transitions:** hand-drawn 16 × 16 tiles assembled as Godot terrain sets"*

**And §9.2's grid:** *"One world tile is 16 px and the collision/detail subgrid is 8 px."*

---

**The arithmetic that makes tiles different from props.** A prop is drawn once and placed a few times. **A ground tile is drawn once and placed everywhere:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The viewport** | **960 × 540, so 60 × 34 tiles = about 2,040 tiles on screen** |
| **A York exterior scene** | **several screens' worth — call it 10,000 to 50,000 tile placements** |
| **Each one** | **the same 256 pixels** |

**So a one-pixel error in a ground tile is a one-pixel error repeated two thousand times on screen.** That is the whole difference, and it produces four requirements a prop does not have:

| | Requirement | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **it must tile seamlessly** | **its right edge meets its own left edge** |
| **2** | **it must not produce a pattern when repeated** | **two thousand copies of any distinctive mark is a visible grid** |
| **3** | **it must be quiet** | stage 6's earth lesson — **the floor is the largest area on screen and should be the least interesting** |
| **4** | **it must connect to its neighbours** | **the transition grammar**, which is most of this stage |

---

**What this stage covers:**

| Lessons | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1–4** | **the single tile** — authoring it, the seam test, variants, the repetition test |
| **5–9** | **terrain sets** — Godot's `TileSet`, the transition grammar, the matching modes, authoring in Tilemap mode, and the Tileset Texture importer |
| **10–16** | **modular architecture** — the four tests, then walls, roofs, openings, fences, interiors and elevation |
| **17–18** | **the screen's colour budget, and what §9.3 leaves open** |

---

**And the honest scope warning, up front.** §9.3's closing paragraph:

> *"**Terrain transition grammar**, environment material ramps, final York calibration assets, destruction states and VFX rules **remain open work**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So the transition grammar is not decided** | this stage teaches **how transition grammars work** and **what the options are**, not which one Shepherds uses |
| **Nor are the environment material ramps** | **stage 6 assigned ramps to materials by reading the Intended uses column.** A formal scene palette is open |
| **And §9** is explicit that **no environment art is approved**: *"No current terrain, prop, building, character-effect or environment art is approved"* | |
| **Which means** | **this stage produces proposals, and the grammar is a decision to be made.** Stage 13's lesson on raising things applies |

**That is not a weakness of the stage. It is the state of the project**, and knowing which parts are decided and which are open is the difference between drawing to a contract and inventing one.

**Practice.** Read §9.1 and §9.3 in full, and list which parts of environment art are decided and which §9.3 leaves open. Then count the tiles on one screen at 960 × 540. Then look at `media/sprites/environment/` and confirm what is there.
The sixteen-pixel tile, authored:
Drawing one ground tile: the method, the pixel budget, and the test that matters.

**From stage 6's earth lesson, the four-step method:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **fill with the Mid** — `TERR-023` Terrath Earth for soil, `TERR-047` Dust Olive for grass, `TERR-015` Dry Stone for paving |
| **2** | **three or four two-pixel clusters of the Shadow step**, scattered |
| **3** | **one or two clusters of the Light step**, fewer than the darker ones |
| **4** | **stop** |

**That is about twelve pixels of work on a 256-pixel tile — under 5% coverage.** And it is correct.

---

**The pixel budget, stated as a rule:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A ground tile** | **two values, three to five marks, under 10% of the tile marked** |
| **A paved or structured tile** | **three values and a structure** — mortar lines, plank gaps — **which is more coverage and is justified because the structure is the subject** |
| **A decorated tile** | **the base tile plus one feature** — a pebble, a tuft, a crack. **Placed one tile in eight to one in twenty** |
| **And never** | **a tile where every pixel is doing something.** Two thousand of those is visual noise at scale |

---

**Setting up the file:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Canvas** | **16 × 16 for a single tile** — or **a sheet**, which is the next lessons' subject |
| **Grid** | **16 × 16**, so it aligns |
| **Indexed, with the palette** | stage 5 |
| **And `View › Tiled Mode` on** | **immediately, before drawing anything** |

**That last point is the method.** **Drawing a tile with Tiled Mode off and then checking it is backwards** — you will have made edge decisions that do not work and will have to redraw them. **With it on, every mark you place is immediately visible in its tiled context**, and the edges take care of themselves.

---

**The seam test**, which is the only test that matters for a single tile:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it checks** | **does the tile's right edge meet its own left edge, and its bottom meet its top, without a visible line or discontinuity?** |
| **How** | **Tiled Mode, at 300%** |
| **What a failure looks like** | **a visible grid** — a lighter or darker line along the tile boundaries |
| **The two causes** | **a mark that touches an edge and has no counterpart on the opposite edge**; or **a value imbalance between one edge and the other** |
| **The fix for the first** | **a mark that crosses an edge must be split across both edges.** A three-pixel cluster at the right edge continues as the remainder at the left |
| **The fix for the second** | **move the marks inward.** A tile whose marks are all at least two pixels from every edge cannot fail the seam test |

**And that last point is the cheap answer: keep the marks away from the edges.** It costs a little variety and it makes the seam test automatic.

---

**One Aseprite-specific technique worth knowing.** From stage 1's selection lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **you want to draw a mark that crosses the tile boundary**, which means editing two opposite edges in register |
| **The method** | **Tiled Mode lets you draw across the boundary and Aseprite wraps the stroke** — so the mark is split correctly for free |
| **Which is the second reason Tiled Mode is on from the start** | |

**Practice.** Draw one earth tile with Tiled Mode on from the start: two values, four marks, all at least two pixels from the edges. Then draw a second where one mark deliberately crosses an edge, and check it wraps. Then turn Tiled Mode off, look at the single tile, and turn it back on — note that the single tile looks sparse and the tiled field looks right.
Variants and the repetition test:
The second test: four copies of a good tile make a bad field, and the three ways to break the pattern.

**§9.3's requirement for modular pieces:**

> *"Modular pieces additionally pass **repetition and corner seam tests**."*

**The seam test is the last lesson's. This is the repetition test**, and it is a different failure.

---

**What the repetition test checks:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Not** | whether the tile's edges meet — that is the seam test |
| **But** | **whether the tiled field reads as a surface or as a grid of repeated units** |
| **How** | **tile it 8 × 8 and look at the whole thing at 300%**, then at 100% |
| **The failure** | **you can see the tile.** Any distinctive mark becomes a lattice, and the eye locks onto the lattice rather than the surface |

**And the failure is subtler than it sounds.** A tile can pass the seam test perfectly and still produce an obvious grid, **because what repeats is not the edge but the content.**

---

**The three ways to break the pattern:**

**1 — Make the single tile quieter.** The cheapest fix and the first to try:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The principle** | **a tile with no distinctive mark cannot produce a visible lattice** |
| **So** | **two values, three marks, all small and none at a memorable position** |
| **And the limit** | **a completely flat tile is seamless, pattern-free and lifeless.** Two values with three marks is the practical floor |

**2 — Multiple variants, placed randomly.** The standard answer:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How many** | **three to five variants of a ground material** |
| **What differs** | **only the marks' positions.** Same two values, same count, different places |
| **What must not differ** | **the overall value.** A variant that is noticeably lighter produces patches, which is a worse artefact than a grid |
| **How they are placed** | **Godot's `TileSet` supports alternative tiles and random placement**, and a `TileMapLayer` can be painted with a randomised brush |
| **The arithmetic** | **four variants reduces the lattice's period from 1 tile to about 4**, which at 16 px is 64 px — **large enough that the eye stops seeing a grid** |

**3 — Scatter objects on top.** The one that does the most work:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What** | **tufts, pebbles, small plants, cracks — as separate placeable objects or as decorated tiles**, not part of the base |
| **Why it works better than variants** | **because the scatter is at a different frequency from the grid.** A tuft placed every seven tiles breaks a one-tile lattice completely |
| **And it is cheaper** | **one tuft drawn once, placed by hand or by a scatter rule, beats four variants of a whole tile** |
| **The density** | **one feature per eight to twenty tiles.** More than that and the scatter becomes its own pattern |

---

**The practical recipe, combining all three:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One quiet base tile**, marks away from the edges | |
| **Two or three variants**, identical in value | |
| **Three or four scatter objects** — a tuft, a pebble, a crack, a patch | |
| **Placed at one in ten** | |
| **And then the test**: **tile an 8 × 8 field with the variants and the scatter, and look at it at 100%** | |

**And the honest check: does it look like ground, or like a tilemap?** **If you can count the tiles, it fails.**

**Practice.** Tile your single earth tile 8 × 8 and look at it at 300% and 100% — decide whether you can see the grid. Then make three variants and tile again with them mixed. Then draw a tuft and a pebble as separate 16 × 16 decorated tiles and scatter them at one in ten, and compare all three fields.
Godot's TileSet, and terrain sets:
What the engine does with your tiles, the three terrain modes, and the peering bits that decide which tile goes where.

**§9.1 names the target:** *"hand-drawn 16 × 16 tiles **assembled as Godot terrain sets**"*. **This lesson is what that means.**

---

**The objects involved, in Godot 4:**

| Object | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **`TileSet`** | **the resource holding the tiles** — their textures, collision shapes, navigation, custom data and terrain assignments |
| **`TileSetAtlasSource`** | **one texture divided into a grid of tiles.** Your imported sheet |
| **`TileMapLayer`** | **the node that paints tiles into the scene** |
| **A terrain set** | **a group of terrains within a `TileSet`**, each with a matching mode |
| **A terrain** | **one material within a set** — grass, earth, stone |
| **Peering bits** | **per-tile flags saying what must be in each neighbouring cell for this tile to be chosen** |

---

**How peering bits work**, which is the mechanism:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Each tile gets bits** for its neighbours — sides, corners, or both depending on the mode | |
| **A bit's value** | **`-1` means "empty space / no terrain"; `0` or greater is a terrain ID** |
| **And the rule** | **a tile is chosen when its neighbours match its bits.** The docs' example: *"a tile with all peering bits set to `0` or higher appears only if all 8 neighbouring tiles are using a tile with the same terrain ID"* |
| **And the converse** | *"if top-adjacent bits are set to `-1`, it will only appear if there is empty space on top of it (including diagonally)"* |

**So you paint "grass" and Godot picks which grass tile** — the middle one, an edge one, an outer corner, an inner corner — **by looking at what is around it.** That is autotiling.

---

**The three modes, named exactly as the editor names them:**

| Mode | What it looks at |
| --- | --- |
| **Match Corners and Sides** | **all eight neighbours** |
| **Match Corners** | **the four diagonal neighbours** |
| **Match Sides** | **the four orthogonal neighbours** |

**The Godot documentation maps these to Godot 3's bitmask modes — 2 × 2, 3 × 3 and 3 × 3 minimal — without saying which is which.** And the tile counts for full coverage are **practical knowledge rather than documented**:

| Mode | Tiles for full coverage, in practice |
| --- | --- |
| **Match Sides** | **16** — every combination of four orthogonal neighbours |
| **Match Corners** | **16** |
| **Match Corners and Sides** | **47** — the "blob" set. 256 raw combinations, reducing to 47 distinct tiles |

---

**So the choice is a drawing budget:**

| Mode | Tiles to draw | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Match Sides** | **16** | **edges and outer corners, no inner corners.** A terrain boundary that turns inward has a visible notch |
| **Match Corners** | **16** | **diagonal transitions handled**, sides less so |
| **Match Corners and Sides** | **47** | **everything** — clean inner and outer corners in every configuration |

**And the practical recommendation for this project: start with Match Sides at 16 tiles.** Three reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **16 tiles is a day's work; 47 is a week's** |
| **2** | **York's terrain boundaries are mostly simple** — a path across grass, a wall's base — and inner corners are rare |
| **3** | **and §9.3 leaves the grammar open**, so **the first terrain set is a proposal.** Draw 16, use them, and find out whether the missing cases matter |

**That is a decision to raise rather than to assume** — and it is exactly the kind of thing §9.3's *"Terrain transition grammar … remain[s] open work"* is pointing at.

**Practice.** Open a `TileSet` in Godot and find the Terrain Sets panel. Create one terrain set in Match Sides mode with one terrain. Then look at the peering bits panel for a single tile and set its four side bits. Then paint with it and watch Godot choose tiles.
Transition grammar:
The set of tiles a boundary needs, named and counted — and the three ways two materials can meet.

**A "transition" is how one material becomes another**, and there are three fundamentally different answers.

---

**The three kinds:**

| Kind | What it is | Tiles needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A hard cut** | **the two materials simply abut.** Grass tile, then earth tile | **none** — just the two base tiles |
| **An edge set** | **a dedicated tile for each configuration of boundary** — the material's edge drawn properly | **16 or 47**, per the last lesson |
| **An overlay** | **a transparent tile drawn on top of the base**, carrying the boundary | **16 or 47 overlays, reusable over any base** |

---

**And the overlay deserves attention, because it is the cheapest at scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How it works** | **a second `TileMapLayer` above the base**, painted with transparent tiles that carry the grass's ragged edge |
| **The payoff** | **one set of grass-edge overlays works over earth, stone, path and water** — **so N materials need N edge sets instead of N × (N−1)** |
| **The cost** | **two layers to paint, and the overlay's own shading cannot know what is beneath it** — so it has to work over any base, which means **its inner edge needs its own darkening** rather than relying on the base |
| **And §9.1's warning applies** | *"Do not bake a floor or scenery behind a standalone object"* — **an overlay is the opposite: it is deliberately transparent except at the boundary** |

**The arithmetic of why this matters:** **York might have six ground materials.** Dedicated edge sets between every pair is **6 × 5 = 30 transitions × 16 tiles = 480 tiles.** **Overlays are 6 × 16 = 96.** **That is the difference between a feasible terrain set and an infeasible one.**

---

**What one edge set contains**, in Match Sides mode's 16 tiles:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 tile** | **all four sides are the same material** — the interior fill |
| **4 tiles** | **one side is foreign** — the four straight edges: N, E, S, W |
| **4 tiles** | **two adjacent sides foreign** — the four outer corners |
| **2 tiles** | **two opposite sides foreign** — a one-tile-wide strip, horizontal and vertical |
| **4 tiles** | **three sides foreign** — the four ends of a one-tile strip |
| **1 tile** | **all four sides foreign** — an isolated single tile |
| | **16** |

**Drawing them in that order is the sensible sequence**, because each group is a variation on the last. **And the interior fill is the base tile from two lessons ago, so one of the sixteen is already drawn.**

---

**Three drawing rules for an edge:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The edge is a shape, not a line** | **grass meeting earth is a ragged two-or-three-pixel incursion of grass into the earth's tile**, not a straight boundary. **A straight boundary reads as a mown lawn** |
| **2 — The edge carries the occlusion** | **a one-pixel darker line on the lower material's side** where the upper one overlaps — stage 4. **This is what makes grass look like it is growing over earth rather than printed beside it** |
| **3 — The edge must not create a pattern** | **sixteen tiles used repeatedly is sixteen repeating shapes.** So **the ragged incursion should be different on each of the four straight edges**, and ideally there are **two variants of each** |

---

**And the open question to raise.** §9.3: *"Terrain transition grammar … remain[s] open work."*

**So the decisions to be made are:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Hard cuts, edge sets or overlays?** | **overlays are the scalable answer and they are a real commitment** |
| **Which matching mode?** | **16 or 47** |
| **Which materials transition to which?** | **not every pair needs a transition.** Grass to earth, yes; stone to water, probably never |
| **And how many variants per tile?** | |

**Four decisions, none of them made.** Stage 13's lesson is how to raise them.

**Practice.** Draw the 16-tile Match Sides edge set for grass over earth, in the order the table gives. Then draw the same boundary as a transparent overlay set and compare the work. Then count how many tiles York would need with dedicated sets against overlays, assuming six ground materials.
Authoring a terrain set in Aseprite:
Laying out the sheet, using Tilemap mode on it, and the file organisation that keeps the tile indices stable.

**Two ways to author a tile set, and the choice matters.**

---

**Option A — one file per tile.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **16 files**, each 16 × 16 | |
| **Pros** | **each tile is independently reviewable**, which is `media/README.md`'s argument for separate files per direction |
| **Cons** | **you cannot see the set together**, and **the seam and repetition tests need them assembled** — so you would be assembling them constantly |
| **Verdict** | **wrong for tiles.** The tests require the set |

**Option B — one sheet file.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One file, a grid of 16 × 16 cells** — for a 16-tile set, **a 4 × 4 arrangement at 64 × 64**, or **a 16 × 1 strip at 256 × 16** | |
| **Pros** | **the whole set visible at once; the seam tests runnable; one file to import; and the tile indices are positional and stable** |
| **Cons** | **one file holds many assets**, which brushes against the one-master rule |
| **Verdict** | **right**, and **the one-master rule is satisfied: the sheet IS the asset.** A terrain set is one thing |

---

**The layout decision, which determines the tile indices:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Godot reads a `TileSetAtlasSource` as a grid** | with coordinates, so **a tile's identity is its position in the sheet** |
| **Which means** | **the layout is a contract.** Once a `TileSet` references the tile at (2, 1), **moving that tile in the sheet breaks the TileSet** |
| **So** | **decide the layout first and write it down** |
| **A sensible layout for a 16-tile Match Sides set** | **4 × 4, in the order from the transition lesson** — fill, four edges, four outer corners, two strips, four ends, one isolated |
| **And leave room** | **a 8 × 4 sheet with the second half empty** gives you room for variants without moving anything |

**That last point is the practical one: a sheet with spare cells can grow; a tightly packed one cannot.**

---

**Using Aseprite's Tilemap mode on the sheet**, from stage 1:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The confusion to clear up** | **Aseprite's Tilemap mode and Godot's `TileSet` are different things.** Aseprite's tilemap is an authoring convenience; Godot's is the runtime structure |
| **What Aseprite's tilemap gives you** | **edit a tile once and every cell using it updates** — which is useful for **mocking up a scene** to test the set |
| **The workflow** | **a second file, a tilemap layer, the set's tiles in its tileset, and a mocked-up 20 × 15 scene.** Draw in the master sheet, see it in the mock-up |
| **And the submode warning from stage 1** | **Manual (`Space+1`) once anything downstream knows the indices.** Auto reorders and deletes |

---

**And the file organisation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Category** | **`environment`** — one of the seven in `media/README.md` |
| **Family** | **by material or by location** — `terrain/grass`, or `york/ground` |
| **Asset key** | **kebab-case** — `grass-terrain-set` |
| **The sheet** | **`grass-terrain-set.aseprite`** — **no action, no direction**, per §9.2's static-master rule |
| **The mock-up** | **`media/work/`**, gitignored — **it is not a master** |
| **And `_exports/`** | **Wizard writes there; you never do** |

**Practice.** Create a 64 × 64 sheet with a 16 × 16 grid and lay out the 16 Match Sides positions, writing the layout down. Then draw the fill tile and the four straight edges. Then make a separate mock-up file with a tilemap layer and assemble a small scene from them, and check the seams.
The Tileset Texture importer:
The third of Wizard's six importers, what it produces, and the steps from master to painted tiles.

**From stage 7's importer lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Name** | **Tileset Texture** |
| **Internal name** | `aseprite_wizard.plugin.tileset-texture` |
| **Produces** | **a `PortableCompressedTexture2D`** |
| **Recognised extensions** | `.aseprite`, `.ase` |

**And it is a project setting which importer a new `.aseprite` gets by default** — so **a terrain sheet dropped into a project whose default is SpriteFrames imports as the wrong thing, silently.** Stage 7's trap, and it bites hardest here because a tile sheet imported as a `SpriteFrames` produces a nonsensical animation.

---

**The steps, master to painted tiles:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the sheet master in `media/sprites/environment/<family>/<asset-key>/`** |
| **2** | **select it in Godot's FileSystem dock, Import tab, set the importer to Tileset Texture, Reimport** |
| **3** | **a `TileSet` resource** — new, or the scene's existing one |
| **4** | **add a `TileSetAtlasSource` to it** and give it the imported texture |
| **5** | **set the atlas's tile size to 16 × 16** and its separation and margins to zero |
| **6** | **"Create tiles in non-transparent texture regions"**, or select the tiles by hand |
| **7** | **a terrain set**, in Match Sides mode, with one terrain |
| **8** | **set each tile's peering bits** — the 16 configurations from the transition lesson |
| **9** | **a `TileMapLayer` in the scene with that `TileSet`** |
| **10** | **paint with the terrain brush**, and Godot chooses the tiles |

**Step 8 is the laborious one** and it is where the layout decision pays off: **if the sheet is laid out in a known order, the bits are set in a known order.**

---

**Four things that go wrong:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The tile size is not 16** | **the atlas defaults may not match.** Set it explicitly |
| **The sheet has separation or margins** | **set them to zero**, or Godot's grid will not align with yours |
| **Transparent tiles are skipped** | **"create tiles in non-transparent regions" skips an empty cell** — which is fine for spares and a problem if a tile is legitimately mostly transparent, like an overlay. **Create those by hand** |
| **The indices shift** | **from Aseprite's Auto tilemap submode, or from re-laying-out the sheet.** Stage 1's warning: **Manual mode once anything downstream knows the indices** |

---

**And two things the importer does not do:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Collision** | **a `TileSet` holds collision shapes per tile**, and they are set in Godot, not in Aseprite. **§9.2's 8 px subgrid is where that happens** |
| **Terrain assignments** | **the peering bits are Godot-side data.** Reimporting the texture does not lose them — **they live on the `TileSet`, not on the texture** |

**That second row is reassuring and worth knowing: you can redraw the sheet and reimport, and the terrain bits survive**, as long as the tile positions have not moved. **Which is the whole reason the layout is a contract.**

---

**One alternative worth naming.** The ordinary Godot texture importer:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **You could export a PNG from Aseprite** and let Godot import it as a texture | |
| **Why not** | **§3: *"Accepted `.aseprite` masters import through Aseprite Wizard; no competing sprite export pipeline is established"*** |
| **And the practical reason** | **the `.aseprite` is the master, and a PNG in the project is a second copy that can drift** |

**Practice.** Import your terrain sheet as a Tileset Texture, build a `TileSet` with a 16 × 16 atlas, create the tiles, and set up a Match Sides terrain set. Set the peering bits for the fill tile and the four edges. Then paint with it. Then redraw one tile in Aseprite, reimport, and confirm the terrain bits survived.
Modular architecture: the four tests:
§9.1's second asset class and the tests it names: straight run, corner, transition seam, and repetition.

**§9.1:**

> *"**modular architecture:** reusable walls, roofs, doors, windows, gates, fences, posts and interior pieces which must pass **straight-run, corner and transition seam tests**"*

**And §9.3 adds the fourth:** *"Modular pieces additionally pass **repetition** and corner seam tests."*

---

**The four tests:**

| | Test | What it checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Straight run** | **place the piece five times in a row.** Do the joints disappear? Is the run continuous? |
| **2** | **Corner** | **turn the run through 90 degrees.** Is there a corner piece, and does it work both as an outer and an inner corner? |
| **3** | **Transition seam** | **where the piece meets a different material or a different piece** — a wall meeting a door frame, a fence meeting a gate post |
| **4** | **Repetition** | **does the five-piece run read as a wall, or as five copies of a piece?** The tile lesson's test, applied to architecture |

**Run them in that order**, because each one can invalidate the next.

---

**What a modular set contains, minimally.** Taking a wall:

| Piece | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A straight section** | the run |
| **An outer corner** | where the wall turns away from the viewer |
| **An inner corner** | where it turns toward |
| **An end cap** | where the wall stops |
| **A top or coping** | **if the wall is thick enough to have a top face** — stage 3 |
| **And optionally two or three variants of the straight section** | for the repetition test |

**Six to nine pieces for one wall material**, which is the honest cost of modularity.

---

**The joint, which is where modularity lives or dies:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **a piece's right edge meets the next piece's left edge**, and **any asymmetry shows as a repeating vertical line** |
| **The seam test** | the same as a tile's: **place two and look at the join at 300%** |
| **The fix** | **the two edges must be complementary** — a block that ends halfway at the right edge continues at the left |
| **And the structural answer** | **make the joint fall where a joint belongs.** A masonry wall's courses are staggered, **so a piece whose blocks are staggered at its edges joins invisibly, because a joint between blocks is what a wall has anyway** |

**That last point is the craft: hide the modular joint inside the material's own structure.** Brick courses, plank ends, fence posts, roof tile overlaps — **all of them are natural places for a seam, and a modular piece that puts its boundary there has no visible seam at all.**

---

**And the piece size decision:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One tile wide — 16 px** | **maximum flexibility, maximum repetition risk** |
| **Two tiles — 32 px** | **a good compromise**: the repetition period doubles and the piece is still placeable anywhere |
| **Three or four tiles** | **fewer joints, less flexible**, and a wall's length becomes quantised |
| **§9.2's fence run at 41–50 px high** | says nothing about length, **so the length is a decision** |
| **And the recommendation** | **two tiles wide for walls and fences**, with variants |

**Practice.** Draw a two-tile-wide dry-stone wall section at 55 px high, with the blocks staggered at both edges. Place five in a row and run the straight-run and repetition tests. Then draw an outer corner and an end cap, and run the corner test. Then count how many pieces the set needs.
Walls:
The most-repeated architectural piece: its three faces, where the joint goes, and the one-pixel line that makes an interior read.

**A wall in this projection**, from stage 3:

| Face | Visible? |
| --- | --- |
| **The front** | **yes** — a rectangle, vertical edges, drawn true |
| **The top** | **yes, if the wall is thick enough** — a foreshortened coping |
| **The back and sides** | **no** |

**And §9.2's two walls give the heights:** **a dry-stone wall at 50–60 px; a door opening needing at least 88 px clear**, so **a house wall is 100 px or more.**

---

**The three-value structure:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The coping / top** | **lightest** — it faces up |
| **The front face** | **Mid**, and it is the largest area |
| **The base** | **a one-or-two-pixel line of Deep** — occlusion where the wall meets the ground |
| **The vertical ends** | **Shadow on the right-hand one, Mid on the left** |

**And the base line is the single most valuable pixel row in architecture.** From stage 4's occlusion lesson: *"where a wall meets the floor — one pixel of Deep along the base does more for an interior than any amount of wall texture."*

---

**The material choices**, from stage 6:

| Wall | Ramps |
| --- | --- |
| **Dressed masonry** | **`TERR-013`–`016`** warm stone, with `TERR-013` mortar |
| **Dry-stone** | **`TERR-013`–`016`**, larger irregular blocks, **no mortar line** |
| **Cob or earthen** | **`TERR-021`–`024`** earth, **all four steps because it is a vertical lit surface** |
| **Timber frame with infill** | **`TERR-033`–`036`** for the frame, **`TERR-005`–`008`** or `TERR-016` for the plaster infill |
| **Plastered** | **`TERR-029`–`032`** ochre — *"aged plaster"* |

**And York's likely answer: dry-stone for field walls, timber frame with plaster for houses, dressed stone for anything important.** Which is three wall materials, each needing a set — **and §9.3's *"final York calibration assets"* being open work means this is not decided.**

---

**Where the joint goes.** The last lesson's principle, applied:

| Wall type | Natural seam position |
| --- | --- |
| **Dressed masonry** | **a mortar line.** Make the piece two tiles wide and end it mid-course with a staggered edge |
| **Dry-stone** | **between two blocks**, irregularly — **easy, because the material is irregular** |
| **Timber frame** | **at a vertical post.** **The best case: a frame's upright is a natural module boundary**, so a piece that ends at a post joins invisibly |
