| **Plastered** | **the hardest** — a flat surface has no natural seam, **so the piece must have perfectly complementary edges, or carry a deliberate feature (a buttress, a drainpipe, a crack) at the joint** |

---

**And the inner corner, which is the piece people forget:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An outer corner** | the wall turns away — **you see two front faces meeting at a vertical line** |
| **An inner corner** | the wall turns toward — **you see the inside of the angle, which is in shadow** |
| **Why it is harder** | **the inner corner's occlusion runs up the full height of the join**, and it is the darkest part of any wall |
| **And in this projection** | **an inner corner shows more of the top face than a straight run does**, which means the coping turns |

**Practice.** Draw a two-tile dry-stone wall section at 55 px with a coping, a base line of `TERR-013`, and staggered block edges. Run the straight-run test with five copies. Then draw an outer corner and an inner corner, and check the occlusion in the inner one. Then draw a timber-frame section ending at a post and confirm the joint is invisible.
Roofs:
The largest single surface on a building, drawn as a foreshortened plane, with the overlap that does the work.

**From stage 6's slate lesson and stage 3's projection:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A roof is a large sloped plane** | so **in this projection it is drawn as a foreshortened top face** |
| **The ridge** | **a horizontal line** at the top |
| **The eaves** | **a horizontal line** at the bottom, overhanging the wall |
| **The field between** | **the foreshortened slope**, drawn with horizontal courses |
| **And the gable ends** | **triangular vertical faces**, if the roof is seen from the side |

---

**The course structure**, which is the roof's whole texture:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Courses** | **horizontal bands 3 to 5 px deep**, with a one-pixel darker line between them |
| **Why horizontal** | **because tiles and thatch are laid in horizontal courses, each overlapping the one below** |
| **The line between** | **`TERR-017`** for slate, or the material's Deep — **it is the shadow cast by the overlap**, which is occlusion |
| **Individual tiles** | **not drawn.** Two or three vertical nicks per course suggest them — stage 6 |
| **And the stagger** | **each course's nicks offset from the one above**, like masonry courses |

---

**Three roof materials, from stage 6:**

| Material | Ramp | Structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Slate or tile** | **`TERR-017`–`020`** — *"roofing, dark stone, wet rock"* | **crisp horizontal courses**, regular, with a visible ridge |
| **Thatch** | **`TERR-029`–`032`** ochre — *"dry grasses"* | **soft, thick, no courses** — a few horizontal bands of texture, **a very deep eaves overhang, and a rounded ridge.** The silhouette is the read |
| **Timber shingle** | **`TERR-033`–`036`** | **between the two** — courses, but irregular |

**And the silhouette difference is the main signal.** **A slate roof has a crisp straight ridge and a thin eaves line; a thatched roof is thick, rounded and overhangs deeply.** At 3 × 3 scale **that silhouette difference reads from across the screen and the course texture does not.**

---

**The parts a roof set needs:**

| Piece | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A straight section** | the run along the building |
| **The ridge** | the top — often a separate piece, because ridge tiles are a different shape |
| **A left and right end** | **the gable or the hip** |
| **An outer corner, an inner corner** | for L-shaped buildings |
| **And a chimney** | **a separate prop**, not a roof piece |

**Six to eight pieces**, which is comparable to a wall set.

---

**Two problems specific to roofs.**

**1 — The roof hides the wall, and that is a gameplay question.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The issue** | **a roof drawn at full depth covers the interior**, and in a top-down game the player often needs to see inside |
| **The options** | **a roof that is removed or faded when the player enters** (very common); **a cutaway**; **or buildings drawn without their roofs for interiors** |
| **Which is a design decision** | **and `menu-runtime-contract.md` and the production brief would own it.** §9.1 names *"interior pieces"* as part of the modular class, **which implies interiors are drawn and therefore seen** |
| **So: raise it.** The art depends on the answer | |

**2 — Roof depth against building height.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The arithmetic** | **a house wall is 100 px or more** (from §9.2's 88 px door clearance) **and a roof at a 45-degree pitch, foreshortened to half, adds perhaps 30 to 50 px** |
| **So a house is 130 to 150 px tall** — **about two character heights**, which is right | |
| **And it will not fit in a 112 × 112 frame**, which is §9.2's point: *"Large props use a wider canvas or deliberate scene assembly"* | |
| **The practical answer** | **a building is a scene assembly of modular pieces, not one sprite** |

**Practice.** Draw a two-tile roof section in `TERR-017`–`020`: four courses with one-pixel lines, offset nicks, a ridge piece and an eaves line. Run the straight-run test. Then draw the same section as thatch in `TERR-029`–`032` and compare the silhouettes at 100%. Then work out the total height of a house with an 88 px door and a pitched roof.
Doors, windows and openings:
The pieces that have to interrupt a wall run, the clearance §9.2 fixes, and the recess that makes an opening read.

**§9.2's one architectural measurement:**

> *"**Door opening** | at least **88 px clear** | architecture-defined"*

**And the derivation: an 80 px adult must pass through it.** 88 px gives 8 px of headroom — **which is 17 cm at 45.7 px per metre, and tight.** A character in a hat needs all of it.

---

**An opening's five parts:**

| Part | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **The reveal** | **the recess's side faces** — visible because the wall has thickness |
| **The lintel or arch** | **the top**, carrying the wall above |
| **The threshold or sill** | the bottom |
| **The dark interior** | **what you see through it** |
| **And the door or shutter itself** | **a separate piece**, because it opens |

---

**What makes an opening read as an opening rather than a dark rectangle: the reveal.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **a flat dark rectangle on a wall is a painted rectangle** |
| **The fix** | **one or two pixels of the wall's own material, in Shadow and Deep, inside the opening's edge** — the thickness of the wall, seen at an angle |
| **Which side** | **the right-hand reveal is visible** when the light is upper-left and the view is three-quarter — **so a one-pixel line of the wall's Shadow down the opening's left inner edge, and Deep down the right** |
| **And the lintel's underside** | **Deep** — the deepest occlusion on the whole wall |
| **The interior** | **`TERR-001`–`002`**, and **not pure black** |

**That is about six pixels of work and it is the difference between a window and a hole in a sticker.**

---

**The modular problem openings create.** From the modular-tests lesson:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A wall run is made of repeated sections** | and **an opening interrupts it** |
| **So the set needs** | **a wall section with an opening in it** — or **the opening as a separate piece that replaces a wall section** |
| **The second is better** | **because then one door piece works in any wall of the same height**, rather than one door-in-wall piece per wall material |
| **Which means** | **the door piece must match the wall's thickness, coping and base line** — so **it is designed with the wall, not after it** |
| **And the transition seam test** | §9.1's third test, exactly this: *"transition seam tests"* |

---

**Windows**, which are the same problem smaller:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Size** | **a window is perhaps 20–30 px wide and 25–35 px tall** — about a third of a door |
| **The sill** | **a light horizontal line of the wall's Light step**, projecting a pixel either side. **This is what makes a window read as recessed** |
| **Shutters** | **a separate piece, open or closed** — and **two states, so §9.3's rule applies: define them before drawing** |
| **Glass** | **if there is glass, it is `TERR-057`–`060` water or `TERR-109`–`112` tech**, dark, with **one or two pixels of a lighter reflection** at the top |
| **And in York** | **glass is a wealth signal.** Whether York's houses have glazed windows is a canon question |

---

**And the one decision that has to be made before any of this is drawn: what is seen through an opening?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Option A — darkness** | **`TERR-001`–`002`, flat.** Cheapest, and it reads as "interior, not modelled" |
| **Option B — a glimpse** | **two or three pixels of an interior wall or a lit interior** — which implies the interior exists |
| **Option C — the actual interior** | **if the game renders interiors behind openings**, which is a technical decision |
| **Which one** | **depends on the roof decision from the last lesson**, and both are the production brief's |

**Practice.** Draw a wall section with a door opening at 88 px clear, with a one-pixel reveal on each side, a Deep lintel underside and a `TERR-002` interior. Then draw it as a separate piece that replaces a wall section, and check the transition seam against the plain wall. Then draw a window with a projecting sill and compare it with the same window without one.
Gates, fences and posts:
The thin architecture: pieces that are mostly negative space, the post rhythm, and the §9.2 band that governs them.

**§9.2's two entries:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fence run** | **41–50 px high, 1 tile deep** |
| **And §6.8's requirement** | *"Four York defenders brace **the fence** while fourteen corpse puppets press against it"* — **so the Prologue needs a fence, and it is load-bearing dramatically** |

---

**What makes a fence different from a wall: it is mostly gaps.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A wall** | a solid plane. **The drawing is the surface** |
| **A fence** | **posts and rails with air between them.** **The drawing is the silhouette, and the background shows through** |
| **Which means** | **a fence is the one architectural piece where §10.1's negative gaps clause is the whole asset** |
| **And the consequence** | **it must read against every background** — grass, earth, a crowd of corpse puppets. **A fence that disappears against grass is useless** |

---

**The structure:**

| Part | Pixels |
| --- | --- |
| **A post** | **2–3 px wide, 41–50 px tall**, with a visible top (stage 3's foreshortened top face — **a post's top is a small ellipse or a 2 × 1 rectangle**) |
| **Rails** | **2 px tall, running horizontally between posts** — **two or three rails** |
| **Post spacing** | **one or two tiles — 16 or 32 px.** **16 px is a dense palisade; 32 px is a field fence** |
| **The gap between rails** | **the background** |
| **And the base** | **a contact shadow at each post, not along the whole run** — because the rails do not touch the ground |

**That last point is a good detail: a fence's shadow is a row of small ellipses, one per post.** It is cheap and it reads immediately.

---

**The rhythm problem**, which is the repetition test in its hardest form:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A fence is inherently periodic** | **posts at a fixed spacing is a rhythm**, and a rhythm is what the repetition test is supposed to catch |
| **But here it is correct** | **a real fence has evenly spaced posts.** The periodicity is the subject |
| **So the test changes** | **the question is not "can I see the repeat" but "does the repeat look like a fence or like a tiled texture"** |
| **And the answer** | **vary the pieces, not the rhythm** — **a leaning post, a missing rail, a weathered one, every fifth or seventh piece.** The rhythm stays and the uniformity goes |
| **§9.3's wear caution applies** | **a broken rail says something.** §6.8's fence is being braced against a press of bodies, **so damage there is dramatically motivated and elsewhere it is not** |

---

**A gate**, which is a fence piece with states:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **States** | **closed, open — and §9.3 requires both defined before drawing** |
| **The open state's problem** | **a gate swung open is foreshortened, and in this projection it is drawn at an angle the projection does not really permit** |
| **The practical answer** | **draw the open state as a plausible lie** — the gate turned toward the viewer, narrower, with the same height. **Nobody will measure it** |
| **Or avoid it** | **a sliding gate, a removable hurdle, or a gate that is simply always open or always closed.** Which is a design decision |

---

**And posts on their own**, which §9.1 lists separately:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A standalone post** | **a prop, not architecture** — stage 7's pipeline, a bottom-centre anchor, its own contact shadow |
| **Uses** | **a gate post, a tethering post, a boundary marker, a washing line** |
| **And it is a good small asset** — **2–3 px wide and 40 px tall is about 100 pixels of drawing**, and it tests the whole vertical-object problem cheaply | |

**Practice.** Draw a 32 px fence section at 45 px high: one post with a visible top, two rails, and a contact shadow at the post only. Run the straight-run test with six copies. Then draw three variants — a leaning post, a missing rail, a weathered one — and mix them into the run. Then put the run against grass and against a dark background and check it reads against both.
Floors and interiors:
Inside a building: the floor materials, the wall-to-floor line, and what §9.1's "interior pieces" implies.

**§9.1 lists interiors in the modular class:**

> *"modular architecture: reusable walls, roofs, doors, windows, gates, fences, posts and **interior pieces** which must pass straight-run, corner and transition seam tests"*

**And `menu-runtime-contract.md` and the production brief own whether interiors are seen** — the roof lesson's open question.

---

**Interior floors**, which are tiles like any other:

| Material | Ramp | Structure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Beaten earth** | **`TERR-021`–`024`** | **the quietest possible** — two values, three marks |
| **Timber boards** | **`TERR-033`–`036`** | **long planks** — one-pixel `TERR-033` lines every 4 or 5 px in one direction, with staggered ends |
| **Flagstones** | **`TERR-013`–`016`** | **irregular blocks with mortar lines** — the stone lesson, laid flat |
| **Rushes or straw** | **`TERR-029`–`032`** | dashes in random directions |

**And the floor's job is the same as the ground's:** **quiet.** Stage 6's rule — **an interesting floor is a bug.** A timber floor with every board's grain drawn is a pattern.

---

**The wall-to-floor line, which is the single most important pixel row in an interior.** From stage 4:

> *"where a wall meets the floor — **one pixel of Deep along the base does more for an interior than any amount of wall texture**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | **separates the vertical from the horizontal.** Without it, the wall and the floor are two flat areas of similar value and the room has no shape |
| **Which value** | **the floor material's Deep**, or `TERR-002` |
| **How wide** | **one pixel. Two in a corner** |
| **And at the corners** | **the line turns, and the inner corner gets two pixels** — the deepest occlusion in the room |

---

**What else an interior needs**, and it is a short list because most of it is props:

| Element | Which stage |
| --- | --- |
| **Floor tiles** | this one |
| **Wall sections, interior-facing** | the walls lesson — **and note the interior face of a wall is a different piece from the exterior face**, because its lighting and its base line differ |
| **Door and window openings seen from inside** | the openings lesson — **and the reveal reverses** |
| **A ceiling** | **usually not drawn.** In top-down you are looking down into the room |
| **Furniture** | **props** — §9.2's bench, table, bed, cabinet, shelving, with their bands |
| **A hearth or fire** | **stage 6's fire lesson, plus a `Light2D`** |
| **And the light** | **§2's *"Godot `Light2D`, restrained overlays"*.** An interior is a lit space, and **the drawing is restrained precisely so the light can do the work** |

---

**And the one thing interiors make obvious that exteriors hide: the lighting direction.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§10.1's upper-left key** | is the **authored** light, and it applies indoors as outdoors |
| **But indoors the real light comes from a window or a fire** | which is a `Light2D` at a specific position |
| **So an interior is the clearest case of the restraint clause** | **the baked upper-left key is almost wrong indoors, and it is kept anyway, because consistency matters more and the runtime light supplies the truth** |
| **Which is worth understanding rather than fighting** | **bake the upper-left key, keep it weak, and let the hearth light the room** |

**Practice.** Draw a 16 × 16 timber board floor tile with staggered plank ends and tile-test it. Then draw a 32 px interior wall section with a one-pixel `TERR-002` base line, and the same section without it, and compare at 300%. Then assemble a small room: floor, two walls, a corner, and the base line turning the corner.
Cliffs and elevation:
Height in a projection with no vanishing point: the cliff face, the step, and the one ambiguity that cannot be drawn away.

**§9.1 names cliffs in the terrain class** — *"rock, masonry, ruins, foundations, cliffs"* is `TERR-013`–`016`'s intended use — **and elevation is the hardest thing in this projection.**

---

**The problem, from stage 3's height-against-depth lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Moving up the screen means either further away or taller** | and a cliff is **both at once** |
| **A 32 px cliff face** | is **32 px of screen height that is vertical surface**, with ground above it that is further away |
| **So the player must be able to tell** | **where the top edge is, where the bottom edge is, and that the middle is not walkable** |

---

**The three devices, and all three are needed:**

| | Device | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **The cliff face is a front face** | **a vertical surface with its own material and shading** — darker than the ground above, with vertical striations |
| **2** | **The top edge is a lip** | **a one-or-two-pixel band of the ground's Light step** along the top, projecting slightly. **This is what reads as an edge rather than a colour change** |
| **3** | **The bottom edge is a contact line** | **Deep where the face meets the lower ground**, plus **scree or rubble** if the material warrants it |

**And the consequence for the tile set: a cliff needs its own terrain set**, because the top edge, the face and the bottom edge are three different tile roles plus corners.

---

**The piece count, honestly:**

| Piece | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **The top lip** | straight, plus outer and inner corners — **3 to 9 tiles** |
| **The face** | **one to three tiles of vertical striation**, repeating downward for taller cliffs |
| **The base** | straight, plus corners — **3 to 9 tiles** |
| **And the cases** | **a cliff that turns, a cliff that ends, a cliff with a path cut into it** |

**Which is why cliffs are usually the last terrain a game gets**, and why §9.3's *"final York calibration assets"* being open work is a mercy here.

---

**The cheaper answers, which are worth considering first:**

| Option | What it costs |
| --- | --- |
| **A low step or kerb — 4 to 8 px** | **one piece plus corners.** Reads as elevation without needing a face set, and **it is enough for most of what York needs** |
| **A retaining wall** | **the walls lesson's set, reused** — a wall is a cliff with a tidier face |
| **A slope or ramp** | **a foreshortened top face with a value gradient**, and **it is walkable, which avoids the collision question entirely** |
| **And avoiding elevation** | **a flat village with no cliffs.** §9.1 names cliffs because the ramp's use mentions them, **not because the Prologue needs one** |

---

**And the ambiguity that cannot be drawn away.** The honest limit of the projection:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A tall cliff face occupies screen height** | and **the ground at its top is drawn at the same scale as the ground at its bottom**, because §9.1 says *"floors do not converge"* |
| **So two points on the map, one above the other, are indistinguishable from two points at different heights** | |
| **Which means** | **the player cannot always tell how far back the upper ground is.** No amount of shading fixes it |
| **What games do instead** | **keep elevation changes small and local; use the camera and collision to make the geometry unambiguous in play; and accept that a 2D top-down game's verticality is schematic** |
| **And §4's line** | *"The camera never rotates; authored directional coverage must therefore support every facing gameplay can expose"* — **the camera is fixed, so the ambiguity is permanent** |

**Practice.** Draw an 8 px kerb: a thin front face, a light lip along the top, a Deep contact line at the base, and corners. Place it and walk a character to it. Then draw a 32 px cliff face with vertical striations, a lip and a base, and count the tiles a full set would need. Then decide, for a York scene, whether you need a cliff at all.
The screen's colour budget, applied:
§9.3's 32–40 colours spent on a real scene, and how a scene palette is curated.

**§9.3:**

> *"The Master Palette remains the colour authority. **A scene curates only the material ramps it needs**; identity colours such as Beacon cyan, Grace gold, veil violet and ember are used only when their meaning is genuinely present. **A normal environment screen should usually remain near 32–40 selected master colours**, but readability and the actual material set decide the final count."*

**Three rules there: curate; reserve the identity colours; and 32–40.**

---

**The arithmetic.** 32–40 colours at four steps per ramp is **eight to ten ramps** — and the characters' own 12–18 are on top of that, or inside it.

**A York daytime exterior, curated:**

| Ramp | For | Steps used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`TERR-001`–`004` Neutral** | **outlines, contact shadows, interiors of openings** | **3** |
| **`TERR-021`–`024` Earth** | paths, bare ground | **2** (ground is quiet) |
| **`TERR-045`–`048` Olive** | grass | **2** |
| **`TERR-013`–`016` Stone** | walls, foundations | **4** |
| **`TERR-033`–`036` Timber** | fences, doors, beams, carts | **4** |
| **`TERR-017`–`020` Slate** | roofs | **4** |
| **`TERR-029`–`032` Ochre** | thatch, plaster | **3** |
| **`TERR-049`–`052` Living Green** | trees, shrubs | **3** |
| **`TERR-041`–`044` Moss** | on stone, at bases | **2** |
| **Subtotal** | **nine ramps** | **27** |
| **Plus a character** | `TERR-073`–`076` skin, `TERR-005`–`008` cloth, `TERR-025`–`028` leather | **about 10** |
| **Total** | | **about 37** |

**Which lands inside the band**, and notice how it got there: **the quiet materials use two steps and the structural ones use four.** Stage 6's contrast scale, applied as a budget.

---

**The three ways a scene goes over budget:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Every material uses all four steps** | **the commonest.** Nine ramps × 4 = 36 before the characters. **The fix is stage 6's: a flat ground material needs two steps** |
| **2 — Too many ramps** | **two greens and two greys is four ramps where two might do.** The fix: **ask whether the distinction is load-bearing** |
| **3 — An identity colour has leaked in** | **§9.3's own warning: *"identity colours such as Beacon cyan, Grace gold, veil violet and ember are used only when their meaning is genuinely present"*** |

**And rule 3 is the one with teeth.** A brass hinge drawn in Grace Gold, a violet flower, an orange ember in a cooking fire — **each one spends an identity colour and makes it mean less when it is used deliberately.**

---

**How to curate a scene, in four steps:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — List the materials the scene actually contains** | **by looking at the layout, not by imagining** |
| **2 — Assign ramps**, sharing where possible | thatch and plaster both take ochre; sacking and grass both take olive |
| **3 — Decide the step count per material** | **flat ground 2; vertical structure 4; secondary detail 1–2** |
| **4 — Total it, and cut** | and **if it will not come under 40, say so** — §9.3's own escape clause is *"readability and the actual material set decide the final count"* |

---

**And the practical tool, from stage 5:** **the Lospec palette analyzer on a screenshot.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Take a screenshot of the assembled scene in Godot** | |
| **Run it through the analyzer** | |
| **It reports every colour and its count** | |
| **The caution** | **`Light2D` will have produced colours outside the 132**, which `colour-palette.md` permits: *"Runtime lighting, compositing, transparency, and effects may create transitional display colours"* — **so analyse an unlit screenshot, or the assembled sheet** |

**Practice.** Curate a York exterior as the table above does, listing ramps and step counts, and total it. Then find one ramp you could cut and one material you could move to two steps. Then assemble a small scene in Godot, screenshot it unlit, and run it through the Lospec analyzer to count the actual colours.
What is open work:
The stage's conclusion: a precise list of what §9 leaves undecided, why that matters, and how to proceed anyway.

**§9's own statement, in its first line:**

> *"**No current terrain, prop, building, character-effect or environment art is approved.** Environment art is drawn directly; it does not use the retired generation, sheet-conversion or reference-chaining workflow."*

**And §9.3's closing paragraph names the open decisions:**

> *"**Terrain transition grammar, environment material ramps, final York calibration assets, destruction states and VFX rules remain open work.** Implementation placeholders do not approve visual style."*

---

**So, precisely, what is decided and what is not:**

| Decided | Open |
| --- | --- |
| **The projection** — rectilinear three-quarter, no convergence, vertical verticals (§9.1) | **the transition grammar** — hard cuts, edge sets or overlays; which matching mode; which pairs transition |
| **The tile size** — 16 px, with an 8 px subgrid (§9.2) | **the environment material ramps** — which ramp each environment material takes, formally |
| **The four asset classes** (§9.1) | **the York calibration assets** — §9.2's bands are *"starting calibration, not approval"* |
| **The four modular tests** (§9.1, §9.3) | **destruction states** |
| **The anchor, footprint and visible-size rules** (§9.1, §9.2) | **VFX rules** |
| **The eleven per-asset checks** (§9.3) | **and whether roofs are removed or faded, and what is seen through an opening** — which this stage raised and §9 does not address |
| **The 32–40 screen colour budget** (§9.3) | |
| **The lighting direction and restraint** (§9.1, §10.1) | |

---

**Why the asymmetry is the right shape.** Everything **decided** is a constraint that lets work begin: the projection, the grid, the anchor, the tests, the checks. Everything **open** is a choice that drawing will inform:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§9.2's own words about its bands** | *"Validate them beside the real character at native scale and **revise the table if drawn evidence shows a systematic problem**"* |
| **Which is a standing invitation** | **the bands are a hypothesis, and drawing tests it** |
| **And the same logic applies to the grammar** | **you cannot choose between edge sets and overlays without having drawn one of each** |

---

**So how to proceed. Four rules:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Draw the smallest thing that tests the decision** | **one 16-tile edge set, and one 16-tile overlay set, for one boundary.** Then the choice has evidence |
| **2 — Keep it in `media/work/`** | gitignored, and **not a master until the decision is made** |
| **3 — Record what you chose and why** | **so the proposal has the six elements stage 5's new-ramp lesson listed**: the gap, why nothing else works, the cost, what it pairs with, its limits, and the date |
| **4 — Raise it rather than deciding it** | **§2.1: *"Art must not invent costume details, insignia, equipment, anatomy or lore to fill a gap; surface the gap instead"*** — and §2.1's priority order puts **direct decisions by Master Roachi** first, with **Timon having final say on design** |

---

**And the stage's own honest summary:**

> **This stage taught how terrain and architecture work, what the tests are, what the options are, and what each option costs. It did not teach which option Shepherds uses, because that has not been decided — and the most useful thing a terrain stage can do in that situation is make the decision cheap to make.**

**Which is the same position stage 12 of the SA politics curriculum takes about a live argument, and for the same reason: where a question is open, the useful contribution is the strongest form of each answer and what evidence would settle it.**

**Practice.** Write the decided/open table above onto one page. Then pick the transition grammar decision and draw the smallest test of it — one boundary, both ways. Then write the proposal with all six elements. Then list which of §9.3's five open items your drawing could inform and which it could not.
The eighty-pixel problem:
The stage's thesis: a figure at eighty pixels has no room for a face, so identity has to be carried by shape — and the contract says so.

**The measurement, §4:**

> *"Approximate adult height remains near **80 px sole-to-crown**, but pose and authored direction may change the measured height. The approved idle reference deliberately reaches **81–87 px by direction**."*

**And §10.1's consequence:**

> *"Every playable hero must remain identifiable in solid black, grayscale, dark lighting and a busy party scene. **Identity cannot depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail.**"*

---

**What 80 pixels actually buys**, from stage 2's detail budget:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The figure's bounding box** | **about 85 × 40** |
| **Pixels occupied** | **about 1,600** |
| **Minus a one-pixel outline** | **about 1,350 interior pixels** |
| **The head** | **10 to 14 px tall, 8 to 11 wide** — **80 to 140 pixels** |
| **The face area** | **about 6 × 6 = 36 pixels** |
| **An eye** | **one pixel, or none** |
| **A hand** | **two or three pixels across** |

**So there is no face.** There is a head-shape, and within it room for two dark pixels and an eyebrow.

**And the project's own answer, from `media/reference/Animation/README.md`:**

> *"**Face mark** | Kept (`#408190`): on s, se, e, w and sw; **not visible on the back views**"*

**One mark, one colour, on five of eight directions.** **That is the decided scale of facial detail in this game**, and it is the right one.

---

**So identity is carried by four things**, and this stage teaches each:

| | Carrier | Lesson |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Silhouette** — height, build, hair or hat shape, cloak, stance | 5 |
| **2** | **Equipment that breaks the outline** — §10.1's own permission | 13 |
| **3** | **Value structure** — which parts are light and dark, as a pattern | stage 4 |
| **4** | **Costume shape** — not its colour | 14 |

**And the thing that carries none of it: the face.**

---

**Which produces the stage's organising principle:**

> **Draw the silhouette until the character is recognisable in solid black. Only then draw anything inside it.**

**That is stage 4's order applied to a figure, and it is the discipline the whole stage rests on.** A character sprite that fails the black test has to be redrawn from the silhouette, **and no amount of interior work will save it** — stage 4's cause 5.

---

**The stage's shape:**

| Lessons | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1–4** | **the body at this scale** — the problem, proportion, the head, hands and feet |
| **5** | **silhouette first** |
| **6–9** | **the eight directions** — the rule, why mirroring is banned, what the alternative costs, and how to draw eight separately |
| **10–12** | **the measured facts** — the 81–87 px variance, anatomical scale across poses, ground contact |
| **13–14** | **identity** — equipment and costume |
| **15–16** | **four legs** — the body, and the Prologue's four animals |
| **17–18** | **Timon's reference read as a specification**, and the checklist |

**And what this stage does not cover: movement.** The figure is drawn standing. **Stage 10 is animation**, and it depends entirely on this one.

**Practice.** Open one of the reference masters at `media/reference/Animation/body-part-reference/converted/s/` and measure the figure's height in pixels. Then count the pixels in its head. Then find the face mark and confirm its colour. Then look at the north-facing version and confirm there is no face.
Proportion at eighty pixels:
The head-count that fits, the measurements the reference actually uses, and why a stylised proportion is the only workable one.

**The classical proportions, and why none of them works here:**

| System | Head count | At 80 px the head is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Academic realism** | **7.5 heads** | **10.7 px** |
| **Heroic illustration** | **8 heads** | **10 px** |
| **Stylised / animation** | **6 heads** | **13.3 px** |
| **Cartoon** | **4–5 heads** | **16–20 px** |
| **Chibi** | **2–3 heads** | **27–40 px** |

**And the measured answer from the project's own reference: a head of 10 to 14 px on an 81–87 px figure is between 6 and 8 heads** — **so Shepherds sits at the realistic-to-stylised boundary**, which matches §2's *"warm, earthy, weathered"* rather than cartoon.

---

**Why that is the right choice here, and the trade it makes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A larger head — 5 heads, 16 px** | **more room for a face, more character, less realism.** And **the body gets correspondingly less**: a 5-head figure at 80 px has a 64 px body |
| **A smaller head — 8 heads, 10 px** | **more body, more realistic silhouette, and a head with 36 pixels of face area** |
| **The project's 6–8** | **the body carries the character and the head is a shape** |
| **And it follows from §10.1** | **identity may not depend on microscopic detail**, so there is no point buying face pixels |

---

**The vertical landmarks, on an 84 px figure.** These are the numbers to work from:

| Landmark | Height from the sole |
| --- | --- |
| **Crown** | **84** |
| **Chin** | **about 72** — so the head is **12 px** |
| **Shoulder** | **about 68** |
| **Nipple line / mid-chest** | **about 60** |
| **Waist** | **about 52** |
| **Hip / crotch** | **about 42** — **halfway**, which is the one reliable proportional fact |
| **Knee** | **about 22** |
| **Ankle** | **about 4** |
| **Sole** | **0** |

**The halfway hip is the landmark worth memorising.** **The crotch is at half the figure's height**, in every proportional system and at every scale. **Get that right and the figure reads; get it wrong and no amount of detail helps.**

---

**The horizontal measurements:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Shoulder width** | **about 18 to 22 px** for an adult — **roughly a quarter of the height**, or **two head-widths** |
| **Waist** | **12 to 15 px** |
| **Hip** | **14 to 18 px** |
| **Head width** | **8 to 11 px** |
| **Upper arm** | **4 to 5 px thick** |
| **Forearm** | **3 to 4 px** |
| **Thigh** | **6 to 7 px** |
| **Calf** | **4 to 5 px** |
| **Ankle** | **3 px** |

**And those numbers are the whole figure.** An upper arm four pixels thick has room for **one value boundary**, which is stage 4's point arriving concretely: **a limb at this scale is a two-value shape with an outline.**

---

**The variations that distinguish characters**, which is the identity lesson's material:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Height** | **±6 px is visible** — 78 against 84 reads as shorter |
| **Shoulder width** | **±3 px is visible** — a broad character against a slight one |
| **Head size** | **±2 px** |
| **Limb thickness** | **±1 px** reads as heavier or lighter build |
| **And the proportion** | **a shorter figure with the same head size reads as younger** — which is how a child is drawn: **not a smaller adult, but a 60 px figure with a 12 px head, so 5 heads** |

**Practice.** Draw an 84 px vertical line and mark the ten landmarks from the table. Then build a figure silhouette on them, using the horizontal measurements. Then draw a second figure 6 px shorter and 3 px broader and check both read as different people in solid black. Then draw a child at 60 px with a 12 px head.
The head:
Twelve pixels: the shape, the hair, the one mark the reference permits, and what to leave out.

**The head is 10 to 14 px tall and 8 to 11 wide — about 100 pixels** — and from the stage's first lesson, **about 36 of them are the face area.**

---

**The shape, in four directions.** The head is the clearest demonstration that eight directions are eight drawings:

| Direction | What the head's silhouette is |
| --- | --- |
| **South — facing the viewer** | **a rounded shape, widest at the cheekbones, narrowing to a chin.** The face area is central |
| **East or west — profile** | **a different shape entirely** — the brow and nose project forward, the back of the skull projects back, and the jaw line is visible. **Not the south view rotated** |
| **North — from behind** | **a rounded shape, with the hair's mass and the neck.** **No face at all** |
| **Diagonals** | **between the two**, and genuinely in between — **this is where the eight-direction cost is highest** |

---

**The hair, which is the single largest identity carrier on the whole figure.** From stage 4's black test:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why hair** | **it is the outermost part of the silhouette's top**, and the top of a silhouette is what the eye reads first |
| **What reads** | **the mass and its outline** — a bun, a tied-back tail, a hood, a hat's brim, short cropped, long loose |
| **What does not** | **strands.** Hair is a shape plus two values |
| **Pixel budget** | **20 to 50 pixels**, which is a lot at this scale and worth spending |
| **And it changes by direction** | **a tied-back tail is invisible from the front and prominent from behind** — which is **a reason the back views are distinguishable at all** |

**A hat or hood is better still**, because its silhouette is harder-edged and reads more clearly — **and §10.1's equipment clause permits it to break the outline.**

---

**The face, at the project's decided scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The reference's answer** | **one face mark, `#408190`, on s, se, e, w and sw** |
| **Not on** | **n, ne, nw** |
| **What a mark can be** | **two single-pixel eyes; or a one-pixel bar; or a two-pixel shadow under the brow** |
| **Value** | **`TERR-002` or `TERR-003`**, from stage 6's skin lesson — **not `TERR-001`, which reads as a hole** |
| **What to leave out** | **the mouth, the nose, the ears, the eyebrows as separate features** |

**And the strongest argument for leaving out the mouth: the reference does not have one**, and Timon and Master Roachi reviewed that reference in motion across all eight directions and approved it as the final idle reference. **That is a decided question.**

---

**The neck, which is three pixels and matters:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Width** | **3 to 4 px** |
| **Height** | **2 to 3 px visible** |
| **Its job** | **the occlusion under the chin** — stage 4's *"under the chin, above the chest: the head overhangs the neck"*. **One pixel of Deep there does more for the head than anything inside it** |
| **And without it** | **the head sits directly on the shoulders and the figure reads as hunched** |

---

**The practical drawing order for a head:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the silhouette including the hair**, in one value |
| **2** | **the black test** — is this person recognisable from the head alone? |
| **3** | **the neck and its occlusion** |
| **4** | **two values on the face mass** — lit upper-left, shadowed lower-right |
| **5** | **two values on the hair**, with the boundary following its mass |
| **6** | **the face mark, if the direction has one** |
| **7** | **stop** |

**Practice.** Draw a 12 px head in four directions — s, e, n, se — as four separate silhouettes, and confirm none is a rotation of another. Then add hair with a distinctive shape and run the black test on the head alone. Then add the neck's occlusion and compare with and without. Then add the face mark to the s and e versions and leave the n one bare.
Hands and feet:
The extremities at two and three pixels: what they can be, and the one thing they must do.

**The measurements, from the proportion lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A hand** | **2 to 3 px across, 3 to 4 px long** — **about 8 to 12 pixels** |
| **A foot** | **4 to 6 px long, 3 px high** — **about 15 to 30 pixels** |

**So a hand has room for a shape and a value**, and a foot has room for a shape, two values and a contact.

---

**The hand.** What it can and cannot be:

| Can | Cannot |
| --- | --- |
| **a cluster, slightly wider than the wrist** | **fingers** |
| **a value distinct from the sleeve** | **a thumb** |
| **a silhouette that changes when it grips something** | **a gesture in the fingers** |
| **a position that reads as open or closed** | |

**And the positions that read at this scale:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Hanging at the side** | **a 2 × 3 cluster below the sleeve** |
| **Gripping** | **a cluster wrapped around the gripped object's silhouette** — and **the object is what reads, not the grip** |
| **Open and raised** | **a slightly wider cluster, 3 × 3** |
| **Pointing** | **a 1 px extension** — barely, and only in profile |
| **And the rule** | **a hand's meaning comes from where the arm puts it**, not from the hand itself. **Gesture is an arm problem** |

---

**The foot, which has a job the hand does not:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its job** | **ground contact.** §4: *"**Ground contact must be stable in every frame.** Collision and gameplay origin remain at the feet"* |
| **Which means** | **the foot's lowest row is the figure's lowest row, and it sits at the pivot's row** — (56, 96) in a 112 × 112 frame |
| **The shape** | **a horizontal cluster, longer than it is tall, extending forward** — and **the direction it extends is a direction cue** |
| **The two values** | **the upper surface lit, the side in shadow, and a line of Deep where it meets the ground** |

**And the direction cue is worth noticing.** In a south-facing figure the feet point toward the viewer and are foreshortened; in a profile they point sideways and are at full length. **So the feet are one of the clearest direction signals in the whole figure**, and getting them wrong makes a direction read as the wrong one.

---

**The foot in each direction**, which is four distinct drawings:

| Direction | The foot |
| --- | --- |
| **South** | **foreshortened** — 3 to 4 px long, pointing down-screen, both feet visible |
| **East or west** | **full length** — 5 to 6 px, pointing sideways, the near foot overlapping the far |
| **North** | **foreshortened**, pointing up-screen — **and you see the heel rather than the toe** |
| **Diagonals** | **between**, with one foot more foreshortened than the other |

---

**And the stance, which is a silhouette decision and belongs here:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Feet together** | **one mass. No gap, and the figure reads as a single column** |
| **Feet apart** | **a negative gap between the legs** — stage 4's gaps lesson — and **the stance becomes part of the identity** |
| **Weight on one leg** | **asymmetric**, with the hip raised on the weighted side. **At 80 px that is a one-or-two-pixel difference and it reads** |
| **The reference's idle** | **has *"3–5 meaningful poses"*** across its 24 frames, **so the stance changes within the animation** — which stage 10 takes up |

**Practice.** Draw a hand hanging at the side as a 2 × 3 cluster, then the same hand gripping a 2 px staff, and check the staff reads rather than the grip. Then draw feet in all four cardinal directions and confirm each is a different shape. Then draw a figure with feet together and the same figure with feet apart and a gap, and run the black test on both.
Silhouette first:
The stage's method, stated as a procedure: how to build a figure from the outside in, and when to stop.

**Stage 4's order, applied to a figure:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the silhouette, in one value** |
| **2** | **the black test** |
| **3** | **the negative gaps** |
| **4** | **the black test again** |
| **5** | **two values** |
| **6** | **four values, materials, outline** |
| **7** | **the face mark** |

**Steps 1 to 4 are this lesson, and they are perhaps 20% of the work and 80% of whether the sprite succeeds.**

---

**Building the silhouette, in six passes:**

| Pass | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The box** | **an 85 × 40 rectangle, with the ten landmarks from the proportion lesson marked.** This is scaffolding on its own layer and it does not export |
| **2 — The masses** | **head, torso, pelvis, four limbs — as simple blocks.** No detail, no outline, one value. **Check the halfway hip** |
| **3 — The contour** | **replace the blocks with a single continuous outline**, following the masses but smoothing where the body smooths — the shoulder into the arm, the waist into the hip |
| **4 — The hair and the costume's silhouette** | **a hood's outer edge, a cloak's hem, a hat's brim.** **This is where the character becomes a specific person** |
| **5 — The equipment that breaks the outline** | **§10.1's permission** — the crook over a shoulder, the satchel at a hip |
| **6 — The gaps** | **armpits, between the legs, under the arm where the satchel strap passes** |

---

**What the black test asks at this point.** From stage 4:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Is it a person?** | **the proportion and the stance** |
| **2 — Is it *this* person?** | **the hair, the costume silhouette, the equipment, the build** |
| **3 — Is the pose readable?** | **standing, carrying, reaching, braced** |

**And the honest standard: put four heroes' silhouettes side by side in black and name each.** **If you cannot, the design does not distinguish them — which §2.1 and `characters.md` own, not the drawing.**

---

**When to stop adding to the silhouette:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The temptation** | **more projections** — a scarf, a tool, a bag, a feather. Each one adds silhouette information |
| **The limit** | **the outline must still read as a human figure.** Too many projections and it reads as a bundle |
| **And the practical limit** | **two or three deliberate projections.** The hair or hat, one piece of equipment, and perhaps a cloak's movement |
| **§10.1's wording** | *"allow **signature** equipment to break the torso silhouette"* — **signature, singular in spirit.** One memorable thing |

---

**And the one thing that is worth doing before the silhouette: look at the reference.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`media/reference/Animation/body-part-reference/`** | **Timon's approved idle, 8 directions, 24 frames, 192 source frames** |
| **What it gives you** | **the project's decided proportion, build, stance and height by direction** |
| **How to use it** | **as a reference layer under your silhouette** — stage 1's reference layers |
| **And `media/README.md` is explicit** | **it is *"the final reference for every character's idle"*** — *"**Every future character's idle animation follows it**"* |
| **Which means** | **the silhouette's proportions are not a free choice.** They are specified by an approved asset |

**That is the most important sentence in this stage.** **The figure's proportions are decided, and the reference is where they are written down.**

**Practice.** Open a reference frame as a reference layer in a 112 × 112 file. Draw your figure's silhouette over it in one value, following its proportions. Run the black test. Then add hair, one piece of equipment and the gaps, and run it again. Then put your silhouette beside the reference's and compare the heights and the hip position.
The eight directions:
The rule, the eight names, and what each view actually shows — which is why eight drawings and not one.

**§5.1 and §5.4:**

> *"**eight separately authored directions: S, SE, E, NE, N, NW, W and SW; no mirroring**"*
>
> *"Use eight authored directions whenever asymmetry or the approved motion reference requires them."*

**And the naming, §5.4:** *"Naming states the action and direction plainly: `idle_s`, `move_ne`, `staff_attack_1_se`."*

---

**The eight, with what each shows:**

| Direction | Facing | What you see |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`s`** | **toward the viewer** | **the face, the chest, the fronts of both arms, both feet foreshortened.** The most informative view and usually drawn first |
| **`se`** | **down-right** | **three-quarter** — the face partly turned, one shoulder nearer, the far arm partly hidden |
| **`e`** | **right, in profile** | **the profile head, one side of the body, the near arm overlapping the far, feet at full length.** The **most different** from south |
| **`ne`** | **up-right** | **three-quarter from behind** — the back of the head mostly, one cheek at most |
| **`n`** | **away** | **the back of the head and body. No face.** The least informative view |
| **`nw`** | **up-left** | ne's counterpart |
| **`w`** | **left, in profile** | e's counterpart |
| **`sw`** | **down-left** | se's counterpart |

---

**Why eight drawings and not one rotated.** Three reasons:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The head changes shape** | the head lesson: **a profile head is not a front head rotated.** The brow and nose project; the skull's back projects |
| **2 — Occlusion changes** | **in profile the near arm hides the far one; in front both are visible.** That is a different drawing, not a transform |
| **3 — The light does not rotate** | stage 4: **the key light stays at the upper-left while the body turns**, so **the lit side of the body changes.** Facing south the right shoulder is lit; facing north the left one is |

---

**And the cost, stated honestly.** Eight directions × the number of actions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The idle alone** | **8 directions × 24 frames = 192 drawings** |
| **The run** | **8 × 12 = 96** |
| **§6.1's Eli** | *"idle and normal movement throughout; a south-facing lying/get-up sequence…; stoop-down, hold and rise…; a general interaction; kneel/lift/stow…; remove-from-satchel and place-on-bench; **three crook-chain attacks**; crook-heavy wind-up and release; sling throw, sling charge and charged throw; dodge; and a non-damaging shove/stagger reaction"* |
| **Which is** | **roughly fifteen action families**, several needing eight directions, at 6 to 24 frames each |
| **Order of magnitude** | **well over a thousand frames for one character's Prologue requirements** |

**That number is the reason §5.3 exists:**

> *"Animation requirements come from **actual gameplay actions**, not from speculative 'complete sprite sheet' lists."*

**And the mitigations the contract itself provides:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Not every action needs eight** | **§6.1: *"a south-facing lying/get-up sequence"*** — **one direction, because the script controls where he lies** |
| **Not every action needs 24 frames** | **§5.4: *"Frame counts outside the approved idle and movement references are authored to the action's gameplay anticipation, active and recovery timing"*** |
| **And §6.1 again** | *"The Prologue uses one normal movement speed… it does not require a separate run animation"* — **and *"Guard, parry, hurt, downed, revive, victory, Shepherd Light and Ultimate animations are later-game requirements"*** |

**Read those three together: the contract is actively reducing the count.** **The Prologue needs far less than a complete sprite sheet, and knowing which is the difference between a finishable job and an unfinishable one.**

**Practice.** Draw one figure's silhouette in all eight directions, as eight separate drawings, and confirm no two are transforms of each other. Then list §6.1's Eli requirements and mark which need eight directions and which need one. Then multiply it out and write down the frame count.
Why mirroring is banned:
The clause, the three reasons behind it, and the one case it permits.

**§5.4:**

> *"**Mirroring is permitted only for an explicitly approved asset whose handedness, costume and action geometry survive the flip.**"*

**Three conditions, all of which must hold. This lesson is why each one matters.**

---

**Reason 1 — Handedness.** The reference's own note:

> *"The limb colours are tied to a side, so **a flipped west would swap them**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For the reference specifically** | **each arm and leg is its own colour**, so a flip swaps left and right. **That is a property of the reference figure, not of every character** |
| **For a real character** | **the handedness is in the costume and the equipment** — a crook held in the right hand, a satchel on the left hip, a strap over one shoulder |
| **A flip reverses all of it** | so **the west-facing character is holding the crook in the other hand** |
| **And it is visible** | **not subtly.** A player watching a character turn sees the crook jump from one side to the other |

**Reason 2 — The lighting, which stage 4 established.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The key light is at the upper-left and stays there** | §10.1 |
| **A flipped sprite's light is at the upper-right** | because the whole image reversed |
| **So in a scene where everything is lit from the upper-left, the flipped sprite is lit from the wrong side** | |
| **And it reads as wrong even on a perfectly symmetrical character** | |

**That second reason is the one people miss, and it applies even when handedness does not.**

**Reason 3 — Action geometry.** §5.4's third condition:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An attack has a direction** | a crook swung from the right shoulder sweeps left-to-right |
| **Flipped** | it sweeps right-to-left — **which may be fine, or may contradict the gameplay's hit geometry** |
| **And for an asymmetric action** | **a sling thrown from one hand, a shove with one shoulder** — the flip changes what the action is |

---

**What the runtime actually does**, which is the generous part. From `authored_sprite_body.gd`:

> *"a west-side tag **as drawn, unmirrored**, whenever the set has one (`direction8_of`, `_drawn_facing`), and mirrors **only a direction with no drawing of its own**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So the engine supports both** | **draw eight and it uses eight; draw five and it mirrors the three it lacks** |
| **Which means mirroring is a fallback, not a prohibition** | **the asset is better with eight and works with five** |
| **And the practical consequence** | **you can ship five directions and upgrade to eight later, per action**, without changing any code |

**That is worth knowing, because it changes the risk calculus:** **a first pass at five directions is a legitimate increment, and §5.4's rule is about what gets *approved*, not about what the engine can play.**

---

**And the one case §5.4 permits.** All three conditions:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Handedness survives** | **the character is symmetrical, or the asymmetry is invisible** — no held object, no asymmetric costume |
| **Costume survives** | **no satchel on one hip, no strap over one shoulder, no asymmetric hem** |
| **Action geometry survives** | **the action is symmetrical** — a two-handed lift, a straight-on idle, a fall |
| **Plus** | ***"explicitly approved"*** — **it is a decision, not a default** |
| **A plausible candidate** | **a sheep.** Symmetrical, no costume, no handedness — **and §6.3 needs *"directional walking"*, so the saving is real** |

**Practice.** Draw a figure with a satchel on one hip and a crook in one hand, then flip it and put the two side by side — note the three changes. Then draw a symmetrical creature and flip it, and check whether anything reads wrongly. Then read `direction8_of` and `_drawn_facing` in `authored_sprite_body.gd` and confirm the fallback behaviour.
What five directions costs:
The industry-normal economy, exactly what it gives up, and how to decide per asset.

**The method Slynyrd's Pixelblog 55 teaches**, and which most games use:

> **Draw five orientations — front, back, two diagonals and one side — and flip to get the other three.**

**Five drawings instead of eight is a 37.5% saving**, which across §6.1's fifteen action families is enormous.

---

**Exactly what gets mirrored:**

| Drawn | Mirrored to get |
| --- | --- |
| **`s`** | — |
| **`n`** | — |
| **`e`** | **`w`** |
| **`se`** | **`sw`** |
| **`ne`** | **`nw`** |

**So three of eight are flips**, and `s` and `n` are drawn once each because they are their own mirror.

---

**What that gives up, item by item:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Handedness** | **the crook moves to the other hand in `w`, `sw` and `nw`** — three of eight directions. **Visible when the character turns** |
| **The lighting** | **those three are lit from the upper-right.** Stage 4's reason |
| **Costume asymmetry** | **a satchel, a strap, a scar, a hem** — all reversed in three directions |
| **Action geometry** | **an asymmetric attack's direction reverses** |
| **And what it does not give up** | **the silhouette, the proportion, the animation timing, the value structure.** A mirrored sprite is a correct sprite with its handedness and lighting reversed |

---

**How to decide, per asset.** Four questions:

| Question | If yes |
| --- | --- |
| **Does it hold or carry anything?** | **eight.** A crook, a satchel, a sling, a tool |
| **Is the costume asymmetric?** | **eight** |
| **Is the action asymmetric?** | **eight for that action**, even if the idle is five |
| **Is it a hero the player will watch for twenty hours?** | **eight.** §10.1's identity clause is about heroes specifically |
| **None of the above** | **five is defensible, and §5.4 requires it to be explicitly approved** |

**And the per-action nuance is worth stating: the decision is per asset, action and direction**, because that is the granularity of §3.1's masters. **A character's idle might be eight and their fall might be one** — §6.1's *"south-facing lying/get-up sequence"* is exactly that.

---

**The two intermediate strategies, which are better than either extreme:**

**1 — Five now, eight later.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How** | **the runtime mirrors only a direction with no drawing of its own.** So add `w` later and it is used immediately |
| **The cost** | **nothing, mechanically.** The file naming and the tags are unchanged |
| **And what it buys** | **a playable character sooner**, which `CLAUDE.md`'s *"Work one asset, action and direction at a time so each authored animation can be reviewed in Godot before the next family expands"* favours |

**2 — Eight for the idle, five for everything else.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The reasoning** | **the idle is what the player sees most**, standing still in a conversation or a menu. **An attack lasts 0.3 seconds** |
| **And the reference supports it** | **the approved idle is eight authored directions** and the approved run also eight — **so the two most-seen animations are already specified as eight** |
| **The honest risk** | **inconsistency.** A character whose idle has the crook on the right and whose attack has it on the left, depending on direction, is worse than one that is wrong consistently |

---

**And the contract's position, which resolves it:** **§5.4 permits mirroring only for an explicitly approved asset, and the approved references are eight.** **So the default is eight, five is a decision to raise, and the engine will carry either.**

**Practice.** Take your eight-direction silhouette and delete `w`, `sw` and `nw`, then view the character turning in Godot and watch the handedness flip. Then run the four questions against a hero, a sheep and a corpse puppet and write down the answer for each. Then decide what you would propose for the sheep and why.
The 81 to 87 pixel variance:
The reference's measured heights by direction, why they differ, and the decision that kept them.

**The measurements, from `media/reference/Animation/README.md`:**

> *"**Body height (tallest pose)** | **s and n 81 px; se, e, w and sw 84 px; ne and nw 87 px.** The crouch is 6 px lower."*

**And §4 cites it:** *"Approximate adult height remains near 80 px sole-to-crown, but **pose and authored direction may change the measured height.** The approved idle reference deliberately reaches 81–87 px by direction."*

---

**So the same figure measures three different heights:**

| Directions | Height | Relative to south |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **s, n** | **81 px** | — |
| **se, e, w, sw** | **84 px** | **+3** |
| **ne, nw** | **87 px** | **+6** |

**A 6-pixel range on an 81-pixel figure is 7.4%**, which is large enough to see if you are looking for it.

---

**Why it happens.** The honest answer is that it is a consequence of how the poses were drawn rather than a geometric necessity — **and there is a plausible geometric reason too:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **In the three-quarter projection** | **the figure is seen from above and in front** |
| **Facing away (n, ne, nw)** | **more of the top of the head and shoulders is presented**, and **the body leans very slightly away**, so the measured silhouette is taller |
| **Facing toward (s)** | **the head is seen more from the front**, slightly foreshortened at the crown |
| **The diagonals** | **in between** |
| **And the practical cause** | **eight separately drawn poses by a human artist differ.** Which is the point of the next section |

---

**The decision, which is the lesson.** `media/reference/Animation/README.md`:

> *"**None of the following is a defect. All of it was seen in the preview and kept on purpose:**
> - the 3 px drop when the loop returns from frame 24 to frame 1;
> - **the height changing by direction**;
> - the few pixels that change during west's hold (its 24 source frames are separate images, not copies);
> - east and west starting their crouch one frame earlier than the others.
>
> **Timon rejected re-timing the key poses and evening out the heights.**"*

**Four deliberate irregularities, reviewed in motion across eight directions, and kept.**

---

**Why that matters more than the heights themselves.** Three things:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — It tells you what "approved" means** | **it means someone looked at it in motion and decided.** Not that it was measured and found regular |
| **2 — It tells you not to fix it** | **a future character whose heights are evened out to 84 across all eight directions would not match the reference** — and `media/README.md` says *"Every future character's idle animation follows it"* |
| **3 — And it tells you the standard is "reads correctly", not "measures consistently"** | **which is §10's condition 6: *"silhouette, value, ground contact and direction coverage read at native scale"*. Read, not measure** |

---

**And the practical consequence for drawing.** §4's hard rule:

> *"**Never normalize each frame's bounding-box height independently; doing so makes prone bodies grow.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What that forbids** | **adjusting a pose's size so its bounding box matches another's** |
| **Why it matters here** | **if the eight directions legitimately differ by 6 px, the temptation to normalise them is strong** — and normalising would **scale the figure**, which changes its apparent size |
| **The rule** | **the canvas is fixed at 112 × 112, the pivot at (56, 96), and the figure is whatever height it is in that pose and direction** |
| **And for a crouch** | **the reference's crouch is 6 px lower — a real pose change, not a scaling** |

**Practice.** Measure the figure's height in all eight reference directions and confirm the 81/84/87 pattern. Then measure the crouch pose and confirm it is 6 px lower. Then draw your own figure's s and ne silhouettes and see whether yours shows the same tendency naturally. Then read the four kept irregularities and decide which you would have been tempted to fix.
Anatomical scale across poses:
The rule that stops prone bodies growing, the mechanism behind it, and what a crouch or a fall actually does.

**§4's two sentences, which are a single rule:**

> *"A pose that crouches, falls or lies down **keeps the same anatomical scale** as its upright pose. **Never normalize each frame's bounding-box height independently; doing so makes prone bodies grow.**"*

---

**The mechanism, because the failure is counter-intuitive.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An upright figure** | **84 px tall, 20 px wide.** Its bounding box is **84 × 20** |
| **The same figure lying down** | **84 px long, 20 px tall.** Its bounding box is **20 × 84** rotated — **or in practice about 70 × 24**, because a lying body is foreshortened and curled |
| **The failure** | **a tool or a habit that scales each frame to fill the same bounding height** |
| **What happens** | **the 24-px-tall lying figure is scaled up to 84 px tall** — **so it becomes 3.5 times its real size.** A prone body the size of a cart |
| **Hence §4's words** | *"doing so makes prone bodies **grow**"* |

**And where this actually happens:** **an automated conversion pipeline, a batch resize, or a per-frame trim-and-recentre.** **Which is exactly what the retired sprite-acus workflow did** — and `media/reference/Animation/README.md` records a related artefact of it: *"the recipe anchors each frame on its own bottom-centre, so across a stride the figure's paste column moves by up to 13 px (e and w) as the legs open and close."*

**That is the same class of error, horizontally rather than vertically**, and the README says it was *"Seen and left alone"* — **because the reference is a reference and not a master.**

---

**What the rule requires positively:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The canvas is fixed** | **112 × 112 in every frame of every direction of every action** |
| **The pivot is fixed** | **(56, 96)** |
| **The figure moves within it** | **and its measured height is whatever the pose produces** |
| **So a crouch** | **is drawn 6 px shorter, with the knees bent and the torso lowered — and the feet still at row 96** |
| **And a prone figure** | **is drawn lying down, about 70 px long and 24 tall, occupying the lower part of the frame — and the pivot is still at (56, 96)** |

---

**Which raises the question §6.1 answers: where does the pivot go on a lying figure?**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§4** | *"Collision and gameplay origin remain at the feet"* |
| **For a standing figure** | **the feet are at the pivot** |
| **For a lying figure** | **the feet are at one end of the body, which is not the centre** |
| **So either** | **the pivot stays at (56, 96) and the body is drawn wherever it falls relative to that point** — which means **the body's position in the frame encodes which way it fell** |
| **Or** | **the pivot represents the character's ground position rather than literally their feet** |
| **And §6.1's requirement** | *"a **south-facing** lying/get-up sequence for waking and sleeping"* — **one direction, because the script controls where he lies**, which sidesteps most of the problem |

**The practical answer: draw the lying figure so that the pivot (56, 96) is where the character's ground position is** — **roughly under the torso** — **and keep that convention across every prone frame of the sequence.** **Then the get-up animation returns the body to standing with the feet arriving at the pivot, and the whole sequence is continuous.**

---

**And the general principle this establishes:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The pivot is a world position, not a body part** | and the body is drawn relative to it |
| **Which is why the canvas has 16 rows below the pivot** | **room for a crouch, a fall, a jump's shadow and a prone body** |
| **And why trimming is fatal** | stage 1's rule — **trim destroys the only fixed reference the sequence has** |

**Practice.** Draw a figure standing, crouching 6 px lower, and lying down, all three in 112 × 112 with the pivot at (56, 96), and confirm the figure's limb thicknesses and head size are identical in all three. Then measure each pose's bounding box and note how different they are. Then draw the get-up sequence's first and last frames and check they are continuous at the pivot.
Ground contact:
§4's stability requirement, what makes a foot look planted, and the three failures that make a figure float.

**§4:**

> *"**Ground contact must be stable in every frame.** Collision and gameplay origin remain at the feet."*

**And §10's condition 6 lists it as one of four things that must read:** *"silhouette, value, **ground contact** and direction coverage read at native scale."*

---

**What makes a foot look planted.** Four things, and all four are needed:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The foot's lowest row is at the pivot's row** | **row 96** in a 112 × 112 frame |
| **2 — A line of Deep under it** | **occlusion where foot meets ground** — stage 4's *"about eight pixels of work for the single largest readability gain available"* |
| **3 — The contact shadow, on its own layer** | **an ellipse beneath the figure** — stage 3 |
| **4 — And the foot does not move between frames unless the character is stepping** | **which is the "stable in every frame" clause** |

---

**The three failures:**

**1 — The foot drifts between frames.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Symptom** | **the character appears to slide**, or to shuffle while standing still |
| **Cause** | **a 24-frame idle in which the planted foot's pixels change** |
| **The exception the reference permits** | *"the few pixels that change during west's hold (its 24 source frames are separate images, not copies)"* — **hand-drawn frames differ slightly and that was kept** |
| **So the standard is not "identical"** | **it is "stable"** — the foot stays where it is and may differ by a pixel |
| **The technique** | **copy the planted foot between frames rather than redrawing it.** Stage 1's linked cels, or a copy-paste |

**2 — Both feet leave the ground.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **When it is correct** | **a jump, a pounce, a fall** — §6.2's Pip has a pounce in Act I |
| **When it is wrong** | **an idle, a stand, a graze.** A figure with no foot at row 96 is floating |
| **And in a walk** | **at least one foot is down in every frame of a walk cycle**, which is what distinguishes a walk from a run. **A run has a flight phase where neither foot touches** |
| **Which means** | **§5.2's 12-frame run legitimately has airborne frames**, and the contact shadow is what keeps it anchored |

**3 — The shadow moves with the body.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The failure** | **the contact shadow drawn on the body's layer, so it rises when the body rises** |
| **Why §3.1 separates it** | **body, equipment, shadow, effects** — **the shadow is its own layer so it can stay put** |
| **The correct behaviour** | **the shadow stays on the ground and shrinks as the body rises** |
| **And §6.1's stoop** | *"stoop-down, hold and rise for the wool"* — **the shadow grows slightly as he lowers and shrinks as he rises, or simply stays** |

---

**The reference's measured contact behaviour**, which is worth knowing because it is the standard:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The idle's crouch** | **6 px lower** — so the figure lowers and the feet stay |
| **The run's heights** | **s 72, se and sw 75, e, w and n 78, ne and nw 81 px; lowest pose 63 px (ne, nw)** |
| **Which means the run's lowest pose is 18 px below its tallest** | **a very large compression**, and the feet are doing a lot |
| **And the run's paste column drift** | **up to 13 px in e and w** — the conversion artefact, *"seen and left alone"* |

**That last figure is a caution rather than a model: 13 px of horizontal drift across a stride is exactly the "foot drifts" failure**, and it survives in the reference because **the reference is a motion reference, not a production master.** **A character's own run must not do that.**

**Practice.** Draw a two-frame idle where the planted foot is copied between frames, then a version where it is redrawn, and play both at 84 ms — note the difference. Then draw a stoop with the shadow on its own layer staying put, and again with the shadow on the body layer, and compare. Then measure the run reference's heights and confirm the 18 px compression.
Signature equipment:
§10.1's permission to break the silhouette, what qualifies, and the four things equipment must survive.

**§10.1:**

> *"Preserve useful negative gaps between body, limbs and equipment, and **allow signature equipment to break the torso silhouette**."*

**A permission rather than a requirement — and it is the second-strongest identity carrier after the head.**

---

**What "break the torso silhouette" means:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A shape that projects beyond the body's outline** | so the figure's silhouette is no longer a clean human shape |
| **Why that is valuable** | **stage 4's black test.** **A smooth oval is anonymous; an outline with a crook sticking out of it is a specific person** |
| **And it is the only interior-of-the-figure detail that survives the black test** | because it is not interior — **it is outline** |

---

**What qualifies, from §6.1's Eli:**

| Item | How it breaks the silhouette |
| --- | --- |
| **The crook** | **a long diagonal projecting above the shoulder and below the hip** — the single most distinctive thing about a shepherd |
| **The satchel** | **a mass at one hip**, widening the silhouette on one side. §6.1: *"The satchel is part of Eli's required costume"* |
| **The sling** | **a short projection at the belt**, or in hand |
| **A hood or hat** | **the head lesson's** — and it breaks the *head's* silhouette rather than the torso's |
| **A cloak** | **widens and softens the whole lower silhouette**, and moves |

**And note §6.1's detail about Beacon:** *"Beacon is invisible while carried because it is inside Eli's satchel."* **So the satchel is not just identity — it is a narrative container, and its presence is required.**

---

**The four things equipment must survive:**

| | Must survive | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **the black test** | **it is there to be seen in silhouette.** If it merges with the torso it is doing nothing |
| **2** | **eight directions** | **a crook over the right shoulder is in front of the body facing west and behind it facing east** — **so it is eight drawings, and its occlusion relationship with the body changes** |
| **3** | **animation** | **it moves with the body, and it has its own weight.** Stage 10's secondary motion |
| **4** | **the negative gap requirement** | **§10.1's same sentence** — the equipment and the body need a gap or a value difference between them |

**Condition 2 is the expensive one.** **A held object's relationship to the body is a per-direction drawing problem:**

| Direction | The crook, held in the right hand |
| --- | --- |
| **`s`** | **in front of the body**, crossing the torso diagonally |
| **`e`** | **on the near side**, fully visible, overlapping nothing |
| **`n`** | **behind the body**, partly hidden |
| **`w`** | **on the far side**, mostly hidden behind the torso |
| **Which is four different occlusion problems** | and the diagonals are four more |

---

**And §3.1's layer rule exists for exactly this:**

> *"Layers should separate only things that require independent editing or runtime treatment — **body, equipment**, shadow and effects"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Equipment on its own layer** | **so it can be edited, hidden or swapped without redrawing the body** |
| **Which matters** | **because a character may gain a different crook, or lose the satchel in a cutscene** |
| **And Wizard's split-layer importer** | **can bring it in as a separate texture** — stage 7's importer lesson |
| **But the occlusion problem remains** | **a crook behind the body cannot be a separate layer above the body.** **So the layering is per-direction too, or the equipment is drawn into the body where it passes behind** |

**That is the honest complication: layer separation and occlusion fight each other**, and the practical answer is **equipment on its own layer where it is in front, and drawn into the body layer where it is behind** — which means **the layer split is not uniform across the eight directions.**

**Practice.** Draw a figure with a crook in all four cardinal directions and solve the occlusion in each. Then run the black test on all four and confirm the crook reads in each. Then put the crook on its own layer in the s and e drawings and into the body layer in the n and w ones, and note that the file structures differ.
Costume as identity:
What a costume can carry at eighty pixels, where the design comes from, and the clause that forbids inventing it.

**From §10.1: identity may not depend on hue, glow, jewellery or microscopic detail. So a costume carries identity through shape and value.**

---

**What a costume can be at this scale:**

| Element | Pixels | Reads? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A silhouette change** — a cloak, a long coat, a wide hem, a hood | **20 to 60** | **yes, strongly.** The best investment |
| **A value block** — a dark tunic against light trousers | **a whole region** | **yes** — and it survives greyscale, which hue does not |
| **A hard edge** — a belt, a collar, a cuff, a hem line | **1 px each** | **yes, as a boundary** |
| **A large pattern** — two or three stripes, a wide band | **2 px marks** | **marginally** |
| **A small pattern** — checks, embroidery, a crest | **1 px** | **no.** Stage 2's fine-texture failure |
| **An insignia** | **2 to 4 px** | **no, not legibly** — and §2.1 forbids inventing one |

---

**So the hierarchy, in order of what to spend pixels on:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The garment's outline** | long or short, loose or fitted, hooded or bare |
| **2 — The value split between garments** | **which is the grey-test-safe way to distinguish parts of a costume** |
| **3 — The hard boundaries** | belt, collar, cuffs, hem — **one pixel each and they define the garment's structure** |
| **4 — Two or three folds** | stage 6's cloth lesson |
| **5 — Nothing else** | |

---

**Now the part that is not a drawing decision.** §2.1:

> *"Art must not invent costume details, insignia, equipment, anatomy or lore to fill a gap; **surface the gap instead**."*

**And the priority order:**

> *"1. direct decisions by Master Roachi; 2. **Terrath canon** for identity, culture, history and other world-fact; 3. the current product document that owns the mechanic or scene; 4. an explicitly approved visual reference or asset; 5. general mood and technique references."*

**So a character's costume comes from `characters.md` and from canon**, and where it is unspecified, **the answer is to raise it.**

**And §2.1 is explicit about what establishes nothing:**

> *"Generated images, old character sheets, filenames, imported assets and text embedded inside an image **establish nothing by themselves**. They may be consulted only as unapproved reference until a specific feature is accepted."*

**Which means: an old character sheet showing Eli in a particular coat is not authority.** **The 2026-09-22 reset put almost all existing art outside the approval boundary**, and §1 lists exactly what survives: **the UI art (minus the inventory window placeholder) and Timon's two body-part references.**

---

**So the practical process for a character's costume:**

| Step | What |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **read `characters.md` for the character** |
