| **The fox** (§6.5) | *"**worry/pacing**, rear, lunge, settle/recover, struck reaction and **flee**"* | **a pace (a walk) and a flee (a run)** |

**Note §6.4's economy:** **the deer needs no walk cycle** because the script repositions it — **which is the contract reducing the count again**, and worth reading as a model: **ask what the scene actually shows.**

---

**The gallop's structure**, which is what a deer's *"depart/run"* and a fox's *"flee"* want:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The two flight phases** | **gathered** (all four legs tucked under) and **extended** (fore legs forward, hind legs back) — **and both are airborne** |
| **Which is the signature** | **a galloping animal is off the ground for roughly half the cycle**, and those two airborne poses are the ones the eye reads |
| **The frame count** | **8 frames is enough for a gallop at this scale; 12 is generous** |
| **And at 8 frames** | **contact (hind), contact (other hind), gathered flight, contact (fore), contact (other fore), extended flight** — with the flights getting two frames each |

**And the extended pose is the money shot:** **front legs reaching forward, hind legs reaching back, body stretched.** **At 32 px long that pose is 40 px long**, which is a visible stretch — **squash and stretch, in the one place it survives.**

---

**The scamper**, which is Pip's and is different:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **a bounding gait** — the hind legs push together and the fore legs land together. **A rabbit's gait, and a happy dog's** |
| **Why it reads differently** | **two beats rather than four**, with large vertical movement |
| **The frames** | **6 to 8** — **gathered, airborne, fore contact, compressed, push, airborne** |
| **And the vertical** | **4 to 6 px on a 25 px dog**, which is a quarter of its height. **A scamper bounces** |
| **Which is the characterisation** | **§6.2's word is *"run/scamper"*, and a scamper is a characterful run.** A sheepdog working is purposeful; a sheepdog scampering is pleased |

---

**And the general economy for creature animation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A walk is 12 frames and four footfalls** | the most frames |
| **A run or gallop is 8** | **fewer frames, because it is faster.** §5.4's *"Smoothness never overrides responsiveness"* |
| **A scamper is 6 to 8** | |
| **And the directions** | **§6.3's sheep needs *"any direction reachable by their movement"* — eight, or five with an explicit mirroring approval** |
| **So one sheep walk** | **8 directions × 12 frames = 96 frames**, or **5 × 12 = 60 with mirroring** |

**Practice.** Draw an 8-frame deer gallop with two airborne poses — gathered and extended — and measure the body's length in each. Then draw a 6-frame Pip scamper with 5 px of vertical bounce. Then list §6's four animals and write the frame and direction count for each of their required gaits, and total it.
Pip, the sheep, the deer and the fox:
The Prologue's four animals, their complete requirement lists, and the frame count that follows.

**Taking §6.2 to §6.5 literally, because they are the specification.**

---

**Pip — §6.2:**

> *"Pip needs **curled sleep, idle, walk, run/scamper, nose-down sniff, bark, dig, three-bite chain and dodge**. **Dodge is a distinct action from pounce. Pounce is an Act I requirement rather than a Prologue requirement.**"*

| Animation | Loop? | Directions | Frames |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`sleep`** | **loop** | **1** (curled, and the script places him) | 4–8 |
| **`idle`** | **loop** | **8** | 24 |
| **`walk`** | **loop** | **8** | 12 |
| **`scamper`** | **loop** | **8** | 6–8 |
| **`_sniff`** | one-shot | **8**, probably | 6–8 |
| **`_bark`** | one-shot | **8** | 4–6 |
| **`_dig`** | **loop** — digging continues | **1 or 8** | 6–8 |
| **`_bite_1/2/3`** | one-shot ×3 | **8** | 4–6 each |
| **`_dodge`** | one-shot | **8** | 4–6 |

**And §6.2's two sentences about pounce are doing work:** **dodge and pounce are different actions, and pounce is deferred.** **So nine animation families now, not ten.**

---

**The sheep — §6.3:**

> *"The living sheep need **idle/graze and directional walking** because gathered sheep follow Eli and **may face any direction reachable by their movement**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Two families only** | **the shortest list of the four** |
| **`graze`** | **loop, and probably 1 direction or a few** — a grazing sheep's head is down and its direction matters less |
| **`walk`** | **loop, 8 directions** — *"any direction reachable by their movement"* |
| **And the mirroring candidate** | **stage 9's: symmetrical, no costume, no handedness.** **5 directions with an explicit approval saves 36 frames** |
| **And the quantity** | **a flock.** One sheep's animations serve all of them, **but the game needs many sheep on screen at once**, which is a §2 crowd-readability problem |

---

**The deer — §6.4:**

> *"The Prologue deer needs **graze, notice, alert/watch and depart/run**. It is **repositioned between authored sightings** and therefore **does not require an ordinary walk cycle** for the Prologue. **Its final departure can face any direction and must support all eight.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Four families, and the economy is explicit** | **no walk cycle** |
| **`graze`** | loop, **1 or few directions** |
| **`_notice`** | **one-shot** — the head comes up. **A beautiful small animation and probably 1 direction, since the script places it** |
| **`alert`** | **loop** — the held watching state |
| **`run`** | **loop, 8 directions** — *"must support all eight"* |
| **So** | **three animations at one or few directions, and one at eight** |

---

**The fox — §6.5:**

> *"The fox needs **worry/pacing, rear as a clear dodge telegraph, lunge, settle/recover, struck reaction and flee**. The lunge currently lasts **0.22 seconds** and the rear **0.62 seconds**; **art must be authored against the gameplay timing rather than redefining it.**"*

| Animation | Loop? | Frames |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`pace`** | **loop** | 12 — a walk |
| **`_rear`** | one-shot | **7** at 84 ms — the 0.62 s telegraph |
| **`_lunge`** | one-shot | **3** at 73 ms — the 0.22 s active phase |
| **`_settle`** | one-shot | 4–6 — the recovery |
| **`_struck`** | one-shot | 3–4 |
| **`_flee`** | **loop** | 8 — a gallop |

**Six families, with two exact timings given — and the fox is 18 px at the shoulder.** **The hardest animation problem in the Prologue**, as stage 9 said.

---

**The total, roughly:**

| Animal | Families | Frames, at eight directions where needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Pip** | **9** | **roughly 400** |
| **The sheep** | **2** | **roughly 110**, or 70 with mirroring |
| **The deer** | **4** | **roughly 90** |
| **The fox** | **6** | **roughly 130** |
| **Total** | **21 families** | **roughly 700 frames** |

**And that is the animals alone, before Eli's fifteen families and the named residents' idles.** **Which is why §10.2's derivation rule and §6's per-animal economies are the most valuable clauses in the contract.**

**Practice.** Write out the full table above with your own direction and frame estimates, and total it. Then pick the sheep — the shortest list — and draw its graze loop. Then pick the deer's `_notice` and draw it as a one-shot in one direction. Then decide which of the twenty-one families you would draw first and why.
Beacon, and animating an object:
§6.6's requirement in full, what makes an object's animation different from a creature's, and the state progression.

**§6.6:**

> *"Beacon needs **inert, awakening and awake** states. **Awakening includes trembling, seams, rings rotating into alignment, rising, flash and settlement.** Awake Beacon uses **light and a subtle bob**. **Beacon is spherical and does not require character-style directional facings.** Array begins in Act I."*

---

**What makes it different from a creature:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **No directions** | **spherical** — one drawing serves every facing. **A saving of eight to one** |
| **No ground contact in the usual sense** | **it rises**, so **the contact shadow is its own animation** — stage 4's jumping-character case |
| **No anatomy** | **so the animation is entirely about the object's own mechanics** — seams, rings, light |
| **And it is a light source** | **stage 6's fire lesson: an emitter has no shadow side, and the light it casts is `Light2D`'s** |

---

**The three states, and the progression:**

| State | What it is | Loop? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **`inert`** | **a dark sphere.** From stage 5's accents lesson: **no Beacon cyan at all, or only `TERR-105` Beacon Deep** | **loop, or a single frame.** An inert object may not move at all |
| **`_awakening`** | **the sequence** — six named beats | **one-shot** |
| **`awake`** | ***"light and a subtle bob"*** | **loop** |

**And the awakening's six beats, which §6.6 lists in order:**

| | Beat | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **trembling** | **1 px of jitter, 2–4 frames.** Random-looking, not periodic |
| **2** | **seams** | **lines appear on the sphere** — `TERR-106` then `107`, 3–4 frames |
| **3** | **rings rotating into alignment** | **the hardest.** Bands of the sphere rotating — **and rotation on a sphere at this scale is a sequence of hand-drawn positions, not a transform** |
| **4** | **rising** | **the sphere leaves the ground** — and **the contact shadow shrinks and stays put** |
| **5** | **flash** | **1–2 frames of `TERR-108` Beacon Light, or `TERR-104` Sacred White at the core** if the moment is sacred |
| **6** | **settlement** | **the sphere settles into its awake position**, 3–4 frames |

**Six beats, perhaps 20 to 30 frames total**, and **it is a one-shot** — so the tag is **`_awakening`**.

---

**The rings, which deserve a note because they are genuinely hard:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **a band rotating around a sphere, seen at 16 to 24 px** |
| **Why it is hard** | **the band's apparent width changes as it rotates** — widest when face-on, a line when edge-on — **and it is occluded by the sphere for half its travel** |
| **How to do it** | **draw the positions, not the rotation.** Six or eight hand-drawn positions of the band, cycling |
| **And the simplification** | **at this scale a ring can be three pixels wide and its rotation read from its vertical position and curvature alone** |
| **And "rotating into alignment"** | **means the rings stop.** So the cycle decelerates — the easing lesson's **3, 2, 1, 1** deceleration |

---

**The awake state's "subtle bob":**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **How much** | **1 to 2 px, over 12 to 24 frames.** Slow and small |
| **And the shadow** | **stays on the ground and changes size with the bob** — **1 px of shadow width change** |
| **And the light** | **`Light2D`, pulsing slightly** — which is the engine's, and **a drawn pulse plus an engine pulse would double it** |
| **Which is the division of labour** | stage 6's: **you draw the emitter, the engine casts the light** |

---

**And the general lesson for any object animation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **An object's animation is about its mechanism** | **hinges, rings, seams, levers, flames** — not about anatomy |
| **So the beats come from the mechanism's description** | **and §6.6 gives six, in order, which is a complete storyboard** |
| **And §9.3's rule applies** | *"Interactive and destructible objects define their required states before drawing"* — **three states, defined** |

**Practice.** Draw Beacon's three states as still frames: inert (dark, `TERR-105`), awake (`TERR-107` with a `108` core), and the flash. Then animate the trembling as 4 frames of 1 px jitter. Then draw six positions of a rotating ring and cycle them, decelerating to a stop. Then animate the awake bob at 1 px over 24 frames with the shadow changing width.
The animation checklist:
The stage's conclusion: eighteen checks, the four numbers, and what carries into the pipeline.

**Before animating:**

| | Check |
| --- | --- |
| **1** | **the standing figure is finished and passes stage 9's checks** |
| **2** | **the gameplay timing is known**, from `systems.md`, §6 or the code |
| **3** | **the frame count follows from the timing** — and the frame duration is chosen |
| **4** | **the tag name is decided, with the `_` prefix if it is a one-shot** |

**While animating:**

| | Check |
| --- | --- |
| **5** | **the key poses are drawn first, and each passes the black test** |
| **6** | **3–5 keys for an idle; a key per phase for an action** |
| **7** | **anticipation gets the most frames; the active phase the fewest** |
| **8** | **holds are placed on the contacts and the extremes** |
| **9** | **the planted foot is copied between frames, not redrawn** |
| **10** | **the figure's pivot column does not drift** |
| **11** | **no bounding box is normalised** — §4 |
| **12** | **the light stays at the upper-left in every frame** |

**The numbers:**

| | Check |
| --- | --- |
| **13** | **every frame is 84 ms** — or the action's own duration, deliberately |
| **14** | **24 frames for an idle, 12 for movement**; anything else authored to its timing |
| **15** | **the heights match the reference's pattern** — 81/84/87 for an idle, 72–81 for a run |
| **16** | **the loop's discontinuity is deliberate** — the 3 px drop |

**At the end:**

| | Check |
| --- | --- |
| **17** | **played in Aseprite's preview at 100% and at 300%** |
| **18** | **and in Godot: at native scale, in motion, against the real ground, under representative lighting** — §5.3's four conditions, of which **Aseprite can only give you two** |

---

**The four numbers to carry:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **84 ms** | **not 83** |
| **24 frames** | the idle, with motion in 1–10 and a hold to 24 |
| **12 frames** | movement, with about four two-frame holds |
| **8 directions** | authored, no mirroring |

---

**And the stage's thesis:**

> **At twelve frames a second and eighty pixels, animation is strong poses, uneven timing and deliberate stillness. Draw the keys, hold them, and let the discontinuities do the work.**

**Everything here follows from that.** Pose-to-pose, because keys are testable and inbetweens are not. The 14-frame hold, because stillness reads as breath and motion reads as fidgeting. The two-frame holds on the contacts, because uneven timing is weight. The 3 px loop drop, because a loop with no event in it reads as a machine. **Anticipation over the active phase, because readability is in the wind-up.** **And "smoothness never overrides responsiveness", which is the contract saying the same thing.**

---

**What carries into stage 12.** The pipeline stage takes everything this stage produced and gets it into the game:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The tag and the prefix** | §3.1 and §5.3 |
| **The 84 ms arithmetic, and the relative durations that carry the holds** | the addon's source |
| **The split-layer importer**, for the waist split and the four layers | |
| **The direction and mirror fallback** in `authored_sprite_body.gd` | |
| **And the validator** | **which can check the durations, the tag, the canvas and the palette mechanically** — which is the only way 700 frames of animal animation stays correct |

**Practice.** Write the eighteen checks on one page beside stages 4, 5, 7 and 9's. Then take one finished animation and run all eighteen. Then write the four numbers on a sticky note. Then animate one new thing — the deer's `_notice` is the smallest — running the checks as you go.
UI art is not pixel art:
The stage's opening correction: interface art in this game is painted at high resolution and rasterised at the display's native resolution, which is the opposite of everything in stages 2 to 10.

**The three statements that establish it:**

> **§3:** *"HUD and other UI artwork uses **transparent PNG** where practical and **does not inherit sprite canvas, pivot or animation rules**."*
>
> **`hud.md` §2:** *"**Interface layers are lifted into the window and rasterised at native display resolution.** They retain the same 960 × 540 layout coordinates through the interface-layer transform, so gameplay measurements remain stable while **text, borders, paintings and vector-like drawing remain sharp**."*
>
> **`menu-runtime-contract.md` §9:** *"**Final UI art comes from Timon and remains `.png`, outside the sprite pipeline.**"*

---

**So the two halves of the game are rendered completely differently:**

| | The world | The interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Resolution** | **960 × 540, enlarged by an integer factor with nearest filtering** | **rasterised at the display's native resolution** |
| **So one art pixel is** | **2 × 2 at 1080p, 4 × 4 at 2160p** | **one screen pixel** |
| **The medium** | **pixel art — 4 values per material, no anti-aliasing, 132-colour palette** | **painting — any resolution, anti-aliased, smooth gradients, any colour** |
| **The format** | **`.aseprite`** | **`.png`** |
| **The pipeline** | **Aseprite Wizard** | **Godot's own texture import** |
| **The rules** | **§4's canvas, §5's animation, §10.1's grammar** | ***"does not inherit sprite canvas, pivot or animation rules"*** |

**And `hud.md` adds the handling:** *"**Large painted UI textures are downsampled with a high-quality filter to approximately the pixels they occupy and cached; they are never enlarged past their useful source resolution.**"*

**So UI art is drawn LARGE and scaled DOWN** — the exact inverse of the sprite rule that forbids *"resized or filtered source art"*.

---

**Which means this stage asks you to put almost everything down.** The rules that do **not** apply to UI art:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The 112 × 112 canvas and the (56, 96) pivot** | §3, explicitly |
| **Four values per material** | it is a painting |
| **No anti-aliasing** | **anti-aliasing is the point** — *"text, borders, paintings and vector-like drawing remain sharp"* |
| **No smooth gradients** | permitted |
| **The 132-colour palette** | **partly** — the violet rule is exempted for UI (`colour-palette.md`, 2026-09-15), and the party accents are exempt entirely |
| **12 fps animation** | UI animation is Godot's tweens and `AnimationPlayer` |
| **Aseprite** | **not the tool.** A painting program is |

**And what still applies:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **§8's legibility requirement** | *"at the locked viewport and at 1080p, 1440p and 2160p"* |
| **§10's definition of done** | all eight conditions |
| **`hud.md` §11's eight verification items** | including *"no telegraph depends on hue alone"* |
| **The world's visual identity** | §2's *"warm, earthy, weathered"*, and `cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md`'s locked principle: *"The game uses multiple visual languages by design. Their unity comes from assigning each one a clear narrative role and grounding all of them in the same canonical world and character designs"* |

---

**And the authorship fact that governs the whole stage.** `menu-runtime-contract.md` §9: ***"Final UI art comes from Timon."***

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So the UI art is Timon's work**, not Master Roachi's | |
| **Which is consistent with** | **§2's *"Master Roachi is final visual and animation authority"*** for approval, and **Timon's final say on design** |
| **And the approved family proves it** | **`timon-frame-v3.png`** — the frame is named after its author |
| **What that means for this stage** | **it teaches how to read, validate and work with the UI art contract rather than how to paint it** — because the painting is somebody else's |

**Practice.** Read §3's UI sentence, `hud.md` §2 and `menu-runtime-contract.md` §9. Then open `media/ui/hud/timon-frame-v3.png` and note its pixel dimensions — then compare them with 960 × 540. Then list every rule from stages 2 to 10 that does not apply to it.
The rendering split:
`hud.md` §2 in detail: the two render paths, the coordinate system that bridges them, and why a HUD review needs the shell.

**The architecture, quoted:**

> *"The world renders into a **960 × 540 `SubViewport`** and is enlarged by an **integer factor with nearest filtering**. Interface layers are **lifted into the window** and rasterised at **native display resolution**. They retain the same **960 × 540 layout coordinates** through the interface-layer transform, so **gameplay measurements remain stable** while text, borders, paintings and vector-like drawing remain sharp."*

---

**The three layers, bottom to top:**

| Layer | Rendered how |
| --- | --- |
| **The world** | **960 × 540 `SubViewport`, integer-scaled, nearest filtering** |
| **The world vignette** | **an interface layer over the world and below the HUD.** *"It follows the leader's drawn position and `WorldClock.darkness()`, remaining subtle by day and readable at night. It never changes world time or replaces gameplay lighting"* |
| **The HUD** | **an interface layer, native resolution** |

**And the owner:** ***"`PresentationShell` owns this split. It sets the window font oversampling to the interface scale while leaving the world viewport pixel-scaled."***

---

**Why the 960 × 540 coordinate system is retained for the interface**, which is the clever part:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem it solves** | **if the HUD were laid out in display pixels, every layout number would change with the resolution** |
| **The solution** | **the HUD is laid out in 960 × 540 units and the transform scales it** |
| **So** | **a HUD element at (480, 520) is at the bottom centre at every resolution** |
| **And `hud.md` §3 uses those units** | *"Its central plate occupies approximately **52% of the 960-unit frame width**"* |
| **Which means** | **the layout is resolution-independent and the rasterisation is resolution-native.** Both at once |

---

**The consequence for the art, and it is the practical point:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A HUD element occupying 100 × 40 layout units** | occupies **200 × 80 display pixels at 1080p** and **400 × 160 at 2160p** |
| **So the source art must be large enough for 2160p** | **at least 400 × 160, and more if there is headroom** |
| **And `hud.md`'s rule** | *"Large painted UI textures are **downsampled** with a high-quality filter to approximately the pixels they occupy and cached; **they are never enlarged past their useful source resolution**"* |
| **Which gives the authoring rule** | **paint UI art at 4× the layout size or more, and never at 1×** |
| **And the cache** | **the downsample is cached, so the cost is paid once** |

---

**Input, which the art has to agree with:**

> *"Input mapping must account for the world viewport, interface transform and window letterboxing. **A click target is measured in the same HUD coordinate system as the art it belongs to.**"*

**And §3's specific instance:** *"Hit testing uses **the painted circle, not its rectangular bounds**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So a painted round button** | **has a round hit area**, defined in layout units |
| **Which means the art and the hit area are two expressions of one shape** | and **if the art moves, the hit area moves** |
| **And a decorative ornament** | **§3: *"decorative ornaments may extend beyond the plate without changing the functional layout"*** — **so decoration and function are separable, deliberately** |

---

**And the review rule, which is the stage's single most quotable line:**

> *"**Running a world scene without the shell is not a valid presentation-quality HUD review.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it forbids** | **judging HUD art in Aseprite, in a paint program, or in a bare Godot scene** |
| **Why** | **because the downsample, the font oversampling, the interface transform and the letterboxing all happen in the shell** — so **without it you are looking at art that is not being rendered the way the game renders it** |
| **Which is the UI equivalent of §5.3's four conditions** | and **stricter**, because it names the specific thing that must be running |

**Practice.** Find `PresentationShell` in the game's scripts and read what it does. Then work out the display pixel size of a 100 × 40 layout-unit element at 1080p, 1440p and 2160p. Then open `timon-frame-v3.png` and divide its width by 960 to find its source scale factor. Then run the game through the shell and look at the HUD, and then look at the same PNG in a viewer, and note the difference.

The main frame as a specification:
`hud.md` §3 read as the detailed brief it is: layout, function, hit testing, and the eight candles.

**The whole of §3, unpacked — because it is the most specified piece of art in the project.**

---

**The geometry:**

> *"The approved bottom frame is `media/ui/hud/timon-frame-v3.png`. Its **central plate occupies approximately 52% of the 960-unit frame width** and is **centred on the bottom edge**; **decorative ornaments may extend beyond the plate without changing the functional layout**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **52% of 960** | **about 499 layout units of central plate** |
| **Centred on the bottom edge** | so the plate spans roughly **x = 230 to 730** |
| **And the ornaments extend beyond** | **without being functional** — which is the separation of decoration from layout |

---

**The functional slots:**

| Slot | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **Six numbered plaques** | **the equipped active skills** |
| **The slot above them** | **Unity** |
| **The slot below them** | **experience** |
| **The left round button** | **opens the paused menu on Journal** |
| **The right round button** | **opens it on Map** |

**And the two main orbs, from §4:** *"Leader identity and exact leader values sit with **the two main orbs** rather than in a party frame."*

---

**The interaction rules, which the art has to support:**

> *"Button clicks work **only while the world belongs to the player, the frame is shown and the HUD is not faded**. **Hit testing uses the painted circle, not its rectangular bounds.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The three conditions on a click** | **runtime logic, not art** |
| **But the hit testing clause is art** | **the button's painted circle is its hit area** |
| **Which means** | **the painted circle's centre and radius, in layout units, are facts the code needs** |
| **And if the art is revised** | **those numbers change, and the code has to be updated with it** |
| **So a frame revision is a code change** | which is why **`timon-frame-v3` rather than a silently updated `timon-frame.png`** |

---

**The eight candles, which are the most unusual thing in the whole project:**

> *"The frame's **eight painted candles** are lit by **one shared transparent 3D viewport**. Each flame **aligns to its wick**, sits over the frame, **fades with the HUD**, and **leans opposite the leader's acceleration and movement**. **This isolated effect does not establish a 3D art pipeline for the game world.**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Eight painted candles in the frame art** | **so the wicks' positions are facts in the PNG** |
| **One shared transparent 3D viewport** | **a single 3D scene rendering eight flames**, composited over the frame |
| **Each flame aligns to its wick** | **so the flame positions are derived from the art** |
| **And they lean opposite the leader's acceleration** | **which means the HUD responds to the player's movement** — a lovely detail, and a real constraint on the art, because **the wicks must be positioned so a leaning flame does not collide with the frame's ornament** |
| **And the final sentence is a scoping fence** | *"does not establish a 3D art pipeline for the game world"* — **the same kind of clause as the violet rule's exemptions** |

---

**What all of this teaches about reading a UI brief:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — The layout numbers are in layout units**, not pixels — 52% of 960 | |
| **2 — The functional slots are a list**, and the art must accommodate each | |
| **3 — The hit areas are derived from the painted shapes**, so the art defines them | |
| **4 — The dynamic elements (the flames) take their positions from the static art** | |
| **5 — And the version number in the filename is a contract boundary** | |

**Practice.** Open `timon-frame-v3.png` and measure its central plate as a fraction of its width — check it against 52%. Then find the two round buttons and estimate their centres and radii in layout units. Then find the eight candle wicks and note their positions. Then read §4 on the leader orbs and §5 on the dash charges and see how they relate to the frame.
Nine-slice and scalable borders:
§8's "scalable borders" requirement, Aseprite's Slices as the authoring tool, and Godot's two consumers.

**§8's requirement:**

> *"UI art must remain legible at the locked viewport and at 1080p, 1440p and 2160p presentation. **Text contrast, scalable borders, safe areas** and controller/mouse interaction are validated in-engine."*

**"Scalable borders" is the nine-slice technique**, and stage 1's Slices lesson is its authoring half.

---

**The technique, recalled from stage 1:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The inner rectangle divides the image into nine regions** | |
| **The four corners never stretch** | |
| **The top and bottom edges stretch horizontally only** | |
| **The left and right edges stretch vertically only** | |
| **The centre stretches both ways, or tiles** | |
| **So one small ornate frame draws a panel of any size with its corners intact** | |

---

**Godot's two consumers**, and the choice matters:

| | `NinePatchRect` | `StyleBoxTexture` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What it is** | **a Control node** that draws one nine-patched texture | **a resource** assigned to a Control's theme |
| **Where the margins live** | **`patch_margin_left/top/right/bottom`** on the node | **`texture_margin_*`** on the resource |
| **Use it for** | **a specific panel** placed in a scene | **every panel of a type** — a theme's `Panel`, `Button`, `PopupPanel` |
| **And the axis stretch mode** | **both have `axis_stretch_horizontal/vertical`** — Stretch, Tile, or Tile Fit | |

**For the Shepherds interface the likely answer is `StyleBoxTexture` in a theme**, because `menu-runtime-contract.md` §1 describes **one shared menu shell with eight tabs** — and a theme applies one border treatment to all of them.

---

**The authoring workflow, end to end:**

| Step | Where |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — Paint the border** at 4× the layout size or more | **a paint program**, because it is UI art |
| **2 — Decide the four margins** | **the non-stretching corner size** |
| **3 — Record them** | **in the brief, or in the PNG's own filename, or in a sidecar note** |
| **4 — Set them in Godot** | `patch_margin_*` or `texture_margin_*` |
| **5 — Test at every size the panel will be** | **and §8's four resolutions** |

**And the role Aseprite's Slices plays**, which is narrower than stage 1 implied:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **If the art were pixel art in Aseprite** | **a Slice with a 9-slice centre is the natural way to record the margins** — and the exported JSON carries them |
| **But UI art is painted elsewhere** | so **the Slice route applies to any pixel-art UI element that does come from Aseprite** |
| **Which there may be** | **map markers, inventory slot art, small icons** — §8's list includes *"map markers and inventory-slot art"*, and those are small enough to be pixel art |
| **So** | **the technique is the same and the tool depends on the element** |

---

**The three sizes a border must survive:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its minimum** | **twice the margin plus one pixel.** A border with 8-unit margins cannot draw a panel narrower than 17 units |
| **Its design size** | the size it was painted for |
| **Its maximum** | **and this is where it fails** — a border stretched to four times its design width has a centre region stretched 4×, **and if the centre has any detail, that detail smears** |
| **The fix** | **a plain or tiling centre.** A nine-slice's centre should be flat, a subtle texture, or set to Tile |

**Practice.** Take `dialogue-text-box.png` and work out what its four nine-slice margins would be. Then set it up as a `NinePatchRect` in Godot and resize it from its minimum to four times its width, and watch where it breaks. Then set the centre's axis stretch to Tile and compare. Then do the same as a `StyleBoxTexture` in a theme.
Painted openings and hit targets:
`hud.md` §11's first and fourth verification items: the art defines where the controls are, and both have to agree.

**Two of §11's eight items at every target resolution:**

> *"1. **all painted openings still expose the intended fill or control**;"*
> *"4. **mouse and controller focus/click targets match what is painted**;"*

**And §3's instance:** *"Hit testing uses **the painted circle, not its rectangular bounds**."*

---

**What a "painted opening" is:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A hole in the HUD art** through which something else shows | |
| **Examples from §3 and §4** | **the six skill plaques** (which show skill icons); **the Unity slot**; **the experience slot**; **the two leader orbs**; **the dash charges** |
| **Why it matters** | **the art is a frame around content, and the content is drawn by code** |
| **So the opening's position and size, in layout units, are shared facts** | |

**And the failure §11's item 1 guards against:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The art is revised** and an opening moves by three units | |
| **The code is not updated** | |
| **So the fill is drawn three units off** — **a resource bar that does not fill its painted opening, or a skill icon overlapping its plaque's border** | |
| **And at 1080p that is six screen pixels**, which is visible | |

---

**The three kinds of agreement the art and the code need:**

| | Kind | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **a fill region** — code draws a bar or a texture inside a painted frame | **the resource orbs, the experience slot** |
| **2** | **an anchor point** — code positions something relative to the art | **the eight candle wicks; the party frames' accent rims** |
| **3** | **a hit area** — code tests input against a painted shape | **the two round buttons, with the circle not the rectangle** |

**And all three are numbers that live in two places at once.** Which means:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A UI art revision is a coordinated change** | the art, and whatever code holds the numbers |
| **Which is why the filename carries a version** | `timon-frame-v3` — **so a revision is explicit** |
| **And the practical artefact** | **a note recording each opening's position and size in layout units, beside the art** |

---

**The round-button case worked properly**, because it is the clearest:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The art** | **a painted circular button, with ornament around it** |
| **Its rectangular bounds** | **include the ornament and the corners outside the circle** |
| **The hit test** | **the circle only** — *"Hit testing uses the painted circle, not its rectangular bounds"* |
| **So the code needs** | **a centre and a radius in layout units** |
| **And the art must make the circle unambiguous** | **a clearly painted circular edge, with the ornament visibly outside it** — so that **where the player thinks they can click is where they can** |
| **Which is a design requirement on the painting** | **not just a code requirement** |

---

**And §11's remaining six items**, because they are the UI stage's checklist:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **2** | *"text is rasterised sharply and meets contrast needs"* |
| **3** | *"world-to-interface anchors remain on their actors"* — **the enemy health bars and damage numbers that follow world objects** |
| **5** | *"minimap and world input map to the correct coordinates"* |
| **6** | *"**no telegraph depends on hue alone**"* — **§5.3's clause, restated as a HUD verification item** |
| **7** | *"the leader and every companion state remain understandable during combat"* |
| **8** | *"orb and candle subviewports remain inside the frame budget"* — **a performance item, and a reason not to add more subviewports** |

**Practice.** Open `timon-frame-v3.png` and identify every painted opening, writing down its position and size as a fraction of the image. Then convert those to layout units. Then find the two round buttons and estimate their centres and radii. Then read §11's eight items and mark which are art decisions, which are code, and which are both.
Legibility at four resolutions:
§8's four targets, what changes between them, and the five things to check at each.

**§8:**

> *"UI art must remain legible at **the locked viewport** and at **1080p, 1440p and 2160p** presentation."*

**Four targets, and the first is not a display resolution — it is the 960 × 540 layout space.**

---

**What each target is, and what happens to the art:**

| Target | The world | The interface |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **The locked viewport — 960 × 540** | **1:1** | **1:1 layout units** |
| **1080p — 1920 × 1080** | **exactly 2× integer, nearest** | **2× rasterisation** |
| **1440p — 2560 × 1440** | **2.67×** — so **2× with letterboxing, or a non-integer scale** | **2.67× rasterisation** |
| **2160p — 3840 × 2160** | **exactly 4×** | **4× rasterisation** |

**And 1440p is the awkward one**, because **the world's integer scaling and the interface's native rasterisation diverge most there**: **the world is scaled 2× and letterboxed while the interface is rasterised at 2.67×.** `hud.md` §2's input note is about exactly this: *"Input mapping must account for the world viewport, interface transform **and window letterboxing**."*

---

**The five things to check at each:**

| | Check | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **the source art is not being enlarged** | `hud.md`: *"never enlarged past their useful source resolution"*. **At 2160p a 100-unit element needs 400 px of source** |
| **2** | **text is sharp and meets contrast** | §11's item 2. **The font oversampling is set by `PresentationShell` to the interface scale** |
| **3** | **painted openings still expose their fill** | §11's item 1 |
| **4** | **hit targets match the painting** | §11's item 4 |
| **5** | **safe areas hold** | §8's word. **Nothing important within a few units of the screen edge** |

---

**And the authoring consequence, which is the one number to take away:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The maximum rasterisation is 4×** (2160p) | |
| **So source art must be at least 4× its layout size** | |
| **And `hud.md` says it is downsampled *"to approximately the pixels they occupy"* and cached** | |
| **Which means** | **painting at 4× is the minimum and painting at 6× or 8× costs only file size and gives headroom** |
| **The practical rule** | **paint at 4× to 8× the layout size, in a paint program, as a transparent PNG** |

---

**The one trap: mixed media in one element.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **a HUD element containing both painted art and pixel art** — a painted frame around a pixel-art icon |
| **What happens** | **the painted part rasterises natively and the pixel-art part is scaled by the same transform** — **so the pixel art is scaled by 2.67× at 1440p, with filtering, and loses its pixels** |
| **The fix** | **keep them in different layers** — the painted frame as an interface layer, the pixel-art icon either rendered in the world viewport or authored at the interface's scale |
| **Or** | **author the icon as painted art too** |
| **And §8's list** | *"map markers and **inventory-slot art**"* — **both are small elements that could be either, and the decision matters** |

**That trap is worth naming because it is invisible at 1080p** (where 2× is an integer and pixel art survives) **and visible at 1440p** (where 2.67× is not).

**Practice.** Run the game at 1080p and at 1440p and compare the HUD's sharpness. Then find a HUD element and measure its source PNG's dimensions against its layout size to find the scale factor. Then check whether any HUD element mixes painted and pixel art. Then read `PresentationShell`'s font oversampling line.
The placeholder, and what to replace it:
§11's first open art item, what the inventory window has to do, and the portrait problem beside it.

**The two items, from §11:**

> *"**Replace the menu-window placeholder** and **code-drawn party portrait silhouettes**."*

**Plus `hud.md` §12's first:** *"**Draw and approve replacement party portraits.**"*

---

**The inventory window.** What is known:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The file** | **`media/ui/menu/inventorywindow.png`** |
| **Its status** | **§1: *"a documented temporary placeholder"*. §8: *"loaded today but is explicitly placeholder art and is not approved"*** |
| **What it is for** | **the Inventory tab of the shared menu shell** — `menu-runtime-contract.md` §1's eight tabs: *"Journal, Party, Codex, Inventory, Stats, Skills, Map, System"* |
| **What it has to do** | **frame the inventory and equipment page** — §2 of the menu contract |

**And what a replacement needs, derived from the menu contract:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Scalability** | **the menu shell is shared across eight tabs**, so **either one window art serves all eight, or each has its own** — and **the first is cheaper and more coherent** |
| **A nine-slice treatment** | because the pages differ in content and may differ in size |
| **Openings for the content** | the slot grid, the equipment slots, the stats columns |
| **A greyed state** | **§1: *"A page unavailable in combat remains visible but greyed and non-interactive"*** — **so the art needs a disabled treatment** |
| **And tab affordances** | since Q/E and LB/RB step between tabs |

**So the honest answer: the inventory window is not one asset — it is the menu shell's frame**, and replacing it well means **designing the shared shell rather than one window.** **Which is a design job and Timon's.**

---

**The portraits, which are a different and larger problem.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What was there** | **generated party portraits** — **removed** under the 2026-09-22 reset |
| **What is there now** | **§8: *"the HUD and menu use a generic code-drawn silhouette until approved portraits replace it"*** |
| **What a portrait is, per `cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md` register 1** | ***"high-resolution pixel portraits** to show facial detail, personality, age, clothing, and emotion beyond what gameplay sprites can carry"* |
| **And §2's permission** | *"**Dialogue portraits and major illustrated scenes may use higher-resolution art than gameplay sprites**, but none is currently approved"* |

**So a portrait is a third medium**, and it has to be reconciled with both others:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Not an 80 px sprite** | **it has facial detail, which stage 9 established a sprite cannot carry** |
| **Not painted UI art either** | **it is *"high-resolution pixel portraits"*** — **pixel art, at a higher resolution** |
| **How much higher** | **undecided.** A 48 × 48 or 64 × 64 portrait has room for a face; a 96 × 96 has room for expression |
| **And the rendering question** | **if it is pixel art and it is in an interface layer, it hits the mixed-media trap from the last lesson** |
| **Which means** | **either portraits are rendered in a pixel-scaled layer, or they are authored at the interface scale** — **and that is a `PresentationShell` question, not an art one** |

---

**And the unity requirement that governs both.** `cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md`'s locked principle:

> *"The game uses **multiple visual languages by design**. Their unity comes from **assigning each one a clear narrative role** and **grounding all of them in the same canonical world and character designs**."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So five visual languages are permitted** | gameplay sprites, painted UI, high-resolution pixel portraits, illustrated tableaux, and fully produced cinematics |
| **And unity comes from two things** | **a clear role for each**, and **the same canonical designs underneath** |
| **Which means** | **a portrait must be recognisably the same character as the 80 px sprite** — **and since the sprite's identity is silhouette, equipment and value structure (stage 9), the portrait must carry those forward** |
| **And the practical test** | **put the portrait and the sprite side by side and ask whether they are the same person** |

**Practice.** Open `inventorywindow.png` and list what it would need to do to serve all eight menu tabs. Then read `menu-runtime-contract.md` §1 and §2 and note every state the art must support. Then read the cinematic document's five registers and write down which medium each uses. Then sketch a portrait size that has room for a face and check it against the mixed-media trap.
Map markers, and icons at small sizes:
The six approved markers, the four-value rule at twelve pixels, and the one §11 item that constrains every icon set.

**What exists.** Under `media/ui/map/`:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **`minimap-border-compass-v2.png`** | **the minimap frame** — and the asset `colour-palette.md` records a change to: *"the minimap's purple banner, is red in Timon's minimap border v2 of 2026-09-16"* |
| **Six NPC markers** | **exclaim and question**, each in **gold, red and silver** |

**And §8 names them in the accepted family:** *"map markers and inventory-slot art used by the runtime."*

---

**The three colours are a set, and the semantics are open.** `hud.md` §12:

> *"**Add explicit offered/accepted quest state** before treating `!` and `?` as final semantics."*
> *"**Wire red secret/puzzle markers** when those systems exist."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **So gold, red and silver are three states** | **and which state each is has not been fixed** |
| **The obvious reading** | **gold = available, silver = seen or completed, red = secret or puzzle** |
| **But the document does not say so** | and **§2.1's rule applies: *"Art must not invent… to fill a gap; surface the gap instead"*** |
| **Which makes this** | **an art asset waiting for a design decision**, and §11's note about it is the surfacing |

---

**And `!` and `?` as glyphs are a borrowed convention**, which is worth naming:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Where it comes from** | **the MMO and action-RPG lineage** — an exclamation mark offers a quest, a question mark completes one |
| **Why it was borrowed** | **because it is legible without explanation** |
| **And the risk** | **§12's note is exactly it** — **the convention implies a meaning the game may not have** |

---

**Now the craft problem: an icon at twelve pixels.**

A map marker on a minimap is small — perhaps 12 to 16 layout units. **Which forces every lesson from stage 5 into its hardest case.**

| Constraint | At 12 px |
| --- | --- |
| **Four values per material (§10.1)** | **a 12 px icon has room for perhaps three** — **and two is often correct** |
| **Silhouette first (stage 5)** | **the silhouette is almost the whole icon** |
| **No anti-aliasing** | **so the only shape control is the pixel placement itself** |
| **Readable at the viewport scale** | **and the marker is also rasterised by the interface transform if it is an interface layer** — which is the mixed-media trap again |

**The two techniques that actually work at that size:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **1 — An outline that separates the icon from any background.** **A dark one-pixel outline is the single most effective device at small sizes**, because the minimap behind the marker is of unknown colour | |
| **2 — One accent value and one dark value, and nothing else.** **A gold marker is two golds and an outline.** Adding a third value at 12 px blurs rather than clarifies | |

---

**And §11's item 6, which governs any icon set:**

> *"**no telegraph depends on hue alone**"*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Applied to the markers** | **gold, red and silver differ in hue — and if they differ in nothing else, the distinction fails for a colour-blind player** |
| **What `colour-palette.md`'s structure gives you** | **each ramp is `Deep → Shadow → Mid → Light`, so the three metals differ in value as well as hue** |
| **But the reliable fix is shape** | **a different glyph, a different outline weight, or a badge** |
| **And the markers already have two glyphs** | `!` and `?` — **so two of the distinctions are shape-based already** |
| **The gap** | **gold vs silver vs red within one glyph** — **three hues, one shape** |

**Practice.** Open the six markers in `media/ui/map/` and note their dimensions and how many values each uses. Then convert each to greyscale and check whether the three colours are still distinguishable. Then draw a 12 × 12 marker of your own in two values plus an outline, place it over three different backgrounds, and check it reads on all three.
The eight open HUD items:
`hud.md` §12 in full: what the HUD does not have yet, and what each missing piece asks of the art.

**The list, quoted:**

> *"1. Draw and approve **replacement party portraits**.
> 2. Add a visible **spent dodge-charge state** rather than only reordering.
> 3. Replace the **provisional level `1`** with the real progression value.
> 4. Add **quick-use item art** and wire its cooldown display.
> 5. Add explicit **offered/accepted quest state** before treating `!` and `?` as final semantics.
> 6. Wire **red secret/puzzle markers** when those systems exist.
> 7. Add **periodic damage numbers** for continuing effects.
> 8. **Manually review every orb mode**, including the restricted state."*

---

**Which of them are art, which are code, and which are both:**

| | Item | Art | Code |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **party portraits** | **the whole job** — and a medium decision | the display |
| **2** | **spent dodge charge** | **a drawn empty state for the charge** | the state tracking |
| **3** | **real level value** | **none** | **all of it** |
| **4** | **quick-use item art** | **an icon set, plus a cooldown treatment** | the cooldown |
| **5** | **offered/accepted quest state** | **possibly a fourth marker variant** | **the design decision first** |
| **6** | **red secret markers** | **the art exists** | the systems do not |
| **7** | **periodic damage numbers** | **a font treatment, and §11's item 3 anchoring** | the timing |
| **8** | **every orb mode reviewed** | **the review** | the modes |

---

**Two of them are worth reading closely.**

**Item 2 — the spent dodge charge:** *"Add a visible spent dodge-charge state rather than only reordering."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What happens now** | **the charges reorder** — so a spent charge is communicated by position |
| **Why that fails** | **the player cannot see how many are spent, only where they are** |
| **The art answer** | **a drawn empty state** — a dimmed, hollowed or desaturated charge in the same position |
| **Which is the UI form of §5.3's telegraph rule** | **a state must be visible in itself, not only by comparison** |

**Item 8 — manual review of every orb mode:** *"including the restricted state."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it reveals** | **the orbs have modes**, one of which is "restricted" |
| **And §4 says** | *"Leader identity and exact leader values sit with the two main orbs"* |
| **So the orbs are the HUD's most state-heavy element** | and **a manual review at every resolution is the only way to validate them** |
| **Which is §2's line again** | *"Running a world scene without the shell is not a valid presentation-quality HUD review"* |

---

**And the pattern across all eight, which is the lesson:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Every item is specific enough to act on** | a named asset, a named state, a named wiring |
| **Several are blocked on a design decision rather than on art** | items 5 and 6 |
| **One is blocked on nothing but work** | item 1 |
| **And one is not a change at all** | item 8 — **a review** |
| **Which is what an honest open-work list looks like** | **and §11's art list and §12's HUD list are the two halves of the same practice** |

**Practice.** Read §12's eight items and §11's art list and mark the overlaps. Then run the game and look for the dodge charges — check whether a spent charge is visibly distinguishable. Then find the level display and confirm it reads `1`. Then list what you would have to draw to close items 2, 4 and 7.
The five visual registers:
`cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md`: five visual languages, one locked principle, and where pixel art stops.

**The locked principle, which is the document's thesis:**

> *"The game uses **multiple visual languages by design**. Their unity comes from **assigning each one a clear narrative role** and **grounding all of them in the same canonical world and character designs**."*

---

**The five registers:**

| | Register | Medium | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **normal dialogue** | **high-resolution pixel portraits** | **ordinary conversation** — *"facial detail, personality, age, clothing, and emotion beyond what gameplay sprites can carry"* |
| **2** | **important staged conversations** | **in-engine cinematics** — the gameplay sprites, posed and framed | **scenes that matter and happen in the world** |
| **3** | **heightened sequences** | **illustrated graphic-novel tableaux** | **moments that need more than the engine can stage** |
| **4** | **act transitions** | **fully produced cinematics** — *"may move beyond pixel art"* | **between acts** |
| **5** | **Shepherd and metaphysical events** | **the sacred register** — white and violet | **Shepherd Light, visions, the metaphysical** |

**Plus one more, which is a UI language rather than a scene register:** **Beacon's technological interface** — a distinct visual vocabulary for the one character whose presence is technological.

---

**Why five rather than one**, and this is the part that generalises:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **One medium for everything means the weakest moment sets the ceiling** | **a game that only has 80 px sprites can only stage what 80 px sprites can carry** |
| **Five media means each moment uses what suits it** | **and the cost is coherence** |
| **Which the locked principle addresses directly** | **a clear narrative role for each**, so **the player learns what each medium means** |
| **And the second half is the real safeguard** | ***"grounding all of them in the same canonical world and character designs"*** |

**So the unity is not stylistic — it is in the designs underneath.** A character is the same character in all five registers, and **stage 9 said what a character's identity consists of at 80 px: silhouette, equipment and value structure.** Those three must survive into a portrait, a tableau and a cinematic.

---

**What this means for the pixel-art craft the rest of the curriculum teaches:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Registers 1 and 2 are pixel art** | **one at higher resolution, one at gameplay resolution** |
| **Register 3 is illustration** | **not pixel art, and not Aseprite's job** |
| **Register 4 explicitly may leave pixel art** | ***"may move beyond pixel art"*** |
| **Register 5 is a colour language rather than a medium** | **and applies across the others** |
| **So Aseprite's domain is registers 1, 2 and 5's pixel-art instances** | **and the painted UI is a sixth thing outside this list entirely** |

---

**And the production proof-of-concept**, which is how the document avoids being theory:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The Eli test scene** | **one scene built to prove the cinematic register works before committing to it** |
| **Which is §10.2's asset planning rule in another form** | **prove the pipeline on one asset, then scale** |
| **And the same move as the body bases** | **two approved references before any character animation** |
| **The pattern** | **one proof, validated, then production** — **and it recurs in every part of this project** |

**Practice.** Read `cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md` in full and write down each register's narrative role in one sentence. Then take one character and list what their silhouette, equipment and value structure are at 80 px, and what each would become in a portrait. Then find the Eli test scene in the repository and see what it proves.
The sacred and the dissonant:
The one colour language in the project that is a narrative mechanic: violet with a white core, and violet without one.

**From `cinematic-and-dialogue-visual-system.md`'s fifth register:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The sacred register** | **violet `TERR-117` to `TERR-120`, with a core of Sacred White / Grace Ivory `TERR-101` to `TERR-104`** |
| **The dissonant register** | **the same violet family — and it *"never carries a white core"*** |

**Two registers, one hue, and the distinction is the white core.**

---

**Why that is a good design**, and it is worth dwelling on:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The hue is shared** | **so both read as the same order of phenomenon** — metaphysical, not mundane |
| **The core distinguishes them** | **sacred has a white heart; dissonant is violet all the way down** |
| **So the player learns one rule** | **look for the white** |
| **And it satisfies §11's item 6** | ***"no telegraph depends on hue alone"*** — **the distinction is a value structure, not a hue** |
| **Which is the same solution stage 5 taught for materials** | **value carries the information; hue carries the identity** |

---

**And it explains `colour-palette.md`'s violet rule**, which stage 3 introduced:

> *"Violet may be used **only** for Shepherd, sacred, or deliberately dissonant content. **Three exemptions** are recorded: lavender flora, Nix Green, and UI."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Why violet is reserved** | **because it is a narrative signal, and a signal that appears decoratively stops signalling** |
| **So violet in the world means something** | **and violet in the UI is exempted because the UI is not the world** |
| **And lavender flora is exempted** | **because York has lavender, and pretending otherwise is the kind of invention §2.1 forbids** |
| **And Nix Green** | **a character exception, recorded** |
| **Which makes the violet rule** | **the clearest instance in the whole project of a colour constraint that exists for narrative reasons rather than aesthetic ones** |

---

**The practical authoring consequence:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **If you draw an effect in violet** | **you are claiming it is Shepherd, sacred, or dissonant** |
| **If it is sacred** | **it needs a white or Grace Ivory core** |
| **If it is dissonant** | **it must not have one** |
| **If it is neither** | **pick another hue** |
| **And if the design has not decided** | **§2.1: surface the gap** |

**Which turns a colour choice into a design question, every time.** That is the point.

---

**And Beacon's language, which sits beside this one:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Beacon's interface vocabulary is technological** | **distinct from the sacred register and from the rest of the HUD** |
| **Why a character gets their own UI language** | **because the character is technological, and the interface is how that reads** |
| **Which is the locked principle applied to a character rather than a scene** | **a clear role, grounded in the canonical design** |
| **And a constraint on the HUD** | **because Beacon's elements must be distinguishable from the rest of it without breaking §2's *"warm, earthy, weathered"*** |

**Practice.** Open `colour-palette.md` and find `TERR-101` to `TERR-104` and `TERR-117` to `TERR-120`. Note their hex values and their positions in their ramps. Then draw two small effects in Aseprite, both in the violet family, one with a Grace Ivory core and one without, and check that the difference reads at 80 px. Then read the cinematic document's description of Beacon's UI language.
Shepherd Light, Beacon and fire:
The three named effect families, what each one's rules already are, and how much is still open.

**These are the VFX the documents actually name. Nothing else is decided.**

---

**1 — Shepherd Light.** The sacred register's gameplay form.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Its colours** | **violet `TERR-117`–`120` with a Sacred White / Grace Ivory `TERR-101`–`104` core** |
| **Its rule** | **the white core is mandatory** — because its absence means dissonance |
| **Its narrative role** | **Shepherd and metaphysical events**, per register 5 |
| **What is open** | **its shape, its animation, its duration, its layering** — all of it |

**2 — Beacon's technological language.** A UI and effect vocabulary rather than a single effect.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What is decided** | **that it exists and is distinct** |
| **What is open** | **everything else** |

**3 — Fire, and the eight candles.** The one effect that is fully specified — and specified oddly.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The candles** | **`hud.md` §3: eight painted candles lit by one shared transparent 3D viewport** |
| **The rules** | **each flame aligns to its wick, sits over the frame, fades with the HUD, and leans opposite the leader's acceleration** |
| **The scoping clause** | ***"This isolated effect does not establish a 3D art pipeline for the game world."*** |
| **And §11's performance item** | *"orb and candle subviewports remain inside the frame budget"* |

**So the project's one fully-specified effect is not pixel art at all.** Which is a fact worth sitting with: **the HUD's flames are 3D, by exception, with a fence around the exception.**

---

**What world fire would be, as distinct from the candles:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **York's hearths, torches and lamps** | **world objects, in the pixel-scaled viewport** |
| **So pixel art, at 12 fps, under §10.1's four-value rule** | — |
| **And `WorldClock.darkness()` matters** | because **`hud.md` §2's vignette *"remains subtle by day and readable at night"*** — **so lit things read differently by time of day** |
| **Which is §9.3's open work** | *"lighting and time-of-day treatment"*, listed as undecided |
| **So world fire is blocked on the lighting decision** | and **§2.1 says to surface that rather than invent it** |

---

**The three questions any effect family has to answer**, which the candles answer and the other two do not:

| | Question | The candles' answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **where does it attach?** | **each flame to its wick, from the frame art** |
| **2** | **what does it respond to?** | **the HUD's fade, and the leader's acceleration** |
| **3** | **what is its budget?** | **one shared subviewport for all eight, inside the frame budget** |

**And those three questions are the right brief for Shepherd Light too** — attachment, response, budget — **which is a more useful thing to take from the candles than their 3D-ness.**

---

**One honest note on scope.** Of the three families:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The candles are done** | and are not yours to author |
| **Shepherd Light has a colour rule and nothing else** | |
| **Beacon has a direction and nothing else** | |
| **World fire is blocked on lighting** | |
| **So VFX is the least-decided area in the whole art contract** | and **the curriculum's job here is to teach the craft and name the gaps, not to fill them** |

**Practice.** Run the game, watch the candle flames, and move the leader to see them lean. Then find the shared subviewport in the scene tree. Then draw a four-frame violet effect in Aseprite with a Grace Ivory core and check its colours against the palette. Then read §9.3's open work on lighting and note what would have to be decided before world fire could be drawn.
Effects at twelve frames:
What §5's animation contract means for an effect, and the three structural differences between an effect and a character animation.

**The contract still applies.** §5.1 and §5.4 do not exempt effects:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **12 fps** | **§5.1's authoring rate** |
| **One-shot tags begin with `_`; looping tags do not** | **§5.3, and stage 12's Wizard behaviour** |
| **One master per entity** | **§3** |
| **The 112 × 112 canvas and the (56, 96) pivot** | **only if the effect is a character's** — **a standalone effect is its own entity with its own canvas** |

**And the duration arithmetic from stage 10:** **a frame duration of 84 ms imports at 12 fps**, while a shorter duration raises the derived rate. **An effect's frame timing is therefore a pipeline decision as much as an animation one.**

---

**The three differences between an effect and a character animation:**

| | | A character animation | An effect |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1** | **Looping** | **idle loops; run loops** | **most effects fire once and end** — **so the tag takes the `_` prefix** |
| **2** | **Anchoring** | **the pivot at (56, 96), the feet** | **the attachment point is the effect's own** — a wick, a hand, a weapon's edge, a point in the world |
| **3** | **Direction** | **eight directions, four drawn, four mirrored** | **often directionless, or rotated rather than redrawn** |

**And the third is the most useful.** An effect that is radially symmetric needs one copy. An effect with a direction may be **rotated in Godot rather than redrawn** — which breaks the pixel grid and is sometimes still right, and sometimes visibly wrong. **§3's rule against *"resized or filtered source art"* is about scaling; rotation is not named, which means the decision is open and should be surfaced.**

---

**The structure of an effect's frames**, which is a craft matter:

| Phase | What it does | Frames at 12 fps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Anticipation** | **a small cue that something is about to happen** | **1 to 2 — about 0.08 to 0.17 s** |
| **The strike** | **the brightest, largest frame** | **1 — and it should be the single frame a player remembers** |
| **The dissipation** | **the effect fading, spreading or falling** | **3 to 6** |

**Which gives a 5-to-9-frame effect**, or **0.4 to 0.75 s.** And the asymmetry is the point: **anticipation is brief, the strike is a single frame, and the dissipation is most of the animation.**

**Compare the run cycle from stage 10:** **12 frames, evenly spaced, looping.** An effect is **the opposite shape** — front-loaded, uneven, and terminal.

---

**And the four-value rule at its hardest.** §10.1: *"four values per material."*

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The problem** | **an effect is light, and light wants a gradient** |
| **What four values gives you** | **a core, a body, an edge, and a halo** |
| **Which is enough** | **because the eye reads the core-to-halo progression as glow** |
| **And the sacred register already specifies the structure** | **a Grace Ivory core inside a violet body** — **which is the core-and-body division, named** |
| **So the palette has done half the design** | and **the remaining decision is the edge and the halo** |

---

**The one additional constraint for effects over a dark world:** **additive blending.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **What it does** | **adds the effect's colour to what is behind it rather than replacing it** |
| **Why effects use it** | **because light adds** |
| **What it costs** | **the palette.** **An additive effect's on-screen colour is not a palette colour** — it is the sum |
| **Which means** | **a validator checking on-screen colours against the 132 entries would fail** — **and `colour-palette.md`'s four accepted cleanup colours show the document already anticipates validator exceptions** |
| **So the honest position** | **additive blending is a rendering decision that puts an effect outside the palette's validation**, and **whether to use it is open** |

**Practice.** Draw a 6-frame effect in Aseprite at 12 fps with one anticipation frame, one strike and four dissipation frames, using four values. Then name the tag with a leading `_`, import it with the Wizard, and confirm the prefix is stripped and the animation does not loop. Then play it in Godot over a dark background, once with normal blending and once additive, and compare. Then check the frame durations the Wizard derived against what you typed.
